This is most important, not only for stability of measurement but also, and of rather more importance, so that the line will coil easily. Most pcople have had the experience of trying to coil up a xiece of new rope. It is like fightins with a boa-—constrictor, in the end one is lucky to come out of the contest unhanged. The addition of the knots to the lead line just makes the whole thing more intractable Disressing for a moment, and ignoring the bloke who just shouted "keep to the point" the casicst way to coil up a new rope is to chuck the whole coil overboard, hanging on of course to the bitter end, and coil up as it is pulled in, taking the tivists out as they aspear over the rail. To coil up one ond in the left hand, slide the right hand along the rope, straightening it as you go, almost to arms length, then bring that length of rope in the form of a coil back to the left hand giving the rope a twist in the direction of the ley of the strands. Transfer from right hand to left and carry on. You will find thet the twist is done most easily between the thumb and first fingor of the right hand as it moves back towards the left. This will give coils of equal size and of about twenty inches diametor. To stretch the lead line before marking, tie one end to a fixed object and pull on the other with a tackle. Wren it is taut drench it with water. Keep it in that state for a fev hours, then let it dry tightening the tackle as it slackens. Another and rather easicr way is to tie a bucket on one end, make the other ond fust to the boat, chuck the bucket overboard, end tow it on. the end of the line for ea few hours. A much essier type of line to handle, and one which is much more disinclined to tangle is the round sennit or plaited line. You know the sort of line Mum hangs her clots on in the garden. This is not, however, easily obtained in small sizes. When not in OSC. keep the lead line coiled down in a box in the cockpit or for example under a thwart. This will ensure that when you want it in a hell of a hurry, as you usually do, it is aveilable and you don't have to spend five minutes untangling it. Anothcr my way is to carry it wound between two cleats a couple of feet apart. On my ovm boat it is kept wound on a kevil or lons cleat about two fect long fastened through the stanchions inside the rail. There is it out of the way yet constantly available. Now how to use the lead Line. This is always good for a laugh! We read of the loadsman in the old time ship-of-the-line standing in the chains and swinging the lead round his head in ever increasing circles like a sort of Ouzlam Bird in reverse ;car, then letting it go to fly forward, the lead, that is to say, not the leadsman. into the water, the line sliding 1 through his fingers until bottom was reached whereupon he would chant "By the Hark Nine" or somc such remark. Remombering that the lead must have weighed anything up to ten pounds or more, I often vonder what he chanted when he forgot to let go. I bet even Captain Hornblower laughcd!! The Entrance To Bradwell Creek This has always had a somewhat justifiable reputation for difficulty, although once knowm it is comparatively simple, Sailing Directions given in most pilot books are now however somewhat in error due to the erection of the Nuclear Power Station, Some marks have been removed and other replaced, Approaching from the west, keep parallel to Pewit Islant and well out, about half a mile from the island, This means at the present time you will be passing quite close to the ships which lie in the river. Keep on this line until about two hundred vards west of the Power Station cofferdam barrier wall, This is a most unmistakable object which resembles a pier and lies about a quarter of a mile east of the entrance, Turn south and head towards the shore. When in line with and about two hundred yards from the west end of the barrier wall a square wooden post will be seen in a south westerly direction, distance abaut two hundred yards, This post, which carries water temperature monitoring equipment for the Power Station, is on and near the end of the spit which runs in a north easterly direction from the eastern end of Pewit Island, Head for a point due east of, and thirty yards from, this post, From this point turn and sail towards the post in a westerly direction keeping south of the post and passing it close to, about eight to ten yards, From here on the southern and eastern side of the spit which is quite steep to, is marked by withies. The channel is narrow and is most shallow at the outer end, Follow the withies in, keeping them to starboard and very close, a few yards, on no account straying to the south and east of them, The mud flat extending from shore between t>e Power Station and the navigable channel of the creek is extensive and dries out six feet above L.W, Ordinary Spring Tides, As the channel turns towards the south a pair of leading marks will be seen on the sea wall. Keep these in line until Bradwell Quay itself is opened up then turn and sail along the line of moored vessels running parallel to the quay. Hallam Part 3 Tools Lead Line (Continued) of the Trade -the ———e ee In the small cruiser the best position from which to use th lead line is the lee side of the cockpit. This ensures that there is no danger of it becoming fouled up with any projection on the bottom of the boat, the keel or centrevlate for example, or even as has been known the rudder Hold the lead line with two or three coils in your outboard hand with the lead dangling free on a couple of feet of line. The rest of the coils are held in the inboard hand. Swing the lead with an underhand motion a couple of times to get the rhythu, then let it go to fly forward, those coils held in the swinging hand being released at the same moment but the Line itself still being retained in the hand in such a manner that the line is free to run. As the line tightens release as many coils as are necessary from the inboard hand. By this time the lead will have entered the water somewhere level with the dows. As the lead sinks more line will run out but at the same time the boat will be overtaking the lead. The power of the swing should be such thet the lead reaches the bottom just before the line becomes vertical in the water. The amount of energy you will expend will depend upon the speed of the boat and the depth of the water When the lead reaches the bottom a slight but distinct thump will be felt in the fingers of the swinging hand, which you will remember, still has the line running through it. Fingers are extremely sensitive instruments, and can detect even in deep water this thump and the slight slacking of tension in the line as the lead hits the bottom. You will now be able to read off the depth either visually or by feel from the knots, which will be in the region of either wielding or holding hand Coil up the line again retrieving it as quickly as you can and make another cast. This brings us face to face with a cardinal truth. Unless atmeme ree anchor one soundingisutterlyuseless. Two or three at least are required, preferably more. One sounding merely tells you the depth of the water over ae oe that one particular pimple or depression on which the lead has landed. A number will give you the trend of the soundings; whether the water is becoming shallower or deeper, and whether this change in depth is fast or slow, thus indicating a steep or shallow change in the contours of the sea bottom. The lead line as a pilotage instrument can be used in a number of ways. Perhaps the most obvious is to give adequate warning of the time to go about when tacking near the shore. Another way is to use the lead s a blind man uses a stick, tapping along a kerb. At night, or in fog, when sailing on a river or estuary, one can sail towards a known bank until in say a couple of fathoms, then follow the two fathoms line along, feeling ones way with the lead. The existence of a spit or a swatch will be apparent, thus giving by reference to the chart an indication of ones position; but more of this later on in the series when we consider the technique of pilotage proper. The lead line is probably the most useful and certainly the cheapest tool of the pilots trade. It is also unfortunately the least used by most yachtsmen. This is probably due to the fact that using it is possibly the quickestway of gettingwater up ones sleeve. The amount of water brought on board by the lead line as it is retrieved is almost unbelieveable. A few casts and ones hands and sleeves are soaking, no fun in the winter. There is another implement which can be used for depth sounding, the possession of which in days gone by was the hall mark of the East Coast yachtsman, the sounding pole. This, a light wood or bamboo pole between six and twelve feet long, marked off in feet by alternate white and black bands, would be displayed proudly in the rigging, stamping the owner as a genuine hairy chested ditch crawler. Its use had its ligher moments too. The sight of old Charlie trying desperately to get into Bradwell Creek at Cont'd on page 6

a cuarter to closing time on a Saturday evening, wielding his sounding pole like a demented drum-major was usually sufficient to clear the public bar of the Green Man. Although the sounding pole has largely fallen into disuse now- adays, I am sure that a shorter version, say five feet lonz, would be if anything more useful to the dinghy, or any Light craft cruiser, owners. It could be used single handed easier than the lead and could double as a boat—hook or a spinnaker pole. This month's Sailing Instructions deal with a stretch of water on your ovm doorstep. So 7 Page HULL CONSTRUCTION - 2 by "Barnacle" Last month we dealt with three methods of planking a round bilge hull with solid wood. First, this month, let us look at clinker-ply, or glued clinker. This is an elegant way of producing a light, strong dinghy, and has most of the advantages and disadvantages of normal clinker. Since the plywood strakes have adequate transverse strength, it requires no ribs, but this sreat advantage is offset by the fact that all seams are glued, producing a rigid hull which is more liable to be cracked. For a boat which is to give any real service, all strakes should be rivetted es well as glued, since it is an unfortunate fact that the modern resin glues do not always behave the same way on a boat immersed in sea water as they do immersed in a laboratory beaker. For rapid production of light, shapely yacht tenders this method is just about ideal. Next in the possible methods of producing a round bilge hull we can consider wooden moulding. This can be many layers of thin veneers bonded to form 2 single sheet of shaped plywood, or two or three skins laid at angles (I am lumping such constructions as vee root, slim strake and double diajyonal under the heading of moulded hulls). At first sight these methods seem very well suited to amateur construction, but a little further consideration shows that there will be nearly as much work in building the mould as in building a more conventional hull, and then to achieve good results considerably more than a casual acquaintance with modern resin glues is needed. One or two skins are not too bad, but the third, fourth and fifth get extremely tedious. No, this is a method best left to the factory. And what about the result? Stron;, light, very shapely, and rigid, ideal for a short term proposition, but perhaps not the thing in which to invest hard earned savinzs in the expectation of realising your money in ten years time. At this point let me clear up possible misunderstandings about my use of the word rigid. It has been pointed out to me that the topsides of 2 glued-strip hull can move in and out as much as those of a carvel hull. Admittedly, but that is NOT what I meant by rigid. They have no movement at all in the fore and aft direction; the very direction in which movement is essential to give to a pounding from a heavy sea. Old sailormen always swore hat Eastwoods brick barges went fastest in a heavy sea when they worked the most, and the Lowestoft and Southwold "Yolls'' used to carry a saw to cut through the thiarts so their clinker hulls could work even more, when they wanted to get along dgvickly in a North East gale. Lastly in the round bilge hulls we have fibreglass. This is no proposition for the emateur. A mould involves more work than building a hull by any other method, and then the knowledze of practical chemistry required is considerable if the best results are to be achieved. A fibreglass hull has most of the advantages and disadvantages of a moulded wooden hull, except that it cannot rot, worits won't eat it, and the topsides need not be painted although the bottom of a cruiser will still need entifoulding. On the other hand ultra violet light will degrade the resin, other ageing effects may occur, and a cheap moulding may delaminate. One is also faced with an unusual surface finish worry, that of one side being beautifully smooth and the other very rough indeed. Some firms overcome this by using inner and outer mouldings so all the rough surfaces are hidden One point with regard to fibreglass dinghies - always buy a dinghy with wooden floorboards and thwarts screwed in and not moulded in place. The fibreglass may appear to have a good non-skid surface when dry, but when it gets wet it is about as safe to stand on as a sheet of wet ice, and it is extremely fatiguing rowing a dinghy when one is continually sliding around on the thwerts. On any fibreglass boat always beware of moulded-in wooden components - these are almost certain to rot very quickly. Some moulders use pieces of wood moulded in place to form a support for a rib in the fibreglass This is frowned on in the better moulding shops, but it is the fibreglass rib that supplies the strength and not the timber, so it is not too serious if the wood does rot. A moulded in keel, gunwale or thwart which rots is a different story. And what if you damage a moulded hull? ~\4 LA, Page 3 HULL CONSTRUCTION - 3 To finish off this series let us consider the various chine hulls. These are by no means confined to dinghies and small cruisers, as some quite large hulls are bduilt with chines, including spritsail barges. Building a hard chine hull (single or multi-chine) is usually quick, far quicker than any other method, but it requires more accurate workmanship, and the fairing off of keel, chines and frames is harder than anything met with on a round bilged carvel hull. The hull may be planked and. caulked, it may be clinker, or it may be ply skinned. All are somewhat easier and quicker to build than the equivalent round bilge hull, particularly ply, where the boat is changed from a skeleton to a complete hull ina week end. Most of the troubles with chine hulls occur in the design stages, as it is possible to bend a flat sheet of normal plywood only into a cylindrical or conical shape. Any compound curvature or twist is not possible. This has fooled many people who imagine that all they have to do to design 2 hard chine hull is to draw a series of straight sided sections. Alas, nothing could be further from the truth, for the sections, particularly in the bows, are quite well curved, ss are the keel and chines. In fact a well designed hard chine hull, skinned with sheet ply, can be nearly as shapely es a planked or moulded hull, whilst costing far less to build. Many people have attempted to "prove! that chine hulls are not as good as round bilged hulls, whilst others have wasted just cs much time trying to prove the reverse. In fact each has its advantages and disadvantages, which do not greatly affect the sailing performance of the boat, 9 except in the case of sailing barges & oS chine hull where the long was decidedly superior to a round bilge. Ply skinned chine hulls do have stress concentrations along the keel, chines and deck edge, but these are not usually likely to cause serious trouble on a well designed hull, whilst clinker and carvel chine hulls behave exactly like round bilge hulls, and are as easy to repair. A plywood skinned chine Bast can be restored to its original condition after being holed by replacing the entire ply panel involved, but its life expectation is probably not so good as that of a planked hull, although marine plywood is steadily improving. To summarise, (most difficult) for an amateur built hull wanted quickly; hard chine, plywood skinned. For a hull not wanted quite so quickly, involving less care in building and with the best possible expectation of life; round bilge carvel. For small dinghies; clinker ply, and for a light, long lasting hull requiring that bit more care in building; normal clinker. For those rich types who can afford to buy a new racing boat whenever they want to; a moulded hull, either ply or fibreglass. "Barnacle!

Hallam Tools of the Trade The Steerins Compass (Cont'd) In its usual form the instrument consists basically of a card to which is affixed a magnetic needle or system of needles, this assembly being mounted on a pivot inside a bowl. The bowl is filled with a liquid, as described last month, the liquid being a mixture of distilled water and alcohol. The iquid will cause a drag on the card and damp out any tendency towards violent oscillatory motion set up by the movement of the boat. One must remember that the earth's magnetic-field is not very strong, and it is quite easy to cause an undamped or dry point compass card to spin completely round, causing it to require several seconds to come to rest. dnilst this may be acceptable ina compass which is used on land and can be set dows on a solid object until the card comes to rest, it is obviously completely useless in a boat’ where the motion never ceases. : ' The card is calibrated, usually in points, half and quarter points, although degrees may be used and are sometimes marked on the card in addition to the points. A line is marked on the glass top of the bowl, known as the "Tubber's Line". The compass must always be installed such that this " "Tubber's Line" is exactly parallel to the fore and aft centre-line of the boat. The line is sometimes replaced by a graticule or a pointer, but the principle is the ‘saiae. : The coipass East be fitted in such a way that it remains horizontal even when the boat heels or pitches. © This is acnieved by mounting it on two pivots fore and aft in a ring, which is in turn pivoted athwartships in another ring or cradle. These are know as gimbals. The. position of the compass in the boat is something that requires some thought. It follows that as it is a magnetic instrument that any ferro-magnetic material, iron or steel, or any electric magnetic instrument or component, such as & radio loudspeaker, or indeed even a piece of wire with current flowing through it, will cause an inter-action with the magnetic needle and: affect its reading, Put it then, as far away from any local ww ironworks 2s you can, and don't forget the iron tiller, if you have one, nor ~~ that rusty heap of old iron under the cockpit floor, the thing you proudly call "my auxiliary engine" although you know, and I know, the thing hasn't coughed since the day iuntie left the sea cock open on the thunderbox, and flooded the whole boat. . ; wore about compasses and positions next month, so don't rush out and _ buy one yet. With a South Westerly wind blowing hard on a flooding tide that »vart of ‘the Blackwater between Osea Island and _.erssa can be West uncoinfortadle and under these circumstances Thirslet Creek is a good shelter. It runs into the big flat on the orth sice of the River Blackwater Opposite Stone, in a jesterly direction from the entrance, which is opposite St. Lawrence Bay. On the south side of the entrance is a steep -— to spit known as Thirslet Spit, marked with, at the .soment, two beacons. One is Cont'd on Page 7

One advantage of sleeping aboard is that less extra gear is needed, and what ther. is, does not have to be carried ashore. The first requirement is a cover. A dinghy with a gcoseneck about four feet above the keel can have a strut made to hold the boom horizontal, and a canvas cover lacing down over tne topsides, prefsrably with end flaps which can be laced across - when sleeping =Board an anchored, floating boat, she will usually lie head to wind so only the forward end of the cover need be clesed. A good mooring comprises a ground or span chain of heavy links securely fastened to two substantial roots, with a lighter riding chain secured to its centre by a swivel and stitable shackles, the swivel well greased, and the shackles securely wired. A single root mooring can be used in isolatud cases, but to avoid a vertical Gull on the root a much larger scope or chain must be used, so a single root mooring should never be used where several boats are to be moored in line. NEWS AND VIEWS CENTRE PLATES - Another hint Owners of centre-plate yachts which take the ground between tides are almost sure to be troubled at some time or other through their plates becoming mud-bound; in fact, so scrious is the problem that it has caused many owners to turn to ksel boats or to seek moorings at which they remain always arloat. Of course, all manner of suggsstions have been advanced for overcoming the difficulty but none is really satisfactory. In the case of a certain yacht wnich suffered acutely from this difficulty, a solution was to pass ths end of the boom-crutch through the chain slot in the top of the centre-board case, and give a direct push to the plate as far aft of the pivot bolt as possible. Generally a long shove was more effective than sharp hammer blows or gigging with the tackle. Contd. on Page 4.

Page lh. In very dry weather, when the mud was really solid, the first job on arrival on board, was to pour water into the case and keep it filled whilst hoisting sails and preparing for casting off. By the time all was ready and the moorings about to be let go, the plate always responded to a good steady push from ons or two members of the crew. BoAoP. A COVER FOR A CRUISING DINGHY If you intend to use a dinghy for cruising it is worth getting a proper cover made, but if you intend to sleep aboard only in extraordinary circumstances such as being caught out in a flat calm and pouring rain and unable to reach a campsite ashore, then quite a simple cover can be improvised. My first cruising on the Blackwater and Colne was done in a 12 ft. lugsail dinghy with no decking at all, and at night we used to lash the yard and boom together, support one end on the mast thwart and hoist the other to a suitable height with the halliard. The sail was then spread over and lashed round under the boat - an operation that could only be done with the boat ashore. The result was draughty and the sail got F covered in mud, but at least we had somewhere dry to sleep. f Later I borrowed a larger, flat bottomed boat with wide side deck” and with her we supported the aft end of the boom by lashing the tiller to the end of it and spread a rectangle of old canvas over, holding it in to the cockpit coamings with a lashing all round. This was tolerable with the wind abean, but if we were afloat and lay head to wind a howling gale blew in at the open fore end of the crude cover. When I eventually saved enough to buy "Melody" I decided she was worth fitting with a proper cover, and got Mr.Taylor to make one for me at a cost of about ten pounds. For this cover, the boom rested in the scissors crutches on the aft deck, and the cover came down to about the middle of the side decks, lacing onto a row of small clips screwed to the shear strake bclow the rubbing strake. Inside the cover a flap hung just inside the coamings and laced to clips under the carlines. With.the front lacing round the mast and tent type doors aft lacing down to the sheethorse the result was almost completely draughtproof. ww Owners with "all over" covers made to fit the boat with thé boom lying from the goosensck to the aft deck could easily sew a couple of triangular extensions to the cover so it will reach the hull when the boom is raised, either by a support, or the topping lift or main halliard taken to the boom end fitting. (If the main halliard is not long enough, use the kicking strap as an extension). A cover so modified might not fit over well forward, but it should be draughtproof. For a dinghy that is having a cruising cover specially made, arrange the doom as high as possible, with a wooden or metal support at the aft end - you could rely on the topping lift, but sooner or later it will slip or break and the boom will fall on your head. The best method of holding down the cover is to lace or clip it to hooks outside the hull, but where this cannot be done it can be held with lines passing under the hull, or a “drawstring” round below te rubbing strake. For real luxury, the cover can be spread like a Mansard roof by using a pair of oars for the lower ridges, held apart /Contd .on Page 5-

Page 5. by spreaders (tiller and tiller extension, jib whisker pole etc. could be modified to serve a dual purpose) and held up C6ithser by lacing to the cover or tying below the boom. The Spreaders then form handy clothes racks etc. One warning - make sure the main sheet is well out of the way, as it can be an infernal nuisance hanging from the boom - I used to coil "Nelody's" on top of the boom before putting the cover on. You will find a cover which can be fitted from inside the boat well worth its cost - no more muddy feet, sleep wherever you can find fairly calm water and with all your gear handy. If you really use the space in the boat you will find yourself far better off than you would ashore in a tent which is probably less than half the size of even a small dinghy. . JoAcS. Page 6 Anchoring | by "Barnacle" Having dealt very briefly with the subject of moorings, let us now turn our attention to anchors and anchoring. Hor the cruising mar there are three types of suitadle anchor; Danforth, C.9.R. and Fisherman, the relative merits of which are thoroughly discussed elsewhere (if I mention Heaton again Someone will think I'm a relative of his). Every boat should carry at least main and kedge anchor, so if you really can't decide which type of anchor will suit you best, then try one ef cach. The main anchor should be ready for immediate © use whenever the boat is cruising in coastal waters. This does not mean lying under the aft deck, with a tangle of filthy old rope on top of it. It means secured to the foredeck in such a manner that it can be let. go ina matter of seconds, with a stout warp or chain secured to it, the warp or chain so stowed that it will run out freely, and with the bitter end made fast to the boat. For those of you who had not realised it, this is the origin of the saying "right to the bitter end" - it's the end (of the cable) made fast to the bitts -- or which should be made fast to the bitte: It comes expensive if you habitually forget to secure the bitter end. The warp or chain should never be made fast to the bitts in such a manner that it cannot be undone quickly - one day you might have to slip your anchor ina hurry. Most textbooks advise a lashing that can be cut with a knife, but there is a danger here that the lashing will rot or chafe, andyou may have the mortification of seeing the end of your higily expensive chain, which you thought was so well secured, disappearing through the roller fairlead. Nos A far better way is to secure the bitter end to a Stenhouse slip, an inexpensive little bit of ironmongery which will hold as strongly as the rest of the chain, and can be readily knocked open with the first heavy object that comes to hand if ever you do have to slip your chain. If you are sailing singlehanded it is quite good practice to lead your anchor cable through the roller fairlead on the stem head, then back outside everything to the cockpit, where the anchor can be stowed away .on the grating. (Although most boats give the lone sailor enough time to nip up forward and deal with a properly stowed anchor). If your main anchor is a C.9.R. or Danforth it is easy to stow and always ready for use, but that does not apply toa Fisherman. These can be brutes to stow, and the generally accepted method is to lay the flukes flat on deck with the stock outboard, one end sticking up vertically. To prevent this end catching stray jib sheets, fishing lines etc. (as it certainly will, if you give it half a chance) it is best stowed alongside a shroud or liferail stanchion to which it can be seized, or better still, protected by a piece of plastic tubing of suitable diameter slid over the stanchion or shroud. Whilst on the subject of Fisherman anchors, make sure the pin is securely home, and WIRE it in place. A lashing here, like a bitter end lashing, gets neglected, and if the pin comes out, the anchor is practically certain to drag. When cruising it is guite a sound idea to have the kedge anchor ready for immediate use as well as the main. Warp is nearly always used for the kedge anchor, and see that it is of ample length. Thirty fathoms is the MINIMUM that should be carried on a two and a half tonner. For larger boats, wire can be used, but it is awkvard tc stow; the drum off a Kelvin sounding machine, complete with its wire, comes in handy here. A kedge warp need not be terrifically heavy rope, but be sure it is properly coiled away, and in good condition. Contd, on Page 7

Page 7 Always put out enough warp or chain when anchoring. Three times the depth at high water is the usually quoted figure for a Fisherman anchor, up to five times for a C.9.R. Remember these are MINIMUM figures, and twice as much won't hurt a bits “Most boats are very, very badly supplied with chain and warp - after all, a C.%.8. on twenty fatioms of chain can not be relied upon to hold in more than four or five fathoms of water, and since we have a two fathom rise and fall of tide in these parts it means you must be in only two fathoms of water if you wish to anchor sareiy at low tide. When anchoring for more than an nour or two, or in the vicinity of other boats, the kedge should bdé laid out down tide of the main anchor. Very few boats carry enough chain to do this the easy way by dropping back on the main anchor, laying the kedge overboard, and then hauling back to a point midway between the anchors.so a trip in the dinghy will have to oe made. If you value your life do this properly, with the anchor slung over the dinghy's transom with a slippery hitch, and the warp properly coiled down well clear of your legs. If you get tangled up with the anchor or warp and fall out of the dinghy your hopes of survival will be very slight. _ | In heavy weather it is nice to be able to lay out a thirdanchor Somewhere up wind, but not in line with the main or kedge. Should the wind blow across the tide, you will be putting a severe strain-on anchors laid up and down tide in the usual manner, and they may well start to drag, whereas quite a small anchor laid up wind will prevent this. Ll belisve the Royal Navy regard a boat as properly moored only when she has three anchors out ina "crow's foot", In any event it is comforting to have a third anchor aboard. It can spend most of its time vut of the way in the bilges, but it may save your boat in an emergency. Anothsr comfort is an anchor buoy secured to the crown of the main anchor by a line which need be no more than a third the length of the cables. Then, if you foul your anchor you can pick up the buoy, and by hauling on the buoy line upend the ancnor clsar of whatever has fouled it. A useful substitute for a buoy is a tripping line made fast to the crown of the anchor, stop.ed onto the main cable with cotton and its end siezed to the cable about half way up. Finally, when letting go an anchor, first wait until your boat is moving astern over the ground, then, if you have a Fisherman anchor, pay out the cable carefully so it cannot foul the anchor. A C.Q.R. or Danforth can be let go more abruptly, but do not be too careless. 'Barnacle". _FOR SAIZ AND MART Sailing dinghy - 8 feet, moulded ply pram dinguy, Prout built. Tools of the Trade The eLeering Compass A type of compass which is popular insmall craft is the ex-aircraft grid stecring compass. These instruments are obtainable at. most surplus stores, varying in price from about fifteen shillings to five pounds, depending upon condition. and, perhaps most important of all, the type of shop from which it is purchased. There are two models, a five inch diameter and a seven inch diameter. Both work on the same system which ~ athough the same in principle as the ordinary marine compass, differs in application. The grid-compass has .a dead beat card carrying a wire graticule in the form of a "T" with the centre of rotation at the position where the stem joins the cross bar thus :- | | | The North Seeking pole of the magnetic system being in the direction shown. The glass cover to the bowl has a set of graticules in the form of a boxed "T" thus: X , aan : “fy se ir — a ~/ bs —~ 1g ~/ ie a = e Wy - < e eS j= Fl | t » | A Contd.on Page 7

Page 7 and the rim marked off in degrees, North being on the side away from the stem of the "T", This cover is rotatable by hand and has facilities for locking. The bowl carries a short white pointer against the edge inside. The compass is mounted so that a line between the pointer and the centre of rotation is parallel to the centre-line of the boat, the pointer being on the forward side. To use the instrument, the cover is rotated so that the course to be steered in degrees is level with the little pointer, and locked. The boat is stscered on to a course such that the "T" on the card coincides with the boxed "T" on the glass. The boat is now Sailing through the water on the course set up on the cover, or grid ring. Note that I have said "through ths water", it does not follow that the boat is actually moving over the sea bed in the direction it is being steered, due to leeway, tidal drift etc. of which moré soon. The shape of the graticules overcomes to a large extent the problem of parallax and even if the compass is not gimballed, can still be uséd with a reasonable angle of heel, say ten degrees. A very useful and comparatively cheap compass for small boats is the "Sestrel Minor" costing in its basic form £2,16.- This has a card of about two inches diameter in a perspex bowl. The card has vertical graduatiors around the edge, and with the addition of a sighting ring and a handle, can be used as a nand bearing compass. Other popular compasses arse on the market varying in price between about £8 and £80. The two mentioned above however are probably the most attractive to the average nard-up small eruiser man, One difficulty which arises with some compasses is the formation of bubbles under the glass. This is caused by the continued expansiors and contractions of the damping fluid, evaporation of the alcohol from the fluid, or just plain leakage. These bubbles tend to upset the damping action on the card and Should be removed. This can be a rather agifficult process if not tackled in the right way. The method I have used is to unserew the filling cap and gently suck with the mouth, holding the instrument at a slight angle, orifice upwards. The bubbles will gradually move towards the rim until they form into one larger bubbie at the filling hole. Top up with distilled water and screw the cap down tightly. Don't try drinking the fluid, it doesn't Test#a bit like gin even if it does contain alcohol: Incidentally, the grid stesring compass does not suffer from this trouble as a rule. —a Page 8 The steering compass must be mounted in such a position that it can easily be seen by the helmsman in whatever position he may be. This, in a small vessel is not easily done. On larger vessels with wheel steering it is usual to have the compass mounted in a housing called a binnacle in front of the wheel. The binnacle consists of a box with a glass window, having facilities for illuminating the compass card, all mounted on'a stout pillar. The cockpit of a small boat has no place for such a monster. it is wsual “therefore to mount the compass on the after cabin bulkhead. A common method in pre war days was to mount the compass inside the cabin behind a window in the bulkhead, thus protecting the instrument from the weather. This is a reasonable way for the ordinary compass but would be too difficult an arrangement for a grid steering compass. The latter should be mounted in a position which gives the helmsman eas; access to it for course setting. The insides of the after cockpit coaming under the tiller is a good place provided that there are no heavy galvanised iron fittings, such as cleats, in the vicinity. If your vessel has a bridge deck at the forward end of the cockpit it may be possible to mount the compass under a hinged glass or perspex window, but again, look out for the large lumps of 1Pon. Don't forget that galley equipment is often ferrous in in nature and tends to be very portable. If you must lose your temper when the stew burns, don't fling the ladle at the helmsman, it might end up near, the compass. Page 10 On securing your boat by "BARNACLE" You may have read and digested all in my two previous articles and yet still lose your boat from its mooring or anchor, How can this be? A glance over the foredecks of a row of boats will soon show you - note the old bvawley with its heavy oak posts passing down through the deck to the keel, and the chain with two or three turns round the post; then note the luxury motor cruiser of comparable Size, probably built by a firm with more experisnce of aircraft, caravan or furniture making than boat building - e Lirm whose employees sec ths sea only from Blackpool Pier on Bank Holidays. The motor cruiser will probably be provided with a beautiful little chromium plated cleat nearly big enough to take Mother's linen line, and there might be as many as four one inch number six screws holding the cleat to the deck planks. Some firms with a little more imagination might even go so far as to put one anda half inch eights through into a deck beam, making the cleat just about secure enough to take the weight of the anchor, if you can manage to pass the chain or warp round the grossly undersized cleat! The minimum that should be relied on in the way of a mooring fixture is a cleat or eyebolt large enough to pass a hand under, through-bolted to a solid timber running from the stem head under all foredeck beams back to the mast, with solid blocks between the timber and deck planking in the way of the fittings. Not only should there be such a fitting on the foredeck, there should also be at “east one on the aft deck so that the boat can be secured alongside a quay or staging. It is most regrettable that in the present boom in sailing there are firms with no good reputation to lose, and with absolutely no knowledge of the requirements of a good cruising boat, who will sell boats which cannot possibly be properly secured to a mooring, and it is even more regrettable that some of these firms are producing boats which should never be taken off their moorings! - Boats with no provision for hand starting the engine, with no cable locker, no clips for fire extinguishers, nothing that any even moderately cautious skipper would regard as essential. Possibly the best thing that could happen to such a boat is for it to go adrift in the first real blow and wreck itself - let us hope with no one aboard other than the manufacturer or salesman-demonstrator. Having ensured that your boat is provided with adequate posts, cleats or rings to secure to, and sufficient warps to anchor properly, warp the boat safely round a boatyard or through a trot of moorings, or secure her alongside a quay, the next essential is:fenders of some sort. I doubt whether there has ever been a boat with too many fenders. Fenders come in all shapes, sizes and materials,all of which have their advantages and disadvantages. Inflatable plastic fenders might get punctured, but until they do they are a joy to use; coir fenders are very good until they get wet and dirty, and then a sodden lump on deck, oozing muddy water all over the places is a real nuisance. Solid rubazote or similar fenders are very good, but watch them - like the solid expanded plastic mooring buoys they come fitted with a natural fibre rope which very soon rots and you losé your nice new fender or buoy. Then there is the poor man's standby - old tyres. Thesé mark the paintwork after a time, but it is only a discoloration - the wood is not damaged. They can be obtained very cheaply, often free, and the only other disadvantage is that they must be provided with holes to allow the water they collect to drain out.

Page 11 When mooring alongside anothes boat be sure you have sufficient fenders out to avoid damaging no either hull mattsr at what angle they may come together, and if ina berth that will dry out, make sure that the heights of the fenders ars such that the boats are still adsquatéely protected even if one settles lower in ths mud than the other. In particular, watch the corners of transom sterns - they can give anothor boat a nasty dig. “Wnen mooring alongside a piled quay or staging, hang two or three fenders over your topsides with a stout spar or plank between the fenders andthe piles so that if your boat moves forward or aft the fenders will still be effective. Also, whenever you moor alongside put sufficient fenders out on your exposed Side to protect your boat against the cheerful clot who comes along without any fenders and leaves his boat alongside yours. Finally, always remember to bring all your fenders on deck when sailing -— nothing looks more slovenly than a boat Sailing along with a row of fenders out. fBarnacls', NEWS and VIEWS, Letter to the Secretary, Dear Mr. Edwards, I was somewhat startled in reading my current copy of "Navigans" to see the very kind note of congratulation to myself which our Editor, Daphne Tovey, has inserted, I shall be grateful if you will convey to the members of the Clubd my thanks for this gracious gesture, Yours sincerely, (Sed.) &. Page T The Cruising Yacht's Tender "Barnacle" A tender for a cruising yacht can be anything from a diminutive fibreglass bathtub up to a thirty foot high-speed launch, but in this article Ij~ropose to mention only a few points relevant to tenders to yachts of ten tons and under. Ideally, a cruiser's tender should be of such size that it can be carried aboard its parent boat, but Since it should also be capable of carrying all the crew safely, it must all too often be towed. Dix feet Long is the smallest practical size for a pram dinghy to carry two people, and a dinghy this size can usually be carried aboard a four tonner, but the four tonner may well have a crew of four! Up to about the five ton mark the cruiser owner will be well advised to carry a folding dinghy aboard, and keep a decent size dinghy at his home port, leaving it on the mooring when he goes out. Much has been said and written on the relative merits of pram and stem dinghies, but since a six foot pram dinghy has easily the carrying capacity of an eight foot stem dinghy, these arguments are of academic interest only to the small cruiser owner who must try to squeeze his quart of gear and crew into a pint pot of dinghy. More conflicting requirements for a tender are that it must be light to tw well, or hoist aboard, and it must be strong to withstand the inevitable abuse it will get. Clinker ply, with rivetted scams, appears to be the cheapest and easist way of obtaining a suitable hull, which will be stronger and easier to build than a hard chine ply skinned boat. If you build your own dinghy, fit the gunwhale timbers outside the top strake instead of in the usual position inside. This method has three tremendous advantages: it helps to keep stray wave tops out of the boat, it leaves more room inside and gives a wider spacing to the rowlocks, and it makes it possible to tip every drop of watsr out of the boat when she is ashore. Inside, the dinghy should have non-skid bottom boards, adequate thwarts which leave ample room for legs an inch or two longer than average, and if at all possible, there should be at least a small watertight locker to hold gear which must be kept dry. The rowlocks should be secured to the boat with plastic line, and there should be either a couple of little leather pockets or clips in which they can be stowed when not in use. When towing the dinghy, oars or paddles should also be securely lashed in, preferably to a thwart. Bottom boards should bs held in place with a turn button, and the baler should, like the rowlocks, be tied in with plastic line so that the whole dinghy can be turned upside down and shaken without the loss of any gear. At least two stout towing peinters should bse fitted and a dinghy which is to be hoisted aboard should also have a strongly fitted ringbolt or clips in the stern. All round the topsides of the dinghy should be fitted a substantial fender; an old bass warp used to be nearly universal, but these days far better rubber or plastic fenders can be bought for very reasonable prices. Underneath, the dingny should be provided with stout oak bilge keels, preferably shod with bronze strips, so that the bottom will not get torn out when she is dragged up and down shingly beaches. A dinghy which is to be carried upside down on the deck of the parent craft can have these bilge keels fitted in the form of twin handrails - most convenient when walking round the dinghy, and also very handy for tying on dirty dishcloths etc. hung out to dry - Contd. on Page 8

Page 8 Pg (they don't look nearly so bad as when they are tied to the ship's liferail). Some people who have to move their dinghies up and down concrete hards fit them with small wheels, either oné nouséed in a hollow in the central skeg, or a pair at the ends of the bilge keels. This certainly simplifies moving the dinghy ashore, and does not really make any difference to the performance afloat. . If at all possible, a dinghy should be provided with ample well fitted buoyancy, preferably solid fcamed plastic, and all yachts' tenders should be clearly marked with the name and port of registry of the parent boat. Remember, the first visitors will probably see of the yacht that is your pride and joy (or it SHOULD be!) is the dinghy, so keep it smart and in good order, ‘Barnacle", NEWS FLASH! The Best from your Boat I do not intend to enter into any controversy over the tyye of dinghy that you should have, because this depends on'too many factors and people have individual ideas about boats in rather the same way as choice of motor car. ; I aim to help you to get the best out of whatever boat you have bought. Remember that ina competitive class a 1% increase in speed probably makes a difference of about 6 places so that as a rule it is minor things that will give you a lst compared with 6th or 7th. You will find that in most fleets it is the best main- tained dinghy that is consistently in the front and there is no other answer to this than time spent on your boat, getting everything to the best state within vour power. Surface finish is not so important as people think. It only makes a difference when it is blowing fairly hard. The smoothness of your dinghy contours on bottom and topsides is very important, and all bumps and crevices should befaired in so that you have a nice flowing line. This will involve you ina considerable amount of time with filler cement and sandpaper. Do not forget things like your rudder and centre plate, because these account for a good part of your wetted arca. Having got your hull, centreplate and ruddser into as good a shape as you can, next we come to the mast and rigging. Here you must abide by your class rules but get your mast as light as you can within these rules. Also get the best acrodynamic form that the rules will allow. The rigging should be kept as simple as the class rules will allow and most important, in goci condition, it is false Contd.on Page 7.

Page /. economy to save 5/-d. on rigging and lose a £20 hollow mast. If you have mast tangsto hold your stays make these of stainless stcel. There have been a number of cases lately of small s. ackles giving way, you can now buy tested shackles and it is money well spent to use these in important places if you cannot afford to use them everywhere. It is much cheaper in the long run to use stainless steel stranded wire instead of galvanised iron or solid stainless steel. If you are using Terylene rope for halliards remember that this must be pre-stretched. We will leave sails for the moment as these are important enough to warrant a complete article of their own. Now we come to the inside of the dinghy. Remember that your job when racing is largely a matter of concentration, therefore you should be as comfortable and relaxed as circumstances will allow. Both you and your crew may have to move very quickly at times so you should keep the floor of the boat as clear as possible so that you can move without falling over the odd rope or fitting. Arrange your sheet leads and plate tackle to intrude as little as possible and yet be immediately to hand in emergency. If you have self-bailers see that these are under the centre thwart. If at all possible and in most cases with a little ingenuity, you can arrange to have clear deckspace where you and your crew sit. Your crew cannot be expected to give of their best if they are sitting on a fairlead or some other deck fitting! To be continued. Cont. on Page 8

Page 8 Using the Yachts Tender by "Barnacle" These days a horribly large number of yachtsmen are drowned when they fall out of their dinghies, and one has only to watch them to see why. Let me quote a personal experience. Seven of us, having enjoyed a convivial evening at the “Green Man" piled aboard a twelve foot stem dinghy to take the last of the ebb tide down Bradwell Creek to a twenty ton cutter anchored near the mouth. With such a load aboard the top of the open dagger plate case was below water. What fun: Never mind - the ever ingenious skipper sat on the top of the case, stopping about half the flow of water. Two of us baled, two rowed, and we all sang with the joy of living, until we grounded on the far side of the creek. With seven of us aboard there wasn't really room to row straight, so many willing hands hindered each other in hoisting the (luckily small) lugsail, and one gallant soul leapt over the transom to push us off the mud. Unfortunately for him it was the bow that was azround, not the stern and he went in up to his armpits. fhe rudder could not be found, so we steered (?) with the oars, and eventually reached the cutter, but not before a gybe all standing had caught the mainsheet round one man's neck and nearly strangled him. Arrived at the cutter all seven of us leant out to grab her, and the dinghy capsized bensath us, leaving us hanging from bobstay, whisker shrouds and bulwarks to scramble aboard as best we could. Fortunately somebody had held on to the painter, so the party was soon under way again with a swamped dinghy lying under our counter. What fun: What mad, suicidal folly - I still go cold when I think of how incredibly lucky we were. To be drunk in charge of a dinghy is every bit as dangerous as to be drunk in charge of a car. But even sober, sedate yachtsmen load their dinghies until they have only an inch or two of freeboard rather than make two safe trips. Whilst this may be permissable in shallow water when the tide is rapidly departing and all aboard are fully aware of the risks being taken it is never justifiable in deep water or where there is any sea running. It is amazing how few people seem to be able to step straight into or out of the centre of a dinghy. When ferrying passengers it is usually best to get the stern of the dinghy against the up-tide face of a jetty or staging so they can step straight in, but this is not always possible, and is of course impossible when boarding or léaving a tide rode yacht. On all occasions the skipper should be first into and last out of the dinghy and he should be constantly on the alert to move over and keep the dinghy balanced whilst passengers are getting in or out. When coming alongside a tide rode yacht, always try to approach from the weather quarter, and see that all aboard the dinghy know clearly who is going to catch hold of the boat on arrival. This should always be the foremost person in the dinghy, even if she first touches aft. If the passenger in the stern of the dinghy grabs the yacht's rail the tide will lever the dinghyaway from the ship's side, and if the passenger still hangs on, the dinghy will turn right round, making it almost impossible to gst her properly secured, whereas if the foremost person catches on with one hand, then passes the painter round a cleat, stanchion étc., the wind and tide will hold the dinghy alongside the yacht. When approaching from up-tide on a strong tide, swing the dinghy round before she gets level with the parent yacht, and approach from the bows with the dinghy travelling stern first. Contd.on Page 9

3 wgeYpa! Page 9 Again it must be the foremost hand in the dinghy who catches on. One sure way of capsizing a dinghy sooner or later is to consistently board and leave it with it held alongside the transom or end of a counter stern of a tide rode yacht. The tide will be trying to steam the dinghy away from the yacht, and if you step too near'the side against the yacht the run of tide under the dinghy may well flip it over on top of you. Whenever you step from a dinghy to a yacht or staging, take care not to kick or push the dinghy avay from beneath you - it takes a little care and practice to step cleanly into the centre of the dinghy, but it is an art that is well worth learning. Finally, ship your oars and slip out the rowlocks before you come alongside, not after you have torn a gash out of the topsides. Never step in or out of a dinghy with the rowlocks fitted - if they catch in your turnups or socks you can have a nasty spill. . "Barnacle"!

Imagine a brilliant morning,;a light North Westerly breeze, crowds of people on the banks, a vast-fleet of motor aad sailing boats of all shapes and sizes, and add ten sailing barges .slowly manoeuvring for position on:tne starting line at Osea, and you can get some idea of the scene at eighto'clock on the morning of July 7th. Every thing was perfect except for tye wind, which was not strong enough, though there was sufficient to move the barges across the line, continually changing pos- itions and making it difficult to see exactly what was happen- oe A fine sight before the start was ''Nell', the 90 years ing. ‘ old Gowes built gaffer,possibly the oldest yacht in commission on the river, sailing down with jackyard topsail drawing and piling on bigger and better headsnils to catch all the wind. possible; a good leader for. the fleet of barges, the oldest of 20 years her junior, which is nearly Towards the start the barges began to sort themselves out ( and out of the mud); Ardeer ( 46 tons, built at Rochesterin 1895) in a fine position on the windward end of ‘the line; — Saltcote Belle(49 tons , built by Howard of Maldon in1895), readily spotted with her grey hull, champion of the pre-war| Blackwater barge matches; then Memory (largest and youngest in the race- a 65 tonner built at Harwich in 1904), with a very. dirty jib; Marjorie ( 56 tons, built in 1902 at Ipswich) then: a mass which took some time to sort themselves out, with Venta (the only other Maldon built entry) with white mainsail; and Gipping (59 tons built at Ipswich in 1899, oldest in the race) in poor nositions at the.leeward end. As they drew clear of Osea Memory led ARdeer by about five lengthg ,then came Salt- cote Belle four lengths behind with Marjorie close astern, gradually drawing ahead to pass Sal’ cote Belle to windward by Goldhanger Spit. While thoy wore engaged in what looked lik luffing match Spvinaway C6 ( 57 tons, built by Orvis and Full-r of Ipswich in 1899 and owned by Cranfield Bros., working fouee aa one race) took ivantaze of tne the onl y stronger tide in mid stream and fairly galloped past both of them to leeward,continuing to overhaul both Ardeer and later Memory. Meanwhile Maid of Connaught ( ex Monarch- another large barge and possibiy unique in being converted back to a sailor- man after rynning for 3 time as a fully powered barge) was enjoying a battle with Millie( 50 tons,built at Brightlingsea in 1892- identifiable by ner white topsail- a change from the mass of advertisements. she once carried!) and Pretoria(the other Kentish barge- built at Faversham.in 1902, and at 44 tons the smallest barge in the race). Venta and Gipping were sailing well in what breeze there was,but their poor start put them well over half an hour behind the leaders,as they passed Stone. Down past the laid up tankers they went, to off Sales’ point where they were turned round a mark boat, just after the turn of the tide, to beat and drift home again. Spinaway C rounded first, followed by Memory and Marjorie, but Memory pointed higher than the former, and by the time she reached the Doubles it seemed shs had a good lead, though Spinaway C and Marjorie still had a chance, but the rest of the fleet were well back, However ,it was by no means '' in the bag'' for a Sudden South - Easterly wind brought the rearguard up in fine style, and in the Basin Reach, . a

Sunshine, fresh breezes, a dash of rain on Monday afternoon, added to a splendid sunset as well as sunrises for those who were stirring, all combined to make a memorable weekend of sailing and camping for the club. Mersea Stone again was the choice this year for the base of operations and what better choice could there have been. The expedition was led by Phil Luke of Great Baddow. In all, eleven boats put in at the camp-site over the Bank Holiday weekend, the little armada being composed ef two Sharpies, one Torch, four Enterprises (two of which arrived on Sunday), one G.P., one Fleetwind, farolin a self-contained camp in herself, and last but by no means least, Avril, in all her glory. As most club members will recall, Avril 's explorers became stuck in the mud on the first picnic cruise. We are proud to announce that Avril did not become stuck in the mud this time. Alas, she.became stranded on the hard at Brightlingsea, evernight on Saturday, having been assured by the locals that the tide was favourable. Thus it was that her skipper and crew spent their first night at camp aboard Avril. The boats arrived at intervals throughout Saturday, the first adventurous souls having put out on the early morning tide. As the day progressed, tents were added to the splendid location, the last ones going up shortly before midnight, salved with all the necessary good fortune from Avril in her predicament at Brightlingsea. By Sunday there were ten tents in all, eleven including "the smallest room". THE BEST FROM YOUR BOAT, Part 2, Sails. It’ is only in the last 3 or 4 years that we in this country have abandoned the idea that a good sail should be cut flat and should have very little flow,The Continentals have proved us wrongin this, and most dinghies will go very much faster Rj under any condition with a lot of flow in botno mainsail and foresail., A good mainsail should nave a large shelf along the boom, and be very baggy just aft of the mast. There are two ways of doing this, you can, if you havea long purse,buy your 39ils from Paul Elvstrom who builds the shape into the sail by the way he cuts the widths of clotns still keeping the luff and foot straight.This is by far the best way, but it is out of the price range of most of us. The common way of getting flow into'a sail is by shaping the luff ané the foot, so that before the sails are put onto the spars they have shaped luff and foot, which, when they are fixed to staight spars puts flow into them, The. way you use your new sails is very important as you w can completely ruin a new sail in its first hour:of life. -We will deal first with the treatment of a cotton sail. It should ideally, be set first on a nice sunny diy, with a moderate breeze. Pull un the luff just hand taut, do not attempt to sweat the sail up the mast, the same is true along tne boom, it should only be hand taut on the outhaul, A cotton sail needs 24 hours use before it is stretched and during this time you should continually take uv the slack on boom and mast as the sail stretches. Do not sheet the sails in hard during this 24 hours, it is best to keep the boat reaching with a beam wind backwards and forewards, At the end of 24 hours sailing time you can then sweat up the luff of the sail but do not pull out the outhaul as tignt as it will go on stretching slightly for another 24 hours or so. NEVER in this period of 9 sails life reef it, if you do, it will nevér recover, also — try not to get it wet.,It should be aired after use and carefully put away dry. You snould,even after careful stretching, treat your sails very carefully if you capsize, especially in salt water, Rinse them in fresh water,dry and air them before storing. y Well cared for cotton sails will give 5 years first class racing. a Coming to terylene sails the requirements are somewhat different.Cotton sails are carefully stretched and they retain the stretched ‘shape for the rest of their life, Terylene on the other hand is elastic,and while you can ruin a terylene sail by the way you set it ,the damage is not permanent.You must therefore be very fussy about tension on luff and foot each time you set sail. The amount of tension you put on them will determine how the sail sets, and by varying the tension you can give the sail the best shape for varying weather conditions, You will .after a, little experimenting, find out the right tension so that the sail will have no creases in the wrong places. As you increase the tension you will flatten the sail. Make certein that your battens are the right length, and if you have a leach line, have this as loose as possible con- Sistent with the sail: setting, Contd. on Page

Pase 13. The ‘after sxiling' care of terylene is quite important for, while the material will not rot, it will, if folded hard, Grease to such an extent that if the next race you take part in is alight weather one, your sails will remain creased the whole of the time, thus giving you a considerable handicap to overcome, Therefore lightly fold terylenes or hang them up. If they have become wet with salt water, wash them in fresh water and dry them as you would for cotton sails before putting them away. Please, if you have a good set of sails either cotton or terylene, do look after them for sailmaking is some- thing of a black art, and excellent sails are few and far between. Most sailmakers do 2 reasoy,ably honest job, but every now and again they turn out the sail ina million. This will | not happen twice to you so if you get one treat it like gold dust, SPLICES AND ROPES' ENDS. "Barnacle", _ As one looks round 2 boatyard these days one sees plenty of roves with unravelled ends, steadily getting shorter and shorter, and perfect horrors to tie good knots in. This should not be, as it is so easy to prevent an end from unlaying. If for any reason you have to cut a Warp and have not time to do anything about the raw end, slio a thumb knot in it to stop it fron unlaying until you have tine to do something About it- cither whip or splice it. Whipping is neat and tidy 2nd is easily done, but the plain whivping-is not ' a good bst' as a permanent finish. Far better, is the ssilmakers' ©. :inping which cannot pull off the end. A third recognised whipoing is the West Country whipping, but I have never seen it used, or known 2nyone who has, so it can , probably, well be forgotten. A back svlice.can always be put in the ends of a warp if it is well tapered ett, and it provides a neat end to the rone, but it does stiffen it and may make it difficult to tie 2 zsood knot near. tne end of the rope. Eye splices, both with and without thimbles, are needed all over 2 boat, 28 Without doubt, it is far and away toe neatest way of putting a loon in the end of 1 rove, and should be used whenever 2 permanent loop is needed. Exauples , such as the end of the lanyard on the ship's bucket, and the tails of halliard falls ,where they shackle onto .blocks or wire parts, come readily to. mind. Splicins is fascinating work, and once learnt, the beginner is often tempted to put splices in places, where they should not really be used, _ Siaply for the fun of making them. When learning to splice don! t make the mistake of trying to start on codline, thinking that the small stuff is. easier- it isn't. Codline is often so tightly laid that it is a real brute to tuck and a single splice say take four or five times as longs 2s one in something like two inch hemp. Rope is expensive, and continually practising splices can soon get through quite a le ngth, so it is advisable bo start learning on an old mooring rone. “hen practising , don't bother to ake vast numbers of tucks, but concentrate on setting the start of the splice correct, When anlicing cotton and synthetic fibre ropes it is necessary to whin or seal the ends of tne strands before starting the splice, but this is not so for sisal or hep. Once the bick splice and eye splice have been mastered there are other splices, but they are seldom used now, 2nd are worth learning only for their interest.

Page 14, There is quite a range of fancy knots that can be tied , using the individual strands of a rope, to produce a decorative ring round the end of 2 rope. Some of these can be used in Place of a crown knot to start a back splice, and others are> finished off by relaying the rope beyond the knot and putting on 2 saiimakers' whipping. These knots are well worth learn- — ing so that you can finish off the ends of your mooring warps in 2 distinctive, easily identified manner. Unfortunately it is very difficult to mako a neat job of these fancy finishes in synthetic ropes, whose strands do not hold their lay very well, and it is next door to inpossible in cotton. However, sisal and hemp take these fancy knots well, and it is a pleasant way of passing a Warm windless after- noon sitting on deck doing a bit of ropework, You may complain that I have not actually told you how to do any of the knots and splices, Certainly not- they sre very well described and illustrated in almost every textbook on sailing, and in ‘Scouting for Boys', and-it is not ny intention in these two articles to write about a subject that has already been covered thoroughly, but merely to emphasise certain, not so obvious, points which are often negiected in the textbooks, Letter to the Editor continued, of Phil Luke, camping weekend and picnics have been marred by by lack of interest and help by club officials. Officers of the Day or other responsible Duty Officer have only been on duty during racing periods or Open Day, at other times the welfare and safety of club members and equipment has not been under the eye of anyone with the authority to make decisions. It is further suggested that all programmed fixtures sucn as picnics, cruises, camping weekends, should constitute part of a sailing programme, divorced from shore- bound social activities, and run parallel with the cet fixtures. Well organised club sailing could bring together a large number of members and families who at the moment sail alone, and introduce those who seldom sail beyond Millbeach to the challenge and interest of sailing in wider estuary waters. The knowledge that their guidance and safety was being watched over by experienced and responsible club officers, and that steps, would be taken to assist in need, would encourage those who have been less adventurous in the past. The result of the questionaire put out in Navigans showed that the items of biggest interest were day vicnics and weekend cruises, but people Will not turn out unless assured of reason- able orgzanisats on.if it is considered that financial stringency does not allow extension of facilities,an increase of sub's wouldnot come amiss. Ten shillings a year is such a small sum for the enjoymentprovided, little more than two packets of cigarettes, and: even the impecunious could surely dig just a little deeper.’ It is considered that a big effort is required to improve the general sailing interests of the club, for the bene- fit of 211 members, and also of importance, for the good name of the club amongst other clubs and users of the Blackwater, Yours faithfully, P. "Barnacle" COMMODORE'S COMIENTS There are three things of note to which I should like to draw your attention this month. Firstly, the Laying Up Dinner and Dance, This takes place on Friday, 8th November at 7 o'clock for 7.30; and this year, for the first time, will be held in the Great Baddow Laboratories Dinning Rooms, West Hanningfield Rd, Great Baddow, As usual the Guests of Honour will be our President, Dr, E, Eastwood C.B.E., Ph.D., M.Sc., M.I.5.B. and Mrs, Zastwood, For those who may not know the locality, it is about a quarter of a mile down the first turning to the right past the Church on the Southend Road, There is an enormous private car park and yuides will be available to show the way from there, Please come in your hundreds! Price of tickets has been fixed provisionally at seventeen and six pence, Secondly, we have during the week November 4th to 8th, the election of committee members for the M,A.S.C. main committee. We as a section are fortunate to be quite persona grata with the M,A.S.C, at the moment, this being due in no small measure to the activities of your Vice Commodore, Jack Bigden who is a member of the main committee, He is however due to retire now, but will be standing again for re-election, Please support him by recording your vote, and in so doing support the Sailing Club. All details are on the posters around the establishments, Finally, a word about power vessels, The Committee have decided that power boats of the non planing type are acceptable; defining these as vessels with outboard or inboard engines which at all times act as displacement craft, As there are bound to be border-line cases, each application will be treated on its merits, Terence Hallam

The M.A.S.C. have announced that Gala Day will be held on Saturday llth July 1964 and the Sailing Section have been asked to organise the Gala Dance. Mr. Bigden has booked the Lion and Lamb for this date. Following the approval in principle at the A.G.M. of adopting an entrance fee levy on future Associate Members, the following proposed additions to rules were formulated. 13. Subscriptions (f) An entrance fee of £2. 2. 0. is payable by an associate member or £3. 3. O. by an Associate Member with husband or wife, on being accepted by the committee. (g) An Associate Cadet who joins the club before his or her 17th birthday and remains a paid up Cadet will not be required to pay the entrance fee on application to Associate Membership. In the first part John dealt with general maintenance, pointing out that it is an all-—the-year-—round jcb and not just a cese of a few hours work at laying-up and fitting-out. He also pointed out how insidious water can be in delaminating ply and rotting planks. The maintenance of sails and rigging followed, particular stress being given to the storing of cotton sails and the treatment of galvanised rigging. At this point we were reminded of the forthconing.talk by Mr. A.G. Taylor, the well known Maldon sail-maker, scheduled for 12th March which should give everyone a greater insight into the subject of sails. The next point was the all-important one of paint, with a strong warning against allowing the excessive build-up of old paint on a boat. STEAMING THE RIBS BY "BARNACLE" It is early morning in the boatyard. The skeleton of the new boat seems to fill the building shed, with its multiplicity of struts and braces securing it to the roof beams. A wisp of smoke rises as the boy lights the fire under the steam chest boiler, and splintering noises show he is busy smashing up the last remains of an assortment of old dinghies, rotton cabin tops and broken masts, ensuring a good supply of fuel for the day*s activities. Some of the shipwrights are wriggling their way round inside the —_ framework of the new boat, marking off the run of the ribs with chalk and pencil marks on the ribbands, vhilst others gather round the circular saw and planer, feeding into them the boards of wet, green oak, delivered freshly cut to the yard the previous day. As the ribs emerge from the planer they are checked, and any with small knots or wavy grain are rejected and the rest are laid out with the grain in the best direction for bending, and chamfers are planed on the inner corners. If the grain tends to run out, the outer corners may have their sharp edges removed to reduce the risk of splitting when they are bent. By the time the first batch of ribs are prepared, steam is probably up in the boiler. Some yards have very good steam chests, others are a trifle on the crude side. In the latter case, the boy will probably be stopping up the worst of the leaks, surroundéd by a fine haze of steam. When the steam chest is nicely hot. the first half dozen or so ribs are fed in, the chest is closed and the ribs left to stew for about half an. hour, depending on their size. Like most forms of cooking an overdone rib is nearly as bad as one that is underdone. Even when the ribs are ready there will be no signs of hurry, but just try working with the shipwrights ! From the time the steam chest is opened until the rib is in place not a second will be wasted. Two men are ready inside the frame of the hull, whilst others wait outside. The chest is opened, emitting a pleasant cloud of steam, a rib is grasped (by a well gloved hand) and withdrawn and passed to the first man outside the boat. The rib feels bone dry, very hot and suprisingly rubbery. The man outside the boat will rapidly give the rib anynecessary sideways bend, passing it over the top and down inside the ribbands, outside the shelf timbers to the men inside the hull who locate its lower end in the socket in the keel and push it firmly into position against the ribbands. The men outside watch carefully, and as soon as they notice it is not touching a certain ribband a clamp is screwed on to pull it into place. Meanwhile the men inside the hull are tacking the rib to the ribbands, and maybe teo the keel with wire nails. The rib usually lies snugly in place alongside the beam shelf, but occasionally it is necessary to tack it here as well. Then the next rib is taken from the chest and the drill repeated. Quite often. two or more teams are working on different parts of the hull simul- taneously. As ribs are taken from the chest, others are put in, alternate batches often being marked by hammering a tack into the ends so there can be no doubt which have been in the longest. Work is always started in the middle of the hull where the beam is greatest, and carried on into the stern where there are usually the sharpest . curves so that any ribs that break or refuse to bend properly can be vut Conteces

-5- in up in the bows where the ribs are shorter and with little curvature, but this must be done very quickly before the timber cools off tco much. Oak or rock elm (not to be confused with ordinary elm) are the woods chiefly used for steamed ribs. Both can be obtained with good straight grain in the required lengths, and both take steaming well, the rock elm being the easier to bend when hot. The whole secret of steaming is plenty of hot steam, under pressure if at all possible, and cook the wood for the right time. Amateur attempts with a bit of drainpipe over a driftwood fire will usually succeed fairly well, in fact the wood will bend quite well if it has been immersed in boiling water, but it is far and away easier to handle if it has been properly steamed in a good chest with no water touching it.
