A hearty vote of thanks goes to Jack Bigden, the ladies of the galley and all the other kind people who helped to make the afternoon such a success. — ADMIRALTY CHARTS #OR THE CRUISING YACHTSMAN A valuable item in the cruiser's inventory should be an adequate set of charts corrected up to date. The standards applied by the Admiralty Chart Agents are necessarily high: alterations are continually being made, and cancellation is. ruthless after a very few years (maybe three or four), with the result that several pounds! worth of charts are reduced to the stetus of lampshade material. Sailing on cancelled and uncorrected charts really has nothing to recommend it, and the obvious solution is to do one's own corrections, fairly regularly, and above all, well before time of sailing. After all, the familiarity thus gained with the chart numbers as well as their range and content is something that will pay off later in confidence and facility and so increase one's scope and enjoyment of cruising. Members of this club are well based to enjoy a pretty wide range of cruising possibilities from creek-crawling (remember Arthur Ransome's "Secret Water"?) to going foreign, even if it does involve crossing one or.two of the main shipping lanes. For general purposes the cruising —_—— area available can conveniently be taken as bounded by a line from Dungeness to Boulogne on the one hand and from Happisburgh to Den Helder on the other. From the Catalogue of Admiralty Charts (1964 Home Edition, price one shilling from any of the Agents ) one can compile a basic and comprehensive selection of large and small scale charts to cover this area according to requirements. (The nearest official supplier of local charts is May and Brett Ltd., 118 High Street, Maldon). Starting from scratch, the yachtsman's requirement will be a large ‘scale chart of home channels and nearby harbours. The rule, "as large a scale as possible", holds good at every stage and for every size of vessel. Admiralty charts covering a large stretch of coastline have ~ the advertised disadvantage that marks close inshore are not shown. For example, No. 1610 (North Foreland to Orfordness) bears the following Caution: "Certain buoys, lights and wrecks in the inner waters are not shown on this chart. All buoys and wrecks are omitted westward of the heavy pecked line. For these the larger scale charts must be consulted." This pecked line zigzags between Walton-on-the—Naze and Westgate—on~ Sea, and passes outside all of the swatchways which would normally be used by yachtsmen.

3 ~ The alternative large scale charts covering lesser areas in detail are unwieldy on the small boat (minus chart table and maybe even without cabin). To overcome this difficulty the Admiralty has recently issued a series of Yachting Charts showing small inshore areas on a large scale, backed with its authority and presented on a sheet small enough to be handled in a dinghy, giving on the reverse side sailing directions, yacht repair facilities and local yacht clubs, with additionally a transparent cover to fit —- all at a price about half the average full size production. With Nos. 5389 (W. Mersea to Maldon) and 5388 (Approaches to Rivers Colne and Blackwater) the yachtsman can comfortably explore the home estuaries, and they will be sufficient also for most cruiser races organised by the Blackwater J.R.C. The series covers every popular yachting centre from Great Yarmouth to Dover. The Yachting Chart for Burnham is No. 5390 and (surely excellent value this!) for Approaches to Harwich with the Rivers Stour, Orwell and Deben it is No. 5387. It has to be borne in mind that for this admittedly cheap series corrections are not provided, although there 12ppears no reason why yachtsmen should not insert their own. However, when the yachtsman wishes to make a passage from one centre to another, the next difficulty arises: even between the Blackwater and the Crouch he is going to be off his charts for a small distance, and between the Blackwater and Harwich he is going to be off for quite a large distance round the Naze. Then the need for a larger chart end at least an improvised chart table makes itself felt. For Burnham via the inner channel (the Raysand ~- colloquially 'raisin') local knowledge is probably better than any charts; otherwise you go by the Spitway and on to Ne. 1975 (Thames Estuary — Northern part). For passages to the Stour Nos. 1975 and 2052 (The Naze to Orfordness) give coverage, as well as including the whole of the lovely Orwell and Deben estuaries. Expleration of these is made easier if one supplements the charts with Jack Coote's book, "East Coast Rivers", which gives details of channels and anchorages (illustrated by photographs and diagrams ) and a mass of information about shore facilities. | A crossing of the Thames Estuary calls again for something over ard above No. 1610 in view of the warning quoted above. No. 1975 will see you out of the Blackwater but covers only half the crossing and has to be used in conjunction with No. 1607 (Thames Estuary - Southern part), which will take you as far as Leigh, the Medway, Whitstable or Ramsgate. Here you may at choice use either Yachting Charts Nos. 5391 (Leigh Creek), 5392 (Medway), 5393 (Whitstable) or 5394 (Ramsgate) for entering harbour, or else (for Ramsgate) the full size No. 1828 (The Downs) which has the advantage that it goes as far as Dover. For the Suffolk and Norfolk coast to Happisburgh (variously Haisborough and Ha'isboro' where, according to Bob Roberts at least, even the fishes will put you on course in "windy old weather"), Chart No. 1543° (Haisborough to Orfordness) will give you coverage for passage making and includes a plan of Southwold harbour where it is needed. For entering the harbours of Great Yarmouth and Lowestoft one has a choice (dependent on the size of sheet one is prepared to handle) between the two Yachting Charts Nos.5385 (Yarmouth) and 5386 (Lewestoft) and the full size No. 1536 (Approaches to Gt. Yarmouth and Lowestoft). If the latter can in fact be accommedated, it has the advantage of exceptionally large scale insets of both these fairly busy working harbours. So far we have ccvered less than half of our designated area. Charts for the North Sea passage and cruising on the other side are as large a subject again and best dealt with in later articles. DO=IT~YOURSELF, SLOCUM STYLE "The seasons came quickly while I worked. Hardly were the ribs of the sloop up before apple—trees were in bloom. Then the daisies and the cherries came soon after. Close by the place where the old Spray had now dissolved rested the ashes of John Cook, a revered Pilgrim father. Se the new Spray rose from hallowed ground. From the deck of the new craft I could put out my hand and pick cherries that grew over the little grave. The planks for the new vessel, which I soon came to put on, were of Georgia pine an inch and a half thick. The operation of putting them in was tedious, but, when on, the calking was easy. The outward edges stood slightly open to receive the calking, but the inner. edges were so close that I could not see daylight between them. All the butts were fastened hy through bolts, with screw—nuts tightening them to the timbers, so that there would be no complaint from them. Many bolts with screw—nuts were used in other parts of the construction, in all about a thousand. It was my purpose to make my vessel stout and strong. : _ ' Now, it is a law in Lloyd's that the Jane repaired all out of the old until she is entirely new is still the Jane. The Spray changed her being so gradually that it was hard to say at what point the old died. or the new took birth, and it was no matter. The bulwarks I built up of white—-oak stanchions, fourteen inches high, and covered with seven- eighth-inch white pine. These stanchions, mortised through a two inch covering board, I calked with thin cedar wedges. They have remained perfectly tight ever since. The deck I made of one-and~a—-half-—inch by three—inch white pine spiked to beams six by six inches, of yellow Georgia pine, placed three feet apart. The deck.inclosures were one over the aperture of the main hatch, six feet by six, for a cooking galley, and a trunk further aft, about ten feet by twelve, for a cabin. Both of these rose about three feet above the deck, and were sunk sufficiently into the hold to afford head—room. In the spaces along the sides of the cabin, under the deck, I arranged a berth to sleep in, and shelves for small storage, not forgetting a place for the medicine-chest. In the midship hold, that is, the space between cabin and galley, under the deck was room for provision of water, salt beef eke, ample for many months" From "Sailing Alone Round The World", by Joshua Slocum. A MAST IS MADE BY "BARNACLE" Many club members have built their own boats, but few of them have made the mast and even fewer have been faced with the job of making a hollow mast. From the outside all masts look pretty much the same, but the tall tapering mast of a modern.ocean racer is one of the most complex examples of woodworker‘'s skill to be found. These days few boats of any size have solid masts, and those do often have them laminated out of many separately pieces to produce the strongest possible spar. Hollow masts can be made in two halves, carefully carved out and glued together, or they can be built up box fashion from selected planks. For masts of small to medium size the former method is tote preferred as the mast can readily be made to any desired shape, and the wall thickness can be kept uniform. Larger masts have to be built up -.because of the amount of timber that would be wasted were they hollowed out of solid, but where the various boards have been glued up to form the two halves they are often carved inside to give a uniform wall. A third method of producing a hollow spar is to roll a tapered tube of thin veneer, with plugs at the ends and any cross tree stations. (The McGruer method). This produces an incredibly light, strong spar, but also an incredibly expensive one! "Melody's" boom is an original McGruer spar, the Maldon smack "Fly" has a hollow gaff made

aoe from the Mcgruer boom from the King of Spain's class racer. Anybody With lots and lots of spare time and money might like to have a shot at this.method of construction. The method most likely to interest us is the two halves carved from solid. A mast made this way should always be started with one over—size piece of timber. Sitka spruce is nearly always used, and a fine timber it is. A good forty foot length will have the grain running straight from end to end without knots or waves, and it is a much lighter wood than B.C. pine. Firstly the single baulk of timber is cut lengthwise into two halves, one of which is turned endwise, and the two are then marked to ensure that they are kept in the same relationship. When buying timber for a hollow mast from a reputable firm of boat builders timber merchants it can be ordered in the two halves, with one half reversed and clearly marked, but it is far safer to order one piece and cut it yourself. This halving and reversing is so important because it ensures that the two sides of the mast will be of equal strength and that any wanders in the grain cancel out. Having halved the baulk the freshly cut faces are planed FLAT AND SMOOTH. This is one job where even the best machine planing is not considered good enough by the experts, and much care is taken to get a perfect joint face. The fore and aft profile is then marked on each half, sawn, and planed to finished size. The length of all the hollow sections between the crosstree: plugs are marked all round each half, a table of saw depths and fence settings drawn up and the hollows roughed out on the circular saw. This job cannot be hurried. The more taper there is to be on the spar the more cuts must be made, and some of the cuts have to be made parallel to the front and some parallel to the back, so the halves frequently have to be turned end for end. Eventually the machining is finished and the hollows cleaned out by hand with roundsoled planes and gauges.-. Working on spruce demands very sharp iron if the wood is not to be torn. When the hollows are fairly smooth, and the correct size to template, recesses are cut for any sheave boxes, masthead light wires are laid up in the hollows and the halves are glued together and held with may be as many as sixty clamps. Spar glueing is an "all hands" job in the boatyard, and is not something that can easily be done by a couple of amateurs. When the glue has set the sides of the spar are planed off to profile then the corners are removed to a predetermined depth (most yards have marking gauges which mark the correct amount to remove to convert a rectangular spar to octagonal ), the resulting octagon has its corners removed and so on until the spar reaches its final round or pear shape. "Ironmongery" is fitted, the spar is sanded smooth and varnished, and another mast is ready for the attention of the rigger. INTRODUCTION The following pages are not a "SHIP'S LOG", they are the "WORKING DIARY" of a fortnight's summer holiday on my brother's converted ship's boat "AaRK". It had been arranged that Vic and his family should spend a fortnight in the summer eboard AaRK and Vic had decided to go further afield than last year when he tookherup to Woodbridge. Christchurch in Hampshire was chosen for a number of reasons, it represented a bit. of a "voyage", it entailed some navigation and also most important of all, it is a lovely landlocked harbour with facilities for his young children. My mother lives thirty miles from Christchurch in a town called Romsey, and Frances and I were to meet Vic and Family there. I shall not touch on Vic's holiday, except to mention that he left Heybridge Lock on a Saturday morning and walked into Mother's house on the Monday evening, three days to Southampton. The following day he took AaRK to Christchurch and hence did the trip in four days. Ian and Frances 9th August, 1953 Last day at work before holiday Left car at home, and had a lift into work from a friend. RBrother—in-law gave lift from work to the Railway Station where we caught the 5-40 p.m. train to Liverpool Street. Caught fast Tube to Waterlco, made good time (6-40 p.m.). British Railways had a fire at Waterlou and we caught a dubious long slow train to Eastleigh and so to Romsey. ‘Delight, Vic was waiting at Romsey Station. Frances was so glad to see him despite being her b—brother-— in-law Mummy had traditional chops and peas ready in minutes. Talked till late, long tiring day. Saturday 10th August Holiday begins Breakfast in bed, with the children joining in. Frances did necessary shopping (bread, eggs, butter, milk etc.). Chicken luuch in Romsey and down to boat with Vic. Arrived at Christchurch quay 3-30 p.m. and got first sight of AaRK. Very smart she looked. Came aboard, fetched luggage, t.rd &% cup of tea with Vic, last minute queries, answers and suggestions from owner. No snags. AaRK was as neat and tidy as I have ever seen her, and I was "in" on the last stage of construction and have kept a beady (envious!) eye on her up to date. The owner had touched up all the paint blemiskes and varnish work, all sails bent, all halyards neatly coiled. He, or his wife more likely, had cleaned out thoroughly below, clean towels, not a speck of dust, everything in place. Frances made a list of all edibles aboard, I noted with gratitude the full tank, spare Calor bottle, full load of petrol, even the water bottles filled freshly. The owner justifies my faith and extreme admiration. After the cuppa and cakes we had more "chat" then I ferried the owner ashore and saw him off from the quay at 6-30 p.m. Frances and I went to C.S.C. then round Elkins yard (Ann Tiki) round Elkins bank and met Mr (Captain) Stonage. Walked into town had Fish and Chips, walked round to Bea.ister's

Tide down (10 p.m.) and had to launch dinghy into . ili stream, to get back aboard fairly tired but so very, very happy. Just starting to get into the rhythm of the tides. (4.30 high). Motored slowly against flood right clear of entrance, turned into wind and with Frances at the helm I started to make sail. The engine stopped and I tried briefly to start it, no go. Our situation not critical and I proceeded to make all sail and press on for Hurst narrows. The seas were quite large and we had the wind (4-5?) on our starboard quarter. Most alarming for crew who had to take the helm whilst I inspected plugs, spark and fuel flow. All seemed O.K. so I swung it over and it started after a few turns. Having got it to _ go I shut off, and-turned petrol off and confirmed with crew that we would make for the Solent, we made across the bay, well clear of the shore as wind was 71.S.W. (lee shore). Recently during a discussion, a would be boat builder remarked that any fool can neil er screw twe pieces ef wood together, the truth of his ‘remark’ lies in his emission of the word properly.. Nailing aud screwing appear to be such simple jobs that people with little experience often tend to think that they require no thought or care, and then they wonder why the wood splits, the screw shears off, or the fastenings do not hold. When screwing two pieces of wood together, the first things to decide are the seize and number of the screws to be used. These depend on the seizes of the components being fastened, the type of timber used, and the load to be carried, and can be determined only from experience. Many people tend to use too few screws of too large a size, and often use too short a screw. Soft woods such‘as pine or spruce need fastenings at closer centres than hardwoods like oak, and the screws can with advantage be longer than would be used for oak. The widths of the timbers involved affect the diameters of screws used — as a very rough guide it is seldom safe to use larger than

-5- number six screws into three quarter of an inch, eights into inch and tens into inch and a quarter. This epparently small screw size is adopted so that the centres can be staggered so adjacent screws are not run into the same line of the grain. Screw length, as well as being affected by the type of timber used, depends on whether the screw is to be in shear or in tension — screws in tension being longer than those in shear. Also, it isusually good policy to increase the diameter of a screw in tension to get the advantage of the larger head area. Difficulties in driving screws are almost entirely eliminated by drilling the correct sizes of clearance and pilot holes, and in the sizes of screws used for small boat work, this does mean the correct size and not something that looks vaguely right - the margin between a screw which binds solid before it is right home and a screw that strips out under load is only two or three drill sizes different. A frequent reason for splitting the outer piece of wood is failure to cut a proper 90° countersink for the screw head. Quite often in soft wood the screw will bed itself in nicely, but every so often there is a weakness in the timber and the wedging action of the head will split it open. The thread of the screw should be greased particularly if it is to be run into oak or eln, and the screwdriver used must FIT the slot of the screw. A screwdriver bit in a carpenter's brace is the best tool to use, as it is sasier to Spin it quickly to run the screw in than it is to use a normal screwdriver, and the tremendous leverage ensures that the screw is done up tight, whilst the "feel" of the tool avoids the risk of shearing off the screw head as can happen if a spanner of tommy bar is applied to a heavy screwdriver. "Pump" action screwdrivers are very good for digging unsightly marks in the timber surface unless cross head screws are used, and they completely.lack the tightening power of a brace. Brass or steel (galvanised) screws should not be used on boat work - brass screws will de-zincify in a year or two, and although the screw may look quite sound it will have no strength. Stainless steel, gunmetal or silicon bronze screws are more expensive, but if a little care is used in fitting them, each screw can be relied on to carry its full load for many, many years, and should repairs be necessary, they can be unscrewed and often used again whilst a mild steel screw will have rusted, and a brass screw is liable to shear off. | Nailing has been revolutionised by the "anchorfast "and " gripfast" barbed nails. Used properly, these nails are excellent, but they are expensive, and their biggest snag is that once hammered home they can nz¥ be undone without damage to the timber. All but the smallest sizes should have pilot holes drilled, and in some cases it is advisable to drill a clearance hole in the material that is to be nailed down. These barbed nails will resist all strains as well as screws; in fact they are often used as an alternative to screws, but they have not the power to close a gap on fastening that a screw has. Once one has decided to screw two pieces of wood together, one has only to decide on the number, size and material of screw to use, whereas if one is to nail, one has also to decide on the type of nail to be used, and whether to clench or nail blind. Also one has to decide whether or not a pilot hole will be needed, whether to use oval nails with the grain of the upper or lower piece of timber if the grains cross, and whether to clench with or across the grain. The correct angle at which the nails should be skewed when nailing blind is often overlooked — nails hammered in square to the surface of the timber can pull straight out under load, whereas pairs of nails driven in to form Vees can be pulled out only with great difficulty. One final point on nailing - when using galvanised nails, take care not to damage the galvanising. If the nail is going to end up minus half its zinc, you might as well use cheaper ungalvanised nails in the first place. "Barnacle."

Anthony, a destroyer of some 1,300 tons, belonging to the 3rd Flotilla Meditteranean Fleet, the ships company had the rather unique experience of being caught up in an unsolved mystery. It happened during the Spring Cruise of 1931, four of our destroyers were lying at anchor off St. Tropey in a very picturesque bay which that part of the French Rivicra abounds in. le were at open ancktor, that is, one anchor down and free to swing in any direction s6:.i ahout two cables length separating each ship, (1,200 feet to the layman) when the signs of a strom arose one evening. The Captain ordered steam to be raised, and the second anchor be prepared to be dropped under foot a traditional precaution which steadies the swinging of the ship and prevents a bumping and boring match with the next in line. After dark weather conditions became steaily worse so orders were given to"let go second anchor", ‘which duly went out of the Hawse Pipe and away into the unknown. A stiff off shore breeze kept the weather. anchor really biting in for most of the night, then as dawn began to break so did the blow. By daylight things had calmed down nicely, the Captain gave orders to weigh second anchor and return to normal harbour routine. Cable work on destroyers was always tedious, plenty of hand-draulic attached to various items of cable bashing as I called it. So when steam was put on the capstan it made life much easier. Slowly the cable began to tighten, link by link it came in over the lip of the hawse pipe with a grouching grinding noise of steel to steel, there was only one speed for the capstan engine — flat out:-— and only one speed for the cable — dead slow, the gear ration took care of that. We had six shackles out, that is, 75 fathoms of it, so there was a good twenty minutes work before we expected to see the anchor break surface. Bach shackle as it came in was reported to the Bridge by the Cable Officer using coloured hand flags, slowly the cable was stowed in the cable locker by its own weight as it piled in heaps down below. The colour df flag No.l was duly held up, and everyone there began to sigh "oh well, nearly home" when suddenly a loud voice from the Capn of the Focstle rang out "Anchors Gone Sir"! To everyones amazement, there was the cable dangling just above the water line and rising steadily up towards the hawse pipe with nothing on the end! The Cable Officer then gave the order "Stop Capstan' and préceeded to look over the side for ONE BRON LSNNOX 30 CWT BOW ANCHOR quoting the Ship's Rate Book — a sort of cataloque of every item carried.

-7T- Everyone present sensed the next remark which was made, the Cable Officer "Where the ** ** ** is it, Capn of Focastle? The bluejackets in the vicinity began to snigger sensing some witty remark by one Petty Officer Bloggs "Somebodys pinched the thing Sir", "Put yourself in the First Lieutenants report" came the reply. Justice had to be done. Destroyers in those days didn't carry diving apparatus, or divers, so a request was duly made by radio to our nearest ship who carried the gear. It happened to be H.M.S. Royal Oak lying at Golfe Juan, who sent their 42 foot launch and equipment in a most obliging manner taking some 3 hours to accomplish the fifteen or so miles "round the corner". When diving began, some speculation as regards finding self same anchor was running high, the odds changed from hour to hour as the bubbles from both divers made a wide arc over the surface, they spent about four hours down there - ene of our chaps who went in the launch as relief pumping party swere he saw them sitting on the ocean bottom Playing cards! Anyway they finally surfaced with no results, the unusual muddy boots being the only proof that they had at least gcne down to the ocean floor. So after we had fixed them up with a welcome meal they returned to their battlewaggon, leaving Petty Officer Bloggs feeling chocker block! On the messdeck, the usual arguments arose as to who should pay for the anchor, and the cost of the divers (who in those days got double pay for each hour while diving), how much did it cost to buy a new one and so on. It was even suggested that P.O. Bloggs should re engage for his pension which meant "sign on for another 10 years". To enable him to get out of "being in debt to the Crown". Shortly afterwards the Court of Inquiry took place in the Captain's Cabin, and a verdict of "Lost by Accident" was passed, everyone felt sorry for the Capn of the Forcastle when the Cable Officer said to him "You couldn't have shackled it on P.O. Bloggs! He had the last say when replying to that accusation, "Well Sir how did it run out and take the cable with it if it wasn't shackled on?". No reply to that one and as far as I know no positive reason was ever established why the anchor dissappeared. NOTE: All you would be Mariners watchout for Davy Jones, who knows he might have pinched it! TORPS. The Anchor's value per Naval Rate Book was in the region of £20 - made of pig iron — quite cheap stuff. Zhe Thursday 27th February brought us the long awaited films of the America Cup races of 1958 and 1962. These films were loaned to the club by Mr. Oren Aisher and were presented to him by the New York Yacht Club in recognition of his services to yachting. These films are in great . demand and apparently we were very fortunate to obtain ‘the loan of them. In lending these films Mr. Aisher does not make any charge but requests that a collection be taken for donation to the R.Y.A. Olympics fund (a very worthy cause for all interested in sailing). Unfortunately on the night we chose the College projectionist was not available but Mr. A.C. Stock volunteered to fill the breach with the proviso that he wasn't fully experienced. However, aided by members of the club and ‘after a numberof false starts (including the rewinding of one film which the last borrowers had neglected to do) we were all set. During all this manoeuvring of yards of film etc. our Commodore very gallantly ad-libbed to keep the party going. The first film dealt with the 1958 series of races and included a brief history of their origin with particular mention of Sir Thomas Lipton and the part he played in keeping them going. We were shown the whole sequence of operations from the building and launching of the competing boats to the eliminating contests to find the American representative. The film finally ended with the series of races between challenger and challengered which resulted in America retaining the cup. The Australian Challenge of 1960 formed the subject of the second film where we saw them in training, at one point having a fair amount of trouble with the spinnaker! However, by the time the races were due they had mastered the art effectively. Unfortunately, as we know, the Cup still stays in America despite their gallant efforts with Sceptre. These were two remarkable films and one left the College that night with possibly a tiny little bit of envy and perhaps with a feeling that dinghy sailing on the Blackwater'is maybe a little tame. After the film showing the collection taken amounted to £4. 3. 104. This sum was made up to 6 guineas by the Club and passed to the R.Y.A. Olympics fund. J.G.e Reeve. - MAMGU TROPHY LOC cont. Tuesday 13th August Awoke gloomy, and the tide went out. Greased propshaft, water pump, and had a good breakfast. The radio has packed up and we must take it ashore and find suitable shop somewhere. It was O.K. last night and dead this morning. Washerwoman did the dhobey, cleaned and polished below decks and generally tidied up. Went ashore at noon, to find buses ran to Newport every 12 min. However we found a good radio shop and bought new batteries which worked 100%? Not sure. Had lunch in Pilot Boat Im, Beer, Lobster Salad with wizard dressing, it was all jolly good. Saw Sam working on club Redwings after lunch an odd sight all lined up on the beach together. Everyone of them identical even up to the little yellow racing flag at the mast head. Returned to AaRK and scrubbed decks, washed down topsides and at teatime when the tide came in I sailed the dinghy once round the harbour. An education, one hand on the tiller and mainsheet. MSC-DOC-1964-06-marconi-regatta-day.pdf: SUNDAY, JUNE 21st,196h. ww. 41-15 Meg 964 MARCONI REGATTA DAY CRUISER EVENT. ENTRY FEE 2/6 This event will be in the nature of a seamanship or obstacle race and is open to all boats equipped for. cruising and towing a dinghy. Gntrants should anchor off the Marconi Sailing Club site at Stansgate Abbey point on the South bank of the R. Blackwater before 2-30 p.m. All boats should anchor between a line from the extension of the concrete hard just up river from the cottage on the seawall, and the club race starting line marked be metes at the gun emplacement on the seawall at the Ramsey Wick end of the site, and Goldhanger Spit Buoy. Boats must be left with all sails lowered. Headsails may be hanked on stays, with halliards and sheets on, but must be tied down to the deck. (Sails with Wickham—-Martin gear must be lowered.) The mainsail must have at least two tiers on, but no cover, and the boom must rest in the normal gallows or crutch. Entrants should be prepared either to Slip or recover their anchors. Dinghies are to be drawn up on the beach clear of the water, below the cottage on the seawall.(Beach Marshals will adjust the positions of all dinghies at 2-40 p.m. so all are the same distance from the water, but the marshals will NOT turn dinghies round.) All crew members must be ashore. The event will start at 3-O p.m., when the sailing instructions Will be handed out. All crew members must be in the clubroom for the start, unless instructed otherwise on the day by the Officer of the Day. Entries, with fee, should be sent to the M.S.C. Sailing Secretary, N.F.Tovey, [redacted], 14,[redacted]., Great Baddow, Chelmsford, Essex up to the Thursday before the race, and will be accepted in the clubroom from 2-0 p.m. onwards on the day. Entrants should be prepared to use any or all equipment one ‘could reasonably expect to find aboard &@ cruising yacht; entrants unable to complete any portion of the event will not be disqualified, but will be given a time penalty. Enbrants are advised to bring an anchor and warp for the dinghy in addition to the normal kedge, and a marker buoy. No limit will be placed on the size of crew, but there must be a minimum of two, anv bear in mind that all the crew must be ferried out to the boat in the dinghy after the start, and the dinghy must be towed in the race. It will help the sailing committee if owners can send in their entries well in advance. The handicapping details required will be those on the other side of this form. Boats which have a T(H)CF given by the Blackwater Joint Raci Committee or the Old Gaffers Association should just quote the T(H)C# unless there has been some alteration to the boat since the figure was issued. A second prize will be given if there are more than six entries, and a third prize if there are more than nine. _ The object of this event is a pleasant day out, with a bit more point than "just pottering", and for those new to sailing, a chance to see how well fitted they and their boats are for cruising. The more entries there are, the more fun all can have, so please tell all your friends about this event, and tell them about the event described on the other side of this sheet, an event intended to attract the "family man" who prefers to use his boat for a week end out rather than as a day racer. Further copies of this leaflet can be obtained from J.A.Scarlett, "Lawley", 7Ob,[redacted], Maldon,

SUNDAY,. June 28th, 1964 H.W. 3-35 RAC FROM EAST MERSZA TO MALDON. ENTRY FEE Qd. This event is open to all cruisers. Entrants should anchor in Pyefleet on the Saturday evening. Weather permitting, there can be a party ashore on ast Mersea Stone Point in the evening, so bring beer, sausages, etc., etc. The success of the party depends on YOU. The rmee will start at 10 a.m. on the Sunday, on a line between the wreck light anc the R & ¥ Sph. Buoy at the mouth of Brightlingsea Creek. The course will be;- Start southerly over the above line, Bench. Head left to Starboard, Doctor ee Hilly Pool (Port). Finish on a line between the first (down river) pair of red and black buoys at Herrings Point. Owners must note their own finishing times. I would like to hear from any intending competitor who has a gun, a licence, and some blank cartridges, who would be willing to fire the 10 minute, 5 minute anu. startin; suns, which will be the ONLY signals. There will be no committee hoat at the start. There will be no committee, and the race will be sailed under the International Regulations for the Prevention of Collisions at Sea. There will be no prizes, just (wé hope) a good time for all. intrants should send a note of their finishing times and details ay? of their boat to me by Wednesday, July 1st, together with a stamped addressed envelope for returning results, and a 3d. stamp to help cover costs of printing results. The three stamps involved comprise _ the entire entry fee. (But I would appreciate it if intending competitors could send me details for handicapping beforé® the event.) It will add more interest to the results if owners could send in the times at which they pass fixed points in the river, and when and where they pass (or are passed by) other competitors. Withee odadus WS STuv LT? By "DaAh*ACL Ss" ctowing away all the necessary gear is a problem which all who cruise must solve. Those who erely hurl everything into a large locker or onto the cabin sole are askinz for trouble, either in the form of breakages or soaked clothing. at first glance there would not apuear to be much storage space even on guite large cruisers, but a thorougo exanination of the boat will usually reveal more than enouzh space to stow everything nece«sary for at least a fortnight's cruise. une vital word here is ‘necessary". The novice cruiser is easily detected as he staggers aboard witn two or three large kitbags bulging with stuff that will not be unpacked until he gets nome again. All peovle differ in the 3guantity of clothes they need aboard to keep then happy for a fortnizht, so vou zust learn BX experience how much you really NaaD. Then add one thick, long ~/ “eater and LUN's take any more than that amount. On board clothes are best kept in canvas kit bags or holdalls if the boat has not got special netting racks or lockers. One very fine eleven tonner has the nain saloen partially lined, with Clothes lockers built into the lining behinc the bunks. Drinking vater is tne higgest headache of all to stow, but if the boat was designed and built for cruising the designer should have solved this rroblem for you. If you are converting an old boat, it is best to make every effort to build in a tank as low dower as possible. sometimes this proves impossible, and then probably the best solution is that used by “sovranino”" — a fairly large number of small screw tov containers, either aluminiun or plastic, which can be wedged into odd corners. In a planked hvll they can he stood along the bilge stringers and hela against the side of the hull by shock cord. fuel for c@oking stoves presents a similar croblez, and for many years I _PXiried all liguids in glass bottles - screw tog for fuel and “flip top" (Corona) for potable liquids. Meths was always put in clear glass screw top bottles, and paraffin in coloured bottlss, and tne only occasion on which the systen let us do’n was when we made a very peculiar tasting pot of tea with lemon "Corona" in mistake for water. After: this, only coloured fizzy drinks were carried! Tinned food takes up quite a lot of room, but is very easily stowed down in the bilgss, remembering to paint an identifying symbol on each tin and remove all paper labels so they won't soak off and clog the bilse pumms. .everal types of tins need no labels - sardines, milk, herrings and corned beef can all be identified by their shape.. If four separate coszpartments are available, all soups can go in one, fruit in another, meat, stews, etc., in the third and odds and ends in tne fourth, and ther none of the tins ¢ will really need labelling other than “snecials” like steak and kidney puddings which must be cooked in the tin, With such tins it is advisable t. slip the label into the ship's log book for reference to tne cooking instructions when you cone to use it. Bread, butter, packets of oataeal, rice, etc., need a locker, although they ca” be kept in special tins with tight fitting lids - Natisnal Dried Milk tins are good for this, and given a coat of cellulose paint and neatly labelled they will last several seasons. Tea, sugar, etc., can be carried quite safely in glass jars with screw top lids, fitted into a srecially made rack and held in with a length of shock cord. Polystyrene containers would be better, but there don't seem to be any available with gsod screw tops.

3 —_— > —_— ¥ Cutlery is a pest, and the only solution is a proper tray, stowed either in the botton of a locker or fitted in slides as a little draver. It is not a bad idea to fit one or two small drawers in odd spots such as under the side decks, under the foredeck at the forward end of the cabin, or under a footstep to hold odds and ends like primus prickers, spare torch bulbs, money, car keys etc., etc. Crockery should really have a special locker, but in its absence mugs can be hung from hooks along the beam shelf and plates wedged in behind a bunk mattress. Saucepans and frying pans can stow on or under the s'oves, preferably lashed down, and there should be room behind the stoves for the kettle, watches are best fitted into a little clip ou a handy frame behind the galley. Soap and other washing utensils really need a little watertiszat locker of their own - if you buns them all in a polythene bag it gets a trifle unpleasant in time. Cameras, and binoculars, etc., should have a place of their a own as I said in an earlier article, and if nothing better can be ae” found a length of netting hung under the coachroof or deck beams will keep them tolerably safe. 8 golden rule in stowing gear aboard is try to keep the weight as low as possible, and try to avoid putting too auch in thetends of the ship. A few lengths of shockcord, soe pisces of netting and a couple of shelves and you will be surprised how much can be stowed away neatly and safely in even the smallest of cruisers or cruising dinghies. Rising at 7 a.m. (it seened we had only just gone to bed) we looked outside. There was plenty of wind, but it was due East —- where we wanted to go. Another tack — norsh the knoll, then round again to wards to another buoy we could see in the distance. wWas it the “pitway* Slow nearer, it came ly until we could read the name - N, Buxey - we had gained 100 ft. in the last hour! With the tide now running southwards down the coast we could make little progress against the wind to the Spitway. A look at the watch showed 11 a.m. - almost high tide. After a quick conference we decided to go straight over. Pointing the bows at the crested waves ahead we made our way over. For the first time (I believe), an all-—Marconi crew took part in the Hast Anglian 0.#.A. race from Harwich to Jstend on August Bank Holiday week-end. Arthur Adan, Maggie 4dam, Alan ry and John Littlewood sailed KAZARKA into 6th. place in clasS img , 7th. overall — 4 seconds behind the first non-class III boat. = There were 45 starters. The race started from a line off Harwich Pier in a force 2-3 northerly breeze. Most of the yachts set spinnakers as soon as the starting gun was fired and there was some close jostling at the Guard buoy just after tha start. The dinghy sailors had their rule books at the ready} . The wind faded as the afternoon wore on, and the field bunched again; evidently the leaders ran out of wind first. As the tide strengthened, even ‘the big boys found they could make no progress, and the whole fleet kedged within an area scarcely more than a mile square, just inshore of the Sunk Lightship. Uncomfortable; a nasty jobble left over from stronger winds earlier, and sails banging about unless they were taken off. We were kedged for an hour or so}; a study of the chart revealed many old wrecks on the bottomand we wondered how many of ao us would foul our anchors on then. Our own seemed to be holding remarkably well on a warp only 2% times the depth, which had us worried — but it came up easily when wanted. A class x yacht, anchored on chain, seemed to be indifficulties - we last saw them with 7 men tallying on in an effort to recover theirs. Svimnaker agains. wind North Force 1 -— 2, no relation to the forecast S.i/.-W. force 5 yet. Conditions showed the advantage of having an anti-snarl net set under the spinnaker to keep it from wrapping round the forestay. At the start we saw a few boats had these, but we hadn't; had to have a nifty deck-hand (J.L.) to free the tangles before they were too serious. One or two boats, we found afterwards, were right out of luck; a "Stella" came in to Ostend with her spinnaker still tightly wrapped on the stay, and had to send a man up to take off the forestay. Reaching quickly with the tide past the smoky flares of the Isle of Grain we arrived at Cockham, a pretty wooded. spot where we picked up a mooring just as the meal was ready. Our intentions were to —we to ria old sberernagied a mel moored least, “P we lazed on"eee wd T beatime, Arising at 10 a.m. (plenty early enough for a Sunday morning), we fixed our plan of action for the day. The return passage would be much easier — to push out of the Medway against the last of the flood. We would then have the whole of the ebb to take us up the coast to the Spitway, where we should arrive soon after half tide. This should give us enough water to get through. With luck we would be at Versea by seven. After a quick breakfast, we cast off, the engine helping us on our way back. It was a dull overcast day and the air was thick with the smell of oil from the refineries. The wind had moderated from yesterday to a force three. we moored onto the dockyard wall at Sheerness to replenish our petrol supply. After a brief exchange with a puzzled gatekeeper at the dockyard we were in Sheerness High Street, looking for a garage. I wondered why people were looking a at us, but I suppose two figures in lifejackets, shorts and slippers hardly fitted in with the returning churchgoers. We got our petrol and were soon back on board. No need for the engine now, but we were prepared. Ye tacked over to the barrier fence at Shoebury, Southend pier being distantly visible to port. Then back to the Oaze buoy, lunching on the way. Our speed past the measured mile - six knots, The tacks were broad and by half past two we were back in the Swin, with half the journey_over. The navigator (it wasn't me — I was doing the washing up!) was making a good job of it. "Half an hour on the north tack anv we should reach the S.E. Maplin." And sure enough in half an hour we were turning east by the Maplin buoy. “Quarter of an hour east and we. will be at the °./.Swin." Once more he was right almost to the minute. “Now you can carry ona bit if you like towards that wreck" (pointing to some masts sticking out of the water). Suddenly there was a bump, sending the plate in my hand crashing to the floor — then another bump. Running out to the cockpit I realised we were aground. "“fverybody on the shrouds.” Leaning our weight out we tried to free the keel. Motor revving, sails down, nothing happened. “We'll try to push her round." But to push thirty feet of boat round in four feet of water I found rather difficult. The stark truth dawned cn us — we were aground! There was little we could do. “Half past three, low tide six, we should be off by eight" said Ian. "Charming", I thought. "Are you alright?" "Yes— we'll float on the next tide", and with a wave of the hanctw he was off. The foam drew back to show a yellow bank —- we were ~ only just on the edge. Folk Dancer had gone over as far as she would, making it impossible to lay in bed without rolling out. A great big tramp ship of 10,000 tons or so had hove to in the shipping lane a few hundred yard in front. s Je could imagine the captain studying us through his binoculars — was it us or the salvage money they were after? After a few moments they were off again. We whiled away the time padding around the boat, lookingat the underneath and trying to-make out where-all the holes went. The sand was quite firm, it could have been Clacton rather than the West Barrow Sands. The water went down to about six inches in depth, then started rising again. Slowly we came up and finally we were © eff, after much revving of the’engine and leaning on the shrouds. By now, of course, the tide was against us and the wind had ret oe Nothin else for g it than to motor, We chugged on past the Maplin Spit at a steady 24 knots. Soon it was dark, and fortunatel the wind y began to spring up. .We tacked to port towar’s che “gr. f1.2" of the 5.wW. middle. Then towards the slowly risin and’ falling light of the Barrow Deep lightship. . Next, line the lights. of Clacton up with the "fl.ev.sec." of the sSpitway. Quite fun, this night navigation. You can identify buoys at much greater distances than in the daylight. Through the Spitway to the Wallet buoy, which greeted us not with a flash but a deep toll from-its bell. Then soon we were hour later we moored off St. Osyth point. The time? 3 a.m. The followingday's journey passed without incident, Reaching up the Blackwater froma 10.30 start we arrived back at Maldon at ten to one. . A check on the inventory before handing over showed all complete (apart from two spoons bent in a letter 5), So ended a weekend: cruise. For. just over £5 each we'had been 120 miles in 31 hours, Thus for many hours- lack of. sleep, seasiclmess, and blistered hands, we had paid 10d. a mile to travel at 4 mp.h.. -5- Saturday: 4/NW 4-5 becoming 5-6. sunny, cloudy later. left U845 fully reefed via Raysand Channel to Niver roach. At 5 end of ksnd touched on Buxey side, very narrow channel. soaked clawing off, spray sweeping consta ntly over boat, water sloshing in cockpit but once in Crouch not so bad. anchored at Barling Ness until Hw. Unable to get under Potton Bridge so went back a acetal Creek. Stayed there the night as forecast still Hs we 5 Sunday: Forec:.st mod.NVv. Slept till noon. 1400 sculled up Narrow Cuts took mast down for Havengore Bridge. Accompanied by another sailing boat, destination Leigh. Inspected Broomway on foot whilst waiting for tide. soon deep enough 1730 (2 hours before HW) Full sail to Medway. Had to beat up last stretch against tide in fallirg wind to Stangate Creek. Arrived 2130 almost dark. solid cloud all day. Monday: Left 0030 for Sandwich. Nw 3-4 gradually decreasing to calm. Spinaker run to SE Margate buoy. Baking hot. With 5 miles to North foreland and 1 hour tide left engine resorted to. At N,. Foreland wind fromS so motored in choppy seas against tide to Ramsgate. 8 miles in 5 hours. Very unpleasant. Arrived af < Ramsgate 2030, glad to be in. «Anchored in outer harbour and hit el object in night at low water. Tuesday: Hot again. Refilled water cans as stock was four weeks old. Bought newspapers and bread. Waited for tide till noon then sailed over to Pegwell Bay, glorious weather. Started up river Stour for Sandwich but ebb too fierce for much progress so ‘went back to entrance which is sandy and spent afternoon exploring wrecks etc. on sands, which ‘are extensive. vffensive smell led to carcase of porpoise. stench and flies too repulsive to allow close examination. Our macabre speculation on whether slit on “underbody from stem to stern was due to bursting or knife wound ‘remained unanswered. Eric suggested chidlings for teal Started on flood up river for sandwich but were soon convinced we would find'no suitable anchorage so went back to Stone Cut which provided a little drying bay of glutinous mid. It was a fisherman's nightmare, shoals of dabs breaking surface, mullet cruising around on the surface and fish jumping everywhere but the man fishing on the bank had not a bite. - Wednesday: Thick fog early on. Sunny and warm later. Had to wait till afloat at 0830. Motored against flood (no wind) to entrance. set sail in light 5H. Favourable tide to N. Foreland then six hours of ebb to fight. wWe could not work the tides any better because it is necessary to leave sandwich three hours either side of Hi to get out of Pegwell Bay then until Hw the tide is 8S bound and two hours after HW although the Channel tide has changed to north bound, the Thames is ebbing tor the next six. However, we were fortunate to ave a SE Force 3-4 which, with the spinaker (three parachute panels) made Aurora chase along like an ocean racer. It waspainfully slow for the first three hours passing Margate but after that the: tice wasn't so fierc e and we hit the Black Rocks off keculvers with a resounding thud at about four knots. The centreplate and rudder seemed to take the force as the rocks were a little under the surface and no disturbance of the water visible from windward. From then on we took the navigation of the N. Kent coast more seriously and were thankful to have the help. of the tide to beat into the E.Swalas e the wind had veered to Sv. It seemed hard that, having sailed six miles up the &, Swale with about two-hours of favourable tide, the tide should again be adverse flooding into the w.Swale. Although we. wanted to reach Queenborough that night ready for sailing to Canvey next day, the wind had fallen light and it was getting dark so we dropped the hook at Elmuley Ferry in desolate surroundings next to two wrecks. /6.

= * 4 4 a Thursday: Although J600 was planned starting time Aurora was not afloat until J830. Again a pleasant sail down the W.swale in light SV wind against tide. slag heaps of wood chips on © shore for paper mills. Sunny. Took Kingsferry Bridge under jib and oar with about threefoot clearance of our 13'6" mast at half tide. it was half hour to By the time we arrived at the Medway high water - too late for Canvey so sailed up to Stangate Creek. Went right up to Funton Creek as tide started to fall and were lucky not to ground as an hour later when the tide had dropped it became full of mud islands and wrecks. attempted to circumnavigate another small island only to find it joined by a causeway to the mainland, However this made a pleasant swimming pool and Eric did his seal act. Anchored in Stangate Creek for the rest of the afternoon then back to sharfleet Creek for the night as it was blowing SW F.4 and barometer had dropped 10 MBs in 24 hours. Friday: Left 0715 SW 3-4 Sunny. Arrived Holehaven 102), Pleasant run through creeks to Benfleet. With the depth of water available only shall draft ow boats can make this trip which is reminiscent of the Norfolk Broads. Il believe this section was called the Venetian Canal in the early part of this century. Lowered mast to pass under bridge but it was nearly high water and bridge too low so it was opened. Had breakfast/lunch just below bridge then continued down Benfleet Creek to night anchorage. Benfleet,. and Leigh crowded with shallow draft yachts. Watched the boats drying on the complicated network ofmudbanks in warm sunshine. Listened to domestic quarrel on next boat with relish? Saturday: Eric shifted anchor to deeper water 0500 and came back to bed. 0510 he decidedto scull down the creek to anchor in deeper water. .0525 he decidedto hoist the sail and carry on to anchor off the Maplins. The U@45 forecast, listened to off Southend Pier -— SW 5-6. actual wind had freshzned to F.4 so were glad we had left. Arrived at the measured mile posts soon after low water so paddled on warm firm sand pushing Aurora up a shallow inlet in the sands to clear the breaking waves. Tidied up bedding etc. below and did a bit more pushing as we found this pastime very pleasant. Anchored and had breakfast by which time another mile | or so of sand was covered so sailed on towards Havengore until the water became too shallow. Thus, anchoring and sculling alternatively, we arrived at the Broomway two hours before high water as the wind increased. The bridge opened so the mast stayed in position and off we sailed to anchor again in Yokesfleet Creek. The 1340 fors— cast: winds variable later sw 2-4. How they change their mind 3 The rest of he day passed lazily reading, writing and eating. Sunday: 0530 it was my turn.to get under way while Eric snored on. By O800 we were at the southern end of the Raysand Channel at low water springs. Soon the plate touched and eventually we carried on with rudder and plate right up on areach through the smooth water. There was a muddy wake but this was only the hull passing so close to the bottom (in about 10" water) that the top layer of mud was churned up. Another boat coming the other way could not find the channel and we left him, hull down, still trying to push on to the Buxey Sands. It was ideal sailing weather —- warm sunshine F.3 SW and we entered Bradwell Creek about 1130. SAILING CLUB GOSSIP COLUMN The first news received this month was, the engagement cf Juliette Lindars and Rick Jones. Later this summer the Lindars family are moving from Chelmsford but it looks as though one will soon be back. Congratulations Juliette and Rick. The participants of the Norfolk Broads holiday seemed to enjoy themselves and were back in force for the Enterprise Open Meeting although the Triple K Cup and prizes went to other clubs.

- Do BrimPartridge did some rapid developing and printing and showed us some of his photographs of the Broads at the Open Meeting Party. ixcellent food was provided and the raffle prizes were won by Mrs, Derek Baker from Stone Sailing Club and by our Commodore Terry Hallan. Open Day was not as well supported as last year although it was a superbly sunny day. ‘Ye had a laugh when a motor boat towing a water skier capsized. HORPOLG BRVADS 1905 A great li.5.C. reunion took place at Horning Ferry one Saturday afternoon after eight Blakes boats had been hired and one privately owned Felicity had been towed to Jroxham. Evening meals were cooked and eaten at varying speeds and later, in the pub, the singing started. There wasn't much wind on Whit Sunday. We crept along the river to Ranworth Broad for lunch and moved even more slowly out of the Broad to Thurne for the night.. The first bridge was encountered at Potter Heigham the following day. Only minor incidents were reported. The sail up to Hickling “a Broad was quite pleasant. Due either to shallow water, a deep draught boat or bad luck, David and Eleanor ran havd aground and were helped off by another crowd of sailors. The majority of the fleet were havoily drinking tea in the middle of the Broad, supposedly moored with a aud weight. Mooring that night was quite complicated due to the shallow water inshore and we used a motor cruise as a bridge. During the singsong in the Pleasure Boat, Sarah and Peter Jennings, who sail a tiny Catamaran and who were camping at Ludham Bridge, Joined the party. The following morning it rained - bucketfulls. we didn't start sailing and/or motoring until after lunch. The starters said - up to Horsey Mere, then on to Potter Heigham and Thurne. ‘hen the tail-encdersreached Horsey there was no sign of the leaders but a nice bit of wind got up and we had a good sail. After an hour or more of tacking up a narrow river it's really nice to get out to —_ some open water. s The leaders got to Thurne and the tail enders got to Potter Heigham which proved slightly awkward for Linda whose clothes and bed were at Potter while she was at Thurne. All ships cooks went on strike that evening and had meals out. The Potter party awoke to John Hutchings dulcet tones. He'd spent the night in huts and under bridges. His birthday (18th) breakfast was provided by Leonie, Dave (Young) and John (Witter) and by midmorning he was united with his parents at-Thume. A gentle breeze took us to South ‘alsham Broad where several boats took part in a hilariéus balloon chase on the Inner Broad. fhe spectators on land looked very shocked at yachts being treated like dinghies. | , The mouth of the River Ant was cheotic. The cruisers had seemed to be under control the day before but on Wednesday it was awful. Admittedly a couple of dozen yachts, several of which had no auxiliary or outboard engines or motors, were trying to . tack up one of the narrowest of rivers but everybody sorted them- selves out and passed through Ludham Bridge for the night.

-3- John's birthday was duly celebrated at the local hostelry. wore tackin, on Thursday worning took us to Barton Broad for some more open water sailings. sarah end reter were spotted afloat at Barton Turf anc we met them again in the evening et Ludham Bridge. John viitter eideé by Dave anc Leonie anc. others wrote ‘'On the Norfolk Broads'' to the tune of uartermasters Stores. une of a group of young people from Hoddesdon provided the piano accompani- ment :- There was Con, Con, with her apron on There was Jack, Jack, motoring at the bacx There was inike, mike (Sissons) quenting up the dyke, There were boats, boats, nine tiarconi Boats etc. Brian Partridge remembered the chorus from previous years. Young Sue Palmer's head poked through open windows on several even- ings wnile she learned the words of ''Ch Sir Jasper''. what should have been a run out of the Ant and a reach to tiorning and i.croxham turned oyt to be a beat nearly all the way - the wind shifted through 180° overnight. Don Freeman and Joyce had spent the night at Stalham instead of Ludham bridge and did very well to beat to Horning in one day. The final night was spent in various boatyards and some people travelled nome on #ridey for the “snterprise open meeting the following day. :- Damage and repairs Kkeplacement parts for John .itter's outboard. A new halyard for Norman Palmer. A bowsprit found Jack Bigden's porthole and one of the dinghy oars snapped. iuike Sisson had the mistortune to acguire a.crack in his hull after a collision. Sten Allerton grabbed at the boom crutches and fell in the river at Horning; Julian and Dave Young both got Hall wet. For twenty adults and seven children this wasn't bad. Organising stopping places for nine unmatched boats seemed 4 little tricky but vas managed most evenings, isoliday to be repeated? Probably! Signed, fleanor C, sldividge.

Galloper L.V. confirmed wind 5-4 at 05.00 ship's time. ‘se posted a letter advising our agents of our departure (they would be respons- ible for paying import dutics}, topped up the petrol tank, made up two flasks of coffee for use on the voyage, and locked through into the outer harbour, This time we did mean to go to Felixstowe! The tide, almost of spring range, was due to flow Si from 09.00 hrs. and should give us a good start. Actually it was 10.09 as we passed IJit 1 outer buoy, under mainsail and Genoa, doing 44 knots by log in a calm sea, wind SSE force 2-3. ‘Weather fair, visibility moderate. A course of 253° was draw on the chart (No. 1408) as the basic rhumb line for the Outer Gabbard L.V., distant 924 miles. At h imots (say) we should get there at 09.00 on Friday. Up to 16.30 the wind stayed nearly South, usually about force 23; we were steering on or slightly to windward of the rnumb line and doing 34 to 4 mots. The log was satisfactory but needed two oper- ators which obviously would not be possible at all times; however, it did allow us to "calibrate our guesses'! fairly well.

Alan went below ebout 16.00 for shut-eye, leaving me on watch. In IJmuiden we had carelessly over-filled the tank and a little of the spillage had remained on deck; we hadn't bothered unduly as there were no smokers aboard, but evidently it had seeped through at one of the stanchion fixings. The amount was probably very small and all possible ventilation was done but the smell persisted and Maggies was rather ‘knocked out'' by it. From 16.30 the wind faded; after a few breaths from different directions, we were completely becalmed at 17.40, with the sails slat- ting as we rolled. I fitted the boom guy to steady things, but the s@ils continued to flap noisily. Not until 19.10 was there any detec- table wind; then it came up very light from dead aft. ‘ith the Genoa go0osewinged (on the spinnaker pole) we were making 15 ikmots. Alan relieved me at 20,10 hrs., dinner being taken at the change- over, The wind slowly improved, but also veered a littlc, forcing us to the right of our course, though not enough to justify a gybe. At 23.50 I came up again; we were creaming along at 6 knots. ‘ie gybed at the changeover and’I put the wind on the quarter. No sooner had Alan gone below than the wind increased from force 5 to a good 6, At any rate he didn't Bhve time to undress! We changed over from Genoa to working jib, bul even then the strength was out of the wind.. By 00.40 we were becalmed again, and rolling like the town drunk. This calm did not last so long as the previous one, but the direc- tion dia not settle down until 02.00; for an hour or more I was setting the spinnaker pole and boom guy for one gybe, only to have to gybe them over for a 50 degree change of wind. At lest it settled down in the S& to give 35 knots on a broad reach. i should have been very cross if Alan had come up to relieve me as soon as we got a decent wind: In fact, he came at 04.10, by which time f had had some reward for my labours. .€@ held the SE breeze until 06.00, when it started to veer slowly and increased a littie: by 10.00 we wors nearly close-hauled on the sort tack and KAZARKA would steer herself with the tiller in the rack. Alan worked up a D.R. vosition for_10.00 hrs. ; 184 miles snort of ‘the Outer Gabbard and a little to the right of the rhumb line. I brought up the 7/# and took bearings on Outer Gabbard, Noord =,& Hinder end Smith's snoll while Alan plotted them. Meanwhile KAZARKA looked after herself very capably, doing 5 knots almost close-hauled in force 4-5. The position lines from Noord Hinder and Smith's snoll did not help much; they intersected at rather an acute angle, and the beacons were 30 and 40 miles away. However, the run of the bearings on Outer Gabbard showed that we left it to port by about 5 miles. At 12.55, by way of corroboration, we picked up a 6-fathom bank with the echo-sounder, evidently the northern continuation of Inner Gabbard; this, crossed with an Outer Gabbard radio bearing, was a fix that could be relied upon. Coming hard on the wind, we started: the long tramp down to the South Shipwash, The Sunk L.V. radio beacon, nominally only 5 miles range, gave good signals at least 15 miles away and was a useful check, Although we could bring it no nearer than 15° on our port bow, the tide was going wsv until 16.00 hrs. and would help to keep us off the Shipwash, As a precaution, we kept the echo-sounder going. At 15.30 a careful search for seamarks showed the «. Shipwash buoy about 2 miles away to the NW (across the shoal;. At 16.00 we took a fix on the Si and 5y-Shipwash buoys. EDITORIAL Having returned from holiday in a flush of enthusiasm and with a new mast on Torch 162 (iforal:- never tow a boat with the mast up, even for 100 yards, someone's sure to throw a power cable in the way) I now embark on the August issue of NLVIGANS. One of my friends(?) remarked recently that he expected the next issue I produced would be the bumper Christmas number, so I had to do something’? To turn to a more serious topic you will note that the front page of the issue is devoted to a FIRE warning. The risk of fire, particularly on the road. to the:Club is a very real thing so please read, mark, learn and inwardly digest the warning. The anonymous contributor who writes the Gossip Column is unfortunately not with as this month so the column has been written by several anonymous writers among them Rosaleen Farthing. In conclusion, thanks for the contributions I found on my desk when I returned from holiday. J.G.e Reeve EDITOR. ww SATLING CLUB GOSSIP COLUiN frthur and Maggie fdam have been to Holland again with K-ZARKi, covering Texel to Breskens in a 3-week cruise. They had a roughish passage home, entering Brightlingsea at the same time as Fleetwind masts were breaking off Stansgate. ‘e may hear the highlights of this cruise but they are not trying to repossess the AMCGU Trophy. How about hearing from you other cruising types? John Perrin has received a very pleasant and chatty letter from Rosaleen Farthing from Vancour B.C. extracts from which are given below. -‘'This is a beautiful place by anyone's standards, but to a sailor it is something approaching paradise. There are beautiful sailing conditions both in Vancouver and in the straits: between here and Vancouver Island. Vancouver is built eround an inlet and there is a large bay to provide plenty of sheltered . dinghy sailing. ‘Ve have “i-jned Kitsilano Yacht Club which is one of the five clubs in the city, and is the one most concerned with dinghy sailing. ws We decided not to-buy a boat this year but to spend at least some of our weekends exploring the countryside. “Je have spent several long weekends travelling hundreds of miles, but the country is so vast that we haven't seen very much. There is a limit on just how far you can explore. as there are very few roads. ‘’e have bought ourselves a small tent and we make good use of the campsites that can be found everywhere. They have a very high standard at these sites and they always provide free firewood! We have managed to do some sailing though. Both of us have been crewing in Enterprises from time to time. We have managed to combine sailing and exploring as last weekend we drove 300 miles so that Dave could crew in the Yestern Canada Championships. Although most of the sailing is on the coast - it is erovwing quite rapidly on the interior lakes too and people are keen enough to trail their boats 300 or so miles just for a regatta. Oddly enough, organised small boat sailing is relatively recent here. The larger boats, such as Lightnings and Stars and a few Dragons, have been around for quite a while, but Flying Dutchman, Enterprises and 505's are only just building up large enough fleets to have go0d racing. The most popular boats around are small, 8", 'Sabots'. They are used for just about everything from novice instruction to keen Winter racing known as Frostbiting.

-3- regarded them es 'bathtubs' at first, but are slowly being convinced bsoe that there must be more in them than meets the eye. We came here with the fond idea that in this land of timber boats “sould be chean. This has not vroved to be the case as a new Enterprise here would cost us $1000 or over Three hundred pounds! They do not make 5/16" plywood locally and it has to be imported from Japan! There are one or two English built boats around and the difference in finish is tremendous. There are quite a fei; English people to, but there is also a good mixture of Canadians, Australians, New Zealanders and other Europeans. Kost of the Flying Dutchman in the club ere sailed by Dutchman. Sailing people seem t> be the same the world over though. iost of our friends are in the sailing club and we have been to quite a few good parties! The liquor lews here are rather primitive in some respects and even for a seni-official party »ne has to supply one's own drink. It seems kind of strange to walk along the street in a cocktail dress carrying a case of beer: Of course we have found lots of things that are different here - some we like and some we don't. On the whole we are very happy and like Vancouver very much. ‘Ye are both enjoying our jobs and are managing to save rather more money that we could have hoped to back in England. I don't know how long that happy situation will last as there are so many lovely things to spend money on: “Ye hope to have o boat next year and we want to learn to ski this Vinter so - there goes quite a proportion of our savings’ Yell - I hope I get round to posting this letter. I started writing it once before but did not get too far! Pleese give our regards to everyone in the club.' Incidentally congratulationsto John and :.is wife on producing an 82 lb. boy! a k= We launched early Monday morning and. were Jucky enough t have an almost calm day, A quick decision had-t>s be made which waz to go. As there was no wind and only two hours of south going tide left we decided to cross ‘the Firth of Lorne and head northwards up the Sound of lull, We were not going to pass the Lism re Light and its adjacent rocks without help from the engine so downed sail. Once past the dangsrous arca the engine was sto:;ped and the resulting silence was intense, Sudden heavy breathing made me jump - a couple of vorpoises were gambling about + mile awey making n: sound as they surfaced except this. snorting. The seagulis on the rocky shore about two miles away s unded like occasional human voices and the sun shone from a cloudless sky. ‘fe ghosted on hearing more breathing but unable t- see the porpoises because of the distance, The wind increased graduaily to force 2 so enabling us t* avoid the rocks and shoals and by mid after- noon it was apparent that an anchorage must so:n be fund before the tide turned, It was obvious from the charts and Clyde Cruising Club's Sailing Directions that anchorages had tc-be chosen with greater care than on the East Coast due to steeply shelving rocky shores, poor holding ground and greater incidence of strong winds, Loch Aline half way along the Sound of Mull on the mainland shore proved a delightful quiet and picturesque anchorage with wooded shores and the usual castle, The anchor with warp stretching down to it could be seen in two fathoms the water was so‘clear. The wind here though, as in most lochs, was fickle blowing from first one way then the other, A visit to the small store next morning proved that provisions were much more expensive in the Highlands, The shopkeeper's ‘‘ihat beautiful weather we are having" was an echo of the words of every other Scot to whom we had spoken, which sounded ominously as though it was usually grey and cold in this part of the world. The morning passed pleasantly in warm sunshine running the rest of the distance up the Sound of Mull in force 5 gradually decreasing, ith plenty of fair tide left, a course up Loch Sunart, which is over 20 miles long, was planned, The wind suddenly changed to Ni Force 4 and we went careering to.ards what appeared to be a solid rocky shore, The opening showed up between island and headland and the rocks were smooth and rouned worn by the pounding of the waves over centuries, Once in the Loch the wind was again fickle with no appreciable tide because of the great depth and towards late afternoon the mist began rolling in from the west blotting out first the mountain tops then moving lower, Fortunately there was a handy bay on the north shore which we reached as the mist becane —_ a solid drizzle. An immaculate motor fisherman yacht also came in for the night, which is very short at this time of the year in Scotland and never becomes really dark, Next morning it was still drizzling with poor visibility so we did not hurry to start and went ashore to provision and have a look at the village of Salen, Just a few cottages straggling round the . head of the bay but an excellent store and the ubiquitous sheep nibbling the grass, Returning to Aurora we found three workmen admiring her who asked. the inevitable questions, "Have you an engine?" and "Is it reliable?" We were asked this several times and thought at the tine that the Scots yachtsmen were too engine conscious but upon reflection an engine is essential in these waters unless you have a strong pair of arms and oars as it is not easy to anchor and wait for a tide because of the great depths. The afternoon passed tacking back down Loch Sunart in thick mist against a fresh headwind, Although the sailing directions said Loch Teacndais entrance should onl: be attempted under pover because of the shallow devious route necessitated by rock stremm channel we entered under sculling sar and popped safely into the loch at great speed because of the current. This loch looked desolate with just a couple of houses on the shore and the low cloud and drizzle did not

help to show it off. we hastily rigged the awning after anchoring near the head of the loch and watched the off lorry Lump its way over the track which served as a road, Next morning we sculled out the other entrance (which was even less recommended in the Sailing Directions) and saw a colony of seals on the seaweed covered rocks, ‘The adults all slid into the water leaving the pups undefended and presently a ring of faces circled the boat, They soon started playing once we were past. A short sail in bright sunshine brought us to ithe next smell loch - na Droma Buidhe, A glorious peaceful anchorage almost landlocked with wooded hills one side and racky island the other. Having climbed the nearest hill and feasted our eyes on the magnificent scene >f islands, mountains and sea, we were tempted to bathe im the trystal clear water showing a bottom of white sand, ‘iading out waist deep through the seaweed forests and half a dczen strokes back was all the temperature of th water allowed, It was breath-takingly cold. = b= We are now reaching the end of our third year at Stansgate- three years in which the Club has made some fivefold growth, This rapid increase in membership of all types, in boats, and equipment, has created a demand for an organisation capable of administering and operating the facilities required by some 600 members rather than 420, Inevitably the rapid growth has resulted in the building in of stresses which have been evident at times in the creaks and groans of the present administrative system, This year too has had another and especial significance to the Marconi Sailing Club, It is the last year of our present lease, and it has been a year of waiting for the result of the Marina Scheme appeal. This last is now happily resolved, The Ministry of Housing and Local Government has allowed the appeal, and Outline Planning permission has been granted to Mr. Sparrow, Nevertheless this does not signal the end of negotiations; on the contrary the next year is of even more importance in that respect, if we are to achieve in the long term a stable permanent Club. All these things and many more besides have been very much in the minds of your i"lag Officers and Committee during the past year, The result has been a number of propositions that it is intended the Committee shall put to the Annual General Meeting, In order to publicise these and to give members time to chew them over it was decided to devote a whole issue of 'Navigans' to these questions, Terence Hallam POLICY = STATEMENT by the Committee This special edition of 'Navigans' has been produced so that various decisions taken in Committee may be brought to the notice of Club members well in advance of the A,G.M, One of the decisions requires suspension of a part of certain Club rule (rule &) and rather than just making a bald proposal on the A,G.M, Agenda Notice it was felt that the reasoning should be laid before the whole Club, and support asked for, in advance, As is well known the Club lease expires this Winter and the terms of renewal have been in doubt for the last 12 months, However in the last few days it has been announced that the proposed Marina at Ramsay Marsh, near Steeple, has been sanctioned. ‘Subsequent discussions between the Commodore and Mr, Sparrow have resulted in the extension of our lease for a further year on the same terms, During this time the long term future of the Club site will be decided, This will, inevitably, be a time of many negotiations which we, the Committee, are confident will result in a stable and strong Club with a permanent Club House and improved facilities, In order that these negotiations may be carried out by the same people who have been handling Club affairs durins; the period the Club has been at Stansgate, the Committee are proposing that the part of Rule 88 which relates to the length of the term of office of Plag Officers be suspended for one year, This will permit Terry Hallam to be in a position to stand for re-election to the Office of Commodore at the A,G.M, The Committee, who earnestly believe that this procedure is in the best interests of the Club, will be proposing this suspension and backing it with proposals for Flag Officers and other Committee posts - details will be found elsewhere in this edition, This three year period of office for a Flag Officer was chosen as a reasonable time, bearing in mind the period of time these offices are held in other clubs, and is not bound by the Constitution of the Club in any way: hence your Committee feel that they are not in any waybreaking with the traditions of the Club by asking for your support for these proposals.
