-5- THE THIRD RACING CLASS (ORCLASSES?) by the Sailing Secretar At a recent Sailing Committee Meeting the question of the Club supporting more pure racing classes was discussed, This resulted in the proposals which will be detailed later, To put you all in the picture let me give you some of the background which led to the final decisions, I started the ball rolling by sending to all members of the Sailing Commit’.ee a document laying.out my thoughts on this subject which I hoped could be used ior a basis for discussion, These ideas and suggestions stemmed from comments I had heard from various people from time to time and a feeling which I think had been present in some parts of the Club for a while, that the handicap class did not © give the sort of racing most people wanted, My own feelings were that it was not one more racing class that we needed but several, together with the facility to include even more, if sufficient support and demand were forthcoming, ‘ith this in mind I went through the boat register and listed all the boats we had which were either potential racing classes as far as the Club was concerned, or of which we might have. sufficient to run races, It was this list which was finally whittled down some two hours later to a manageabl size e’ when the following course of action was agreed, Points series races would be run for the following racing classes in addition to the existing classes, G. f, 4 he Hornet Snipe Points races would also be run for any other class which Could raise sufficient Support, SE Se ee Se Gee i Torches and Mirrors would also have their owm races as there are a reasonable number of each in the Club but they would not be encouraged as racing classes, A handicap series would still be run for other classes and all the above mentioned classes would be eligible if at any one time there were not sufficient Boats of one class to run a class race, Various Committee members had enquired from certain Club members, whom it was known were considering changing classes what they wanted to change to and whether they would be prepared to support new classes which were not exactly the ones of their choice, In general their comments were favourable, In the above choice some classes may be noticeably absent but it was felt by your Sailing Committee that there would either be insufficient sup ort or that they overlapped too much with existing classes, However, provision has been made to overcome this if the Committee are shovm to be mistaken, It was felt that this problem should be tackled at this time of the year when people were beginning to lay plans for next year and were ccnsidering changing boats, It was also important to do it before it was toe late for those who have made tentative plans to reconsider, The adoption of these classes also gives the potential new boat owner and newcomer to racing a chance to choose the boat most suitable to his needs, It will also make it easier for Club members to advise people seeking guidance about trying boats, as the choice for class racing is now wider. In making these suggestions we have not lost sight of the aims of the Club one of which is to provide sailing for all, but at the same time we are trying to improve the opportunities and standards for those that want to take advantage of the racing facilities offered, The organisation of the classes will be considered in detail later by the Committee but tentative suggestions are that these new classes still be represented by th. handicap class representative on the Sailing Committee but have their own class captain responsible to the handicap class rep. until such time as a class grows sufficiently large to require its ow representative, John Witter.

on YORK OR | FAY? by the Commodore The thought of 600 members all descending upon Stansgate one fine day in the surmer, demanding their rights in the way of lebensraum in the Clubhouse, not to mention toilets, rescue launch, car park, bar and other facilities we supposedly offer them, is indeed sufficient to cause the stoutest ana crustiest Flag Officer to blench, At the present time these services and all others are provided by courtesy of those members, few alas in number, who are prepared to work, Indeed they not only work, but in addition pay, subsidising the Club by expending money on petrol for special journeys, sometimes several times a week, in order that the facilities shall be maintained, albeit in a rather attenuated way. These devoted and long suffering members are about the same in number, indeed to a large extent in person as well, as were operating in the old days when our membership was under 120, It is true that at times we call for a working party, and we are seldom disappointed with the response, Those however are for very special occasions, It is the day to day, and week to week work which is carried out so regularly by the faithful band, It is patently obvious that in spite of the continued efforts of these chaps there are times when the facilities break down, and giving as they do all of their available time there is no spare effort to meet these occasions, . —_ For the whole of the existence of the Club, some fourteen years, the bas’ subscription has remained at ten shillings, notwithstanding the considerable ~TM” rise in the cost of living and therefore running costs, During this period the subscription rates of other clubs have risen two, three, and in some cases, over fourfold. The time, I am sure, has now come for a realistic look at the way we run things, and the services we offer, The choice in simple terms is the selection of the better of two alternatives: to work or to pay. In other: words are we prepared to continue as a "do it yourself" club but with very mich more "do" by the individual member, or are we to employ the services of a full or part time servant, The former choice would entail a drastic change to the way of Club life on the part of all members, lfore real time spent in maintaining and improving the facilities; many more helpers spending more man-hours working at Stansgate, Greater participation in the essential Conmittee work, Less time in which to enjoy ourselves sailing our boats, putting in everyones' interest the Club first and our own entertainment second, ed Choosing the second of the two alternatives would hit where it tends w to hurt most, in our pockets, The subscription would rise, perhaps to. double, treble, or even more, the present sum, It would also necessitate changes in the administration, although these are inevitable anyway. The operation of a club of our size is a business and requires the application of proper management principles, It would also be necessary to modify our © present forms of membership and to streamline the financial side of the club, The choice is ours, Shall it be the first or the second alternative, Work or pay. . Your Flag Officers and Committee have debated these at length, and decided to propose to the A,G.M, that the choice shall be the second one: to pay. They therefore as detailed elsewhere in this journal propose that the next Committee be instructed to take such steps as may be necessary

Jack Reeve ANNUAL GENERAL MESTING 1965 C: Herewith report on the Annual General Meeting as promised last month. The meeting, was held at the M.A.S.C., Beehive Lane on Wednesday 2th November at 7.30 p.m. The chair was taken pro tem by the Commodore. The attendance was a record one of 120 Full and Associate members. The minutes of the previous A.G.ii. and matters arising were dealt With fairly rapidly and were followed by the Secretary's, Treasurer's and Sailing Secretary's Reports. These were all passed unanimously. In bts report the Commodore included a run-down on the events lead- ing up to the Committee's proposals. The first was a proposal to employ a paid steward for the Club. The Club was expanding rapidly but also the work load on the comparitively few willing helpers was increasing. The proposed stewards' duties would be the cleaning and maintenance of the Club premises, site and care of the Qlub boats, i.e. rescue launches and Brazil. In reply to question from the floor it was stated that one person only would be responsible for the supervision of the steward. The steward would not be expected to run the galley. It was pointed out that to cater for this extra expenditure, changes would have to be made to the existing Subscription rates and fees. A vote was‘then taken on the proposal to employ a steward, 69 members voted for it, none against, with four abstentions. The next proposal, that of suspending parts of rule 8(e), was then put before the meeting. The proposal covered that part ofthe rule concerned with the three year term of Flag Officers and its suspersion for one year.

MAMGU TROPHY PRIZE WINNING LOG ‘by C. S. Molyneux Part I This an account of a single handed cruise made in the yacht ‘Samuel Pepys' this summer, by the owner. Details are taken from the log kept during the cruise. | The cruise started I suppose in the 'Black Buoy’ at Wivenhoe, as I was ready to cast off well before High Water. Winds were from the S.W., about Force 6, being, I hoped, t-e tail end of the gales which had been sweeping up the Channel for the previous couple of weeks. At high water, about 22.15 hours, I cast off, and set ‘sail - full mainsail and intermediate jib, for E. Mersea where I intended to spend the night. All went well, and by midnight I was drinking a cup of cocoa before turning in. The ocean racing I have participated in this year has removed completely two of my previous aversions - cocoa and porridge. I am now a believer that there is nothing more welcome during the dogwatches than this combination. w EB. Mersea toward Ramsgate The next morning turned out bright and sunny, and completely na? windless. I got under way at 06.16, hoping to make the Spitway before high water and carry the last of the flood up the Swin, However, progress during the first half hour was barely 50 yerds, and I spent a leisurely time watching the intricate and lengthy operations of rae the schooner Valeda under way. At 07.15 a breeze developed from ¥.S.W., and'as I was starting t> make progress I streamed the log. 09. 08 log 8.4. Wallet Spitway buoy, wind*.8.W. force 5, visibility about’3 miles - making fine progress under largest genoa and full mainsail. - I left the boat sailing herself with the tiller held by the peg- . board - as used by the Leigh cockles, and cooked my second breakfast. Had to beat up Swin, but made . Barrow Buoy at 12.35 hours, 44 hours after high water, but leaving plenty of ebb to clear N. Foreland. Lay course for the Shivering Sands Towers, and prepared a picnic lunch of luncheon meat sandwiches, bananas, am a bottle of beer. YY After passing the N.E. Tongue, at 14.30 hours, the wind died away. Brought the log in as progress was to slow for it to record. Dial showed 32 miles. 45.45 - Queens’ buoy about half mile ahead. Wind freshened from the South, and had to beat down from N. Foreland to Ramsgate, entered Remsgate Harbour at 17.45 hours. By 16.15 I was tied up alongside a Baltic schooner, all stowed and made Bristol fashion. The wind had increased to Force 7, and there was a heavy swell entering the harbour. In spite of this I slept soundly through the night - fatigued after a splendid ea sailing. Ramsgate toward Calais I awoke early next morning, and with great difficulty prepared breakfast whilst the boat heaved and tossed on the swell coming in round the moles into the outer harbour. I chatted with the owners of the schooner whilst awaiting the right state of tide for leaving. They had bought the vessel out of service on the Baltic 'for a song', and were taking her up to Gravesend to convert into a hotel ship for use on the Mediterranean - all 100 tons of her.

'e The wind was blowing about Force 6 W. by S. when I set sail ‘under intermediate jib and with about 5 rolls in the mainsail. Negotiation of the harbour entrance went off successfully, with a strong flood running, aml faicly heavy seas. Having cleared the Queen Buoy I started beating up the Downs. The wind seemed to have increased, and offshore heavy seas were running making progress extremely hard work, so muchso that the log is rather vague at this stage as to times and positions. After clearing S. Yoreland, and losing itslee the seas became just ridiculous in size -- or so I thoughtat the time. The ship for'ard of the mast was permanently under water, and spray from water breaking up for'ard was being thrown.clear. of the after pulpit. At this stage I started thinking of putting back to Ramsgate. I gave the bilge a pump and found sho had made an unprecedented amount of water. I hove to and made an inspection to find the leak. Two seams up for'ward were "ie badly. Those same seams had forced ny retirement from the R. ORC. West Mersea - Ostend race, which was sailed under gale sonditéone. They had been re-caulked and stopped since then, and the fact that they were so I decided leaking again suggested that the trouble might be serious, to put back to Ramsgate. On returning to ths cockpit I saw two spent rocket cases floating near the boat. This was the last straw. The run back to Ramsgate was covered in what seemed nearly zero tine. The boat was almost planing. _ Off the harbour entrance I hove-to and took in the log line, and then entered harbour, Once inside I “xopped the mainsail, and sailed up. the harbour about 18 inches from the wall, under foresail, until she touched. I quickly lowered the Poruant. put out fenders, lines ashore, also a2 masthead line, and canted her into the sea wall. Because of the swell that was running she was poundin; rather heavily, so I opened a seacock ard flooded the bilges while the tide went away from her. Once the tide head “ropped sufficiently for her tonot pound with empty bilges I pumped them dry, and'then went ashore to acquire materials for all possiblerepairs that might be necessary. I had decided to batten the seams. Although this might slow the boat down a bit, at least it should keep the water out even if she worked a bit. Being Sunday, the only place open was a chandless near the inner harbour Messrs. R. H.--------. The assistant, in name alone, was not really in full command of the situattion, and offered -me as battens sturdy pieces of i." x 3 English oak! Rejecting his offer I ‘decided to use a spare sail batten. Having fitted out with stopping, fibreglass, tacks, screws etc. I returned to the boat. There I met up with another yachtsman, holidaying in a bilge keel cruiser from the‘Grvech, who was bored to tears waiting for the right weather to 'get across’. in carrying out the repairs. I am indebted to him for his help In the three hours around low water we managed to find and rectify the trouble - so well in fact that those temporary repairs have lasted to the end of the season with no leakage. | We celebrated with a meal and drinks ashore: in the evening, when we also learnt from the Harbour Officials that they had been récording a steady Force 7 in the harbour for most of the day. Of the three boats that had left the harbour that day, two had come back, and the third was brought back by the lifeboat. (To be continued)

Bigden MAMGU_ TROPHY PRIZE WIKNING LOG , by C.S. Molyneux Part II Ramsgate towards Belgium Next morning the wind was still strong, Force 6 - 7, and from the S.W. Whilst walking along the harbour wall meditating on possibilities for the day's sailing I saw the schooner VALEDA and chatted with the owner. He had come round to Kamsgate on the same day as I had but being later had not saved his tide. so there was insufficient water for him to enter harbour. He had anchored in the fiowns and came into Lamsgate on the Sunday. I decided to sail for Belgium, using trade wind rig, and make for A2eebrugge, Blankenberg or Ostend, whichever was the nearer, on fetching the Belgias coast. For trade wind rig I carry two large genoas, each about 300 sq. ft., set either side of the boat, shackled to rings about 18 ins.

~3- apart on the deck, and not hanked to the forestay. This leaves a gap for airflow betweenthem thus enabling them to fill and act properly. The sheets are led aft and made fast to the tiller. The extra weight of wind in one sail as she veers off course causes the sheet to move the tiller and control the course. Normally, twin booms are used but I prefer in these waters, when on a closed run, not to boom them out. If ona course thet is not a dead run then the windward jib is, of course, boomed out. Preparing for this I laid out the two senoas on deck and led their sheets through the appropriate »locks and fairleads to the tiller. i used just the intermediate jib and no mainsail for leaving harbour. Thi turned out to be a "touch-and-go"incident. At the harbour entrance, cli..r- ing the moles, I was close-hauled. There was a heavy sea which tended wo” stop her dead with each wave and there was also a strong cross tide. intering the gap between the moles at the up-tide end I cleared t!- other mole by about 3 ft. before I was in clear water. This made me re.: le never again to try and leave harbour in similar circumstances under foresali alone. I waited until I cleared the North Goodwin Buoy before hoisting trade wind rig, by which time the wind had gone S& I was too far off a run to use the rig, so I had to hoist the mainsail in any case ana then stow the twin genoas. The log had been streamed at the Queen Buoy at 1130 hrs., reading 38.4 miles. The North Goodwin was passed at 12235 hre.; Sd log 42.6. At this stage the seas coming round South Foreland were felt and it was extremely bumoy. The log again becomes vague at this stage. At about 1800 hrs. the wind, which had been increasing slowly but steadily, was up to about gale force. Nothing could be seen for spray and the boat was "surf-riding" cach wave for as long as 30 seconds at a = ime before dropping down into a trough and trying to head to. Steering her on the course I'd set (100 deg.) became a physical impossibility so I scandalised the mainsail and ran before the wind until it eased off. T.: "surfing" was really exhilarating and would have been really enjoyable had it not been for the worry of preventing her from "broaching-to" eve: - time she dropped down into a trough. During the hour 1800 to 1900 the log recorded an increase of 10.4d. miles but at 1900 hrs. the line »sarted and the spinner was lost. at 200) hrs. the Wind eased off and the seas reduced in size - a fact that worried me as it "smelt" of shoaling water. I trimmed the boat to sail herself on a course roughly due E. and went below to determine ny posit: on a with the radio direction-finder. I did not believe the first position obtained but when I repeated it to within£ mile, I realised that perhaj ; I really was on Thornton Ridge. I plotted course for Blankenberg, prep: ‘ed some food and then went back to the cockpit. Sure enough, about « mile aWay on the port bow was the black spar buoy that I expected to sce - ti ‘s confirmed my radio fix. As I closed the Belgian coast the seas lessened and the Wind scem i to as well. At 2100 hrs., just as darkness was closing in, I sightea Blankenberg and Zeebrugge. The Admiralty Pilot gave directions for ent: :- - ing the harbour but I wasn't too happy about the description of the stax board mole remains - the mole having been destroyed during the war. The entrance is very deceptive and it looks as though one whould leave the one remaining to starboard in order to enter. id learnt later that many boats are wrecked here as this mistake is regularly mace. I hove to upstream of the entrance and partly foie-reached and partly drifted past the entrance at a distance of about half a cable. This gave ne a chance to examine it through the glasses, I decided the Admiralty were right, paid off and sailed in.

| The time was just 2200 hrs. The quiet in the harbour was so weélcouc after the constant noise of wind, weves and spray. In fact the lack of noise Was such that it was almost as if some ethereal body had come con and slipped a couple of plugs in my eers. I tied up alongside the quay and was grected by a couple of local fisherman, one of whom was English and had returned to Belgiun after the war’. In spite of being tired I found the energy to sliv ashore for a bowl of "potage", French bread, a beer and a packet of "St. Michel!” before turning in. Next morning the English fisherman returned and we talked for quite a while. He took me up to Zeebrugge in his car to try am obtain a replacement log-spinner. The price was so exhorbitant that I decided to manage Without. He then took me home for a tea of fresh shrimps, home- made "confiture" and Belgian cream cheeses, I was also given lessons in coffce-making,. Blankenberg towards Vlessingen I spent a very pleasant three days in Blankenberg, the weather being genuine old-fashioned holiday weather - the sun shone the whole time: I later learnt that Blankenberg is not recommended as a port to visit in the book used by many yachtsmen as a cruising bible - the Cruising Association Handbook. Their information is very much out of date in that they state that the harbour dries out ani the toOWn is expensive. In actual fact I had more than 6 ft. of water at low water and I found that living was far cheaper than Ostend. The harbour entrance should be negotiated with care end note taken of the state of the tide as there is a bar with 4 ft. 6 ins. of water over it at L.W.S. I left Blankenberg at 1500 hrs., carrying the ebb up the coast. The wind was N.E. Force 4, visibility about 5 niles with the sun shining pleasantly through the haze. I made a long board about 4 miles out to sea, in order to carry one tack right up to the mouth of thi West Schelde. Zeebrugge was abeam at 1600 hours. A gaff cutter, flying the ied Ensign, could be seen ahead following a parallel course close inshore. Passed same off Knocks. The coastline from Knocke right round to Breskens is completely desolate, the thin line of coast being broken only be the wreck of the Dutch radio ship VERONICA which was driven eshore last winter during bad weather. On entering the Scheldé estuary big shipping was encountered. It was rather e hair-raising expericnce sharing a narrovi channel with three or four 20,000 tonners. Vlessingen is fairly easy to enter, but yachts lock through into the inland waterways in order to moor up in the Yacht Haven. This is e tricky business single-hended with no auxiliary engine. The Yacht Club extends hospitality to all visiting craft and the charges are very reasonable. By 1900 hrs. I was tied up Mediterranean fashion - stern to quay - alongside the AILSA, the gaff cutte: mentioned earlier, which had come over from Pin Mill. The one disadvantage of Vlessingen is the distance of the Yacht Club from the town. However, the tivo mile walk was very much relieved by the jovial company and the Chinese meal at the end. We were rather intrigued to find that Dutch Chinese food is very different from English Chinese food. Because of the lamente»dly short duration of industrial leave I did not have the time I would have liked to cruise around Holland. Thus I spent a couple of days travelling around by train, visiting Amsterdan, Rotterdam, Der Hague, liordrecht an Middleburgh - a very quaint, typically Dutch town. (to he continue?...)

SNIPE: SNIPE: "FOR ANYONE WHC IS INTERESTED IN INTENNATIONAL 2-MAN RACING, THE SNIPE IS EASILY THE BZST CLASS TO OBTAIN TOP COMPETION' These are the words of Paul Elvstrom, the greatest Dinghy Sailor ever (4 Olympic Gold Medals and 6 World Championships). When considering the purchase of a Snipe Sailing dinghy (as every perceptive and intelligent dinghy sailor will surely do at some time or other), the following questions will probably be askec. 1. What type of boat is the Snipe? The Snipe is the largest one-design class with world-wide distribu- tion. Snipe recing is particularly active in Europe, North America and South America. The Snipe is a sleek yet soundly constructed boat with a L.0.A. of 15ft. 7 in. and a beam of 5ft. It has an eMficient Bermuda rig of 110 sq. ft. The jib is large, giving the crew added importance. ‘Modern Snipes are constructed in 3" marine ply or fibreglass, have rolled decks and many have a self draining cockpit. The Snipe is not a flimsy boat having the nautical lines of a flat dish designed to slam across the Water when the conditions of wind and waves are suitable, but a real little yacht with a high performance. The Snipe has neither a clumsy sliding seat or awkward trapeze to pamper to unfit stomach muscles but is a fast stable boat which calls for fitness to sail at top speed and yet is undemanding physicaily when Sailing for pieasure. The Snipe has a high boom which eliminates diving face down in the bilge to avoid decapitation by to boom on going about or gybing. The Snipe has an adjustable wire or nylon horse which carries a freely sliding pulley which elininates easing the mainsheet when going about. The Snipe is strictly a one-design class which makes it stand out way and above uany other so-called one-design classes where minor changes, turning, sails, etc., contribute so significantly to disparities in boat speed, all of which tends to minimise racing skill anc tactics. Ze How does the Snipe perform uncer various conditions of wind, sea and point of sailing? The Snipe has a fair turn of speed ani with e Portsmouth number of 97 is rated faster than the Ynterprise. The performance t0 windward is particularly satisfying; being conparable to almost all other dinghy and better than most. The Snipe, with its good stability performs well under all condi- tions of sea. It is particularly free from yawing motion in rough water.

ee Due to the high boom and adjustable rope horse, the downhaul is easily adjusted (even while racing) to give optimm sail shape to suit the weight of crew and wind strength. A spectacular demonstration of the performance of the Snipe in adverse conditions occured when 2 Cubans escaped from Havana to the U.S.A. by sailing a Snipe across the treachorous 100 mile stretch of water between Cuba and Floride in winds of 20 - 25 knots! The trip was accomplished in 16 hours. This feat amazed yachting experts in Florida Who are well acquainted with the rough, turbulent waters and strong currents of the Gulf Stream. Many a 30-footer has struggled to get across the same dangerous course in 30 hours. 36 How much does a Snipe cost, new or second hand? A new fibreglass Snipe complete with Terylene sails, aluminium nast and boon would cost approx. £230. 4. good second-hand boat would probably cost between £100 and £150 complete with boat cover and launching trolley or road trailer.: (sec % Boats for Sale). ng Le Will the Snipe hold its value? There are two main factors which affect the value of a sailing dinghy, apart from the soundness of construction of the boat: firstly, the activity ana rate of expansion within the class and secondly, the strictness with which the one-design principle is adherred to. These points can be answered together. The Snipe Class association (S.C.I.R.A.) is a very active international organisation which publishes a monthly bulletin to keep Snipe sailors abreast of events throughout the world. §.C.1.#.A. strictly enforees the one-design principle to protect the class and ensure that older boats may compete on equal terms with new boats. The qualities of the Snipe and remarkable class o. ganisation is responsible for the explosive growth of the class - currently an average increase of 2 boats per day with the sail numbers now over the 16,000 mark. 5. Is the Snipe suiteble for the Blackwater estuary and in particular, Sad the Marconi Sailing Club? As you probably know, the club is introducing Snipe racing within the Handicap Class this season and if the numbers are sufficient there will be separate Bmipe races. Currently, 5 members own Snipes, two of which Will certainly be actively racing and several other members have shown interest in purchasing a Snipe. There are many open meetings each year on the Blackwater which include Snipe class racing (8 this year) and with 4 active Snipe fleets on the river there is no lack of competition. Also, the South-East Snipe Championships will be held at Stansgate for the second year running. Details of these events and other national and international events will be posted on the Club notice board and published in next month's issue of Navigans. If anyone is interested in further details about the Snipe will they contact the writer at the Mechanical Engineering Laboratories, 'irittle, Extension 301. K. H. Littlebury.

MARCONI SAILING CLUB. A GUIDE FOR. RACE OFFICERS le The Race Officer and his assistant are responsible for ensuring that the racing arrangements are properly carried out. They should be ready to consult the 0.0.D. ora Sailing Committee member when necessary. They should be familiar with the R.Y.A. racing rules and the Club sailing instructions. The Race Officer should be present one hour before the start of the race, The jobs to be done before the start of the race can conveniently be shared as follows:— RACE OFFICER, 1, Choose course, in consultation with the 0.0.D. or a Sailing committee member, 2. Mark up the sailing board accordingly, ensuring that there are sufficient entry sheets and sailing instructions. Spares are in the Race Officer's box-file, 3. Establish radio link with the rescue launch, and instruct them as to laying special marks etc, 4. Arrange collection of entry sheets 10 mins before the start. 5. Collect visitor's entry fees. N.B, Ghoose the course in regard to wind strength, tide etc., and display the course letter, number of rounds and"direction of start" arrow, if possible, half an hour before the start of the race, or at least before the 10 minute signal, otherwise the start must be postponed as provided in the R.Y.A. Rules, If there is a large entry, or at low water, the lengthened starting line may have to be used, in which case the letter 'L! must be displayed after the course boards, Courses above Mundon Point may not be usable at low water, ASSISTANT RACE OFFICER (Time Keeping). 1. Start the clock (as near as possible B.B.C. time), 2. Prepare the flags and sound signals (cannon for open races, hooter for closed), 3. Display the course sign at the race box. Signals. The normal racing signals are explained in the R.Y.A. Racing Rules 4-8, The Club use class flags, not shapes (See Rule 4.4. (A) (1), and varies Rule 8 as provided in the Sailing Instructions, Wen several races are starting at intervals of 5 or 10 minutes the start signal for one race will be the 5 or 10 minutes signal for the succeeding race, Starting the Races, From the 10 minute signal, until the last class has started, the R.O. should station himself on the line, and watch for any breach of sailing rules. He will make the sound signals at the times indicated by the timekeeper, Both guns should

aoa be loaded ready for a recall or a misfire. He will have radio link with the sescue launch which may, if the entry is large, be stationed at the opposite end of the line to help spot false starters. The timekeeper will break out and lower the flags in the correct sequence, and in order to synchronise the start, the sound signals and flags, he should count dow the last minute before each signal, e.g. "one minute to Enterprise start and Fleetwind warning......30 seconds....e..15 seconds.....10 seconds to Enterprise start and Fleetwind warning......+.efive, four, three, two, one NOW", 6 Recalls. If any identified boats are over the line at the start, the R.O.should shout "RECALL" and sound the other gun. The timekeepeyShould put the class flag at the dip. Competitors over the line are themselves responsible for coming back and starting to the satisfaction of the R.0., but the R.O. should use the loud hailer to attract the atteniion of boats that have started too soon. When premature starters have recrossed the line and started properly, their class flag is lowered, Those who do not do so shall be disqualified, and should be informed of this as soon as they come in after the race. It. despite the recall: signal some boats continue to sail the course, it is enough for the R.O. to keep their class flag flying for three minutes, at the dip after which it can be lowered. Should there by a number of unidentified premature starters or an error in starting procedure, the R.O. should make a general recall and the lst substitute flag should be hoisted. The R.O. will reload the first cannon and sound two guns, The first- substitute should be flow for three minutes, after which it should be lowered. The class flag should be left flying if the false start is to be the ten minutes warning signal for the resrtarted race. 7 Finishing the Race. As each boat approaches the finishing line, the R.O, will call out stand by for (call number).....coming up (when the boat is 2 or 3 seconds away...e.c. "NOW" (when the most forward part of the boat touches the line between the R.O,. and the distance mark). As he says "NOW" he should sound the hooter. He should list the order of finishing, but not necessarily the time of each boat. The R.O,should check the working of the handicaps and post the results on the notice board. (If the R.O. works the results out himself, he should get someone else to check them). 8 Protests. Molyneux PRIZE WINNING LOG Part IV a Dunkerque towards Calais Next morning a bright and early breakfast ready for an early start back to civilisation. I cast off at 09.40 hours under reefed main and intermediate jib and cleared the har»our at 09.55 hours. The wind was still W by S and blowing about Force 6, visibility 3 or 4 miles. I was making good progress and passed the Dunkirk D. C. buoy at 12.00 hours. The Dutch boats had left after me and I could see them astern, all motoring, one carrying storm canvas and all making heavy weather, pitching violently. Approaching Calais T am always wary of the bar which runs down to Cap Blane Wez and only cross it just before high water. It not being high water I kept well out to sea down to Cap Blanc Nez and then came up the coast inside the sandban . I anchored in Calais harbour at 16.15 hours. The Dutchman were already in, having gone straight across the bar using their echo-sounders. In the inner harbour I saw the TANCOSCA with some friends of mine aboard, so we spent the eveing ashore sampling the night-life. “lost of the frgdends 1 had made there the previous years hac gone back to Paris so the evening was relatively quiet. JI turned in early as I was feeling rather knocked up. I could feel a dose of 'flu or sonething coming on, so I decided that if I was going to be ill it may as well be in England and Would sail home the next day, Friday.

Calais towards Brightlingsea Next morning 7 was up and about by 07.00 hours as I wanted to do some shopping before leaving. Apert from bread and crassants I could not buy anything - French shops just don't open that early. I sailed eat 09.00 hours under full mainsail and large genoa, with a wind » by S Force 6 to 7 and visibility less than 1 wile. From the harbour I steered 290 deg. to cross the bar (being nearly high water), which I cleared by 09.25 hours, then lay 335 deg. for the Bast Goodwin light vessel. On a broad reach with this amount of canvas and wind the boat was almost planing. I passed the Bast Goodwin at 11.55 hours and the North Goodwin at 13.00 hours. Clear of the Goodwinds I hove to and changed down 4 foresail to intsrmediate jib.. At 14.30 hours, past the N.E. Spit buoy, I hove to agein ami took in three rolls in the mainsail as the going was getting just'a bit too heavy. This, of course, was.a signal for the wind to stop, which it did completely and I was left wallowing in heavy seas. For the next 13 hours there was no consistent wind, just occasional vague breezes from various vague directions. At 16.00 hours a really strong wind came up from the $.%. I reckoned at the tine that it was nearly gale force and 1 later learned that during the afternoon and even- ing they were recording a steady Force 7 in Brightlingsea harbour. This Wind continued with me right into Brightlingsea. The log becoues very vague again, in fact the only entry being a scrawled "very hard going". ily course was through the S. sdinburgh Chennel, eeross Knock John and down the Barrow Deep. I had extreme difficulty with navigation at this stage - buoys were not where they should be. I found out later, that whilst I was away, the sdinburgh Channels, Barrow and Spitway had all been re-buoyed. I was feeling quite ill at this stage, being tired and with a ‘flu fever coming on. I was also very sore and bruised from being knocked about. In the Barrow, on a dead run, I accidentally gybed all standing and the port runner parted. I didn't feel up to replecing it there and then and it wes all I could do to belay the ends to prevent flogging Hoping that the standing backstay would hold the mast up. After clearing the N.E. end of the Barrow Sands + could see no sign of the Spitway buoys. The black W. Cunfleet buoy was 2 miles N.E. of me. As I couldn't face et this stage a thrash to windward to look for the Spitway buoys, being just on high water / laid » course for Clacton and crossed the Gunfleet Sands. I had plenty of water across at this point and was pleased to reach the smoother waters of the Yallet. The beat to windward up the Wallet.against the tide was relatively easy compared with the previous four hours. I anchored in Brightlingsea, in the dark, at 22.15 hours, absolutely fatigued. It took ie over an hour to straighten out on deci, I then cooked a meal and fell asleep without eating it.

Last Leg I had hoisted the Q-flag before turning in so the Customs would see it in daylight and come and clear me. They woke me at 05.30 hours; I was still fully clothed from where I had fallen asleep the night before - ny dinner still there, cold and untouched. My only comment about the next hour is that only a Customs Officer can fall out of bed at 5.30 in the morning and start drinking neat run! I weighed anchor at 07.00 hours and by 08.00 hours I wes safely tied up in my berth at Wivenhoe’, happy after an excellent, if tiring, holiday and feeling extremely pleased with my little ship. This saved quite a number of disqualifications but a few people just don't seem to learn. Other reasons for the disqualifications were not returning i far enough after being over the line at the start and not declaring (signing out) after each race. John Barnard as Beach Officer organised the car and dinghy parking, the visitors being in a field loaned by Hr. Sparrow. Actually in the Clubhouse a number of people helped inthe awkward task of setting helmsuen to sign in and out and in preparing results sheets. Jack Bigden was in charge of the prizes. There were breakazes and capsizes of course but the majority of boats finished in one piece and the final race. result deteriined the over- all placing in several classes. A lot of hard work was required apart from the basic sailing organi- sation. The dinghy park had to be tidied up and the grass cut to make roon for the extra boats and cars. iiuch gravel was moved from the hard to the muddier parts of the dinghy and car park. The Clubhouse was cleaned daily. ~ The resave boats were maintained and manned. The galley and bar staffs were overworked, BUT IT WAS A GRAND WEEKEND? Ee C athe

Jack Reeve eee ee ee et a eS CADET WEEK It has been decided by the Main Committee, with the approval of Mr. Sparrow, to run a camp under canvas for the Cadets during the Cadet week at Stansgate, i.e. from 10 a.m. Monday 8th August until 6 p.m. Friday 12th ‘wy August. There will be, in fact, two separate camps, one for the girls and another for the lads. These: will be at‘all tines under the charge of a member of the Main Committee. The whole camp will be run on Navy lines, the Cadets being divided into messes of eight to ten youngsters. These messes will be self-catering but will be able to draw bulk cooked basic food from a central: galley staffed by mums. Any trimmings Will be sorted out among the members of the individual MESSES« An Executive, consisting of Senior Cadets and junior members of the Club, is being formed to run the show and the intention is to provide an active "adventure" type of experience for boys and girls between the ages of 11 and 18, based on sailing. The Main Committee has voted a sum of money to help things aLOng and this Will be largely devoted to rewards to encourage self-reliance. A charge of 30/~- per head will be made to cover the cost of the basic food supplied.

At present plans are a little vague and any suggestions or ideas will be welcome. We would also be grateful fbr the loan of Calor gas equipment, to cook the bulk food, if any is available. Tom Gaskell Cadet Officer VISITING THE PIRATES by Fred Partlett PART I At 0910 hours on Thursday 7th July my son Mick and myself set off downriver in our Wayfarer sailing dinghy "Sobraon" for a short cruise, short because tie had to be back on the Saturday. We took the boat cover to sleep under, two air beds, sleeping beg, blankets, a change of clothing, fres water food, Primus stove, a coastal chart and radio. The latter was intended for weather forecasts but it spent most of its time churning out the "pops". A light and variable westerly wind was blowing and the sky overcast as we headed towards Bradwell. There were two other craft, cruisers, under way, one rounded St. Peters Flats and the other headed up the Colne. — We made for the wreck buoy on ‘the Cocum Hills and from there kept a straight course towards no. 2 buoy at the entrance to the Colne. I estimated our speed as 5 knots. Soon after leaving Colne Point behind Mick went ashore for supplies (chocolate) before proceeding along the coast about half mile offshore. We-had caught the last of the ebb tide out of the Blackwater am the tidal stream chart showed slack water close inshore at all states of the tide. It was a pleasant run with little to do except avoid sailing by the lee in the varying Wind. At1250 hours we rounded Clacton Pier and our estimated speed from no. 2 buoy was about 34 knots. At 1400 hours, with Frinton ahead, we could make out the radio ships on the horizon and Wwe made toward them. The wind, although still light seemed more variable than ever, and with our burgee swinging through 180 deg. we were caught with two accidental gybes. Deciding that discretion was the better part of valour we returned nearer the shore and continued toward Frinton. 4500 hours with walton Pier abeam and allowing for the dog-leg seawards, I estimated our speed since Clacton Pier as 24 knots. In spite of giving what I considered to be generaus clearance the Fisherman on Walton Pier greeted our passing with shouts of "Get the **** out of it" and "Clear off, you *¥***", Our reply was much shorter and more to the point. Relating this incident since to a regular pier fisherman he informed me that he would expect all boats to keep at least $ mile away. We scanned the beaches beyond the pier for possible landing places. Only two spots seemed obviously to be uncovered at high tide am we selected one for our attempt at a “soft landing". The beach was rather steep and the waves were breaking, apoarently quite fiercely, on the sand. I realised that our stern might be swamped as we went in but we would be into wind the risk appeared to be small. Some water did come over as I took the mainsail down. Mick, of course, was holdings the bow and holidaymakers came forward to pukl us clear of the surf and up to high vater mark. The time was 1515 hours and high tide was at 150 hours. One of our helpers introduced himself as Brian and offered to put a kettle on, in fact his wife made us a cup of tea which we downed after bailing the boat ana stowing the sails.

It was our original intention to sail further up the. coast and after a council of war, more war than council, “Mick and I agreed to stay overnight. ve would float "Sabraon" off on-the early morning tide and after finishing our sleep, head further up the coast. In preparation for this we eased the boat farther down the beach. After a meal of cold chicken, potatoes and peas we walked up to the cliffs above the Naze before turning in. The sound of maroons going off and the sight of flares fired from the Coastguard Station indicated that the lifeboat was being called out. In the half Light we could see a cruiser flashing SOS. The sea was.calm and the boat was anchored so we assumed engine failure to be the cause. The lifeboat put out after about 15 minutes and the. cruiser was :towed to Harwich, We returned to the beach and having already put the boom up and the cover on we inflated our air beds and.got down for the night. Mick slept soundiy but I cat-napped in case We missed the tide and at 0330 hours Friday morning we were outside in swimming trunks ready to launch omemore. Dawn was just breaking but it was still dark on the beach and the waves as they broke on the shore seemed enormous. ‘e were, I think, both relieved when we. realised that the tide ha: turnedwell short and we were not going for an wy early morning aap We lost no time getting back to bed and finishing our sleep. - - ; (To be continued) SAILING NOTES Attached to this copy of. "Navigans" will be found a list of members boats giving their allocated dinghy park spare or mooring. If you have a boat at Stansgate (or want. to bring one) which is not included on the list please get in touch With me as soon as possible. Also attached is a summary sheet for the points series races which have taken place so far this year. As you will see only three classes have raced this year, namely Enterprise, Hornets and G. P.'s. ‘Races are also scheduled for Fleetwinds, Snipes, Cadets and Torches and Mirrors as well ow Handicap points races which are open to all classes with the exception of | Enterprises, Hornets and G.P.'s. There are also Spoon and Scratch races for dinghies and cruisers which are mainly for enjoyment and as a good introduc— tion to racing. There seems to be a feeling that racing is all cut and thrust sailing but this: is iia’? far from true. Racing in a small way is an excellent method of improving one's ability to handle a boat. Only by using the yardstick of someone else sailing under the same conditions will you find out. why your boat does not go as well as an identical one. Nine times out of ten it will turn out not to be the boat but the person at the "blunt end" who is at fault. The very full and detailed programme produced this year was the result of a lot of very hard work by your Sailing Comsittee in an endeavour to give ample. opportunity for all-types of conpetitive and informative sailing. This was based on a belief that this was what the Club wanted. So far the Comuittee are very disappointed with the results of their endavours as there have been more races cancelled through lack of support than have actually taken place. It is therefore probable that unless more enthusiasm is shown for these events between now and the end of the season very few extra races vill be scheduled for next year.

Possibly it is not realised that for each extra race a Race Officer and rescue launch facilities have to be provided. Therefore it is unfair to ask people to make a special journey to Stansgate to undertake these duties and then find their services unwanted. To most of you this will read like a good old moan, which it is, but if these activities are not wanted there is not point in arranging then. It appears that the majority of the Club do not want these events, even though there are more boats in the dinghy perk than ever before. New Dates for yourCalender. MSC-DOC-1966-08-club-discipline.pdf: Marconi Sailing Club, Beehive Lane, Chelmsford. Memo To: All Members of the Marconi Sailing Club. 1st August, 1966. From: The Officers & Committee of the iarconi Sailing Club. Subject:- Club Discipline. At the General Meeting of the executive Conmittee held this evening opinions were voiced from all quarters in relation to the general lack of discipline, disregard of Bye-laws, instructions and carelessness in relation to Club property exercised by Members throughout the Club. Although in the majority of cases the Committee are sure that such careless disregard and indiscipline is unintentional there are cases of blantant wrong-doing and disregard. Members are reminded that the Club exists‘for their pleasure and enjoy- ment providing they comply with the rules made on their behalf by the Committee who in turn are the servants of the Club freely elected ina democratic manner. We also owe allegiance to our parent body - The hiarconi Athletic & Social Club and to the rules and conditions applicable to seme. Other interests from whom we must accept conditions are the l.aldon Borough Council and the Essex Rivers Board, but possibly the most important of all is the obedience we must give to the conditions laid down by our Landlord which have been freely accepted by the Club in relation to the use of and access to our Club Site. These conditions must be upheld as abuse by any member could endanger out existence as a Club at Stansgate. It was also felt that your Officers and Conmmittec had of recent months become lax to some degree in upholding and imposing the conditions of Club Rules and Bye-laws and it was decided that if this were so such laxity would cease forthwith. It was agreed that all future offenders would be warned and corrected and should misbehaviour continue they would be disciplined in accordance with the rules of both the lharconi Sailing Club and the Marconi Athletic & Social Club. The Duty Officers log shall be used to record all incidents of misbehaviour or other offences against the Club and will be inspected at each General Meeting of the Sailing Club when the Club Secretary will be instructed to take the action decided upon arising from the reported incident. Among the more commonly broken regulations which will be watched in future are the following. a) All guest's names to be entered in the visitors book. One member may only introduce two guests at any one time, the same guests may only be introduced a reasonable number of times per year and must always be accompanied by the member. b) Many non-members are habitually using the Ulub site and will be turned away. Members are strongly advised to carry membership cards when visiting Stansgate to avoid embarrassment. c) The use to which Club boats, launching trollies and trailers are put. a) The use by unauthorised persons of the record player and radio gear. e) The use of No. 1 rescue launch and gesr from Rescue locker by: urn:uthorised persons is forbidden. f) It is not permitted to climb the seawall or to reach the beach by climbing through fence (this is a River Board regulation to combat erosion). SOCIAL SECTION LAYING-UP SUPPER 1966, 21st October, Marconi Dining Roon, Waterhouse Lane. The Laying-Up Supper started well. John got all the cups laid out, then time for a quick sherry before we were called to our tables at 7.40.pm - only 10 minutes after the appointed hour (an improvement of 30 minutes on some years). it was obvious “Jithin a few minutes that all was not well. The number of people present exceeded the number of suppers that had been prepared and several people did not partake of the prescribed menu. John Barnard has a good voice for an M.C and after a toast to the Queen and permission to smoke, he bade Terry Hallam introduce and toast the guests. ilir.F.N.Sutherland , Chairman of the tiarconi Group of Companies and President of the M.A.S.C. (information for Associate Members), replied for the guests. After some thoughts on why boats are called "she" - unpredictable, often in stays and involved with sheets, he kindly presented us with a modél Arab Dhow. Dr.£. Eastwood, the MSC President, thanked Mr. Sutherland for the gift and for his toast to the Club. i 'Flu prevented Mrs. Sutherland from being at the dinner and presenting ‘awards. Queenie Hallam took over and “earned" her supper. The prize winners are listed separately in Navigans. Bouquets were presented to Mrs. Sutherland, Mrs Eastwood and lirs Hallam. Maurice Hinton's band struck up and gave us a good assortment of modern ballroom, jive, twist and cha-cha tunes. Jack Bigden was “M.C for this part of the evening and entertained us with a scooter race, Four contestants, each on a child's scooter rounded a course marked with "squezy"' bottles. lhe best Cruiser pair had a scoot-off with the best Dinghy pair and they were followed by the ladies, I was rather busy, being fed canned: beer from.my "2nd Ladies Cup" small stainless steel ladle by Bernard Tillotson, my crew, and can't remember who won. The draw was made during a break for-coffee and biscuits after which dancing continued, I laughed so much at Jack's second game, that I suffered from hiccups for a couple of hours. The participants of "Pass the Sailbag" dressed in the articles of clothing that they withdrew from the bag and paraded voluntarily (or otherwise e.g. Dr.Woods). They certainly deserved their prizes and applause. I thoroughly enjoyed the evening but I've heard that some people were dissatisfied with the arrangements, Don't just grumble amongst yourselves - send your constructive comments and criticisms to the Committee, or Navigans so that next years Laying-Up Supper can be enjoyed by everyone, | . HS, RenasnaeTM s Report 1966 Ladies and Gentlemen, This year has been a full one, if a little disappointing in some ways. I had hoped to be able to report to you at this A.G.M. that a longer term lease had been, secured, This has not been possible however, Due to events - over which we as a Club have no control, e.g. the financial climate, leading — as it has to restrictions in private capital works, the l:arina scheme, to which our future is in many ways tied, had not gone as far as we had hoped. “ie have indsed continued our cordial elabionshis with our landlord, kr.Sparrow, the result of which has been an extension until the end of next year and it is to be hoped that before our lease runs out the situation will be such that we shall be successful in negotiating for a longer term. — On the Social ‘Side we have been partially successful in spite of the quite strenuous efforts on the part of the Social Secretary, Our highlight was undoubtedly. the Barbecue, although in spite of the enormous crowd attending we still did not make such a large profit. The same applied to the other social events, good attendance but financially only just about breaking even, On this subject of Social events I would at this time point out that the Social Secretary and his small. band of helpers received little support when it cameto the work and they are to be congratulated for the success they did achieve. as far as the Sailing is concerned perhaps the most noticeable feature was the lack of interest of the Cadets. I cannot stress too highly the importance of a good strong and enthusiastic Cadet section and I trust that next year we shall see a change in attitude and performance, The rest of the sailing was patchy. '‘e had some first class open events; the -hitsun Regatta was undoubtedly a success, but Club support for racing in spite of. the removal of entry fees, is still rather poor. The high spot was probably the enthusiasm of our new class, the Hornets. The cruisers look as though they mizht be coaleseing into a class, and we hope that next season will see some enthusiastic cruiser racing, On the diduheuse Side you will all have noticed a change in the’ condition of the Club this year. The employment of a Steward/Handyman although beset by problems at first, has proved to be a first class thing. Kir.Underdown is without doubt a most valuable acquisition. l.embers TI am sure, are not aware of “the amount of real hard work he does, at times when the ordinary member is not around to see, For example, he was at . the Club at three o'clock in the morning last week when a gale was blowing to make sure all was well. This is not an isolated case either. a HORNET MAINSHEET The total number of Hornets now in the club has risen to 12 with several members interested in ourchasing a Hornet for next season. I think we should have even better racing and competition than we had this year. Next season the Club is running its first Hornet National open meeting which will be a two day meeting and the retiring Commodore, Terry Hallam, has kindly agreed to put up a Trophy which will be comp “cd for each year. Also next season, as an experiment, we are running 2 separate Hornet points system with the Stone 5.C. Hornets. This will not be run on a team basis but as individual racing. Three races at Stansgate and three at Stone, so there will be plenty of competition to be met. DATES: 1967 World Championships. HOLLAND 20th - 25th August. National Championships WHITSTABLE 24 - 28th July. Iii RETROSPECT € It was about this time last year that a need was felt in the Club for a dinghy-which was fast and competitive, as enthusiasm and numbers were beginning to wane in the Fleetwinds and some extent the iinterprises(especially towards racing), The Hornet was chosen for several reasons, being fast, with a large sail area (spinnaker included) and 2a 16 ft planing bull. It has superb bouyancy and self-draining cockpit. If turned completely upside down it can easily be righted and there will literally be no water in the boat at all due to the rolled side decks (shades of bailing out Enterprises with a bucketi). The Hornet is said to be one of the most comfortable-boats for the. crew having a 5 ft sliding seat there is no need for backaching hanging out techniques, ~It has been said of a Hornet crew if he/she is not doing anything all the time there is something wrong. ‘Working the spinnaker is a technique on its own which the crew must soom master. In barely a year the Committee were proved correct in their anticipation that a Hornet class was required in the Club and a Fleet of 12 in the first year has surprised many of the Hornet Clubs locally. The R.Y.A. National Hornet Federation are about to issue the Club with Hornet Fleet status recognition. ; There is plenty of outside competition for Hornets which are raced at Maylandsea, Clacton, Stone, Thorpe Bay, Burnham, Saltcote, Drightlingsea and many other places further afield. — Secondhand boats can be purchased from 290 up to the cost of a new one which is £330 ex-sals,. mi Te VISITING THE PIRATES On July 7th, Fred Partlett with his son Mick, sailed from Stansgate in their Wayfarer dinghy "SOBRAON" to Frinton. We left them askeep in their boat which they had pulled up the beach above the high water mark...ccovcsee Friday morning was still overcast with a fresh wind. Brian and his family came down to the beach surprised that we wore still high and dry, After breakfast of sausage, bacon and egg we discussed the Situation and Brian thought he could persuade fellow holidaymakers to assist in putting Sobraon into the water, In fact nobody needed persuading, there was a rush of willing helpers, of all ages. We used the warp from our spare anchor (borrowed from Mike Sissons! "Valkyrie") and slung this under the boat abeam the mast and with two lifting at this point, two on the handles and four or five either side aft Sobraon (350 lbs) was lifted bodily and taken in three stages down the beach and into the water which by now was just past low tide. liick and I thought there was little to be gained going further up the coast at this late hour (11.00 hrs) so after giving Brian a sail up to The Naze and back we set course for Radio London. The wind was still variable, force 1-2 and we had an uneventful sail coming up to Radio London slightly upstream. We ran against the tide in order to round her, a supply ship had just gone alongside flying the Netherlands flag. Mick recognised one disc jockcy who had visited Danbury, and after taking some photographs we headed south west to "Caroline", Rounding Caroline we headed back to ‘alton arriving there about 30 mins before high water, Remembering our previous landing and swamping over the stern I released the tiller pin and rudder strap before we beached and as Mick went over the foredeck to fend off I had the tiller and rudder in on board quicker than it takes to write about it, the mainsail down, then over the side to swing the boat round putting her bows to the breakers, No water came over into the boat and a few pulls put us high and dry once more. The round trip had taken approximately 5 hours. ‘Once again our landing was followed by a cup of tea made by Brian's wife who had watched us sail in. Brian enthused by his morning trip had Sone to the boating lake to have a go on his own, We did not fancy shopping for food so dinner consisted of sausages, potatoes, peas and runner beans (ex tin). After washing up and preparing our "tent" we caught a bus into Clacton and spent the rest of the evening at the cinema, arriving back at Walton soon after 2300 hours. Not intending to catch the early tide we slept soundly and awoke at 07.00 hours when a few people made their early morning excursions to the beach, After breakfast we prepared for the homeward trip. Mick packed some biscuits and cheese and orange squash for having whilst under way and soon after 10.00 hours we had the boat in the water once again with the assistance of holidaymakers. 10.20 hrs set course round WaIton Pier’ (no Fisherman), the wind appeared to be straight up the coast (westerly) and very light, the sun was breaking through and we seemed all set for a gentle sail home. TI had checked the weather forecast with the coastguard station, wind force 2~3 westerly barometer rising.’ As we tacked: down the coast the waves became more pronounced and there was a gentle swell. ‘The wind was increasing and it needed constant attention to ease the boat over the waves. She responded well and at no time did we feel under undue stress. On one occasion we were brought up short and twice we took it green over the foredeck, one of these skimmed the foot of our jib which is set high on Sobraon. From around Frinton we could see the barge race in progress off the Blackwater, just dim shapes on the horizon but there was no doubt about their identity. Around 13.30 hours we were in calmer waters and took the opportunity to refresh ourselves, it was not long before the sailing, once again

* 8 = needed our undivided attention. The kicking strap came undone at the mast fittings and at a suitable moment we luffed up whilst Mick made a running repair and pulled it down hand. As we wanted to see something of the barge race we held our course further off shore than on the outward run, and by the time Colne Pt. was abeam to Starboard we were heading across the estuary towards a Sloop anchored between the Bench Hd Buoy and Sales Pt, whom we assumed to be an official boat concerned with the race, We joined the cavalcade ahead of the last barge and during the beat up to Stansgate managed to pass four more, At 16.20 hours we beafhed at Stansgate, 6 hours after leaving Walton and with three enjoyable days of dinghy cruising behind us. After two days rest we set off again, this time to sail round to Burnham—-on-—Crouch, but that is another story. This month's log is tke Mamgu Trophy Prizewinners log of a trip to France by Geoffrey Bond, Derek. and Eric, sailing Geoffrey's 'Vivacity'. Beginner's Luck Sailing a dinghy for a few seasons I developed a yearning for the open sea, especially after sailing with tide and wind to Clacton and Colne Point, and having to beat home again. It was then my thoughts turned to cruisers, and having purchased a secondhand Vivacity, in October, I launched her when everybody else was laying up for the winter. I registered at night school for a course in navigation, and learnt but only the rudiments, as the course proved abortive owing to lack of support. Came June -— and we were ready to spend a week away from Stansgate; but a week before departure the rudder broke -— it had been made of plywood and painted white - we had to beach her at Stone, whilst a new one was quickly made by Charfleet marine carpenters. We then found we could not match the transom fittings, and it was only on the eve of our holiday that we fitted new gudgeon and pintle to "Calypso's" stern. However - Friday June 10th arrived, and complete with new Crescent© outboard engine, and a company of wives, children and well wishers, we drove to Stansgate, — Imagine our embarrasswent however when we arrived 5 minutes too late to prevent the boat from going aground! We all three pushed and dug but without success, therefore took out time in completing the stowage and éxperiencing our first nigit afloat on safe moorings. We remained up until fidnight for the weather forecast, but as the time passed realised we had tuned into the wrong station! It ‘turnedout fortunate that we hadn't sailed, for there was a severe storm at 03.00 hrs. Saturday June llth We Flag! at again at 04.00 hrs. Derek made a light breakfast at 04.30 hrs and there being no wind, we started the outboard engines on fitting the, rudder however, we fouled the prepeytee and, this made a short delay whilst a new shearpin was fitted. ain inatenaiaie We motored to Bradwell power station at highwater, and off St.Peter' 8 point steered 104° passing Bench Head buoy at.07.30 hrs. A course of 115° took us to the Knowle buoy, then 156° to the Wallet spit. We passed Buxey sands at 08.30 hrs the weather remaining clear and sunny. but Wwindless. At 08.45 hrs we changed course at No.l.w Swin to 9 Barrow ea! and. picked | up the S.idinburgh channel. : The tide was then against us and we took a considerable time to keep east of ‘and beyond Margate sands; nevertheless the wind was now blowing blusteringly and the sky became overcast, the rain descended and continued whilst we passed North Foreland and into Ramsgate harbour at 20.30 hrs. We tied up in the outer harbour and made for the nearest fish and chip shop! and we were in our bunks at 23.00 hrs. Sunday June 12th We went ashore again to find petrol‘ and waited until a garage opened at 09.15 hys; we did-not leave Ramsgate until 09.45 hrs. The weather was again windless but foggy, visibility being less than© Ir mile, we made a bearing for the Quern buoy and altered course down the Goodwin channel via the Brake buoy. We saw several small fishing vessels in the channel and two large vessels were noticeable more by their.foghorn than their appearance! One motor cruiser came over to us in his Pog to ask if we were alright as we had no sail up at the time. We did not see the S.Goodwin light vessel but by its foghorn, could determine our position. At this time Eric collected an exhausted pigeon which he regarded as his special pet and fed it whilst it was with us until we reached land, he nicknamed it 'Sammy going South'.

° -3- We made a bearing of 158° towards Cape Criz Nez, and then sailed off shore to Boulogne, we arrived off Boulogne harbour at 20.00 hrs but had to lay off for + hr whilst a large ship was towed into the southern harbour. We were then given the green light by the traffic light on the pier and we sailed passed the interested French onlookers, including six nuns, who gave us a friendly wave. We passed the car ferry bays and, on instruction from the harbour official, tied up alongside a fishing smack in the Port de Narée, Sammy our pigeon then flew away towards other pigeons, whilst we were left to clear up all his mess! As the customs official did not arrive we made our way to the town and a welcome restaurant. We tried unsuccessfully to ring home but had to make do purchasing picture postcards. Monday June 13th. We went to sleep on board at midnight, but were awakened at 02.45 hrs by the Fisherman talking and banging boxes, and also swilling their evil smelling.decks down - the water coming into our cockpit. Many boats left at 04.00 hrs but luckily the one against which we were tied remained until later. However, we were unable to sleep much owing to the excessive swell as the traffic in the port became heavier, so we arose at 06.30 and left Derek - who was now an excellent cook -— preparing breakfast whilst Eric and myself again bought petrol and bread. We returned to find a shady looking character offering cheap cigarettes etc. He turned out to be the custom's runner and took our order for duty free goods and returned with the cigarettes and brandy and the custom's officer, who (perhaps because of the fishy smell) declined to come aboard. ‘ie then lowered the Q flag from the cross trees and cleaned up our decks. . We set sail for the open sea again and left harbour at 10.00 hrs and had a delightful mornings' sail southwards, with a fresh tacking breeze and sunshine. Visibility was very good and the beaches were clearly visible, we could see expanse of mud and sand of the river Canche at low tide, and admired the sand - yachts racing on Le Touquet beach. Wie anchored off Le Touquet and after lunch swam ashore, and we felt the trip had been worth it for this. We spoke to the skipper of a small fishing boat. and he told us we could not travel up the Canche river until 18.30 hrs at highwater. We waited until then and followed him between the markers and then over the bar under power. The channel was very tortuous and we occasionally went aground — our draught is eft 3 ins and his was 95 cms. However it was a flooding tide and we were the second in the queue of about 6 vessels all going to Etaples, their village. We passed the Le Touquet Yacht Club where we saw many small yachts but only one had twin keels, the rest were all lying on neee Side until they floated at high tide. We anchored just before the village harbour and used the dinghy for the once and only time on the whole journey — merely to step on to prevent us from Sinking into the mud, as the water receded with the tide. We changed our clothes, battened dawn, and went into the village for a beer — which Eric reminded me afterwards we never did get -— but we found that Etaples | 7 ae was on the main line to Paris. The village itself was very ordinary, although the villagers were very friendly. Tuesday June 14th We overslept and awoke 07.00 hrs, we put on our city clothes and dashed, without breakfast, through the town to catch the 07.26 - train to Paris. ‘We spent a happy day in brilliant sunshine and visited Montmatre in the morning. Eric took us to the Paris branch of his firm and treated us to lunch on the premises. Unfortunately, owing to the heavy meal and drunk combined with the oppressive heat, Derek fainted in a shop -— much to the unconcern of the French, who merely stepped over him to continue their shopping, He soon recovered with Vichy water and reassuring words from a zealous English first—aider who was passing. We spent the afternoon buying souvenirs: our only regret being that we would have to leave Paris before we had savoured their nocturnal entertainment! We walked by the Seine to watch the yachts come and go, and had a beer before we left - only to be in the centre of a fracas between the police and the strikers from the French Iron and Steel Union.

u=f- = ° | A journey by crowded metro took us to Gard du Nord, where we caught the 19,18 train back to quiet Htaples. The day on lari made a welcome break, we turned in after a supper of beans on toast. Wednesday June 15th Refreshed, we waited for highwater again, and negotiated the markers out to sea, It made us aware of how much the villager's lives were controlled by the tides. ‘le left Le Touquet at 09.45 hrs. there was a light S.E. breeze, and we were able to keep course without tacking. We sailed offshore making for Cape Griz Nez. ‘We were inspected by a French naval launch before we reached Cape dt Alpreche, and at 11.50 hrs we passed Boulogne harbour and set a course of 349° for Dover. After blue skies, the clouds now thickened and visbility became reduced and the swell more noticeable. We had lunch of mushroom soup, meat sandwiches and rice pudding, and were beginning to feel lonely, because, owing to. the ..-. shipping strike we sighted few ships. Ye spent the time washing the decks listening to the radio (actually a Nova Pal) and catching up on the log on a portable tape recorder, We were only able to determine our position by using the Nova Pal and the echo sounder, At 17.30 hrs we had sighted no vessels for several hours, the visibility still being about one mile, and bearing by Nova Pal on Sandiette, Dungeness and Dover, put us 3 - 4 miles S S ¥ of Dover! The low gain on such a set makes fixes difficult, especially with any crackle; the signals are of such short duration and we had to wait 6 min, to hear wi) them again. Visibility deteriorated but we were lucky to spot the Varne buoy in the mist on our port side. The wind veered and was now YS W we were anxiously looking for signs of land, and were on 349°, At 20.00 hrs we deduced we were in the main shipping lane from the number of vessels sighteds wa at 20.18 hrs we.sighted the radio masts of Dover directly ahead, we became very jubilant. The fog became thicker, but we could hear the Dover fog siren giving a blast every ten seconds; sailing became hazardous owing to many drifting logs. At 20.50 hrs we could’ see the clifts of Dover and also hear the foghorn of S.Goodwin L.V. The Dover foghorn was then switched off when we were within | Sight of the harbour lights. The wind was veering owing to the storn somewhere to our starboard, we made our way towards the brighter light - the western entrance — and opened 2 bottle of brandy to avoid customs duty on it. We missed the tide into Dover as it was just beginning to ebb, but got to the western entrance when a man with a megaphone told us to use the eastern one —- there was nothing in the almanac about this! In spite of the delay we berthed successfully and tied up by the car ferry bays and walked into Dover. We purchased some more petrol and rang home, by this time it was getting late and we did not get to sleep until 0.45 hrs. Thursday June 16th A dull rainy day greeted us, as we awakened late: ” we had breakfast at 08.30 hrs and we entertained 2 customs officers with coffee -— a most informal and happy meeting. We telephoned for clearance from the harbour master, and left after waiting for two ships to enter ww harbour. We left for the choppy sea in squally weather, We left at 10.30 hrs and sailed offshore, reefed, and arrived in Ramsgate harbour at 16.30 hrs, feeling very wet and miserable. After tying up alongside another 4 berth cruiser — owned by 2 young men from Bradwell who had a four months holiday, during which time they hoped to get to the Western Isles, we had a welcome | hot shower and spent the evening in the cinema enjoying Morecombe and ‘/ise, Friday June 17th Again the morning was dull, stormy but good visibility, wewaited until. the weather improved then left Ramsgate 2t 07.15 hrs. We passed N.Foreland with mainsail reefed in a heavy downpour and set’ a course of 002° which took us to the Tongue tower and its accompanying buoys. At 11.00hrs we set a course of 303° and. passed through the S.Hdinburgh channel, We returned past the Barrow light vessel and passed them a parcel of beer, cigarettes and magazines, which they collected in a large fishing net. After passing through the Wallet spitway we ran into a sudden storm, with a strong breeze coming down the Blackwater. This made for an exhilarating close haul back to our mooring, exactly at ETA 20.00 hrs. As we emptied Calypso of dirty laundry and sleeping bags — my children appeared on the clubhouse hard with a large banner between 2 brooksticks — 'Welcome Home" — and it was good to be home. . Geoffrey Bond.

-5- HORWET MATNSHEET How not to Capsize! Centrifugal helming's the pass word. What is it? Briefly it is this. If you put the helm down at speed, in a fast boat such as a Hornet, the boat luffs up on an arc and heels sharply to leeward. Conversly if you up the Hall you will heel to’ windward. Thus in a rough sea or during gybing, when all else fails, you can force your boat level with the tiller. Make every effort to gybe when your mast is plumb-vertical and if, as your boom crashes over, you heel to leeward, yank hard on that tiller. Some hints and tips on Spinnaker Work . L. As a general rule the spinnaker pole should be horizontal and at right angles to the apparent wind. It should be well up on the mast, except when the spinnaker sags badly in light airs. Ze Contrary to popular belief, a spinnaker will develop more forward thrust in a lean wind if the pole is kept high. 3 ‘Most of the trimming should be done on the leeward sheet with the object of keeping the sail pulling forwards and not sideways. ase the sheet until the luff shows signs of wanting to fall in, then harden slightly. Take every advantage of every free puff by easing on the sheet again and harden as the sail starts to fall again. Trim constantly as the wind shifts. lajor shifts have to be allowed for by altering the trim of the pole. What are the special implications of these in connection with Hornets? ne Since the Hornet's spinnaker pole is a stowable five feet in length it does not project far forward of the forestay on a close reach. Therefore, the pole should clip onto the mast about as high as your crew can mamage — say two feet above the gooseneck. It will then project into fresh air and this distance will be maximised if the pole is at right angles to the stay. Ze You can prevent the pole from pointing below the horizontal by tying a piece of terylene in parallel with the shock cord of your up haul. Make your down—haul adjustable, Se Most keen helmsmen use a continuous sheet for their spinnaker and more and more helmsmen leave their spinnaker permanently clipped onto the halyard. The halyard comes down from its Sheave to the bottom of a shroud outside and then under the job sheet and then to the spinnaker.
