-7- NATIONAL ENTERPRISE CLASS RULE CHANGES The National Enterprise Class Rules have been amended to include 2 fibreglass form of construction as well as the traditional wooden hull. A fibreglass bo2t, known as the "404" has been designed to comply fairly closely with the Enterprise specification and performance. Following the rule changes that became effective on 1st November, 1966, the "404" now ranks as an Enterprise. Other changes authorise certain optional alterations to wooden boats and the use of metal spars. There are now three optional versions of the Enterprise, each 'One Design', as follows:- 1, The glass fibre boat. 2. The wooden boat, as at present. 3. The wooden boat with Built in buoyancy. Permutations or combinations of the three will not be permitted, A glass fibre hull may not h2ve wooden decks, and a tanked wooden boat must have all the tanks as shown on the plans. The minimum weight of the glass fibre boat and the wooden boat with built in buoyancy is 220 lbs. Glass Fibre Boats The position on the construction of glass fibre hulls is: a) Construction will be permitted only under licence from the R.YeAo It will be a condition of the issue of the licence that the shells are made available to the trade and to individuals for finishing. b) Houlding must be done from moulds made from a master plug. Glass fibre boats will be measured in the same way as wooden boats. Existing 404's Minor modifications have been made to the 404 during its development but it is the intention that all existing 404's shall be brought into the [Enterprise class subject only to measurement of the hull dimensions etc. It is understood that the R.Y.A. is setting aside a block of Enterprise sail numbers for issue to existing 404's, Wooden Boats Built in Buoyancy. The tanking in wooden boats takes the form of a forw2zrd bulkhead, giving a bow tank, together with side tanks extending from the transom, under the side benches to the forward end of the side benches. The tanking has been designed for ease of installation in existing boats. Optional Variations 1‘ an optional wider rubbing bead. cae An optional position for the forward thwart (only the position shown in the plans are permitted). 3. An optional higher tiller port. Metal Spars The following sections, tapered or untapered may be used, Masts. Booms Holt Allen Enterprise section. Enterprise section. International M35 section M35 section. Proctor B section C section. The rules authorise these specific sections and specify a minimum mast weight of 17 lbs excluding rigging and all normally removable fittings on a

=@e centre of gravity at a minimum of 9*6" from the heel. - The weight and 7 cof g are to be stamped on the mast by the maker. Copies of the revised Rules and plans are available from the R.Y.A. New Street, Chelmsford. Associate Members may also take advantage of these terms. SOCIAL NES A 'Brains Trust’ evening was held at M.AS.C. Social Club, Beehive Lane on Friday 20th January. The panel were Commander C.H.Fricker, Jack Kennewell - of the Blackwater S.C.Geoff “ardell and Terry Hallam of the M.S.C. About fifty people came dong to ask questions on a wide range of subjects connected with the sea, and there were some interesting discussions between members of the panel and the audience. Commander Fricker told us about the sailing of square riggers to Australia, and Francis Chichester's attempt to sail back from Australia was criticised. A question on the bare essentials necessary when going to sea sparked off a discussion on navigation, leading to instructions from the panel on how to work out the deviation of a compass. There were some interesting reminiscences from Terry Hallam on navigating the Blackwater in dark and fog. Some interesting tips were given on how to find a good cruiser if you intend to race it - this involved water line lengths, theoretical lengths, and the ratio of one to the other.

-9- Olympic dinghy racing set everyone arguing in favour of their preferred class, and an interesting discussion developed on the skills of dinghy racing, and how these should best be tried. To plane or not to plane, that is the question. Terry considered skill in sailing to windward was more important. Mike Sissons had a knotty problem -— what does a knot in the Ensign mean? Answer -— you have dutiable goods on board and wish to see the Customs Officer, Moral - don't fly your flags “ith knots in them - it might mean something important. The discussions ranged far and wide on everything from glassfibre to flags, with several jokes and amusing stories thrown in, and %f course plenty of lubrication was available at the bar. Everyone enjoyed themselves, I am sure, and thanks are due to Chairman Jack Bigden and the Panel, One important question put during the evening that I have not mentioned was on the changing shape of the Blackwater. The answer to that one -— come along on 17th February and you will learn all about the river . that we sail on, in a talk entitled ‘Ecology of the Blackwater', See you there at 7.30.pm. -7- SOCIAL REPORT The second winter meeting of the M.S.C. took place at the Social Club, Beehive Lane, on Friday 17th February. Mr.Roy Masefield of Marconi College gave a very interesting talk on the ecology and geology of the Blackwater, He started by showing us a film about beaches - stones and shells, where they come from and how. Then, illustrating his points with diagrams, he showed us how the British coastline, the local hills and valleys, and the local rivers gradually took shape, influenced to a large extend by the advance and retreat of the ice-age glaciers, It was with great interest that we learnt that the river Thames at one time flowed through the valley where our Clubhouse now stands. (Stansgate-on-Thames, indeed!). After a short interval Kr. Masefield went on to show how marshes build up, different plants growing on them according to how long the tide covers that area of land. This was illustrated by some very nice colour slides. Slides were also used to illustrate the formation of spits, how they are broken and build up again, and how the marshes form behind them. The talk was rounded off with a short film entitled 'The River' which followed the course of the river from its small beginning right down to the sea, passing under willow trees, over weirs, through locks, past cricket fields, towns and, of course, the sailing clubs. -4- DOCTOR AFLOAT! A BOOK REVIEW FROM A MAGAZINE, sent to us by Jack Bigden. All Dr. Roger Pilkington wanted was to claim the rights, guaranteed by Parliament, that included the passage of the Kennet and Even Navigation. But when he arrived at the Bridge of Serpents, Reading, the boat wouldn't go under, He rang the Town Hall and sluices were raised down stream and closed farther up river. The water dropped four inches, He removed the mast, the windscreen, the ventilators, opened the sea-cocks and partially flooded the ship. It still wouldn't go under. The deputy borough engineer then gave orders to close down the pumps of the sewage works that serviced 100,000 people. The river went down, but still not far enough. The early evening rush-hour had now started. It was half past five, and the Town Hall said could Dr.Pilkington wait till next day ds they usually stopped work at six o'clock? He obligingly opened the sea-cocks again, took off another inch - in - vain and cordially declined. The borough engineer came up with a back room brainwaves 2 mobile crane to be brought from a nearby RAF station next days; the road to be closed, traffic diverted, while the crane loaded the boat with steel girders until it was low enough. But Dr.Pilkington countered with an even better idea, ‘hy not a ton or more of people? The municipal employees with brief-cases and bowler hats arrived in cars, and Dr.Pilkington began cramming them aboard, He shut them in the hold. He squeezed them into the fore cabin. Five hours after reaching the bridge, the boat passed under with a quarter of an inch to spare, Certainly, Dr.Pilkington is stubborn. Freedom to roam is worth being awkward about, I recommend his "Small Bast on the Thames" (Macmillan £1.10.). All Dr.P's aneedotes are certainly lively. Several people recently have said how intcresting the accounts of sea trips are. I can't invent these but there must be several ‘people who during the summer will make one or two-day excursions up the coast, which, while not perhaps long enough for entry for the hiamgu Trophy, would make extremely interesting reading in Navigans and encourage the new Cruiser owners to venture out of the Blackwater Estuary. I have noticed that a number of Cadets have parents with cruisers. There are other cruising prizes as well as the main Trophy -— cruise to a neighbouring estuary or abroad or a weeks cruise away from home water. what about the Cadets entering 2 log or sending one to Navigans? The MAMGU Trophy is a 12 ft to one inch model of Mamgu presented by Mr and Mrs, A.M,Adam to the Marconi Sailing Club for two purposes: first, to commemorate the ship which for five vital years of the Club's growth served as our Clubhouse, second, to promote a wider interest in the sea and seamanship by encouraging members to go cruising and to share their experiences for the benefit of others. The Trophy is to be awarded annually, and held by the winner for one year, for the best log and account of a cruise made in the preceding twelve months, The cruise must be in a sailing or auxiliary yacht or dinghy, and should be generally of at least three days! duration, though a shorter passage of particular interest may be considered, Use of engine, if any, must be stated. The log may usefully include details of the yacht and any other interesting and relevant matter. The author of the log must be a member or associate member of the Clubs he/she must have taken an active part in sailing the yacht, but need not have been the owner, charterer or skipper. A small panel shall be appointed by the Committee to judge the entries, the decision of the panel to be final. The panel need not consist entirely of club members. Logs are to be judged on their interest and value for others who may attempt similar cruises, and on the seamanship and enterprise implied by the whole undertaking. Thus the riding out of a gale or a passage in heavy weather, conducted in a safe and proper manner and described well enough to assist another iariner in a like situation, should score highly, whereas a colourful account of escapades arising out of gross ignorance or neglect of seamanlike prudence or out of sheer foolnardiness, may be placed lower than a cruise in which hazardous conditions were avoided by good planninh,. A copy of each log entered for the MAMGU shall be presented to the Club if the judges deem it worthy, to be kept for members to read, and to be published, if required, in "Navigans".

RULES 1., NAME. The name of the Club shall be "Marconi Athletic and Social Club". 2. DEFINITIONS. "The Club" means the "Marconi Athletic and Social Club". "The Club House" means the Club House at Beehive Lane, Chelmsford or such other club house as may from time to time be occupied by the Club. "The Company" means The Marconi Company Limited. "The Associated Companies” means The Marconi International Marine Company Limited and English Electric Valve Company Limited. "The General Committee” shall mean the committee elected in accordance with Rule 9(A). The expressions “Ordinary Member", "Family Member", “Associate Member" and "Honorary Life Member" shall bear the meanings assigned to them by Rule 6. The expressions "Outside Section Member” and "Junior Family Member" shall bear the meanings assigned to them by Rule 7. "Section" shall mean a section formed in accordance with Rule 25(A) and Section Committee shall mean in relation to any Section the Com- mittee elected or formed thereunder, 3. COLOURS. The Club colours shall be Royal Blue and White. 4. CONSTITUTION. The Club shall be a members’ club and shall 1

consist of Ordinary Members, together with such other classes of members as are hereinafter mentioned. 5. OBJECTS. The objects of the Club shall be to promote social fellowship, physical fitness and mutual helpfulness among employeesof The Marconi Company Limited and employees of the Associated Companies employed in the Chelmsford area by organising and providing the means for such employees to meet, to engage in sports and recreations of all kinds and to pursue other activities of a social, edu- cational and charitable nature. 6. MEMBERSHIP OF THE CLUB. (A) The Club shall consist of (i) Ordinary Members (ii) | Family Members (iii) Associate Members (iv) Honorary Life Members (B) Ordinary Membership. All employees of the Company and empieyees of the Associated Companies + e ford—ezea- shall be eligible to become Ordinary Members of the Club. (C) Family Membership. A person may become a Family Member of the Club at the discretion of the General Committee if such person is the wife, husband, father, mother, son, daughter, brother or sister of an Ordinary Member or an Honorary Life Member and such person is sixteen years of age or over. Application for Family Membership shall be made on the applicant’s behalf by such Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member (hereinafter referred to 2

as "the Sponsor*) and shall be submitted to the General Committee. The Sponsor shall be liable for the subscription payable in respect of a Family Member of which he is Sponsor. Such sub- scription ‘shall be paid by deduction from the wages or salary of the Sponsor if such Sponsor is an Ordinary Member and shall be paid direct to the Treasurer of the Club by the Sponsor if such Sponsor is an Honorary Life Member. A Family Member shall cease to be a member of the Club forthwith if the Sponsor ceases to be an Deanery, Member or Honorary Life Member of the Club. A Family Member shall be entitled to all the privileges of Club membership except the right to introduce guests and the right to vote at any election or general meeting of the Club: (D) Associate Membership. Associate Membership of the Club may be granted to any person of sixteen years of age or over not being an employee of the Company or an employee of the Associated Companies employed in the Chelmsford area who has first applied for member- ship of a Section and whom the Section Committee is willing to accept as a member of that Section. No application for Associate Membership shall be granted, if the granting of such ‘Associate Membership shall cause the aggregate numbers of Associate Members of the Club to exceed three per cent. of the total Ordinary Membership of the Club provided that the General Committee shall have discretion in exceptional circumstances to exceed this limit where the General Committee has reasonable cause to believe that the limit will be restored by the normal turnover of membership within a period of twelve months. A candidate for Associate Membership shall first apply for membership of a Section. The Committee of that Section, if willing to accept his application, shall before so doing recommend to the General Committee in writing that he be granted Associate Membership of the Club. If the 3

recommendation be not eppzowed by the General Committee the candidate shall not be admitted to membership of the Section but shall be free to make fresh application to the same or some other Bee thon after the lapse of not less than six months. An Associate Member shall be eligible to apply for membership of more than one Section. An Associate Membér shall be entitled to all the privileges of Club membership except the right to introduce guests and the right to vote at any election or general meeting of the Club. (E) Honorary Life Membership. Any person who has left the service of the Company or of one of the Associated Companies on retirement and who at the date of such retirement has been an Ordinary Member of the Club for a period of not less than ten years or periods totalling not less than ten years in the aggre- gate shall, provided he has been an Ordinary Member of the Club for a continuous period of two years ending on the date of such retirement be entitled to become an Honorary Life Member of the Club on making an application to the General Committee for Honorary Life Membership. Such application may be made at any time provided that in the case of a person who has not already retired at the date of his application, such application shall not be made more than three months before the date of his retirement and stele only take effect on the date of his retire- ment. The General Committee shall have the power to elect any Ordinary Member who is about to retire from the service of the Company or the Associated Companies or any former Ordinary Member who has so retired to Honorary Life Membership if such Ordinary Member or former Ordinary Member has been or was an Ordinary Member for a period of not less than five years or periods totalling not less than five years in the aggregate. 4

An Honorary Life Member shall be entitled to all the privileges of Club membership except the right to vote at any election or general meeting of the Club. (F) Election to Membership. No person shall become a member of the Club unless he shall have been elected to membership by the General Committee. Application for member- ship shall be made in writing in the appropriate form prescribed by the General Committee, by the applicant or in the case of applications for Family Membership by the applicant’s Sponsor. The name and address of any applicant for member- ship shall be prominently displayed in the Club House in a part of the Club House frequented by the Club members not less than two clear days before the election of such applicant as a member. (G) Cessation of Membership. A member shall cease to be a member in the following events: - (a) if he resigns his membership by giving not less than one week’s notice in writing to the Chief Executive; such resignation shall take effect at the expiry of the said period of notice (b) if being an Ordinary Member -he cancels the authority to his Company to deduct his subscrip- tion from his wages or salary, he shall cease to be a memberon the expiry of the period in respect of which his subscription has been paid. (c) if being an Ordinary Member he shall cease to be employed by the Company or to be employed by one of the Associated Companies in the Chelmsford area unless immediately on ceasing to be so em- ployed he shall become an Honorary Life Member (d) if he shall have failed to pay his subscrip- tion or in the case of a Family Member his sub- scription shall not have been paid by him or by his Sponsor within thirty days after the same shall have become due and the General Committee 5

shall resolve to terminate his membership on the grounds of nonpayment of his subscription (e) if being a Family Member his Sponsor ceases to be an Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member (f) if his membership shall be terminated in accordance with Rule 23. (H) Membership Cards. The membership cards issued to members shall remain the property of the Club and shall be surrendered to the Chief Executive upon the ter- mination of membership for whatever cause. 7. MEMBERSHIP OF SECTIONS OF THE CLUB. (A) A Section of the Club shall consist of (i) Ordinary Members (ii) Family Members, (iii), Associate Members (iv) Honorary Life Members (vy) Outside Section Members (vi) Junior Family Members (B) Ordinary Members, Family Members and Honorary Life Members shall be entitled to become members of any Section of the Club upon making application for membership of that Section to the Section Committee. (C) Associate Members An Associate Member of the Club may become a member of a Section on making application and being elected by the Section Committee. The election as a member of a Section of a person applying for Associate Membership under Rule 6(D) shall not become effective unless and until such person shall have been electedan Associate Member by the General Committee. 6

A decision of a Section Committee not to permit an Associate Member to Section Membership shall be final. (D) Outside Section Members The Committee of any Section, the normal activities of which take place on premises other than those of the Club or of the Company or the Associated Companies, may grant Outside Section Membership to persons of sixteen years of age or over, not being employees of the Company or the Associated Companies nor qualified for Family Membership provided that the grant of Outside Section Membership to any person will not cause the number of Outside Section Members of that Section to be more than twenty five per cent. of the total number of Ordinary Members who are members of the Section. An Outside Section Member shall not be admitted to membership of more than two Sections and may participate only in the activities of his Section or Sections which are held on premises other than those of the Club or of the Company or the Associated Companies. The name of every person admitted to Outside Section Membership shall be notified forthwith by the Section Committee to the General Committee. An Outside Section Member shall be subject) to these Rules and the decisions and control of the General Committee in all matters affecting his membership. (E) Junior Family Membership of Sections. The Committee of any Section the Rules of which so allow may grant Junior Family Membership to any son or daughter (being fifteen years of age or under) of any member of the section other than an Qutside Section Member. The parent of a Junior Family Member shall be responsible for his child strictly observing the Rules of the Section and the Rules and Bye-Laws of the Club. 7

The subscription, if any, charged by the Section for anton Family Membership shall be paid by the parent. Upon attaining the age of sixteen years, a Junior Family Member shall cease to be a member of his Section or Sections unless within one month from the date of his sixteenth birthday he is admitted to Family or Associate Membership of the Club or Outside Section Membership. A Junior Family Member may participate only in the activities of his Section or Sections and shall not use the premises of the Club otherwise than for the purpose of such activities. The name of every person admitted to Junior Family Membership of a Section shall be notified forthwith by the Section Committee to the General Conmittee. (F) Election to Section Membership A person other than an Ordinary Member, Family Member or Honorary Life Member applying for membership of a Section shall only become a member of that Section upon making application to the Section Committee in accordance with the Rules of the Section and being elected a Section Member by the Section Committee provided that in the case of a person applying for Associate Membership of the Club such person shall not become a memberof the Section until he is elected an Associate Member of the Club by the General Committee. 8. SUBSCRIPTIONS The subscriptions payable by the President, Vice Presidents, Ordinary Members, Family Members and Associate Members shall be fixed and may from time to time be varied by resolution of a general meeting of the Club passed in accordance with Rule 11(C).

Particulars of the subscriptions for the time being payable shall at all times be posted in a prominent position in the Club House. The subscriptions payable for membership of a Section including the subscriptions (if any) payable by Outside Section Members and Junior Family Members shall be those fixed by or in accordance with the Rules of the Section or Sections of which they are members. Subscriptions shall be payable in advance and in the case of annual subscriptions shall be due and payable on the anniversary of the date the member became a President, Vice President or Associate Member as the case may The subscription payable by an Honorary Life Member in respect of a Family Member of which he is Sponsor shall be paid by such Honorary Life Member to the Club Treasurer, The subscriptionofan Ordinary Member including the subscriptions payable by him in respect of Family Members of which he is Sponsor shall be paid by deductions from his wages or salary and authority to his Company to make such deductions shall be given. in his form of Application for Membership. An Ordinary Member who cancels such authority shall be deemed to have resigned his membership from the date his subscription ceases. The subscription of an Associate Member shall be paid to the Section which sponsored his applica- tion for Associate Membership and shall be re- weve by such Section to the Treasurer of the Club. 9. MANAGEMENT (A) General Committee The affairs of the Club, in all matters not in these Rules reserved for the Club in General Meeting, shall be managed by a General Committee consisting of twelve Ordinary Members elected to serve for a term of two years. 9

At its first meeting after each Annual Election the General Committee shall elect a Chairman and a Vice-Chairman for the ensuing year. The General Committee shall meet at least once a month. Seven members shall constitute a quorum. Each member shall be entitled to one vote except that in the case of an equality of votes, the Chairman of the Meeting shall have a second or casting vote. Any member of the. General Committee who absents himself from three consecutive meetings without reasonable excuse shall upon the resolu- tion of the other members thereof cease to be a member of the General Committee and his position may thereupon be filled as a casual vacancy. The members of the General Committee shall have power to appoint any Ordinary Member of the Club to fill a casual vacancy. The proceedings of the General Committee shall be recorded ina Minute Book kept for that purpose, which shall be available for inspection by any member of the General Committee. (B) Bar Sub-Committee At its first meeting after each election, the General Committee shall appoint a Bar Sub- Committee which shall consist solely of the Chairman and four or more other members of the General Committee. The Bar Sub-Committee shall be responsible for the orderly conductof the Club Bars in accordance with the licensing laws for the time being in force and for the purchase for the Club and the supply by the Club of intoxicating liquor. The Bar Sub-Committee shall meet at least once a month. Three members shall constitute a quorum. (C) Other Sub-Committees. The General Committee may appoint one or more Sub-Committees in addition to the Bar Sub- Committee for such purposes and with such 10

responsibilities as it may deem appropriate. Such Sub-Committee shall at all times be responsible to the General Committee which may direct that particular matters shall be referred to it for approval or decision and shall have the right where circumstances permit to over-ride decisions taken by a Sub-Committee. Unless otherwise de- cided by the General Committee, the proceedings of a Sub-Committee shall be recorded in a Minute Book kept for that purpose, which shall be available for inspection by any member of the General Committee. 10. ELECTION OF GENERAL COMMITTEE In every year, six members of the General Committee shall retire from office and shall be eligible for re-election. The members so re- tiring shall be those who have been longest in office since their last election. A member appointed to fill a casual vacancy on the General Committee shall be deemed to have taken office on the date on which the membet in whose place he is appointed was last elected. Notices inviting the nomination of candidates to serve on the General Committee shall be posted by the Chief Executive in the Club House and in such other places as the General Committee may determine on the First day of October in every year. Nominations shall be in writing signed by two Ordinary Members, countersigned by the candi- date to signify his consent and deposited with the Chief Executive within a period of fourteen days from the date of such notices. Only Ordinary Members who are over the age of twenty- one shall be eligible for nomination. The election shall take place during the first complete week of November on dates determined by the General Committee, which shall make all necessary arrangements in connection therewith, including the appointment of three scrutineers who shall not be members of nor candidates for election to the General Committee. The result 11

shall be declared by the posting in the Club House of notices signed by the scrutineers re- cording the number of votes polled by each candi- ave. it indicating which candidates have been elected. The election shall be by ballot. Each Ordinary Member shall have six votes but shall not be entitled to cast more than one vote for a parti- cular candidate and shall not be obliged to cast all the votes to which he is entitled. Should the ballot result in two or more candi- dates receiving an equal number of votes, being the lowest number cast which is sufficient to secure election, the scrutineers shall draw lots to determine which of such candidates shall fill the vacancy. 11. GENERAL MEETINGS (A) Annual General Meetings. An Annual General Meeting of the Club shall be held in every year not later than the Thirtieth day of April and not more than fifteen months shall elapse between the date of one Annual General Meeting and that of the next. Notice of the date and time of the Annual General Meeting shall be posted by the Chief Executive in the Club House and in such other places as the General Committee may determine at least fourteen clear days before such date. The business of an Annual General Meeting shall be to receive and consider the Balance Sheet and the reports of the General Committee, Officers and Auditors; to elect the President and Vice Presidents; to appoint Auditors and to transact any other business which may be determined by the President or the General Committee and stated in the notice of the meeting or of which notice signed by at least two Ordinary Members has been given to the Chief Executive at least seven clear days before the date fixed for the Meeting. 12

(B) Special General Meetings. A Special General Meeting may be called by the President or the General Committee on not less than seven days notice at the time and place specified in the notice of such Special General Meeting or upon the written requisition of at least thirty Ordinary Members or one fifth of the total number of Ordinary Members whichever is ‘the less and shall, if so requisitioned, be held not less than seven clear days nor more than twenty one clear days from the date of the receipt by the Chief Executive of such requisition. Notice of the date and time of a Special General Meeting shall be posted by the Chief Executive in the Club House at least seven clear days before the date of such meeting. (C) Voting at General Meetings. At any General Meeting a resolution put to the yote of the meeting shall be decided on a show of membership cards unless a poll is (before or on the declaration of the show of membership cards) demanded; (a) by the Chairman of the Meeting; or (b) by ten Ordinary Members. Unless a poll be so demanded a declaration by the Chairman that a resolution has on a show of membership cards been carried or carried unani- mously or by a particular majority or lost and an entry to that effect in the book containing the minutes of the proceedings of the meeting shall be conclusive evidence of the fact without proof of the number or proportion of the votes recorded for or against such resolution. A demand for a poll may be withdrawn. If a poll is duly demanded it shall be taken forthwith. On a show of membership cards or on a poll every Ordinary Member present at the meeting shall have one vote. 13

Except in the case of resolutions to alter the rules resolutions shall be passed if voted for by a majority of the Ordinary Members present in person at the meeting and voting. In the case of an equality of votes, the resolutions shall be treated as not passed and in such case the Chair- man shall not have a second or casting vote. cD) 12. ACCOUNTS The General Committee shall cause proper books of account to be kept with respect to all sums of money received and expended by the Club, all sales and purchases. by the Club and the assets and liabilities of the Club. At every Annual General Meeting, the General Committee shall lay before the Club a Balance Sheet made up to the Thirty-first day of December in the previous year, duly audited and signed by the Auditors. A copy of the Balance Sheet shall be posted in the Club House and in such other places as the General Committee may determine at least fourteen clear days before the date of the Annual General Meeting. 13. VICE-PRESIDENTS The Club shall have such number of Vice- Presidents as may from time to time be determined by the General Committee. A Vice-President shall be elected at the Annual General Meeting and shall hold office for life unless he shall resign from the office of Vice-President by giving not less than one weeks notice in writing to the Chief Executive or shall fail to pay his sub- scription within thirty days after the same shall have become due and the General Committee shall resolve to remove him from the office of Vice- President. No person shall be nominated for election as a Vice-President unless such nomina- tion shall have been made or approved by the General Committee. The General Committee shall have power to appoint any person as an additional Vice-President or to fill a casual vacancy in the office of Vice-President until the next following Annual General Meeting. 14

The Vice-Presidents shall be entitled to all the privileges of Ordinary Membership and shall have the right to attend and speak at meetings of the General Committee but not to vote thereat. 14. PRESIDENT The Club shall have a President who shall be elected annually at the Annual General Meeting. No person shall be nominated for election as President unless he is a Vice-President and un- less such nomination shall have been made or approved by the General Committee. Upon the conclusion of his term of office, a retiring President, if not re-elected, shall resume the office of Vice-President. The General Committee shall have power to appoint any Vice-President to fill a casual vacancy in the office of President until the next following Annual General Meeting. The President shall be entitled to all the privileges of Ordinary Membership and shall have the right to attend and speak at meetings of the General Committee but not to vote thereat. 15. TRUSTEES The Club shall have not less than two nor more than three Trustees who shall be appointed by the Company acting in consultation with the General Committee and may be removed from office by the Company. A Trustee shall be entitled to resign his office by giving not less than one month’s notice in writing to the Company. All property of the Club, including land and investments but excluding the Club’s bank account or accounts, shall be vested in the Trustees for the time being in their own names so far as necessary and practicable for the use and benefit of the Club. The Trustees shall have the right to attend and speak at meetings of the General Committee but shall not have a vote. 15

16. OFFICERS (A) Chief Executive The Chief Executive of the Club shall be appointed by the Company acting in consultation with the General Committee and shall be an employee of the Company. The Chief Executive shall have such duties and responsibilities relating to the organisation of the Club and its activities as shall from time to time be assigned to him by the General Committee in agreement with the Company. (B) Executive Officer The Executive Officer of the Club shall be appointed by the Company acting in consultation with the General Committee and shall be an em- ployee of the Company. The Executive Officer shall carry out under the directions of the Chief Executive such duties and responsibilities as may from time to time be assigned to him. (C) Treasurer The Treasurer of the Club shall be appointed by the Company acting in consultation with the General Committee and shall be an employee of the Company. The Treasurer shall carry out under the direc- tions of the Chief Executive such duties and responsibilities as may from time to time be assigned to him. 17. AUDITORS Two Auditors, not being members of the General Committee nor Officers of the Club, shall be appointed annually at the Annual General Meeting. No person shall be nominated for appointment as an Auditor unless he shall have consented to such nomination and such nomination shall have been 16

made or approved by the General Committee. The General Committee shall have power to appoint any person to fill a casual vacancy in the office of Auditor until the next Annual General Meeting. The Auditors shall have access to all the books, accounts, vouchers, deeds, securities, minute books and other documents of the Club, including those of the Sections. 18. BYE-LAWS: The General Committee shall have power from time to time to make, vary and revoke Bye-laws (not inconsistent with these Rules) for the regu- lation of the internal affairsof the Club and the conduct of the members. The Bye-laws for the time being in force shall be binding on all members, and a copy thereof shall at all times be posted in a prominent position in the Club House. 19. OPENING OF CLUB PREMISES The General Committee shall have power from time to time by Bye-law to determine and vary the days and times during which the premises of the Club shall be open to members. 20. SUPPLY OF INTOXICANTS Subject to any special hours certificates which may from time to time be granted to the Club in accordance With the licensing laws, the supply of imtoxicating liquor in the Club Bars piel, be permitted only during the following ours: - Sailing Section Bar Monday to Thursday 6.00 p.m. to 10.30 p m. Friday 6.00 p.m. to 11.00 p.m, Saturday lunchtime 11.30 a.m. to 2.00 p.m. Saturday evening 4.30 p.m. to 11.00 p.m. 17

Sunday lunchtime 12 noon to 2.00 p.m. Sunday evening 4.30 p.m. to 8.00 p.m. Christmas Day Closed Good Friday As for Sundays Other Weekday Bank Holidays: Lunchtime 11.30 a.m. to 2.00 p.m. Evening 6.00 p.m. to 10.30 p.m. or 11.00 p.m., according to weekday. Other Club Bars Monday to Thursday 6.00 p.m. to 10.30 p.m. Friday 6.00 p.m. to 11.00 p.m. Saturday lunchtime 11.30 a.m, to 2.00 p.m. Saturday evening 4.30 p.m. to 11.00 p.m. Sunday lunchtime 12 noon to, 2.00 p.m. Sunday evening 7.00 p.m. to 10.30 p.m. Christmas Day Closed Good Friday Closed Other Weekday Bank Holidays: Lunchtime 11.30 a.m. to 2.00 p.m. Evening 6.00 p.m. to 10.30 p.m. or 11.00 p.m., according to weekday. The General Committee shall haye power from time to time by Bye-law to determine and vary the actual hours within the permitted hours during which the Club Bars shall be open. No intoxicating liquor shall be supplied to a member, visitor or guest who is under eighteen years of age. No intoxicating liquor shall be supplied by or on behalf of the Club for consumption off the premises except to a member in person. 18

No person shall be paid at the expense of the Club any commission, percentage or similar pay- ment on or with reference to purchases of intoxi- cating liquor by the Club; aor shall any person directly or indirectly derive any pecuniary bene- fit from the supply of intoxicating liquor by or on behalf of the Club to members or guests, apart from any benefit accruing to the Club as a whole and apart also from any benefit which a person derives indirectly by reason of the supply giving rise to or contributing to a general gain in the carrying on of the Club. 21. INTRODUCTION OF VISITORS (A) Members’ Guests Ordinary Members and Honorary Life Members may introduce and entertain guests at the premises of the Club. The maximum number of guests which an Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member may in- troduce on any one occesion shall be stated in the Bye-laws and a notice of any decision by the General Committee to reduce such maximum number shall be prominently displayed in the Club House at least seven clear days before the reduction takes effect. There shall be kept at all premises of the Club a Visitors’ Book which shall be signed by every guest and by the Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member effecting the introduction, The General Committee shall have power by Bye-law to deter- mine the fee, if any, which shall be payable by an Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member in respect of each guest introduced by him. An Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member who introduces a guest shall accompany him throughout his stay on the Club premises and shall be re- sponsible for his guest strictly observing these Rules and the Bye-laws of the Club. No person whose membership is suspended at the relevant timeor has been terminated under Rule 23 shall be introduced as a guest. 19

No guest of an Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member shall be permitted to make payment, direct- ly or indirectly for any intoxicating liquor pro- vided on the Club premises. Any guest found or reasonably suspected to be in breach of this sub- rule shall be required to leave the Club premises immediately and the Ordinary Member or Honorary Life Member by whom such guest was introduced shall be liable to suspension upon the breach being duly proved. (B) Visitors from other Clubs Officers and members of other Clubs visiting premises of the Club by official invitation shall during the period of their stay be permitted to buy intoxicating liquor for consumption on the Club premises. A Section shall not issue such an invitation except with the authorityof the General Committee and advance notice of any such visit shall be given by the Section concerned to the Chief Executive. 22. BETTING, LOTTERIES AND GAMING No betting shall be allowed on any premises of the Club. No lottery shall be promoted by any member or Officer on behalf of or in any way con- nected with the Club or with any entertainment or event held by or in connection with the Club without the previous authority of the General Committee. Gaming shall be permitted on the pre- mises of the Club so, however, as not to con- travene any of the provisions of the Betting, Gaming and Lotteries Act, 1963 or any statutory modification thereof for the time being in force. 23. MISCONDUCT OF MEMBERS (A) Misconduct _on Club premises Any Officer of the Club, any member of the General Committee or any person authorised by the 20

General Committee may require any person to leave any premises of the Club forthwith for the re- mainder of that day if in the opinion of such Officer, Committee member or person so authorised such person’s behaviour is detrimental to the proper conduct of the Club or any Section thereof or causes annoyance to other members. (B) Suspension and Termination of Membership (i) Suspension by Chief Executive The Chief Executive (or other Officer deputising for him) with the consent of not less than two members of the General Committee may suspend the membership of any member of the Club whose con- duct, whether on the premises of the Club or elsewhere, is or has been in their opinion con~- trary to the interests of the Club or injurious to its reputation. Such suspension shall take effect until the next following meeting of the General Committee. A member so suspended shall be given written notice of his suspension and of the date and place of the next following meetingof the General Committee at which the suspension will be con- sidered and shall be informed that if he desires he may appear before the General Committee to answer any allegation made against him or make written representations to the General Committee. af Geet meeting the General Committee shall either: - (a) re-instate the suspended member; or (b) extend the suspension for a specified period not exceeding three months; or (c) subject as hereinafter provided, resolve to terminate the membership of the suspended member. (ii) Suspension or termination of Membership by General Committee If in the opinion of the General Committee the conduct of a member of the Club, whether on the 21

premises of the Club or elsewhere is or has been contrary to the interests of the Club or in- jurious to its reputation the General Committee may resolve to suspend the membership of such member for a specified period not exceeding three months or subject as hereinafter provided may resolve to terminate such member’s membership. If practicable not less than 24 hours written notice shall be given to such member informing him of the date and place of the General Committee Meeting at which the suspension or termination of his membership will be considered and informing him that if he desires he may appear before the meeting to answer any allegation made against him or make written representations to the General Committee. If such notice is not given and the General Committee at such meeting resolves to suspend or terminate his membership, he shall be given written notice of such suspension or ter- mination and of the date and place of the next following meeting of the General Committee at which if such member so desires such suspension or termination will be reconsidered and shall be informed that if he desires he may appear before the General Committee or submit written repre- sentations in answer to any allegation. If the member appears at such meeting or makes such ropreseteartone the General Committee shall either:- (a) re-instate such member as a member; or (b) reduce the period of suspension; or (c) confirm the suspension or termination of his membership subject in the case of termination to the member’s right of appeal to the Club in General Meeting. If the member shall not appear at such meeting or make such representations the decision of the General Committee shall stand subject in the case of termination of membership to the member’s right of appeal to the Club in General Meeting. 22

(C) Appeal against Termination of Membership A member whose membership the General Committee has resolved to terminate shall (unless there shall still be available to such member the right to have the decision of the General Committee re- considered by the General Committee under sub- section (B) of this Rule), be informed (by letter, if he did not appear before the Committee) that he has the right within seven days to give written notice of his desire to appeal to the Club in General Meeting (his membership meanwhile being suspended) and that failing such notice of appeal his membership will terminate and his name will be removed from the list of members at the expiration of the said period of seven days. In the event of a notice of appeal being duly received, the General Committee shall call a Special General Meeting of the Club for a day not more than twenty-one clear days after the date of receipt of the notice of appeal. The suspended member shall be given written notice of the date of such Special General Meeting and shall be in- formed that if he so desires he may be present. At any such Special General Meeting any allega- tions against the suspended member shall be re- lated (in his presence, ifhe attends) by a member of the General Committee and the suspended member shall (if he desires) be heard in answer. A decision whether to re-instate the suspended member or to terminate his membership shall be taken by vote ina ballot conducted by scrutineers appointed for the purposeby the General Committee and shall be conclusive. (D) Re-admission after Expulsion for Misconduct A member whose membership has been terminated on grounds of misconduct may at the discretion of the General Committee be re-admitted to member- ship after a period of not. less than six months from the date of such termination. 23

24. DISPUTES AND COMPLAINTS (A) Disputes between Members and Officers and complaints about or by Officers Any dispute between a member and an Officer of the Club and any complaint by a member concerning an Officer of the Club or by an Officer of the Club concerning a member shall, unless settled amicably, be referred by the member or Officer concerned to the General Committee. The General Committee shall take such action as may be appro- priate including the suspension or termination of membership under Rule 23(B)(ii) if the conduct of the member concerned justifies it. If the member or Officer concerned is dissatisfied with the decision of the General Committee, either party may request that the matter be referred for arbi- tration by one or more of the Trustees, appointed under Rule 15, whose decision shall be final provided always that if such decision of the General Committee involves the termination of a person’s membership the matter shall not be re- ferred to the Trustees but such person shall have a right of appeal to the Club in general meeting pursuant to Rule 23. (B) Disputes between Members and other complaints Any dispute: between members which cannot be settled amicably and any complaint by a member other than a complaint concerning an Officer of the Club shall be referred by the member or members concerned to the Chief Executive (or other officer deputising for him) who, if unable to settle the matter to the satisfaction of such member or members, shall refer it at the request of any such member to the General Committee whose decision shall be final provided always that if in the opinion of the Chief Executive (or other Officer deputising for him) the dispute or com- plaint concerns conduct by a member whether on the premises of the Club or elsewhere, which is or has been in the opinion of the Chief Executive (or such other Officer) contrary to the interests of the Club or injurious to its reputation, the 24

Chief Executive (or other officer deputising for him) shall refer the matter immediately to the General Committee and the matter shall be dealt with under the provisions of Rule 23(B) (ii). (C) Right to attend meeting of General Committee Any member or Officer about whom a complaint is made or who makes a complaint or who is a party to a dispute may attend the meetingof the General Committee at which such complaint or dispute is considered or if the matter is referred to the arbitration of oneormore of the Trustees, before the Trusteejor Trustees, to state his case or answer any allegations made against him, 25. EXCLUSION OF LIABILITY AND _INDEMNITIES (A) Exclusion of Liability Neither the Club not any member acting on behalf of the Club nor any Officer thereof nor the Trustees shall be liable to any member or guest of a member or visitor for any loss of or damage to any property occurring, from whatever cause, in or about any premises of the Club; nor for any injury sustained by a member or guest or visitor whilst on or entering or leaving any premises of the Club. (B) Indemnity of Officers, Employees and the Company The Officers and employees of the Club and the Company shall be entitled to be indemnified out of the assets of the Club against all expenses, costs, claims and liabilities arising out of or in the course of the Officers’ or employees’ duties or acts as Officers or employees which the Officers or employees or their predecessors may incur, except such (if any) as they may incur through their own wilful neglect or default. If the assets of the Club shall be insufficient, the Officers, the employees and the Company shall be entitled to be indemnified to the extend of such 25

deficiency by the Ordinary’ Members of the Club and those persons who were Ordinary Members at the date the liability was incurred but have subsequently ceased to be Ordinary Members. The liability of the Ordinary Members and such past Ordinary Members shall be joint and several. (C). Indemnity of General Committee and the Trustees The members of the General Committee and the Trustees shall be entitled to be indemnified out of the assets of the Club against all expenses, costs, claims and liabilities arising our of or in the course of their duties or acts as members of the General Committee or Trustees as the case may be which they or their predecessors in title may incur, except such (if any) as they may incur through their own wilful neglect or default. If the assets of the Club shall be insufficient the members of the General Committee or the Trustees as the case may be shall be entitled to be in- demnified to the extent of the deficiency by the Ordinary Members of the Club and those persons who were Ordinary Members of the Club at the date the liability was incurred but have subsequently ceased to be Ordinary Members. The liability of the Ordinary Members and such past Ordinary Members shall be joint and several. 26. SECTIONS (A) Formation and control Any group of ten or more Ordinary Members having a common sporting, social or cultural interest may with the previous approval of the General Committee form a Section. No person who has not first been elected a member of the Club shall be admitted to membership of a Section except as an Outside Section Member or a Junior Family Member. Each Section shall be under the control of a Section Committee elected annually by and con- sisting of members of the Section other than 26

Associate Members, Outside Section Members and Junior Family Members. Upon a Section being formed the Members thereof shall forthwith elect a Section Committee. The Section Committee shall be responsible to the General Committee for the conduct of its Section. The first Section Committee shall be elected as soon as practicable after the approval of the General Committee to the formation of the Section shall have been given, at a meeting of the Section convened for that purpose by the General Committee. The Section Committee of a newly-formed Section shall, as soon as possible after taking office, prepare and submit to the General Committee Rules for the operation and conduct of the Section. Such Rules shall not come into force until approved with or without amendment by the General Committee and thereafter shall not be amended without the previous approval of the General Committee. Each Section shall submit a written report on its activities to the General Committee at such jntervals as the General Committee may decide. (B) Subscriptions to Sections The additional subscriptions, if any, charged for membership of a Section shall be fixed and may from time to time be varied by the Section Committee subject, in the case of Outside Section Members, to the approval of the General Committee. (C) Section Accounts Each Section shall appoint a Section Treasurer who shall keep a true record of the financial transactions of that Section in accordance with such directions as may from time to time be given to him by the General Committee or laid down in the Bye-laws. (D) Dissolution of Sections Upon the dissolution of a Section all funds, equipment and other property of the Section shall 27

be checked and recorded by the Auditors who shall submit an inventory thereof to the General Com- mittee. Such property shall thereafter be used and applied for the benefit of the general body of Club members and the members of the Section shall have no claim against any person for the distribution of the said property or its equiva- lent in money among the members of the Section that has been dissolved. 27. ALTERATION OF RULES These Rules may be revoked, added to or altered by resolution of a General Meeting of the Club passed by a majority comprising at least two- thirds of the Ordinary Members present and voting. So long as the Club is registered in respect of any premises under Part II of the Licensing Act, 1964 or any statutory amendment or re-enactment thereof for the time being in force the Chief Executive shall give written notice of any alteration of these Rules to the Chief Officer of Police and the Clerk of the Local Authority in each area in which such premises are situated within twenty eight days of such alteration and no alteration of these Rules so as to authorise sales of intoxicating liquor not authorised at the time of the application or last application by the Club for the issue or renewal of a regi- stration certificate shall be effective until such written notice shall have been given. 28

-3- BRAZIL Fitting out the club dinghy 'Brazil' has been my labour of love for two seasons now and on each occasion I have endeavoured to add some improvement or refinement that would make her better and/or safer for would be helmsmen. This year drainage holes have been fitted, the bungs being of the screw type, inserted from inside the boat and attached by a lanyard to prevent loss. The cover has been repaired and draw lines attached that pass under the hull and enable the cover to be tied sufficiently tight so as to prevent sagging. A "boom" has been provided to support the cover, please note how it is fitted and replace it correctly when you have finished, also please see that it is not left lying where it can be damaged whilst you are out sailing. "Brazil" is not fitted with banding to her keel or bilge strakes, I hope to remedy this for next year. In the meantime please remember that she lacks protection in these vital parts, and refrain from grounding her unnecessarily. Finally please report any damage to the 0.0.D. who will note it in his report, and I should be able to sort it out from there. Good luck, good sailing and thank you in anticipation of your careful use of "Brazil". Fred Partlett (iwayfarer 181). ~8- SOCIAL EVENING Se The last winter meeting of the Sailing Club was held at the - Beehive Lane Clubhouse on I'riday, 21st April. About fifty people were . present to enjoy the usual bar facilities, exchange of news, and talks by three very good speakers, The first sveaker was Mr. Alan Hill, who won the Bronze Medal with his craft at the last Boat Show. Mr, Hill told us a lot about the designing and building of boats, his special interest being fibreglass boats, which he believes will become much more popular in the next few years, one of his reasons being the speed of this type of manufacture as opposed to the traditional methods, He explained the system of Lloyd's certificates and recommended that any prospective buyer should ask to see the hull or series certificate. Ve were given tips on the purchase of new and secondhand cruisers; the small points to watch for in the building and current condition of the boat. Alsn, we were told how.to maintain a fibreglass boat by buffing he surface to keep it polished and clean, Point to note: once the fibreglass boat goes svongy and has to be painted it requires -the same amount of maintenance as any wooden or metal boat. If you ever need to repair your fibreglass boat we discovered that the name of the builder should be found, so that ne can thereby ascertain which type of resin was used in the. original construction - it is always advisable to stick to the same type. Mr, Hall also discussed the fitting out of the boats, including the fitting of gas appliances and engines, Altogether he gave us a great deal of useful and heloful advice and information, illustrated with stories and.examples from his own experience. Mr, Sam Poulton of Maldon was the next speaker and he kept the audience laughing with tales ef his early sailing days, from the first boat he had, te the times when he beat Buster Payne in many a race by using the 'hard boiled egg' technique - guaranteed to succeed, He also gave helpful hints on navigating "then you shin up the mast with your binoculars and have a look round", and told us of the advantages and disadvantages ef amming a Thames barge, Since mest of his tales need “the Sam Poulton” tauch to Give them full flavour none of them is repeated here, but any reader whe did not attend the meeting is advised to make the mast of his ar her eppertunity next time they have a chance to hear him speak, - The third speaker of the evening was Keith Musto, who, of eourse, needs no intraduetion. He came along prepared to answer any questions on sailing. However, before getting dom to technicalities, he showed us some very interesting and entertaining colour’slides oi Tolcyo taken during the Olympic'Games, and told us about the ineidents, people and places illustrated, This was most enjoyable, although it was not all about sailing but included tales such as that of the Japanese god whose huge stone statue survived two earthquakes and a tidal.wave, and now has gifts brought to him by many pilgrims, one of whoifmade him a giant pair of sandals, which will come in handy should he ever want to take a walk, The evening passed very quickly indeed, and thanks were expressed to all three speakers for the excellent advice and entertainment they gave us,

SOCIAL REPORT The M.S.C. this year again held a Spring Bank Holiday Regatta and a fancy dress: party on the theme of Naughtical Knights was organised for the Saturday evening. Some people took the nightime part very seriously and arrived clad in pyjamas. The girl in the Baby Doll outfit was probably the coolest and most comfortable guest as the dancing got faster and hotter through the evening. The Clubhouse was full and several people sat at the tables outside on the terrace, The dancing also moved outside when the Conga started. However, I suspect the "whoops" were not all gleeful ones as we hopped barefoot over the gravel at’ the. back of the Clubhouse. om: MO FALLING IN THE WATER Compared with the high accident rate of road users, sailing is a relatively safe pastime. However, accidents do occur, and when they do are usually more ‘Serious as often rescue is either a long way away or more difficult.to obtain. It is therefore more important to take precautions and also to know what to do when an accident does occur. According to the Registrar General's Statistical Review for 1962, there were 898 deaths in the waters around England and ‘ales, including 72 deaths due to submersion of the occupant of 2 small boat and 40 due to other water-transport injury by submersion. Total tragedies are not that infrequent in our own Blackwater which compared with many sailing areas, is sheltered, and potential rescuers not far away. Why do people die when they fall in the water? Other than attack by sharks or mechanical injury there are three main causes of death. l. Hypothermia, i.e. lowering ofbody temperature due to the cold’ environment, a Drowning, i.e. filling of the lungs with water and 3s Vaso-vagal shock, i.e. tne shock of water entering the lower pharynx or upper respiratory passages causing a nervous reflex which stops the heart. To deal with these in turn, the first is by far the commonest cause of death as to immersion. In the unfortunate Lakonia disaster, .of the 124 deaths, there is strong evidence to show that apart from 11 deaths due to injury, most of the remaining 113 were due to hypothermia leading to helplessness unconciousness and then drowning only as a terminal event. when you consider that the.water temperaturé was 64°R, a temperature never obtained around.England, and that help was relatively quickly obtained, you will realise how important is heat loss, Tt has been shown that few people survive for more than seven hours in water at 59 F, again much higher than British sea temperatures, and the survival time in water at 32°F is only a matter of a few minutes. As on land, the best way of keeping warm in the water is to wear warm clothing, Into this category come"wes suits" of which I have no personal experience, but which should be the best of all. If you can get out of the water and sit on your dinghy so much the better as unless the wind is particularly cold your heat loss is slower, Contrary to what might be expected, movement in the water accelerates heat loss as the extra heat generated by muscular effort is more than offset by the removal of the warmer layer of water around, and heated by, the body. Therefore, unless it is to swim a short distance to a rescue boat or the shore it is much better to lie as still possible in the water supported by a life-jacket. As the time of immersion is obviously an important factor, one should.stay as near as possible to the point where rescue might be expected. This usually means strying near the boat. There is no evidence to show that alcohol in normal quantities accelerates heat loss, which may be of some comfort to those if us who imbibe. In the Lakonia disaster it is known that 15 people died from hypothermia after being picked up so it is important, should you rescue someone who has been immersed for some time, to warm them up as quickly as possible. This is really only important if the rescued is “unconscious as conscious people are unlikely to be in danger, The quickest method of warming someone is a warm bath — temperature 97°F - 100 F, but this is onlyof use if they can be bathed within 20 minutes and is seldom feasible. A warm atmosphere, hot water bottles, the close proximity of another human body ‘and warm blankets after removal of the cold wet clothing are the usual methods. So if you cannot rescue yourself, wear warm clothing, keep still and make it as easy as possible for your rescuers by staying near the boat or where they expect you to be. To pass on to the last two headings, prevention is - wear a good life jacket and hold your breath as you go in. Once a person has ceased to breath, irreversible brain damage occurs within 3-5 mins so that any attempt to revive them must be made immediately. If drowning is complicated by hypothermia the chance of successful revival is very small however, Before considering how to revive a person let us consider briefly what happens when lungs fll with water. The water may be fresh or sea water, In the former case the osmotic pressure of the blood causes a rapid absorption of water from the lungs

~ 4 - into the blood stream which so lowers the osmotic pressure of the blood that the red cells burst, releasing a large amount of potassium which the heart cannot tolerate and it stops. This takes place very rapidly, as roughly speaking the minute sacs in the lungs, if all spread out would cover a tennis court and they are designed specially to absorb, In the latter case the reverse occurs as the osmotic pressure of sea water is higher than that of the blood and this causes an outflow of fluid from the blood stream, flooding the lungs and preventing oxygen getting into the blood. The heart can keep beating for 2 few minutes after this occurs, so the chances of successful revival are much higher. The treatment of drowning and also of vaso-vagal shock is the same, namely artificual respirationl I am sure that the simplest and most effective method is mouth to mouth respiration - perhaps better known as the kiss of life. As with all unconscious people, including unconsciousness due to hypothermia, the first essential is to maintain a clear airway. This is done by hooking the forefingers of each hand behind the angle of the jaw of the rescued and lifting the jaw, and thereby the tongue, forward, If possible the lower teeth can be hooked over the upper teeth. It is a waste of time attempting th empty water from the lungs of the rescued. It is much better to attempt to inflate that part of the lung which is not filled with water - usually a considerable proportion, If you kneel facing the feet it is possible to lift the jaw forward, hold the lips together in an airtight joint and breathe gently down the nose. In this position one can watch the chest to see it inflate. Remarkably little effort is required and adequate time should be allowed for the chest to deflate, ahout three times as long as the inflation period. If the sirway is clear, i.e. the tongue is not blocking the back of the throat, the movement of the chest should be gentle and easy. I don't know how long one should continue this as jit is mainly a moral question. If one considers that the brain is dead after five minutes and quadruples this time, I think this is reasonable and is the criterion I have taken on the few occasions I have had to do it. It is important to realise that if the rescued is breathing it is positively dangerous to give artificial respiration. This will only hinder their own respiratory efforts and possibly inflate the stomach, blowing vomit into their air passages and killing then. It is only necessary to keep a clear airway and keep them warm, One last point which I must mention is the question of vomiting, In a conscious person they will get rid of their own vomit but in an unconscious person they may well inhale it with fatal results, Turn them on their side with the head lower than their waist, and no fluid can possibly enter the lungs, This article has turned out to be much longer than I anticipated but even so is only an outline of what happens when one "falls in the water", Greater pens than mine have said "prevention is better than cure" and it is never more true than of sailing accidents, 4,DOCTOR. Port and starboard lights reflected In the east looms Bradwell Station in the bow wave's thrusting crest, hassive With its pulsing power, Startled waders, quit their sandbars Golden lanterns pierce the darkness At jerseyed helmsman's laughing jest, Through the stillness, hour by hour. Startled "stormcock's "arm call ringing Cross the hills in stark formation As prowling dog fox scents its nest Strides its pylons tower by tower Ristant farm dogs break the stillness: And high above the starlight glitters - luuffled echoes come to rest, Icy crystals in sequinned shower, De 6. By the water, watching waiting, , Now quiet, the istuary lies asleeping , As the glow fades out at last, Waiting for another morn Turns one's thought to Romans, Saxons, Creeping tideline reaches shoreward Norsemen, Normans from the past. Before tomorrow's day is born, Pirate ships and flaming beacons, Rising moonglow dulls the starlight Muted creak of smugglers mast. Falsely heralding the dawn , Flashing searchlights seeking bombers. And patient fowler, sitting silent Patient bargemen making fast. Frost—numbed::* hands clutch gun stock worn. T. So the watching week-end sailor Migrant from the City's roar, Counts the twinkling lights of liersea Hears the space jets, trained for war, Wing their flights to far off countries Po And high-above-the sunset soar , . . -6- PILOT'S CUP 1967 We gulped when the Pilot's cup course was announced. Fifteen miles with the wind getting stronger, Up to Southey (close hauled) down to West Mersea S.C. No.5 (close - broad reach) back to Stansgate (close haul/beat. The entries included the Dragons of Terry and Mike, Hornets of Richard, GP14's of Howard, Norman and Ken, Enterprises of Julian and Norman and ourselves. Tide going out, keep out of tide going up through the narrows. Bit choppy up to Osea Pier, in fact very glad of self-balers. Notice in sailing instruction "observe channel marks", Thinks, what are the twins, Julian and Howard doing leaving the Doctor to Porte Oh! well, the Dragons are leaving it to starboard and so ill we. Leave Southey to starboard as instructed. Get on plane after a couple of hundred yards. Stay on plane for miles except for brief rests. Pass Dragons. ixhausted but know that those in front will be disqualified. Norman, Ken etc stop before Stone and go home. Still planing. whoops, there go Howard and Jane. Several cruisers (including the Dragons) around and quite honestly we're not in sufficient control of our own boat to be able to help then. Approach Bradwell Power station, still on plane. Just deciding to go between large metal "breakwater thing" and Bradwell shore when whoops there we go. "Phew it's cold", Boat upright, then over the other way. I get the sails down. John gets the boat up. I hang onto bows as John tries to steer. ‘Jind has taken us to leeward of breakwater, Several cruisers moored. Grab the first one, After a lot of bother the boat is lying head to wind, John is on board, and I'm being hauled in like a sack of potatoes, Estimated water temperature ~ low. Have read A-Doctor's article and know I have only a few minutes to live. My legs feel like jelly.and I can hardly stand, John seems in better shape and returns to dinghy to bale out, Meanwhile the cruiser owners have supplied hot tea, The Dragons go past, The twins, Julian and the Dragons come back. Mr and krs, Tibby volunteer the information that they were about to trawl up to Stansgate but will give us a tow. Their son gets out wind speed indicator - 30 mp.h.+ Gradually legs become stronger, John sits in Spree to steer, Mast got spiked by bowsprit and pruise/ compression crease is main reason for not sailing back, Very grateful for tow. Dragons noted that Richard and Julian went wrong side of Doctor. So victory to Dragons but well done H1073 (and Charles) and 21563 (and Jill). Course (15 miles remember) was completed in 1 hour 52 minutes by the Hornet which isn't bad going, Bleanor. REGATTA -— SPRING BANK HOLIDAY > More than 100 visiting boats arrived at Stansgate for the Bank Holiday Regatta. A handicap race for a Mission to Seamen Pennant attracted forty entries on the Saturday for a closely contested result, The points series started on Sunday morning, with ten classes declared. The Fireballs started after a fifteén minute postponenent - first the wind changed sufficiently to necessitate a reversal of course and then Mundon Buoy was reported aground so course C3 was agreed. The other classes, following at five minute intervals, were Hornets, Kestrels, Flying Juniors, Enterprises GP14's, Fleetwinds, Mirrors, Single-handed handicap (Solos and OK's) and Dinghy Handicap (everything else from Flying Dutchman to a minute clinker built half-decker) - a most impressive Sight! The tide was stronger than the wind for the cruiser start and several boats had to come back to the line after 2 general recall, The afternoon dinghy races were fairly straightforward as far as I can remember, Monday morning dawned bright and windless. C2 was attempted with a probable shortening to 1 lap. The clouds on the horizon began to cover the sky and the wind got up and up. Some classes finished intact but others lost and broke gear after capsizes (up to 25 boats were over according to one eye witness). However, most boats entered the afternoon race, The cruisers had a bit of trouble getting tee to the correct side of the start line and were glad of some assistance from the rescue launch, Sorting out the results was a bit of a rush (but not as bad as coping with the entries on Sunday nmorning). ELC.W, HORNET MAINSHEBT Marconi 5.C. wins at Saltcote The first leg of our annual team race against Saltcote S.C. took place on Saturday 13th May in very hot weather and rather light airs. The Marconi tean had a resounding success winning both races. The Marconi team consisted of Peter Darney and Jane Cottam, Peter Jennings and Geoff “white and Richard and Charles Houlding. The start was the usual running start and the Marconi team got away well with spinnakers up as the gun went except for Peter Darney who pulled down his centre plate instead not being conversant with the Hornet rigging, but he soon found the right rope to pull! Saltcote spotted this and ganged up on him pinching his wind from astern. But some good sailing soon saw Marconi lst, 2nd and 3rd and the finishing order was Jennings, Houlding, Darney. The second race proved more interesting with some unusual wind changes. Saltcote brought in their reserve boat and vigourously swopped sails around from boat to boat, but larconi's once again held the first three positions at the last but one buoy with only a beat lef} to complete to the finish against a strong tide, Unfortunately just prior to this the Houldings lost their spinny pole overboard which was kindly picked up by one of.the .trailing Saltcote boats, The wind then completely dropped and boats began drifting stern first away fron the finishing line. The wind then changed direction through 180 degrees to a run and slowly began to puff again, Peter Darney was quick to spot this and hoisted spinny much to Saltcote's amazement and soon built up a small but useful lead on the three Saltcote boats, Sailing right up the middle of the river against the tide he managed to tempt the Saltcote boats into mid-stream leaving the Houldings and Jennings on the lea shore out of the tide. Here the Houldings soon began to loose ground not being able to hoist their spinny. Peter Jennings then moved over to attack from the leeward side luffing and eventually sitting on the windward side of the second Saltcote boat. By now the Houlding brothers had also moved into mid-stream behind the fleet and had the nerve to ask for their Spinny pole back from the Saltcote boat. Surprisingly they thravit in the water and the Houldings sailed up and picked it. up. Peter Darney was just ahead of the first Saltcote boat and to windward covering him well with only inches between them at times, Peter Jennings was using similar tactics on Saltcote's second boat slowing it down by Geoff “hite alternatively filling the spinny and then letting it flap, allowing. the Houldings to catch up, eventually drawing alongside Peter and Geoff tO windward, As soon as they were level Peter drew away from the Saltcote boat and the finishing order was Ist Peter Darney, 2nd Saltcote, 3rd Peter Jennings and 4th Houldings. The return race will take place at liarconi's later in the year. H.Ornet. Welcome to Howard Mitchell who has just purchased Hornet 418.
