oe A SHORT DINGHY CRUISE Dave Polley (GP14) and Fred Partlett (Wayfarer) arrived early at Stansgate on Saturday the lst July for their planned cruise to Clacton, and at 0830 hours both boats were apparently ready to sail, Dave, with his wife and daughter was soon off on his way down river but Fred's mainsail jammed and, mindful of his capsize the previous week end, he lowered his mast and found the luff groove choked with Blackwater mud, By this time Dave had come about to see what the hold up was but, re-assured he set off down river once more. Fred and Linda with Alan Polley as the third crew member left the hard at 0900 hours confident that they would overhaul the GP14 before very long. However, it was soon apparent that Dave was continuing to draw ahead, and nearing Bradwell he came about once more and asked Fred if.he had been fishing!! Once out of the Blackwater howeverthe Wayfarer surged ahead past the wreck buoys off Mersea and on to the Inner Bench Head, The wind was S.5, about force 2 although the forecast was force 3 and it made for very pleasant sailing all the way up the coast, Fred 'hove to' in the Wayfarer when he was getting out of touch with the GP14 and finally ‘rounded Clacton Pier at approximately 1230 hours shortly followed by Dave, who found himself gicing with a Shearwater whose helmsman showed a lack of courtesy by sailing too close, With the oe bagscads the party had lunch and lazed for a while in the sun. As the tide turned, the boats swung broadside on and it was decided to put them on anchor, it would have been wiser to have anchored on arrival as by this .time both’ centre boards were jammed with ania) Snune=4 and it was quite a task to free them, Although there was an. onshore wind, getting off was no problem and the boats were soon away watched by a larze number of holiday makers lining the promenade above. Running and reaching, the trip back lasted 2 hours 40 mins, and was very enjoyable. All voted it a successful ‘day cruise and hoped for another like it. P,o, Subject te weather and suitable tides ‘this trip could ‘be repeated, If anyone is interested would they please contact Dave Polley or Fred Partlett both of whom would be pleased to go again, Fred Partlett. Oss FF a? LAYING-UP Supper AND DANCE Wednesday 8th November 1967. 7.0.pm for 7.30.pm at The Heybridge Country Club. Owing to the fact that the Company can no longer accommodate Dinner and Dance functions at their Canteens, we have been forced to find an alternative venue for this year's Laying-Up Supper and Dance. Places in the Chelmsford area which can cope with large numbers sare very few, but by personal contact we have been able to go to the Heybridge Country Club, For those who do not know, this club is very attractive, and the Manager has personally assured me that he intends to do his utmost to make it an excellent evening. It is realised that Wednesday is not the most popular day of the week but we had no choice of date and were very fortunate to get any booking -— even when booking November last year, They hope, if we wish to go there again in 1968,to be able to give us 2 Friday booking, This brings me to a vital point -— as we are now moving away from our own Canteens we will be unable to fit in any people who "decide to come at the last minute". The tickets will be on sale from approximately lst October and the last day of sale will be Friday 3rd November - we are sorry but there can be no exceptions to this as we are committed to the Caterers on that date for our final total. There is also.a definite table plan to be drawn and it will not be possible to alter the seating after that day, so will you please let your Ticket Agent know with whom you wish to sit. Last point - the price will be 32/6. I know this is more than we have charged in the past but then we were helped by the very low charges made by the Company Canteens — for which we were all most grateful. We are still trying to keep the price as low as possible "at the same time giving value for money" and we look forward to seeing as many of our members as possible on that night. The number will be strictly limited to 230 - so please do get your tickets early - (pay days are 4th October and lst November). John Barnard. -7- ASSORTED NOTICES FROM THE R.Y.A. The Use of Flares and Rockets— 30th June. We have learnt from the rescue services, which do so much for yachtsmen, that a great and growing number of unnecessary sorties have been caused owing to the misuse of flares and other distress signals. It must be borne in mind that although a white flare is not an official distress signal, even such a flare may cause alarm for two reasons. Firstly, Some white flares which have been stored for some time give off a pinkish glow, Secondly, there are a great many occasions when a boat in distress, which has no official signals, burns petrol soaked rags or Similar material. For these and other reasons even "white" flares cannot be ignored by the rescue services. There have been many instances where sorties have been made and either no vessel found, or information has been received that the flare was a private signal to a wife or friends. Yachtsmen are also reminded that a fire-arms certificate is required for 2a Verey pistol, It is earnestly hoped that you will discourage your members from using any flares or other signals except when in distress. If, however, flares are to be fired as finishing.signals at the end of a night race it is earnestly hoped that prior warning of this possibility will be given to any distress and rescue control centre which might be alerted by the coastguards, the police or members of the public. The identification of such property is often difficult because the owners are not in possession of serial numbers and other identification marks. At a recent meeting held at Yallasea Yacht Marina, it was suggested that boat yard owners keep records of serial numbers of outboard motors and other equipment owned by their customers. This would assist in immediate identification should such property be stolen. The Chief Superintendent, C.1I.D., B.J.Barkway, C.I.D. Springfield, Chelmsford would like comments on this matter and whether we would be prepared to co-operate in the keeping of such records. -~2- MAMGU TROPHY RUNNER-UP Donald and Barbara Woods wrote this interesting log a few weeks after their trip to Holland earlier this year and earned themselves a "runner-up" award, : APRIL IN HOLLAND The aim was to open the 1967 season with a cruise in company to Rotterdam, through the Dutch waterways and back via Flushing. The craft are "Jayess", a Snapdragon 23, skippered by Dr. McKendrick Marconi 58.C., and "Ruadh Sgeir", Content 29 skippered by Ramond Sutton of Creeksea Y.C. Barbara and I shipped with Raymond, Ingrid and their 17 year old son, Ian. We left moorings at Creeksea 1030 hrs, April 5th. just before high water and with a N.E., Force 6-8 romped up to Harwich under working jib only, averaging 6 knots. A beautiful sail marred only by the tragic loss of 4 gallons of home brewed beer, This split from an inalequately chocked off polythene cask which fell and split. Even in a G.R.P boat you can't reclaim it from the bilges! We picked up a mooring just below Pin Mills this is an error inaN,E. gale as it was damnably uncomfortable all night. We Should have anchored down river ‘bélow thé big Ieft hand bend to get shelter. April 6th was a very: rough day redeemed by getting two "pinlets" 7 pint containers) of beer at the Butt and Oyster. These keep seven weeks unopened and three days after opening. They travelled well. There was no Sign of our consort in Harwich harbour. By 1800 hrs although the forecast was gales,-local conditions were still and calm. It seemed possible we were in the centre of a depression; however the 0200 hrs. forecast was N.f 5-6, We still had a flat calm so off we went under motor leaving moorings 0310 hrs. April 7th. Time being short it had been agreed to ‘motor/sail if speed fell below 4 knots.- By ‘0600 hrs all bar two of the crew were incapacitated by sea sickness and remained so for the duration of the crossing, the main trouble being a peculiar lumpy sea left over from the gale. The wind came up just before 0600 hrs and at 0845 we put in eight rolls to the main and sailed thus until the next day. By 1000 hrs. the Galloper L.V was abeam, log 32.2 wind NE 3-4, 090 Magnetic 4 knots. -At- 2050 hrs. the loom of the Goeree L.V. was detected log 78.6, 086 M, wind :NE 3-4. At this point I had expected to see only the Goeree light, but the coastal lights also were clearly visible, in particular the 3 sec. ela of Neauimapelte light house. ne Rea A slight brush, with a — was solved by ating ihe spreader lights to the navigation and masthead lights. This worked very well but apparently means "I am fishing but my green light has gone out", About the same time I was puzzled by searchlights on two small vessels to starboard. These kept sweeping the sea in a random fashion.. In.fact they were probably fishing boats indicating that they had gear. lying out on-the side to which the lights were directed, At 2150 hrs April 7th the wind fell lights; attempts to use the engine were unsuccessful: it would run for a few minutes then stop sounding like a petrol fault. Petrol was appearing at the carburettor and water was circulatings further than that-we.could not go in the dark. The wind remained variable and light-but the tide was north going early flood and we had been set to the south of. the intended course. About midnight we picked up the whistle buoy of the Schouwen Bank so knew exactly our position. Later we had a transit of the L.V and: the Bollen wreck. buoy as we travelled slowly up the coast mainly with the tide. There is an overall general .N.i. tidal set up the Dutch and Belgian coasts. By 0230 hrs the Goeree L.V. was abeam and by 0400 we were off the Hook. 7 ‘ “= The chart shows 3 buoys about 5 miles offshore plus a cryptic light on the northern mole end "Fl W.R, 3sec'"' None of us had been there before. We had about 33 assorted lights plus plenty of traffic. Vihat do you make of a stationary, close cluster of four yellow lights, two vertical fixed, and two horizontal flashing? Or of a flashing white light, the size ge frequency of a buoy light but which appears and disappears with no recognisable periodicity and possibly in a slightly different place?

io Bm There was a cluster of five huge white arc lamps over-lying a just discernible long darkness - a steamer's lights came out from shore towards this, disappeared behind the arc lights and reappeared as she stood out to sea. The end of the mole? Meanwhile a steady stream of shipping was passing astern of us and sailing straight for the shore. The absence of crashes and bangs indicated they knew what they were doings: we didn't so stood off until dawn. This plus the turn of the tide revealed that the cluster of white arc lights were distribited along the 10,000 ton freighter in the anchoring area N.W. 5 miles of the Hook mole, The yellow lights were attached to a small vessel moored a mile further north and doing goodness knows what, That hide and seek white flashing buoy is a manually operated light on the pilot boat. The key and virtually only light to the Hook is on the end of the northern mole and flashes 5 times white followed by a 3 second red light, The North Sea Pilot 1963, P.194 line 20 does not state this, and the chart is not explicit. With daylight the engine problem was tackled, as it turned out very wisely, The petrol tank of stainless steel in the cockpit locker had never been given petrol except through a fine filter funnel. None the less the filter chamber at the base of the tank was choked with corroded filth very difficult to remove. Once this was done the engine ran well and none too soon, The North-Sea Pilot recommends caution attempting the Hook in an onshore wind and I can endorse this. The wind had fallen light, the tide was ebbing and the seas were something better experienced by daylight. For two miles offshore and between the mole ends they would have been most alarming to have met abruptly in the dark. Indeed on the southern mole was a 7-8,000 ton Greek freighter plus its tug where they had clearly been cast a day or so earlier, A chastening sights; without the engine we Should never have got in against the ebb with only a light following wind. At 0900 hrs April 8th we entered Berghaven 119 miles and 29 hrs out of darwich. This little harbour on the port hand just inshore is easily found, but, being an official herbous for lifeboat etc only yachts in transit are permitted to use it. ve Stayed to breakfast and tidy up, everybody having rapidly revived from seasickness. Customs came and cleared us and told us we were the first of the season. Leaving Berghaven we motored up the Nieuwe Waterweg leaving Eurpoort and its new canal over to starboard. It is a fascinating if dirty trip; so much industry and so many ships and barges. Here we made our first acquaintance with the extraordinary fact that a°1,000 ton barge lightly laden or decks awash could pass 20 ft away at 8-10 knots. and yet the disturbance to our yacht would be less than that from many an. outboard motor boat on the Blackwater. This is just as well with the colossal amount of traffic otherwise the canal walls would suffer and life on a cruising yacht would be intolerable. How it is achieved with blunt blows, slab sides and much power I do not understand, We passed the Schiedam Y.C to port, ctlearly identifiable and looking very attractive, and went on to the Royal Yacht Club de Maas arriving 1200 hrs., log 133.7, This lies on the port hand soon after sighting the bridges of Rotterdan, We were made welcome and had we thought to pack white ties could have joined in their Fitting Out Party that evening, We shopped and admired Rotterdam, especially the traffic free shopping precinct and grand multi-halled arts centre.’ (Memo to lady crew members: the Y.C lies in the heart of the seaman's mission areas, Don't do ag oyrs did and go ashore alone unless prepared to handle unusual situations!). After 22 hrs on my feet qT Slept well, Sunday April 9th. Still no sign of our consort. We looked at T.S. Mercator, a Belgian barquentine’ some 40 years old with more than 140, 657 sea miles of training voyages behind her. - Following local knowledge we-left for Willemstad. The major bridges open only at fixed times on weekdays and often not at all on Sundays. So instead of going on through Rotterdam to Dordrecht we turned to take the Code Maas. Traffic on the canals keeps to the right, so when turning left you make a good wide cirele to avoid. getting a ispee portside amidships, as it comes out of the branch canal. The bridges lift in response to 3 hefty toots on the horn; they rise just far enough to permit your passage and

25 Be and a bit more, The journey from Rotterdam to Willemstad can be accomplished by 3 routes, Attention should be paid to the bridge opening times and the state of the tide. We followed the Code Maas under three bridges, ignoring the Spui and skirting Dordrecht on the west side by the Dordsche Kil. Even on Sunday we met barges six abreast in the canal including a phenomenal monster of at least 3000 tons capacity, consisting of a square box propelled from the rear by an articulated power unit. Heaven knows how it steers in a cross wind! However there is absolutely no cause for alarm in amongst all this traffic such is the perfect discipline. ‘Je then came out on to the Hollandsche Diep and had a gantle down wind, down tide evening sail, on a vast deserted sheet of water, with negligible evidence of civilisation, which brought us to Willemstad at 1620 hrs, log 167.2 The Pilot says Willemstad has only 4 ft of waters; we drew 4% ft. However, at the Royal Maas a member had told us he regularly took his 40 ft long 54 ft draft motor sailer in. In fact against the quay there is only 3 ft L.W.S. but six feet away from the bank there is enough water at all states of the tide. The harbour is tiny: so is the town and it is. charming. There are several boats concerned with dyke works using the harbour and it is possible to tie up to one of these, We walked round the town's ancient stellate moat, practically stepping over sleeping ducks and swans, who pay scant heed to humans, We then adjourned to "Het Wapen van Willemstad" on the quay and enjoyed what the skipper described, with massive meiosis, as a "memorable steak" highly to be recommended and extremely reasonable, We slept well that night tool. continued next month. -2.- COMMODORE'S REPORT. NOVEMBER, 1967 This time last year I was somewhat apprehensive of the task at having been elected Commodore of the Marconi Sailing Club. Today I feel a sense of achievement having completed my first year of office. This, however, would not have been possible without the whole hearted support of the Officers and Committee of the Club. 1967 has indeed been quite a hectic year for me since I have also held office as Vice Chairman of the M.A.S.C. The M.A.5S.C. have in the past year adopted a new constitution which will no doubt benefit all members and sections in the future. Looking back I consider that the Marconi 8.C. have had a successful year. Perhaps you will agree with me on the completion of my report. You will have read in the Minutes of last year's A.G.M. the question of ship to shore radio was raised, Our licence was withdrawn by the G.P.O Since our existing equipment was unsuitable. Early in the year we started making enquiries with the Marconi Marine Company who offered us two MIMCo Bantams, We then made a successful appeal to the MASC for 50% grant of the cost on the understanding that the club members would be asked to donate the balance, this was agreed. I am pleased to say that as a result of my appeal to you, we were able to purchase these two very fine equipments. I would like to take this opportunity of thanking our President, Dr, Eastwood who made a substantial donation and all those members who donated sums, large and small. Thank you. The social aspect this year has been somewhat indifferent, from the financial point of view. This has no reflection in any way on our retiring Social Secretary, John Barnard, and the Social Committee who have worked extremely hard in an endeavour to "make it pay". The public functions organised so well in the past year have not been very fruitful, as trends do change, we must change, and possibly consider more social activity at Stansgate in the future. John provided us with a first class Winter programme of lectures and discussions, all of which were well attended. In addition we had an excellent Barbeque at Stansgate for members and guests , As a finale, it has been said that we had our best ever Laying-Up Dinner and Dance this year at the Heybridge Country Club. Thank you John and your band of willing helpers. I am pleased to say that we still have the services of Mr.Underdown our caretaker, He has done a grand job over the past year, he may not always be around when you go to Stansgate, but it is always evident that he has been around. After a severe storm or blow I can always expect a telephone call from him to report any damage, or loss, to club and member's boats and gear. I am sure it is a comforting thought to Cruiser and dinghy owners to know 'he is about' when there is a storm. The Galley services have been maintained by Mrs. Whenty it is hoped that she will continue next season. We have had the misfortune to have three visits from burglars during the past season. On the second occasion a person was charged and found 'guilty' by the court. We have received certain information recently, which has been passed to the C.I.D. and could help them with their enquiries regarding the third visit. Our losses however have not been light; the Bar has been rifled on each occasion, losses would have been much heavier, but for the fact that most of the stock is kept at home by the Officers of the Club. The box for 'Brazil' fees was broken into twice and completely removed on the third occasion. In addition several items of club property were stolen including our grass cutter, fortunately this has been recovered. Due to

the constructional nature of our clubhouse we cannot get insurance cover for theft, The retiring Committee have discussed the security problem and have made recommendations for consideration by your new Committee. Also on the question of Security, steps must be considered for next season to protect our privacy at Stansgate , since it is a known fact that not all the people seen at Stansgate are members of H.S.C. Regarding the Cadet Section they started off so well, but unfortunately the enthusiasm waned. This was partly due to the fact that their Skipper Tom Gaskell became engaged on urgent Company business and unfortunately could not give the time he would have liked. However, the flame is still there and I have high hopesofasuccessful Cadet Section in 1968. Thank you Eleanor Witter for a very successful year of continuity in producing 'Navigans' my thanks also to Avril Stevens for the typing effort, The Administration and work involved in running a Club of our size is quite a responsibility for your honary Officers and Committee, they cannot do it all, our thanks therefore must go out to all those members who give their services, whether it be in the Race box — rescue launch - bar or at working parties, without their support we would cease tq be 2 club, Throughout the season we have had quite lengthy discussions with Mr. Sparrow regarding the state of repair to the Stansgate Road, Late in the season it was agreed to go ahead and effect the necessary repairs. You will recall that through the medium of Navigans I informed members of this and asked you to support any decision taken on the Club's behalf. In an effort to reduce costs, several estimates were obtained; consequently the contractor engaged is an associate or a good friend to the Club. several estimates were obtained for shingle; the hot tar we shall require in the Spring will be purchased at a special price, with trimmings, by virtue of the fact that we have a gentleman amongst us who has certain connections with the Tar Contractors. Very shortly the proposal by the retiring Committee will be put to you for an extra sub of 10/- per adult member, in order to pay part cost of the repair, You might say, why only 10/an We have said 10/- because many of us use the road more than others, in fact some of our members don't get to Stansgate at all (neither have we levied Cadets). So we appeal to those of you who use the road frequently to dig a little deeper into the pocket and clear your conscience, I am sure you will enjoy the ride more and save pounds on fair wear and tear, incidentally all extra donations will be receipted and shown in the Treasurer's Accounts. The question could now be is it worth it? The answer is ‘yes! Since we are very hopeful of another five years at Stansgate. Mr.Sparrow, our landlord, has entered into negotiations with us in order to prepare a new lease, in fact the matter is now in the hands of our Solicitors. The Marina project has not been shelved, but it is possible that it may be modified to be developed in stages. It is considered that Marconi 5,C. could well be involved in the first stage, whereas providing it is acceptable, we would be offered a very long term lease, I cannot Say more at this stage but you can rest assured that we will inform members of developments, when it is possible for us to do so. With the promise of a new lease, the problem of Planning Permission becomes evident, Our existing Planning Permission expires in April 1968. Steps are being taken to renew immediately for a period of a further five years, Should, however, we desire to rebuild or modify our existing © premises we shall, of course, have to submit any proposed plans for consideration to the Planning Authorities. The matter will rest with your new Committee,

~~ In order to build or modify we must of course have surplus funds. At present we have no surplus, but as a result of negotiations between your Vice Commodore, Stan Allerton and the MASC, we should be in a position to have a surplus in the future since the MSC have undertaken to pay our fixed expenditure in future, i.e. rent, rates, sewerage, insurance, telephone, rent. Meanwhile we shall continue to improve the facilities and Goodwill at Stansgate and may I wish youall a very happy season next year and many years to come at Stansgate. Thank you, J» Bigden — Commodore. SECRETARY'S REPORT 1967 Committee meetings have been held on the first Monday of each month and committee members attendance has been almost perfect. Sailing, Social, Finance, Bar and Membership sub-committees were formed to deal with these details of the Sailing Section activities. Eleanor Witter has made an excellent job of editing 'Navigans' and all the Committee wish to thank her for her efforts, The Club now has a total membership of 540 niembers. During the year seven more associate members were able to join the Club but there is still a waiting list of would be associate members. Duty rotas drawn up by the Committee have generally been well adhered to and the duties well performed. Insurance cover for the Club is as follows:-— 1. Club premises and contents, £1730 for fire damage. 2. Club indemnity £25000 for Third Party property £5000 for one clain. oo 3. 16' rescue boat £400 * 4, Brazil £150 plus £25 (trailer). x 5. Walker Fisherman £167 * 6. Walker 8! Dinghy -& 40 *% 7. 20' Rescue Boat £350 * All plus £25000 maximum third party indemnity. 8. 2 Radio transmitter/receiver sets £100 each. I would like to thank all the Officers and Members who have assisted me during the last 12 months and I regret that as I am no longer employed by the Company I must resign from my position as Secretary of the Sailing Section. I hope I shall be allowed to become an Associate Member enabling me to continue to enjoy the Club activities, Tony Cherry. SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT FOR 1967 In 1967, 198 boats were registered, at the last count, for use from Stansgate, This number is made up from 114 dinghies and 44 | cruisers. Of these some 4 cruisers and 50 dinghies were entered for organised Club activities, Although a reasonable percentage this does not give a true picture since those that entered regularly is considerably less than this as may be seen from the Results published from month to month in Navigans,

-~5- On the whole it has been a successful season although many events for both our Club and others on the river have been disrupted by adverse weather conditions. The season started well with Points racing getting under way on the first scheduled weekend. With the exception of the Handicap Class the majority of scheduled points races were sailed and in some cases the overall results showed narrow margins for the winners. Again this year we have held open meetings, the Challenge Cup, Spring Bank Holiday Regatta and Hornet Open Meeting, a new venture this year, being well supported. Na& so well supported were the Cruiser Cup and the GP.14 open meeting. In 1967 we held the Enterprise Triple 'K' Cup and Fleetwind Designer's Trophy within the Regatta and it is proposed for Next Season to include also the GP.14 Commodore's Cup and the Cruiser Cup within this weekend. This arrangement will leave more weekends available for Club Sailing. We have again held team races with 3 Clubs; Locally Osea and Saltcote and further afield the B.B.C's Sailing Club, Ariel at Teddington. Of these we lost to both Ariel and Osea but the Hornets were successful in retaining the Hornet Team Challenge Cup for the 2nd year. Two new ventures were started this years the Hornet Invitation Points with Stone Sailing Club and the Barnacle Points’ series for boats normally kept on moorings. It was intended that Cruiser Owners from M.B.Y.C. should be invited to take part in the Barnacle Points but this unfortunately did not materialise. On the other hand the Hornet Series was a great success with a total of 22 boats taking part at one time or another, This series we hope will be repeated against next year. Perhaps, at least for me, the most disappointing aspect of the season was the havoc that the weather brought to the Helmsman of the Year Trophy weekend. This revealed a weakness in the arrangement for determining a winner in as far as we put all our eggs in one basket. As a result of much thought on this subject it has been suggested that the Committee consider holding a series of races during the year from which a winner can be determined. No doubt you will be hearing more about this from the new Sailing Committee, The Ladies Cup was another event which was marred by the weather. After a postponment from a previous date the winner of the re-sailed race was found to be the only boat to survive the course. Not very much can be done about this sort of thing except to look into a crystal ball in January when the programme is being finalised, in the hope that some indication of weekends with good weather can be found. Rescue Launches have been in considerable demand this season with help being provided fh times of need to anyone in trouble and in particular to our neighbouring Clubs. These services have been provided mainly using the 16ft No.? but during the season the-"New' 26 ft No.4 has been used to back up where necessary..-- This new Launch has now been provided Watertight and the engine reliable so it is with confidence that we can complete fitting out during the winter’nonths so that the boat will be in full commission for the 1968 season.. Brazil has seen much use this season.but due to our unwelcome visitors we are not able to show in the Balance Sheet any return from her hire. However, much of the use was by Cadet members for which there is no charge. The total number of hours sailing enjoyed in her by Club members, as recorded in the book, was about 100 hours. The Reap Commodore was in charge ofMoorings again this Season and has done his best to help and keep all applicants happy. Moorings are, however, in great demand and the supply of g&$d moorings in the deeper waters is very nearly exhausted. . Tonight sees the conclusion of my term of Office as your Sailing Secretary, I have enjoyed doing the job although during the last Season I felt that I was not able to give as much time as I would like. I am however seeking election to the Main Committee so.that the experience I

-§- have can be available to my Successor who will, subject to your approval, be Peter Batey. I am not going to single out any individuals to whom I am indebted but I would like to thank all those who served on the Sailing Committee with me for their help and support with the Club Activities and to thank all Club Members who have helped while not being members of the Committee. Perhaps a word of thanks is also due to Club members who have supported the Sailing Activities, Without their support 2a great deal of time and effort would have been wasted and good support makes one feel the job is worth doing. I hope, sincerely that you will all give Peter the support that I have received and help him as much as possible while he is finding his feet. Thank you all once again, I shall be happy to answer any questions members may want to ask. John Witter. PROPOSAL PASSED AT THE AGM TO COVER PART COST OF REPAIRS TO THE STANSGATE ROAD. At the A.G.M. on Monday 23rd November, the following resolution was put to the meeting and passed unanimously. "tn order to pay for part cost of the repairs to the Stansgate Road, an additional subscription of 10/— per adult member, be paid with the 1968 subscription". The Committee feel that those members who consider they use the Club facilities sufficiently may contribute an amount greater thah the proposed increases their extra contribution will be greatly appreciated and it may then be possible to clear the debt in one year. Failing this it may be necessary to ask members for an increased subscription in 19692 In the rider you will see that we are asking members who most use the facilities to dig deeper into their pockets to swell the funds so that a further levy does not have to be made. The opinion expressed at the meeting was that the improvement was considered to be worth the cost of a tyre and we are hoping that many people will agree with this sentiment. As members who have been to Stansgate since the end of the season will have found, the majority of the work has been done and only the top dressing remains to be done during the first spell of fine weather in the Spring. A BOOK FOR CHRISTMAS It's not exactly hot from the presses but its probably the only novel whose setting is Stansgate and Steeple. Rider Haggard used to visit his brother Admiral Haggard at Stock, and around the beginning of this century he must have visited out sailing site. His story "The Brethren" concerns the family living at Steeple Hall at the time of the Third Crusade, At that time Stansgate Abbey was flourishing, but the road from Steeple seems to have been as bad as it was this year. AS a wine merchant delivering the Christmas order at Steeple Hall says; "The roads in this part of the country are such that it has taken me four long hours to come from the Abbey here, most of which time we spent in mudholes that have wearied the horses and I fear strained the wheels of my waggon", The creek at Ramsey ‘iick is described in some detail and although this is probably how it was 60 years ago rather than 800, it still makes an interesting bit of history. a - Oo-- APRIL IN HOLLAND 1967 (continued from November 'Navigans') Monday April 10th, misty, dry, light N.@. winds. The Harbour Master advised us to leave briskly, for only two hours fair tide remained. We left 1000 hrs nearly losing the outboard motor, which, stored on the pushpit, was neatly snatched over board by a bight of mooring wire. It was fortunately retained by a bit of thin nylon, but its securing bolts were completely distorted by the jerk. On leaving the harbour we appreciated the H.li's advice as the tide siezed and swept us south at 3-5 knots. Progress in these waters in fog would be very difficult. They are featureless; the buoys have no lights or sound signals, On two occasions we found buoys had been reversed in sequence, This could be puzzling! At Zijpe there is a narrows for a mile, which probably gives interesting tidal effects in view of the mean tide strength of 3+ knots, but we passed at slack water. The whole of these waters eventually will be non tidal as an outer and inner chain of barrages are being constructed to seal off all but the Rotterdam and Flushing entrances to the coast, Approaching Zieriksee we passed under the 2% mile long Easter Schelde Brug which is a colossal and beautiful bridge. There is a bascule portion to the north but anything up to 45 ft high just sails under. The ends were lost in mist when we passed, We arrived at Zieriksee 1430 hrs. log 192.4 and tied up alongside the pontoon which is the first thing one comes to and is meant for visitors, This is not mentioned in the Pilots: there is 84 feet of water there, It is anattractive town with good shops and restaurants, but the upper parts of the harbour have the dirtiest waters we came &CTOSS. Tuesday April llth. we left at 0925 and motored upwind back to the entrance to the Veersemeer. Under an arch of the great bridge we saw an ancient windmill turning, At the entrance to the narrow channel the wind came aft, so up genoa to try and keep pace with a small trader up to the locks 8 knots recorded in good spells, As we came up to the Zandkreek lock she drew ahead and not being sure of the room available (another barge with cabin top fenced off as a playpen was already in the lock) we hung back only to get the Dutch equivalent of "Get a move on" on the loud hailer. At least I hope that's what was said. The now tideless meer all the way from Easter Schelde to Veere is being developed to have berths for 6000 yachts over the next two years; it is to be the biggest water sporting place in Europe. A striking feature of the waterways we had visited was the absence of much evidence of pleasure sailing. However there were two large new marinas on the meer, Veere is yet another charming little town, once a fishing port with historic Scots connections, now only a tourist attraction and yacht harbour. The harbour no longer dries out of course. For the first time we were the second English yachts another had been in a couple of day's earlier. After lunch we moved to the chandler's in the canal and filled up with petrol and water. Here you may do your washing and there is a restaurant as well as the boatyard. Just as we were leaving our long sought consort appeared from astern. It transpired she had in view of the weather opted for Flushing rather than the Hook and had been to Middelburg, Veere and Goes being everywhere the first English yacht of the season, With great delight we adjourned to Middelburg arriving 1915 hrs. log 215.4. In passing, the lock between Veere and Middelburg as usual had a large and small portion. We had to use the large basin and found all possible attachment points for warps had long since been knocked off the walls by barges. A friendly hand on the dockside was of great help. Middelburg is a thriving town, the main canal and quay are too busy to moor, but just to the north there is a branch canal, leading into a basin with three lesser canals. Such yacht centre as there is lies in the left hand of the three, but it is feasible, and no-one disturbed us in 1965 or 1967 when we moored against the basin wall.

The shops are excellent, the buildings particularly those lining the old circumferential canal, very attractive. There is a model layout of the island of Walcheren and,a theatre. Best of all take a compass, steer for the S.i. corner of the market square. There you will find a restaurant where if you are-not put off by its formal appearance you will have an excellent, very substantial and reasonable meal as we did. We now had time in hand, but the forecast looked as if there might be a deterioration after about 24 hours -as a front came in from the Atlantic. We decided to try a new policy and start the voyage in the evening thus getting the night over whilst we were fresh. We left fiddelburg 1525 hrs April 12th and motored to Flushing; there is a pleasant little yacht basin and club there where hot showers may be hads the town has little interest. Wie locked out at 1725 hrs in a flat caln, misty with rain squalls so motored steadily just to the north of the buoys of the southern big ship channel. This course is better lit and buoyed than the northern one and there was a more direct tidal set from the coast in our favour, Our consort attempting the Deurloo channel | in daylight had been unable to see any buoys. These are shown on charts | about 1962 but not on more recent ones. These in any case are not lit | but were present two years ago and are quoted in the Pilot 1965 and the | channel is said to be used by fisherman. . By 2130 a steady force 4—5 NE was blowing and we were off the Goote Bank buoy course 315M. At 2215 the Noord Hinder L.V. was sighted ew and by 0004 it was abeam, distant 3 miles, log 259, speed 5 knots. Course was changed to 295M and at 0315 hrs, April 13th the loom of the Galloper L.V. was seen, and at 0530 it was abean, In tacking the jib | sheet spring shackle jumped open. By 0820 the Sunk L.V. was abeam. At | 0840 the wind fell light and the tide flooding, the engine was started to work to the northward. At 0900 the engine bekan to overheat seriously | despite having followed the handbook instructions -re greasing the water a pump. Cure was effected by 3% caps of grease smartly administered. We were being set south of the Cork Ledge and had to use the engine to clear this. We arrived Harwich 1120 hrs. log 319.5 and promptly ran aground on the Guarda sand looking for the Customs. We should have confined ourselves to the outermost of the moorings where there is enough water. The rising tide took us off, but the Customs eventually appeared on a pleasure steamer well out in the harbour because she drew 7-8 ft. We moored to the small wooden fishing boat quay to clear Customs and have breakfast. We left at 1320 hrs for Walton backwaters, the 1400 hrs forecast gave Galloper visibility 110 yds.,we were glad to be in, ~ At 1440 hrs we picked up a mooring in the Twizzle, log 326.9, thus | completing a happy cruise for Barbara, Ian and myself who had to leave ~~ ship to return home, | EPLLOG F The relatively uncomplicated success of this trip was due in large part to the boat and the skill of its owners in organising Shipboard life. The Contest 29 is a G.R.P sloop of Dutch manufacture with 2 10 hep. Marstal petrol auxiliary. L.O.A. 29 ft, Beam 7% ft, Draft 4% ft, Headroom 6 ft -— except at the mast lintel! It is one of the best designed yachts for living we have seen especially in view of its highly competitive price. It handles well but owing to a very Short keel is very quick on the helm and difficult to make self-steering. Later models are having the keel extended to correct this minor flaw. The interior is a complex of well designed lockers etc and the logical and efficiently maintained stowage by the owners showed its value. In the dark it was possible to lecate any required object at first try by an informed guess at the most likely locker. This works so long as everyone puts things back in place thus maintaining the stowage plan. The galley in particular is a masterly example of good planning, easy to use at sea or at anchor.

A useful aid was the Seafix —-------- a new combined R.D.F/hand bearing compass. coe a THE OTHER HALF OF THE STORY After reading part one of Donald Wood's interesting account of his trip to Holland (November Navigans) I thought I must write a brief addendum. "Jayess" is a 23 foot bilge keel Snapdragon with a Seafarer Echo Sounder, a sum—-log and a Pilot Pal R.D.F as navigational aids. We had arranged to holiday with "Ruadh Sgeir" — hoping to meet either in the Orwell or in Rotterdam. Weslipped moorings at 1140 hours on Wednesday April 5th after considerable difficulty loading stores from the dinghy in a really nasty chop. I had two crew, Philip and Michael, but Michael had to leave us as ‘soon as we got to Holland, giving more room but more watch-keeping for the rest of the holiday, It was blowing hard and with the working jib and 8 rolls in the main we kept registering 8 knots. This was too much so we put in 4 more rolls and had a glorious sail arriving at Stone Banks buoy in under four hours, Here we met wind against tide and with a full gale blowing we had an extremely wet and uncomfortable 2 hours motor-sailing the last four miles before anchoring in the lea of the river bend below the visitor's moorings. Hence we did not see "Ruadh Sgeir". who I thought - wrongly - must have decided to stay in the Crouch. The gale continued all Thursday with force 10 forecast for Thames so we motored into Felixstowe for a few hours peace but were told we had to leave before night if we did not want to move every hour or two, | At 1100 hrs on Friday with a force 5 Northerly actual and forecast we sailed for Holland with the working jib and 8 rolls. Although there was rather a lumpy swell following the gale we made 4% - 5 knots. We all remained fit though bitterly cold when night fell and quite unable to get warm anywhere or anyhow. At that time I was still hoping to make the Hook so our course took us north of the Galloper Sands and we did not see the L.V.. However, the night forecast was force 6 onshore so the Hook was out as far as I was concerned, .We altered course for Flushing, passing the N,Hinder at 2300 hours where the wind fell and we turned the engine on. The Thornton Bank whistle Buoy appeared dead ahead in due course, From there I tried to find the Deurloo channel but instead of buoys were only breakers. When we saw a half—covered wreck among the surf we turned round very smartly and closed the shore north of the Kaloo Bank — quite 2a long way round. We locked in at Flushing at 0900 hours on Saturday. The sun shone and all the bridges opened immediately as we motored gently up to Veere where later on we had our usual excellent steak at the cellar restaurant - and a phone call home for one and ninepence! On Monday Philip and I -— now on our own — sailed to Goes - a charming town. We were the only inhabited yacht in the rather overgrown yacht harbour, and the first foreign visitor at this as well.as at our other ports of call, The red ensign was hoisted in our honour but it looked a bit lonely. On the way back on Tuesday we jilled around outside the huge Veerse. Meer lock. After the gates opened and one of the red lights changed to green I made the mistake of heading for the lock but was yelled at in no uncertain terms (and excellent. English) to "Go back" and soon enough a 3000 tonner emerged. I have found the smaller locks quite often oxpect you to go though on one green, but not apparently the big ones, Back in Veere we at last met up with "Ruadh Sgeir" -— a memorable meeting followed by a-memorable meal in Middleburg. Late afternoon the. next day (Wednesday) we locked out of Flushing together but with their greater size and speed they slowly drew ahead and disappeared into the night. Our return trip from Flushing to Stansgate was uneventful - 110 miles on the log in 23 hours, We motored forthe first hour or so but a force 4-5 soon came up from the NY and with.the genow and four rolls the Jayess sailed herself from the Noord Hinder to the Sunk L.V. (some 40 miles) - a great help on 2 cold night with only two on board. Visibility was not brilliant and. the good old Bradwell towers were the first landmarks we saw sincc Tlushing disappeared in the murk the night before. We clearec. customs on the hard after I had driven up to the village to phone.

~4- This was altogether a most enjoy2ble if rather cold cruise. It confirmed our belief that meeting friends by arrangement is great fun but that sailing in company is not on -— anyway for boats of different sizes setting off from different ports. Toujours 1'independence! Donald McKendrick, MINI-CRUISE 1967 WORKING THE TIDES. by Maggie Adam. KAZARKA'S fitting-out, Spring 1967 was with a view to taking her again to her land of origin, Holland. Instead, we went on safari through my land of origin, Scotland. This, plus our other commitments, left just four days' leave for a cruise if we were to have any at all. Starting from Reed's Almanac, I worked out the basic principles for Arthur's approval. I concentrated on full moon, because that practically doubles available sailing time and gives us enough water to float out from our berth at Maldon (we need a rise of 16' or more at Sheerness). A weekend was easily added, and low cunning suggested a “way to get twos by using the first to make our way up the coast to some place from which Arthur could return to work by train and we could also get out on a night-tide if we wanted, I phoned Walton about 2a mooring wo but got no results tried Pin Mill and received a firm assurance fron Mrs. Jack Ward. We still had a lurking intent that if the chance offered of a favourable. slant to the Roompot or the Schelde we would take its; and I put passports and cheques with the ship's papers in case. We even considered the possibility of not getting back at the end of the week and looked up transport services via the Hook and Ostend on Arthur's behalf, Rather looking forward to staying behind for a week or so as Ship's caretaker, I took my own drawing materials and some marine varnish and brushes to keep me gainfully employed! FRIDAY JULY 14 : MALDON -— TOLLESBURY One consequence of keeping our boat at Maldon is, we never start punching a tide! you go out pretty well on top of the tide or not at all, and with luck you may carry your fair tide out of the Blackwater as far as’ the Naze or through the Wallet Spitway. Another consequence of the fact she lies in a mud-berth is that the final loading has to be done on the rise of the same tide as we go outs it tends to be 2 throwing in of duffel bags, plastic containers, milk bottles and such. On Friday July 14 HW Maldon was 18.40 (ship's time is Bve.T) and the rise at Sheerness 16!3's but the wind was WN 4 and westerlies lower the level. at Maldon,so although we were ready and dropped our moorings before even a dark line showed on the wharf opposite, we still grounded lightly on the mud-rim of her berth. Arthur had to shove repeatedly while I threw my lesser weight on to the tiller in phase with him before we got free. (A few weeks later she floated free on 2 16.2 tide, wind being easterly). Beyond the Prom extension the working jib was set and, on the orders"Finished with ensines" the petrol was turned off. After a sultry day it was sheer delight to be on the water and we had supper in the cockpit going past the Doubles, First thoughts had been to go into Thirslet but there we decided to make it Tollesbury and we set the mains! 1, Two hours out from Maldon we were crossing the Nass to go up South Channel, one short reach of which we had to motor, and soon after that we dropped anchor for the night, No need for sail-cover, just riding—light and sleeping—bags’' to put out. The alarm was set for the 06.40 weather forecast and Metmaps and pencil placed within reach. A last look around at the sky and the lights at Bradwell in a stillness scarcely broken by the low calls of waders along the drying edges: I was asleep before I Zot my lee—board tied up.

SATURDAY JULY 15 : TOLLESBURY — KIRBY CREEK "KAZARKA" began to swing just about the time the alarm went off and when the weather forecast began she was round with the ebb flowing under hers HV Sheerness was 07.10 so the difference on that (and Maldon) was half an hour. The forecast was wind SW 2-4 and a hot day ahead. Some time had to be spent on stowages and a little on breakfast -— namely, what took Sir Francis round the Horn, muesli and fruit. At 08.45 (approx) Arthur weighed anchor and we were off under mains'l first and then working jib which could be boomed: out on the spinnaker pole. 55 minutes later we left the Bench head buoy to port and by 10.35 were at Priory Spit buoy. Arthur remarked "I did bring the spinnaker you know, and conditions seem about ideals how about setting it?", We, i.e. he, did and we carried it with great enjoyment for about 2 hours from Jaywick until the Medusa buoy (12.34). Shortly after this a dark cloud developed upwind of us and we knew the "big balloon" must come down. At the same time the wind freshened and altereds I gybed involuntarily, became disorientateds the spinnaker flogged for a few seconds and then the halyard gave way. (Afterwards it appeared that the siezing on the eye at the end of it had chafed through). Arthur collected the spinnaker as it came, and for a few minutes we were reaching off towards the Cork Sand on starboard tack. No immediate danger —- it was 2 miles off — but we couldn't go on for very long, Arthur re-set the working jib and I gybed back on to port tack, intentionally this time! We found we could lay the course close—hauled. The Stone Banks buoy showed up well enough, but as usual Pye End buoy needed finding and turned up well in under Dovercourt between two large white buildings and in front of a square tower. From there it was a beat into Hamford Water, and around 15.15 we dropped anchor in Kirby Creek off Skipper's Island, SUNDAY JULY 16 KIRBY CREEK — PIN MILL Time was of no account today. The early forecast gave wind SW becoming S 2-4, At 09.45 half ebb, we went off, under working jib as far as Pye End and them mains'l as well. From there we came round the breakwater and kept pretty close in to the beach over the Shelf in order to be out of the main force of the ebb, which still had two hours to run. The depth of water was perfectly adequate and well enough indicated by the fishing—boats on moorings and mostly we had about 2 fathoms, but about 4 cables from the Guard buoy we had to stand off again. Just above Felixstowe Dock "SELLA POLARIS" apparently the Swedish royal yacht, was lying at anchor, and not long after that, having meantime "dressed overall" she approached Shotley for some more or less ceremonial disembarkation to take place. We wished to look inside Harwich Pound although we had no intention of entering. M.V. "ENGLAND" (registered Esbjerg) was also on her way in, and not knowing her line of approach we guessed she'd use the starboard side of the channels; nevertheless she swung ring around to the port hand, and we found ourselves crossing her bows 200 yards ahead and having to tack close under the quay in order to cross her wake. The reason for her manoeuvre appeared to be to enable her to turn farther up and reverse alongside Parkeston Quay, Another tack brought us to the entrance of the Pound which in its present state we found unattractive for anything more than an emergency and a temporary landing. Going into the Orwell, we felt the airs becoming very light and, such as they were, they gave us a dead beat. I was amusing myself trying to point higher than another boat on the same course who seemed not very unequal, I was gaining on her 2t each tack but she was being sailed too half-heartedly to make much of that. Anyway, as the breath of maeving 2ir died completely away, we were both reduced to letting the tide bear us limply along like a2 piece of flotsan. In this situation, it was distinctly odd to catch sight of a sizeable spinnaker moving steadily up towards us

* ~ 6 - from astern, setting perfectly 211 the time. It was apparent all we needed to do was sit and wait for her to bring up the breezes and sure enough that was what she did. First, it picked up the halfshearted one and then we felt it too3 I eased sheets and we were off on a dead run. It was as perfect an example of a sea breeze front as one could ever hope for, Off the Hard at Pin Mill we were able to find and pick up one of Jack Ward's moorings as instructed previously. Another time we shall make our arrival known at once, as, while we were hawing a light meal another visitor was directed to it. However, Mrs. Ward can be relied on to sort out any tangles, and by reason of our prior phone c21l, we were not displaced and no hard feelings arose. Arthur arranged to be picked up by the local taxi at ten to seven, since the first bus didn't connect with his train and we returned aboard, His shore-kit was laid out and. the alarm re-set and then we settled down for 2 quiet night. (to be continued next month)

-4- ‘ MINI CRUISE 1967 (Continued from Jan. Issue) MONDAY July 17+h - At Pin Mill Arthur rowed ashore to return to Chelmsford for one day, leaving Maggie to sort out weather forecasts and stow the gear properly. The evening was spent in the Butt and Oyster. The thunderstorms promised by the forecast came during the night. TUESDAY July 18th - Pin Mill - E.Shotley. The following morning was muggy with scarcely a breath and poor visibility. We motored over to the gantry by the Hard just before HY, but after a look at it Arthur decided a more convenient methed (once used with "GOOSE") would be to go alongside a barge and asked to do the job (replace broken spinnaker halyard) from her rigging. We met "CAMBRIA's" tender on its way in and permission was readily given, It didn't take long to do, even although I was the cause of a twist that sent Arthur up a second time, We left our "thank you" on the deck (no lack of paper- weights!), beat down to E,Shotley and dropped anchor about a mile above it. At mid-day "CAMBRIA" passed us again, under mains'1l, tops'1 and fores'1l working her way slowly but steadily to windward. Of Harwich nothing could be seen, even Shotley was indistinct, and a fog-signal boomed from the direction of Parkeston,. Arthur went over the side with the scrubbing brush.for a swim! ‘WEDNESDAY July 19th ~ E.Shotley -— Slaughden Ship's alarm had been set for 00.30. Not a lot of sleep was to be had while the steamers were-pounding down.on the first half of the ebb but the night was clear and warm. The moon was about to set and a little cloud was beginning to gather when we arose; the wind was SS¥.2. We weighed anchor at 01.15 and went off on starboard tack, close-— hauled, under main and Genoay.and by 01.52 we were leaving Shotley Spit buoy fairly well to starboard. At this time of night there was no traffic on the Harwich side but we couldn't feel sure of Felixstowe Dock and so, in the vicinity of Guard buoy we put in a short tack*to bring us.just beyond the main channel on the west side. The next buoy, being Gp.F1,2l., was port—hand for entering, but we left it close to port - i.e. "wrong side" for going out ~ because that happened to-be practicable, Five minutes later we left Gp.f1.3R on the "proper" side - i.e. to starboard — thus putting ourselves back inside the main channel, From there, round Landguard out to Platters, there was more to take account of than buoy-—lights and for the next half hour the watch was divideds Arthur counted buoy—lights and I concentrated on steamer-lights. When Landguard Point was abeam, White over Green presented itself dead ahead, and as we were already on the east side of the channel we bore away Slightly to indicate we were keeping clear, _ As we did this, the other aspect changed to White over Green and Red ....heading straight for us! I told Arthur "Go on watching" he said; and in fact she was already giving us White over Green again. It was then evident to me too that having rounded the Point and observed our aspect, she was accepting the implied invitation to pass Green to Green rather than the conventional Red to Red, To judge from her size and speed, she seemed to be one of the Trinity House pilot vessels. We had now rounded Landguard and started on our way up the coast. In the vicinity of Platters I became aware of White over Red coming up from behind. In due course, we were overtaken by a large steamer showing her Red to our Green, on her way out to the Cork L.V. At the same time, White over Green was showing on our starboard bows close by the light vessel, the two steamers crossed, Red to Red, and a few minutes later we crossed with the incoming one, Green to Green again. Still keeping fos a the main shipping channel, we left the Cork L.V 3 cables to starboard Sods.)

Very soon after this, the sky to eastward began to grow faintly lights; some distant flashes of summer lightning were dying away, but not without a sharp rainstorm. When the rain ceased, we took the Genoa down, Since there was time to spare for making the Ore entrance. . Still comfortably on the run under mains'l only, we came up on the S.¥. Whiting buoy at 04.50. From the run I luffed up towards the haven till we were on a good broad reach, port tack. There was a fair amount of tidal offset as well, pushing: us back down the coast, so it was necessary to point well downwind of the marks. With the sun now over the horizon behind us, conditions were ideal for picking out the bar buoy and the shore—marks. We went in far enough to Size up the situation, then - ybed and turned outward again. According to Jack Goote, you can enter 1-14 hours after L.W, However, the depth on the bar is not great - probably it varies from year to year - and the fraction of rise in that time is not a lots so Arthur chose to wait until about 4 hours before H,W. at the bar, By now the object was not so much to get inside — there was no hurry at all for that, even for the sake of getting up to Aldeburgh and buying bread before early closing - but rather to give the crew a good opportunity of finding out what crossing the bar was all about at first hand. For the next 25 minutes I steered a course out to the S.W. Whiting buoy again and at the predetermined time, came around once more for the shore, The tidal offset was increasing but I was also getting used to it and so came on holding the marks steadily in transit. As we left the bar buoy (black can), Arthur warned me to be prepared for some difference in the steering and sure enough as we passed between the outer shoals we came out of the cross-tide and I could luff right up to steer straight at the marks. This was not all, however, for when we had cleared the North Shoal and were across the mouth of tue river, there was another cross—current to reckon with in the opposite direction until I could safely bear right away and run up the river. Once comfortably inside, my main thought suddenly became "breakfast", and I passed over the helm and went below to prepare the first course - muesli and apple sauce —- but it was still a fairly long time before Arthur got around to his. With 3 hours and only 9 miles to Slaughden and a quartering breeze, he reckoned he had time to explore the Butley River and be able to lay his course back down to the main river. Fair enough! The sun was up and it was getting warm. Expectantly, we rounded the bend and beyond the disused dock lay a pleasant reach with a couple of yachts on moorings at the far end, looking very much at home, "KAZARKA" loves such places and these looked just about her size so she didnit think twice about water, as she had expected, there was enough, When she came about, a slight wind-shift had made it a beat out, with very short tacks most of the way. Hearing a rush of feet on deck, I went up (unnecessarily) to hold the helm while Arthur put up the Genoa between tacks, and for him breakfast was indefinitely postponed while things crew concentrating! We weren't alone in that. A raft of baby shelduck steaming full ahead on the same course suddenly realised they were being overhauled fast; Nama went into her noisy diversion act on the mud—bank and Papa did a bit of running up and down as well. At the same time, all six ducklings took up diving stations instinctivsly and at random — surfaced also 2t random — and submerged again right under our bows. Arthur said, "I can't do a thing about it!" and I just had to count heads as they appeared in our wakes five..... and eventually, six emerged and headed for the shore where Mama (and Papa) were waiting. No doubt, she at least was satisfied she'd lured that monster away from her precious brood, At Orford Quay a laden ferry boat shot across our bows towards the W.D establishment on Orfordness. It wasn't much after 09.90 when we got up to Slaughden, HW Slaughden is 12 hours after Orfordhaven and so it was just about half-tide and running a good 3 knots, followed by a gusty wind, force 5. Off the Aldeburgh Yacht Club "Jumbo" Ward, the Slaughden boatman,

~§- came out to us and pointed to a vacant mooring, then rowed smartly alongside, shouted, "Here, lady" and thrust a piece of card into my hand, This turned out to be our 'pass' for the club—house which’we were invited to make use Of. But we weren't there yet. I can't recall how many tries I had at that mooring-buoys it was probably about my fourth when I hooked it and Arthur leapt up from the well to take the weight off my hands. Some day, somewhere... we'll go out and spend an afternoon just picking up things. hageie Adam, To be continued next month. — ROUND BRITAIN RACE — 1966 A very good turnout of members and their friends were given a real treat on Friday February 23rd at the MASC Hall when Jock Smith, Vice Commodore of the Walton and Frinton Yacht Club and Bill Berry of the Colne Yacht Club gave a lecture illustrated by charts and films on the last Round—Britain Yacht Race, The yacht 'Dinah' they sailed was a West Solent 6 tonner which had been bought as a bare hull and modified and modernised by Jock Smith himself who, being in the sheet metal business, had made the self- steering gear, and even the mast and hoom himself, ‘Three colour films were shown in which the photography was really Superb and these were interspersed with details of the voyage narrated by Bill Berry the navigator, who being a schoolmaster, was able to put “it over very ably in quite a professional style. Out of an entry of 17 yachts, 'Dinah' came in 9th which, on ib corrected time, put them third, which was very commendable as theirs was the smallest boat and was largely home-made, Great credit is due to Jock for operating the projector and sound equipment so efficiently - this was in no small measure due to the fact that he arrived in the hall quite an hour before the meeting was due to begin and therefore had a chance to have a trial run with the film -— this should be an example to all of us who, all too often, find ourselves rigging our dinghies when the five-minute gun is about to be fired! Our Commodore, Jack Bigden, was chairman and the vote of thanks . was proposed by Vice President E.A.Payne. ELA.P, TH: LONDON DINGHY EXHIBITION As Joan and I did not go to the boat show this year we went instead to the London Dinghy Exhibition held at the Crystal Palace National Recreation Centre, We axpected it to be "the mixture as before" and were pleasantly surprised when it turned out to be something entirely different. The exhibition is held over a week end so it is not | necessary to utilise a day of your holiday to attend. We chose to go on Sunday the 3rd March. The emphasis was on do-it-yourself whether you go it alone or with @ group and the 40-50 dinghies exhibited, from the Flying Dutchman down to the little Puffin were all built or at least completed, by amateurs. Their proud owners were in attendance and only too pleased to extoll the virtues of their particular class. Commercial stands were conspisuous by their absence, A number of enthusiastic groups were building boats during the exhibition and one group in particular, with youngsters well below school leaving age, many no more than knee high to a grasshopper would have done credit to a Giles cartoon. A member of the Dinghy Cruising Association exhibited his 12 footer which was so full of equipment and stores that there seemed no room for helmsmen and crew. Incidentally he sails with his boat.cover on from bow to mast and draped inhoard to protect his stores. He said it makes an excellent spray dodger. Young girls so busily sailmaking on domes etc, sewing machbnes went about their task with enthusiasm .oblivious of the onlookers. Demonstrations of capsize drill were ably carried out in the swimming pool in spite of the absence of wind. Two Fireflies, a Finn

-4A4- and a Fireball took part, the Fireball coming to grief when his forestay parted, As well as the exhibition, there were talks and lectures organised in the large gymnasium and you can see from the programme that they were all of interest, The lectures that Joan and I went to were well attended and the film "Sailing to win" proved so popular that an additional showing was put on at 4,pm after the exhibition closed. Frank and Margaret Dye who regularly cruise and live aboard their "Wayfarer" dinghy during their holidays gave a talk on "The pleasures of dinghy cruising" which was easy to listen to and very informative. Margaret Dye operated the slide projector and this talk proved very popular indeed, the hall being almost full on this occasion, The whole exhibition was very well organised, lectures and demonstrations started and finished on time and announcements over the public address system reminded one what was on and when. A five minute warning was given before the start. Refreshments were available on a balcony overlooking the exhibition hall and there was plenty of opportunity to sit down and rest ones feet, Joan toured in her high heels and at the end declared that she had thoroughly enjoyed the show and was not tired out. Most of us have dropped anchor and enjoyed a picnic on the beach and many of the Blackwater Joint cruiser races are started from the pier. The light on the end of the pier is much appreciated although many of us wish that it could be a little hit brighter! Few will know that in the early twenties the Marconi Company was considering the purchase of the island which at shat time, could have been purchased for a very low price indeed. The idea was to use it as a research station but negotiations did not materialise and eventually a hut was erected on the beach at East Mersea where racks were arranged to hold samples of metal which were to be subjected to corrosion tests, The hut was placed (most conveniently!) near the golf course adjoining the site which we have used for our camping cruises. Many people wonder what was the origin of the big house near Osea pier and it seems that in the early part of the century, Mr.F.N.Carrington

from the family business of Brewers bearing that name, was so apalled by the sights he saw outside the public houses in London on Saturday nights that he decided to withdraw from the business and devote himself to the cause of temperence and build a home for inebriates and others needing rest and attention. An amusing story is told of how a sumptuous yacht with a crew, wet and weary from a long sea passage, dropped anchor off the island and sent one of their party ashore to what they thought must be an hotel, to order dinner for six, whilst the remainder donned their club ties and reefer jackets in preparation for the repast - the answer he received can pest be left to the imaginations Th 4 &,A.Payne — Vice President, ENTERPRISE NEWS News from the Area Committee A discussion on the latest rule changes led to the following points:- Jib-Sheet Blocks/Cleats; Jib~sheet cleats are allowed as previously (the mounting of the cleats not to overlap into the cockpit by more than 43" abeam by 5") Blocks may now be fitted but must be a ratchet type (Blocks shall not be mounted so as to overlap into the cockpit or out—board of the side deck). Graphite paint may be used but beware! -— some measurers are refusing to measure graphited boats at Open Meetings - too dirty! Transom flaps; are a must according to the experience of the area committee. I have just fitted these to my boats I hope to try them at Stansgate early in the year. (Max. area 10" x 5" or 8" dia. we have full plans.) Clew outhauls rule: boom fitting to allow adjustment of the mainsail clew during racing: to consist of a fairlead or pulley, a jamming cleat and suitable lanyard. Clearly the lanyard may be lead from the pulley along the length of the boom to the cleat near the mast, It has been decided by the NEA to grant a licence for five years to Waterside Plastics to be sole moulders of the glass-—fibre boat.iIn return the NEA gains the benefit of their increased advertising. This can't be bad! Bell Woodworking have sold therr entire 1968 production!! We are an expanding class, however, the response to the replies to the news letter sent to all enterprise owners in our Club does not confirm this! THIS WAS BAD! CLUB NEWS © We would still like to have the questionaires returned. The sailing programme for the coming season is even more full than before. It is designed to give all members a chance to sail in Club events almost every weekend. Two main series of points races have been devised: the usual Enterprise series of 18 races for the Knight Cup and a Handicap series of 8 races for the Helmsman of the Year Trophy. Our open meeting for the Triple 'K' cup is being held during the Regatta at the Spring Bank Holiday, The fleet officers would be glad to hear of anybody wishing to buy or sell Enterprises - we already know of two tentative buyers. Also we have now got details of the latest modifications including re-—positioning the forward thwart and transom flaps. The most important thing is to get a large fleet on the water — that's Denis Boswell 'D' Bdg, Basildon,

-7- Continuing Maggie Adam's Log Mini Cruise — 1967 WEDNESDAY — Slaughden This being our fifth day out from Maldon, we wanted fresh bread and fruit (and poss ibly a chance of encountering Albert Herring as well,...?) Arthur took a fancy for some locally—-bred yoghurt (raspberry flavour) in addition, Even before we had left the counter precincts, the lid of the jar exploded loudly (and stickily) in his hand. ' Of course, the shopkeeper observed with poise “it's live". All the way up and down the long High Street of that sedately quaint town, Arthur carried his yoghurt which was emitting sub-sonic bangs at regular intervals and making him very sticky. It was very hot and airless and he was very patient. Back at the yacht club, we met the Hon.Sec, anxious to get her shopping done before early closing but more than willing to re-open the bar, did we wish.... we thought of the yoghurt and decided best toget what remained aboard without delay: She looked at it and agreed. The Wind was still blowing up the river, never less than force 4} it was good to feel the deck underfoot after the unyielding hardness of "shore". I. was using a pad of Metmaps and the backs of these large sheets were ideal for working out tides for up to 48 hours ahead and enabling the whole prospect to be seen at a glance. As a routine I took the weather forecasts and prepared my sheet, although with a rather slow- moving Low to the north of the British Isles and wind persistently from SW there was no point in leaving this mooring for the present. THURSDAY JULY 20 — FRIDAY JULY 21 Slaughden — Harty Ferry The 02.02 bulletin indicated that the Low was moving away north and that a previously mentioned High over N. Biscay could be expected to bring a more westerly airstream, This accorded with our hopes of reaching either the Medway or the Swales but although the night was clear enough, it would still be a dead-beat cut of the Ore if we went now; we scrapped the first E.T.D, and went back to Sleep. In the morning Arthur topped up the watertank and went ashore to refill the jerricans at the clubhouse and settle up with the boatman, Following J, Coote, we had reckoned the time for crossing the bar at Orford-haven would be from 18.50. llowever, soundly based "local “ knowledge" at the Y.C.» advised him that he could quite. safely advance that to about 18,20 and gain another half hour of south-going tide. Around 15.15 we dropped our mooring (it was rather close to the starting-line for a race of halfea dozen Loch Long class keel-boats being helmed quite dashingly by sepa for the most part); and began a beat down the Alde with the No.2. Genoa hanked on but only mains'] in use. With time to spare and tide under us, I was enjoying Sailing "KAZARKA" and glad to have the chance in a bit more of wind than on the Orwell without the trouble of handling sheets. A mile or so down we observed a Hillyard sloop that had passed us at Slaughden, now rammed square on the shore and lying at an 'orrible angle, awaiting the next flood. Another mile or so down we received a fairly big puff and the main halyard’ let go. (A Talurit splice had pulled out). "KAZARKA" is nothing if not a ladys she was in mid-stream at the time. At a shout from Arthur I bore away and we ran upstream under bare poles until Arthur got the jid up; then, as it was against the ebb, he also started the motor. We discussed ways and means: we couldn't recall either barge or derrick at Slaughden or at Orford, and the obvious method would be the bosun's chair. It was then I heard myself saying "Well, now that I've been up the Cairngorm chairfift, I think I'd probably ‘have more confidence in your aaa to put me up there than in mine to put you", Although I added feebly ",...so long as it's calm and you tell me what to do". I was committed; the last and only time I put Arthur up, I got riding turns on the winch and his descent wasn't really relaxed for either of us,

— Bm We dropped anchor -— opposite the stranded Hillyard, as it happened (T hoped the diversion would cheer them though I never saw a soul on board her) and up I went, very surprised to find what a long way it was after the cross-trees. When a power boat tore past, I shut my eyes...but want on. I threaded my rope through the sheave (much easier than threading my sewing machine a few days ago!) and then took a canny look around over the Ness and out to sea, Not so bad at all. Then Arthur, always the opportunist, asked me to bring down one of the spinnaker anti-snarl cords as well, and that did prove bothersome as I had to untie a knot on the front of the mast entirely by touch. However, it was done and no sooner had I planted both feet on the deck than I was ordered to "take the helm as we really must get under way", It was 17.40 and a fair amount of time had been lost, As we ‘motored down, I started cooking supper and we had that on the way. Inside the bar we dropped anchor (19.05) and Arthur completed the repair, using my 'leader' to pull through a piece of nylon rope. My log entry says: "Seems a nice evening and a bit of breeze in right direction. The next entries reads-— 20.00 (did look at my watch!) correct by B.B.C!) A. weighed anchor — motor -—— mains'l & followed by No.2, 20.30, comfortably over bar. 20.32. rounded off bar buoy (P) A. kept to N. shore ——- get help from eddies --— pinger never less than 34 metres) on corner —— down to 3m (etres) on main outward channel. This refers to the tip of Orfordness spit where, relying on his own "local knowledge" Arthur was steering close into the corner; although the tide was pouring in fairly fast, he was able to get some help from the eddies on that side. The look at the pinger was purely for future information} there was no reason at that time to expect lack of water and the readings made no practical difference. At last, we were outside. Two hours of fair tide had been lost; Arthur changed up to the big Genoa and we stood offshore on starboard tack, There was little cross—traffic and none of it close at hand. The log needed few entries; we steered on the track of the moon. Around midnight and in the neighbourhood of the N.!.Gunfleet buoy, the tide began to turn against us. It had been intended to kedge in a sheltered spot on the edge of the Gunfleet Sand or the Buxey until the tide ran south again, and now the two lost hours began to count, for it took us just about that time to reach the Gunfleet Spit buoy. One cable south of it (so that the mournful sound of its bell might carry downwind and: not disturb our slumbers!) Arthur brought the jenny down and dropped anchor. The last thing he did after stowing sail was to take bearings on the Gunfleet Spit buoy and the Gunfleet Old Lighthouse, noting as a final check some shore lights in line, We would have rather less than 4 hours sleep until turn of the tide. A good landfall always thrills me. However, to select on the chart a "night" among the shoals and in the darkness to steer a course and find its; then lie securely at anchor inside this hidden shelter and sleep easily and confidently seems really to be casting off shore habits and being like the sea—birds who just fold their wings and rest on the waves. To be continued next month,
