Due to the lack of support we are cancelling the Meeting on the 26th April, which was to have-been a film show, WINS & CHEESE PARTY A very successful wine and cheese party was held in the MASC hall on Friday March 29th when those present, regrettably not as numerous as on some other occasions, were given a surprise treat by Mr.J.E.Kemp, owner and skipper of the Thames barge "Thalatta" who came along and gave a talk, illustrated by numerous photographs and a delightful film showing life on board the barge Memory, Mr. C.F,Leggett, from Marconi Marine, supported Mr, Kemp, who referred to him as the historian and he was able to fill in details about dates and names of barges and their owners. Thalatta was built in 1906 at a time when thousands of these barges were being used commercially for carrying cargoes of hay, coal, sugar or manure, but their numbers were reduced to a few hundreds during the war and now, a mere handful remain, Regrettably, Memory, which won the barge match in 1963 is no longer being sailed, but like Mamgu, which served us so well as a Clubhouse at Heybridge basin, “is also to be used as a youth centre for training children in the ways of the sea, Some members were grieved to hear that Thalatta had been fitted with a powerful engine and that it was intended to use it for propulsion when the sails were worn out, although many got the impression that their legs were being pulled, as ir. Kemp is the last person to resort to an engine when there is any wind available! Mr. Kemp has now signed a contract with the Redbridge Education Authority to take batches of children out for weekly cruises, the first trip being due to start on April lst. HARTY FERRY — MALDON We were roused in time to catch the final news summaryat 02.00 which was "severe storms anc flooding in the West Country". The forecast for Thames and Dover gave wind E 3-5 backing NW-W 5-7 showers, good visibility. Outside we estimated ENE 5, sky overcast, shower insight and visibility 3 miles: not suitable to go out in the dark — there would be a steep sea at the entrance, We ignored the preparations for a meal and went back to sleep once more. —~—S At 06.40 the B.B.C still gave wind E. 3-5, backing NW 4-6 falling off to force 3 by evening, and Galloper had reported E 4...WWe were having it calm and overcast. Nevertheless, by 07.45 Arthur observed wind 245° (T) force 2, i.e. WSW. By the end of the forenoon it had increased to force 5, and was nearly 340°(T) i.e. nearly North. Our intention was to aim at the W.Swin with ae view to saving our tide at the Spitway. We aimed to leave Harty 24 -— 3 hours before slack water in the Swale and to stem the last of the flood. This would help us to get across the mouth of the Thames before the full strength of the ebb swept us too far to the NE to round the West Barrow. Being Sunday, we could also have one more we2thor report before casting off. It was rather mixed -— wind variable 2-4 locally 5, mainly N3-4 later, thundery showers, hail! We were now getting wind 40°(T) i.e. a little E of N and this would enable us to round the W,Barrow. We put on all our oilies and dropped our mooring about 12.15 with 4 rolls in the main and the No.2. Genoa then after passing close to the club barge to shout our thanks to the steward for a comfortable berth, we started on the beat out. Arthur's entry in the deck log concludes: "Flood tide still running strongly, but fan make reasonable progress on long P tack, short S.tack". By 13.50 the wind had dropped to force 3 and the reefs could be shaken out; half an hour later we changed up to the big Genoa, To the north a build-up of castellanus had dissolved away and the sky over us was becoming more settled all the time.

-5-. At 14.34 we left the Ham Gat buoy 50 yards to port. It was nearly local HW and we went through Ham Gat on starboard tack, putting in one short board on port tack to keep us off the landward shoal, From there to the vicinity of the Blacktail Spit buoy was one long leg on starboard tack, After that it became long boards on port tack, short on starboard tack, up to the Spitway. There was no difficulty in picking up buoys across the Spile. Here the tide was essentially slack but rate of progress had to be maintained and Arthur used a couple of his fixes to calculate speed over the ground. At 16.16 we left the E. Spile buoy 2 cables to port — i.e.passing. down-tide of it. We were approaching the deep channel and the cross-—tide would be strengthening all the times we couldn't afford to give anything away here. Sunday afternoon traffic did not appear heavy; it tends to come in fewer but larger vessels and I found that my estimates of distance and relative speed had to be revised. On the other hand, I didn't have the impression of "busy-mess" that I have at Harwich and in the Netherlands; rather a sort of processional that a little ship ought to respect and not intrude into. At 16.24 we left the S. Oaze buoy close to port and at 16.55 had the Blacktail Spit buoy abeam, Soon we came on to port tack for the W. Q Swin, Arthur had been doing sums in the log estimating times and distances to the Spitway. The wind was becoming lighter and if its direction altered too, we would want all the flood in the Blackwater to get us up to Maldon. On the principle that if the motor must be used, then better to accept it where it will do most good, we switched on at 17.15 with a view to reaching and getting through the Spitway before LW. For the next two hours we charged down the Swin with the sails filled — and the engine running, using the echo--sounder to keep us in the deep water and best of the tide, generally tacking at between 4 and 5 fathoms. We made good progress but it can't really be called restful; the premium was on efficiency just as much as before. We saw a coaster leaving the Spitway and cut right across the Whitaker Spit, but we didn't feel justified in doing this. At 19.19 we started through the Spitway, considering that there was very little swell left over, the sea was calm and we shouldn't expect to bump. Nor did we. I kept my eye on the pingers I got a pretty constant reading of 2.2m and it never flickered below 2m. By 19.38 we were through. I went below to make supper at last. Within the next half hour )) the motor was shut off and we were on a dead run, goose—winged with the Genoa comfortably boomed out on the port side. All at once everything felt peaceful with no more strain or effort. When the stove was shut off as well, we sat in the cockpit with our coffee and relaxed in the quiet and: the natural motion of the ship. Night came on as we 'ghosted' up past Bradwell and St. Lawrence Bay and the moon rose above the trees. Our progress became quite slow, but we felt no concern for the tide would carry us if nothing else and we had the whole of that in our favour. We also seemed to have the river to-ourselves; at least we did have, until in the vicinity of Mill Beach we heard.a yacht which was feeling her way down close to the Northey Shore. "Heard" only and specifically, because she was showing no navigation lights at all and was practically invisible in the moonlight; but her motor was loud enough and the voices of her helmsman and crew over and above it made her presence known to us 2 good mile and more away! T don't know how often we've noticed there's no camouflage so complete as a white-painted hull with white sails, especially in moonlight. For some reason the light at the Blackwater S.C was not on that night (although it was functioning a month later). Still early on the tide, we were prepared to anchor in Colliers ' Reach; then Arthur had a second thought and as no barges or lighters were around, he simple attached us to the barge mooring buoy off the Basin. This was at 01.16 with HW Maldon at 03.25. We passed the time with hot drinks and large wedges of cheese, stares sail for harbour and

xa Bl me gathered together what had to be taken ashore with us. The sailing barges at the Hythe were asleep as we slipped past and the noise of our motor seemed loud in our ears, so for the sake of our neighbours Arthur cut off petrol as we approached the houses and then reached for an oar and paddles us alongside the pontoon. It didn't take very long to put gear and ourselves ashore and to say a thank you and good night to "KAZARKA" as well. Just as we shut the back door for the night to go up to bed, the town clock struck four - this was Monday morning and a working day was beginning to lighten the sky. Postscript. Next day I rang up Maldon Customs to report we'd been mo more foreign that the coasts of Suffolk and Kent! "But you had a nice cruise?" "Oh yes" "That's all right then. I'll cancel Notice of Depatture. Just give me a ring next time. CONCLUSIONS All that remains is to try and sum up what this cruise added to my experience, Miles sailed and number of ports visited don't tell much. I suppose the best thing is to state some of our aims and how they were realised, No.l was to get the feeling of really living aboard in as much detachment from shore as we could manage. I think we did that even though Arthur had to spend one day at work, I had nine days and all of ten nights aboard with only two shore interludes -— at Pin Mill and Aldeburgh - and never once felt confined or bored. We were living completely in phase with the tides, under no sense of pressure at all. No.2. was to extend our cruising range and that includes where possible, noting places where we can seek shelter from weather in future and/or leave the boat from one weekend to another. This also was achieved, Since although it was not for either of us a first crossing of Thames Estuary it was our first to the Swale, and first from North to South. We also connected at Pin Mill (Jack Ward), Slaughden ("Jumbo" Ward) and ”| Harty Ferry (Tideway Sea Club) with good temporary moorings and reasonable access by public transport. No.3 had been to enable me, the crew, to participate in a wider rangeof ship's activities than is always convenient when you are aiming at distant objectives. Although I had previously worked out tidal streams for a fair number of passages and a few of the BAORA races, I hadn't been so deeply involved for anything like so long at a time, and I found it very absorbing, Another thing I learned, when coming out of Harwich Harbour, was the importance of knowing about the lateral system of buoy lighting - viz. that colours alone don't tell which hand is which, but that the flashes must be counted as wells e.g, ALL the RED plus the VEN characters of WHITE are Port—hand, Last but not least, I now know my way up the mast and down again!. Maggie Adam,

STANSGATE ROAD The surface of the Stansgate Road is complete at least, providing an easy and comfortable approach to the Club. Prices of both tar and shingle have risen since the estimates were prepared in the Autumn and in addition some re-patching was necessary after further deterioration during the Winter. The total cost has risen from £750 (estimated) to about £1000. The Road Levy was intended to raise £450 towards the cost, The 10/- minimum was suggested for members who rarely visit the Club and it was hoped that regular users of the Club would contribute considerably more. Do you remember Stan's comment at the A.C.M, that he thought the re-surfacing would effectively save him the cost of re-placing a car tyre. He suggested that that should be the sort of sum members should be prepared to donate. We have 300 members (excluding wives and cadets), About 100 only come to the club occasionally - so allow 250 from them(10/- ea.) About 100 come more often-so allow £100 from them (£1 each) About 100 come very often — so allow £300 from them (£3 each) The total of £450 could thus have been reached comfortably. In fact only £280 has been received from 300 subscription accounts. In view of this rather poor response to the original estimated target and bearing in mind the increase in expenditure of about 2250 it is hoped that the conscience of most members will make them want to increase their contribution, especially when they have seen and driven along the "new" road, If the new target of 2700 can be achieved voluntarily during the sailing season, then the committee will be spared the unpleasant task of reimposing a levy for 1969 at the AGM in November. To reach the new target a further donation averaging 30/- per member is necessary. It is hoped that active members will subscribe moré than this. Some ‘members have already contributed very generously and we do not expect a further contribution from these faithful few. A box will be placed in the Clubhouse for further contributions to THE ROAD FUND. x A,S,Bigden,

In the first race on April 2lst the wind died completely for a while soon after the start, and although a light westerly developed the Hornets were unable to make up time to overcome their handicap. The first man home was T,Roper with Julian Bigden second and Norman Palmer in his G.P. third. In the second race a brisk S.W. wind was blowing over a flooding tide but at the start conditions in the narrows did not seem too bad and a course was set for Mundon Stone. However as the twelve boats began the long run back the wind freshened and the seas became very steep in the centre of the channel, More than half of the competitors gave up. on this leg but Richard Houlcing and Ken Stevens completed the lap successfully before retiring. It seemedthat everyone had retired, and the Race Officers went home but Julian Bigden having lost a shroud while crossing from Goldhanger Creek refused assistance and sailed on to the shore using a makeshift rig. After making repairs on the beach he returned to the race and with the water a bit calmer got home 18 minutes before the 3 hour time limit - certainly earning first points for his initiative. Although it is regretted that there should be so much damage to gear and boats, it was hoped that the experts would be able to cope with the sort of conditions we frequently get in the narrows, Few of us wish to be reservoir sailors, and most of the challenge at Stansgate comes in assessing the effects of wind and tide. If conditions require it there should be no reluctance to reduce sail or even anchor for a time, If weather is bad races will be eancelled but on the other hand the helmsman of the year should be able to cope with a wide range of weather conditions, Peter Batey — Sailing Secretary. In future members will not have access to many pieces of Club property or to Store Houses except through the Officer of the Day. Access to the Store Shed (Pete's Palace) is now strictly forbidden and any members with property in that shed should remove it immediately. Members requiring storage for oars should contact Terry Hallam at Baddow for details of arrangements. The boatshed is about to be cleaned up and members are asked to remove their property to prevent its loss. As from 15th July the door by the bar in the Clubhouse will be bolted on the inside so that keys for that door will be useless. The new back door by the Gents changing room has a new Yale lock and is openable with new Yale keys. You may hire a key for the new door for 5/- or exchange your old key plus 1/6 for a new key. New keys must be applied for personally at the Clubhouse on 22nd, 23rd June or at 7 [redacted], Chelmsford (evenings). John Witter holds the key book and members will be required to sign an undertaking that the key is for their own personal use only. The 5/- is a hiring fee and the key must be returned if you leave the Club. The loss of a key should be repor- ted to John Witter immediately. These actions to make the Club and its property more secure result from the findings of a Working Committee and the co-operation of all members is requested to make the scheme work. Please ensure that the Club is secure when you leave and that no unauthorized persons have entry to the premises. If in doubt of a person's right to be at Stansgate do not hesitate to challenge, and then report the details to any Club Officer or Committee Member. Members are also reminded that there is a limit to the number of guests they may introduce to Stansgate and that guests may only arrive accompanied by the members introducing them. Visitors names etc. should be entered in the Visitors book with the member's signature, whether or not they enter the Clubhouse. Employees of the Marconi Group of Companies should not be introduced as guests but should be enrolled as members of the M.S.C. and M.A.S.C. Sailing Club Main Committee.

Associate Member Fees A chance remark made in the Club house recently, has prompted me to 'clear up' the misconception by some of our Associate Members that the club should be in a better financial position since according to our application form Associates pay 300% more in Membership Fees than #'ull iiarconi Members. This is just not so, and should one have studied our Balance Sheet, it would have shown that 2 gns. of every Assoc. Fee (excluding moorinzs, Dinghy Park etc.) is paid into our parent body the M.A.S.C. whereas the full member pays 9d weekly. J- Bigden. ‘Team Race with Osea Sailing Club - 8th June, 1968 On being awakened on Saturday morning by a steady drip-drip as rain overflowed the gutter outside my bedroom window, I began to wish I had not so gallantly accepted Julian's invitation (if you can call it that) to crew for him in the team race against Osea Sailing Club. However, by the time the two teams had arrived at Stansgate at about 10 o'ciock, the rain had eased off and we were to have a very pleasant afternoon's sail. Osea team with their Commodore Alf Lepper as team captain, had been able to bring only one Enterprise with then, borrowing two Enterprises from the Marconi Seiling Club members. Nothing daunted, they ventured to inform us, in the nicest possible way of course, that they would ‘beat us hollow’. Nothing like giving an air of confidence! At the first gun all six boats were off to a very good start and it soon became obvious that competition would be very keen. Ona beat up towards E mark off Osea Island, boats kept well spaced apart, keeping a wary eye on each other with crews (especially me!) not daring to say a word lest we disturb the concentration of our helmsmen: Having rounded the first mark successfully with Eric Pike of 0.5.C. in the lead, it was felt that some team action was in order, and Julian decided to indulge in a luffing match, forcing Eric Pike (in his own boat) and Gordon Cocper (in John Witter's boat) in towards the Osea shore, thus causing them to lose the advantage of the tide. Terry Roper (M.S.C.) with Timny Bigden as crew seized this opportunity to shoot up to first position which he retained for the remainder of the race. Also along this stretch of water between E mark and No.1, A. Lepper (in Bob Miller's boat) and Norman Beadle with Charles Hewlett as crew. changed positions, with A. Lepper coming up to fifth position.

8 The second lap of this race saw Terry Roper of #.S.C. in the lead with Eric Pike and ourselves followin; close tozether. It was not until I found myself beinz drenched that I realised we were planing through to leeward to overtake Eric Pike on the reach past the club. By this time the wind had changed direction slig:tly - in fact it seemed to be very changeable during the whole race. So the first race finished with Terry Roper (1i.5.C.) in first position, Julian (.S.C.) second, Gordon Cooper (0.5S.C.) third, Eric Pike (0.S.C.) fourth, Norman Beadle (M.S.C.}) fifth, and Alf Lepper (0.S.C.) sixth, giving Osea 13 points and Marconi 7S. The next race was not to be so successful for the Marconi boats. Alf Lepper sailing Bob Miller's boat got away to a very good start, keenly followed by ourselves with Osea boats in third and fourth positions. At the first mark A. Lepper was one boat's length in front of us so we immediately tacked away on to a port tack. As A Lepper did not tack to cover, this left us with clear air and on the next tack we were able to catch A. Lepper who was then on port. Positions changed frequently amonyz the rest of the fleet with the final result for the second race being ourselves first, A1f Lepper second, Gordon Cooper third, Terry Roper fourth, Norman Beadle fifth, and Eric Pike sixth. The Trans-Atlantic Race At the time of writing this article, we ‘land-dubbers' in the southern half of the country are enjoying bright sunshine and very warm weather. Meanwhile close to the Azores we have lone yachtsman Alec Rose nearing the last stage of his solo trip around the world, and I hope we shall see him safely in harbour during the next few weeks. However, he too at the moment is enjoying fine sailing conditions due to an anti-cyclone centred around the Azores. Much further North in Mjd Atlantic there is a low depression causing storms and gale force winds of Force 8 - 9, which at this moment are venting their fury upon the competitors of the Single Handed Trans- Atlantic Race, news of which most of us follow closely through the medium of the Press and B.B.C.

She was designed by L. Giles soon after the war as a "flat out" Class II Ocean Racer and as she was a conspicuous success, her design had a profound effect on the design and appearance of many yachts that followed her. She has an excessively blunted bow and a chopped off stern. She is not (it is said) a pretty.boat, but a workman-like boat that will stand up to any amount of hard sailing. Noel Bevan has odds of 10 to 1 against winning the race, but the mere completion of the passage will be, I am sure, a wonderful Sense of achievement. -4- TRIAL BORING by THE GRIBBLE ; This is an attempt to gather together the Club's cruising gossip. This can be hard to come by, as cruising members keep less regular hours (by solar time) than dinghy racing types; their clock is tide- governed, and they are less frequently available for a bar-—side natter, If you have anything for this colum, send it c/o the Editor, and _the.Gribole will endeavour to digest it. How nice to see the variety of "non-racing" designs which are being successful in the cruiser races, Keep it up3 the Dragons needn't have it all their own way and Terry and Mike will.enjoy their sail whether they win or not, The BJRC cruiser races, as well as our own, are worth supporting, The next few dates are July 2lst, August 4th 18th and 31st and September 2nd. Mostly they start at Osea, but the Maldon Y.C, Cruiser Cup on August 4th is from Stansgate. There is really no excuse for missing that one! . . Shifting Sands As reported last month by Stan Campbell, the Ray Sand Channel is not what it was. The notice to Mariners giving chart corrections appeared only in April this year, so your chart may well need to be amended, Two "dries 4 ft" soundings close the Southern end, yet I have been through comfortably at half—tide with 4 ft draught. The two buoys laid by the Crouch Clubs should be left close to starboard when going south: first a yellow one, then a white one. They can be seen -as you- leave the Buxey beacon, and lead you into the Crouch entrance near the Outer Crouch buoy. When they were laid, about 2 years ago, the channel was already believed to be 2 ft.shallower than charteds now it is officially 5 ft shallower than it used to be. Even So, the buoys are clear enough to make it the pleasantest way to the Crouch forour sizeYoraft, North of Harwich, also} there have been Changes. The Cork Light Vessel has been moved more than a mile, and several buoys have also been moved. Better check up before going to the Deben or anywhere North of Harwich. ‘Stansgate is a Customs Port: Well - virtually one. Not all the empty cruiser moorings indicate . laid—up yachts. For ‘example, on June 29th there were Marconi yachts sdiling in..both directions across the North Sea, Foreign—going cruises call for Customs clearance on return (probably also a Notice of Departure), and the incumbent of ialdon Custom House, Mr. Balaam, is very willing to provide clearance at Stansgate, or Bradwell for that matter, in answer to a telephone call on any day of the week. This service is _ most welcome since the derise of Mir. Graham of Brightlingsea, which means that the Colne Customs are now based at Colehester and there may be some delay in getting clearance off East Mersea as - yachtsmen used to do.-: Tell us about it. Yes, again. If you "break new ground” (or should it be water? ) even your first cruise beyond the Blackwater and Colne, you may be entitled to an awards first cruise out of home estuary, first cruise a week away from home, or first cruise foreign, And there is the Mamgu Trophy (which will grace any sailor's sideboard) for the best log, i.e. account of a cruise this year, or since July 3lst last year. A good account is one that helps, or entices others to follow, so keep a log and send it in. The sooner the fresher, but anyway before October lst.

= im DINGHY CRUISE 1968 Dinghy cruising can be very rewarding and this is a short account of one such cruise. From Stansgate we set off in a 'Wayfarer' to make our way round to Burnham via the Ray Sand Channel. As already reported in Navigans the water in this channel is now conspicuous by its absence at low tide and although we went through some two hours beforehand we became uneasy of the situation. Close hauled on port tack with the channel marker bouys to starboard the centre-board touched bottom and we sounded our way through using the jibstick as a sounding pole. The centre-—board had to come fully up with only 12" under the boat, -and our leeward drift became pronounced, however we slipped past the southern buoy and the depth rapidly increased to 4 feet as we headed for the "Outer Crouch". Admirals Hard (Near Enterprise Sailing School) at Burnham is a public hard, freshwater and toilets are available nearby and the soft mud gives a good berth for dinghies, we spent two nights there, With the boom set up in a crutch the boat cover made a good tent, open at the transom. The Wayfarer has room for an air bed each side of the centre—board case and these plus sleeping bags ensured that we were snug and warm. —> From the Crouch we sailed up to the Colne in poor visibility and having to rely on our compass most of the way. The wind was easterly force 4 plus but in the shelter of Colne Point the water was calm and we beached, baled out, dried out and then set up camp for the night. The wind had not abated by next morning and we headed for Brightlingsea rather than risk the east coast. Brightlingsea, for those who have not visited there has an excellent public hard and causeway both of which are tended by a hardmaster, Freshwater is available from tap on the hard and there is "The George" nearby for those who prefer something stronger. Unless you have a heavy anchor don't drop your hook off the hard and expect it to hold, you will need a pick-axe to penetrate the bottom, Don't be misled by the local fisherman's dinghies that appear to be safely at anchor there. At low water it can be seen that all their anchors are "on" the bottom and not "in" it, they rely on the weight only. Our next port of call was Wivenhoe not a readily accessible frontage and the sailing club hard is not very wide. The river is very narrow and large vessels navigate the Colne beyond, particularly up to Hythe Quay and it is tricky dicing with these comparitive monsters in narrow waters, However, we spent a pleasant day in and around Wivenhoe but returned to the estuary and camped once more near Colne Point before our return home to Stansgate. The trip lasted seven days and all six nights were spent aboard and throughout the week only two of our meals were purchased ashore in a cafe, We had no newspapers and used the radio for weather forecasts only. The cost of the holiday was virtually the cost of the food and we both spent less in additional items than during a normal week at home. If you feel like trying your hand at cruising don't forget the Club cruise on July 20th, Happy sailing. Fred Partlett. LOST Large yellow lifejacket 12 ST. Left on hard at Stansgate on the 15th June. wes come THE OVER FORTIES RACH In some trepidation I got ready for the race and donned the horrible Mae West. It was a lovely day with only light winds so I wore only sun top and shorts, little knowing how I was going to suffer the next day with a very burnt back. Never having raced before in any kind of race I hoped we wouldn't capsize or get stuck.in the mud as Jack is famed for doing. Marjorie Allerton and Joan Gaskell were also racing for the first time and Marjorie said "Oh Con, what happens if we capsize", I said hang on to the boat and she said "which part", I replied the nearest and don't let go. Joan also had butterflies in her tum, I won't tell you how I felt as with Jack anything can happen. Well we seemed to make a fair start what I saw of it, what with grabbing the jib sheets and falling over the ct ailloeaie “Seushe a glimpse of Norman in front and Dave Polley about level. We had a pleasant and uneventful sail to Heybridge (all dying for a drink at the "Jolly Sailor") which of course was the target. Norman beached on fairly solid ground but Stan, Tom and we got as near to the "Sailor" as possible. Knowing Heybridge mud of old I stayed put and told Marjorie to do the same until the men had pulled the boats in, Tom asked Joan to bring the anchor and she gaily got out of the boat and went into the mud up to her knees, It was quite a revelation to hear the crew telling the helmsman off in no uncertain terms, it's usually the reverses but anyway Tom and Joan washed their legs in the river and over a drink and sandwiches sitting on the sea wall good temper was restored. After a short rest we started back with a starting signal from the rescue launch manned by Gordon Golding (coxswain) and Jack Reeves as race officer. By this time the wind had freshened somewhat and there were several boats moored and sailing. Of course Jack and I had to - get tangled up with a bow-sprit (fatal things for Jack). Anyway he managed to free us without ripping the mainsail and as the boat gave a hefty lurch I either leapt or fell onto the other side which righted the boat and Jack actually said "Well done". ie all got away without further incident with John Hurrel in the lead in a Hornet and Norman next in a GP and believe it or not we kept third place all the way back and I believe came in second on handicap. ‘I think we all enjoyed it. Since then Marjorie has enjoyed several _ Sails with Stan in " Roxy Lou" so perhaps it might be a good idea to ¢ have a few more events for us near middle age sailors! Connie Bigtten. DINGHY PURSUIT RACE Having had no experience of pursuit races, it was with some trepidation that I agreed to organise the dinghy pursuit rage which was held on Saturday 24th August.. For those who have not heard of this type of race, it can best be described as a dinghy handicap race in which ' the starting times of boats are staggered, so that all boats have an equal chance of being first across the finishing line. Therefore, with Peter Batey's advice and the help of a slide rule, the starting times for all dinghy classes that might possibly enter the race were calculated for various "corrected times” (te time thata GP would take to complete the course). For the mathematically minded, the formula is as follows (PN, = PN,) t, ty 100 . where ty = starting time delay of boat 2 after start of boat 1 PN,= Portsmouth Number of boat 1 1 PN, =Portsmouth Number of boat 2 tb = corrected time for the race.

-5- Conditions on the day were fairly easy, with a light easterly wind and a strong ebb tide. A corrected time of 75 minutes was therefore set for the nine boats which wore entered for the race, As the starting times had been calculated on the basis that Mirrors would be the slowest competitors, the race officer ensured the presence of some Mirrors by pursuading three to enter (two had never raced before and had to be shown the positions of the marks!), Also entered were 2 GPs and four Interprises. There was quite a lot of crew swapping with Nick Bevins crewing for Ken, Sheila Crick for Charlie Hewlett (in Julian's boat) and Ken Stevens for Peter Crick. John Smith eventually managed to pursuade his wife Ann that she should try her hand at crewing in a race. Since the staggered starts would present problems if the usual type of start was used a "Le Mans" start was introduced. Thus at 1500 hrs, three lNirror helmsmen were seen sprinting from the starting line at the top of the hard towards their boats, which were being held in the water by the respective crews. (The race officer declined to consider any additional handicap for age or infirmity unless birth or medical certificates could be produced in evidence). Course G was set, but starting by leaving mark A to starboard. It became obvious that some of the Mirrors needed to know more about the racing rules when John Smith was prevented from rounding A mark, at the first attempt due to an "outside" boat forcing him out of the way. ‘‘hen the GPs were due to start 15.5 minutes later, Nurray Todd in his Mirror had already rounded Breezy Point mark and was over half-way to Goldhanger Creek with his spinnaker helping him to puil away from the other Mirrors who were also well on their way to Goldhanger Creek. Of all three starts, that of the Enterprises was the most energetic, but Bob liller found, as he slipped and dived head first into his boat, that it does not pay to run too fast on seaweed. The Enterprises started 1.5 minutes after the GPs, Once all the boats were on their way towards Goldhanger Creek, “Charlie and Sheila were already overtaking Joyce Reeve's GP (from where does Julian's boat get all its "go"?). By the end of the first lap, Murray's liirror was still leading but with Nick's GP hot in pursuit, leaving the other Mirrors being rapidly overhauled by the remainder of the fleet. When the Enterprises had round No.l conical buoy, it was noticed that some of them seemed to be creeping along the Osea foreshore before heading across to A mark. This was however apparently not crafty tactics, but because they thought that they were supposed to round E mark. Just before Goldhanger Creek was reached for the second time, Nick overtook Murray, but the rest of the fleet were now a long way behind, With the other Mirrors forming a rearguard, In order to ensure that the race actually finished as near as possible to the set time (1631.30 hours for a 75 minute corrected time), it was agreed that the finishing line would be between a committee boat and a nearby mark, The mark so chosen would be the one to which the leader would be closest at the finishing time. It was fortunate that this mark happened to be A mark, as none of the rescue launches would start and the Fisherman had to be rowed out by the race officer and Stan Allerton, Due to a little trouble in anchoring, the committee boat (flying flag S from Do-Yot's whisker pole) ended up rather close to A mark, but the two "committee" members decided that the small gap would make the finish more interesting. ‘ith only three minutes to go before the agreed finishing time, Nick's GP crossed the line, with Murray's Mirror finishing not far behind. As Nick crossed the line, the race officer remembered that he had left his writing implements behind, and so he asked Ken to tell the assistant race officer, Edna Cooper to record the finishing order, There was an exciting moment when all the Enterprises seemed to be coming in together, but Charlie and Bob processed across the line in that order and only Arthur Hodges and Peter Crick carein neck-and-neck with Arthur squeezing through first. Joyce Reeve's GP followed the Enterprises and John Smith and S.Randal in their liirrors following quite a way behind her. I think that I would be correct in saying that the competitors enjoyed the race as mich as the race officer enjoyed organising it and so perhaps we might-have more pursuit and other novelty races in the future. How about holding them on those Sundays when there is no other racing arranged? C.K. Cooper.

a Fs BARBECUE - Saturday 3lst August. "Yell, there are beefburgers, sausages, lamb chops or a slice off the lamb - with or without onion". I explained once more as I took the proffered ticket, "Ere... 2 beefburger, please — with onion" I repeated the order to Chris allerton, who quickly filled the roll I held out with a sizzling beefburger and topped it with onions. Yes, our barbecue was under way once again. Vie had spent-.the day making preparations, and now it was all happening -— the crowds had arrived, the band was playing, the bar was doing a roaring trade, and so were we, serving food to our eager customers. They were all hungrily eyeing the lamb, which after four hours on the spit was cooked to perfection. This was being expertly carved by Arthur, our butcher, who had come armed with a wonderful array of knives, aprons and hats, and a very solid chopping block. , He had arrived early in the afternoon and promptly set up his block and started to prepare the chops, Around him the electricians festooned the hard with an assortment of cables....Rod shinned up the temporary "mast" of Number One rescue launch to fix a string of coloured lights and his assistant Jack and various members of the working party waited until he reached the "On to tell him that the "mast" was rotten. Over by the barbecue Roger and biick got the spit working, and in the band tent the girls, having recovered from their onion peeling session, were cutting the seven hundred rolls in halves, And then, there we were, filling and serving them as fast as we could, nearly roasting ourselves, as well as the meat, for Jack Bates kept the charcoal fires well stoked and glowing eel hot. Everything went with a swing, for after a heavy shower in the afternoon the evening turned out fine and warn, though for those who were chilly there was a large bonfire on the beach, After filling themselves with a large quantity of meat, washed down with plenty of beer, dancing to the Trad Jazz Band and toasting their toes round the fire, our two hundred and fifty suests finally departed, leaving the workers to pack up and revive themselves with a cup of coffee before going hone. All except Chris Allerton, that is, who sank down exhausted behind the shed, and awoke the next morning to find himself still dressed in his apron and hat! Roll on the next Barbecue! Noreen Douce. FURTHER BORINGS by the GRIBBLE Anchoring off the Club From time to time "non-resident" cruiser owners wish to bring their yachts to the Club. Two courses are open to thems they may borrow 2 ‘mooring (by arrangement, please!) or anchor. If you elect to anchor, there are some technical points and some common decencies to be obs: rved. Please resierber that Club moorings are laid as closely as is considered safe for Stansgate conditions; there is NO ROOM for anchoring among: the moorings. One can't take liberties just because the nearest moorings were ,vacant when you arrived. |

-3- The proper procedure is to lie outside, or further down than the moorings. Remember also that a boat is not secure enough to be left unattended for several tides, when lying to a single anchor. (Also, she may range over a very wide area, especially when wind is against tide). One anchor upstream and one down is advisable, with cable equal to four tiises the high water depth on each. These remarks are made because recently an anchored boat fouled a moored one. Some damage resulted and thence was set off a train of "emergency assistance" operations, which in turn started a lot of criticism, some of it on third - or fourth-hand inforration, Having myself only one side of the story as close as second-hand, I will add nothing to the above entirely general observations. UNIQUE SAILING EVENT sT POOLE The Industrial Recreation Clubs of the U.K are having their second Annual Team Race on September 2lst.This year Marconi are sending a team comprising two Enterprises and one Hornet, helmed by Julian Bigden, Peter Jennings (Capt) and Terry Rope respectively. Last year ten clubs accepted the challenger to compete for the Silver cup presented by Sir Bernard liiller, the Chzirman of the John Lewis Partnership. Gach club was allowed to enter two teams of three sailing dinghies - any class was allowed. In the event, about thirty-six lined up for the event. These cane from twelve different classes. By uSing the authorised handicap tables, they started at different times - the slowest first. It was a beach start, the beach being the private one adjoining Brownsea Castle, the holidy club belonging to the John Lewis Partnership on Brownsea Island, The Castle's dining room was used for tea and prize giving at the end of the day. To decide the winners, two identical races were held, one before and one after lunch. Each team only had to record the results of two boats, the results of.the two races combined giving the final placings. We had to sail from the Royal Motor Y.C across to Brownsea Island, The wind was around force 5-6 and several boats capsized. before reaching the island, The race officer then decided to postpone the race for 1 hour. Having travelled so far we were determined that the race should be held. Hence Terry Roper and Tim Bigden sailed round the course without any mishaps and the Race Officer was at last convinced that we could race, There were 12 teams of three boats. Some teams threw all thejr eggs in one basket and brought 3 Fireflys or 3 Enterprises or 3 Riveroats, whilst others split their team to cover all conditions such as the Cjvil Service whoswteam consisted of a Swift Catamaran, an Albacore and an Enterprise. The Marconi team consisted of Julian Bigden and Jill Godwin, Terry Roper and Tim Bigden both in Enterprises and Peter Jennings and Mick Turner in a Hornet. The triangular course was badly sited as the first buoy was a fetch on starboard, the second buoy was a fetch on port and the dead run back to the start. The course was very short, about 3 miles, and this does not allow for any capsizing or mistakes in handicap racing. A good start was made by Narconis and at the first buoy the only boat ahead of our team was an albacore. The next leg, the Swift Catamaran of the Civil Service began to catch us as the wind verred to a close reach, The turn down to the finish was a nightmare with boats jibing, rolling from side to side and eventually capsizing, mainly due to running onto he sand around Brownsea Island. Julian was 2longside Peter after the first lap and on handic2p was well placed. Terry Roper capsized at the jibe mark which lost him very little time with transom flaps wide open he reached off at enormous speed and emptied the boat in next to no time to finish 10th with Peter 12th and Julian 3rd, The second race proved disastrous to Marconis with a similar course to the first race except that the tide was on the way out. Julian, once again in a very favourable position, broke his mast on the run but only had about 300 yards to go to the finish a commendable 10th. Terry broke his tiller and with only 6 inches left to steer with managed to finish also. Peter capsized when he planed full speed onto the sand which by now seemed to be just below the surface on all legs of the course and in places even above the surface. iarconi finished 5th overall, despite the mishaps, with the Civil Service overall winners and BEA (last year's winners) second. WA The reception, tea and prize giving was in Brownsea Castle. The event was well worth while, and we hope next year to come back with the trophy. EDITORIAL Sailing's over and now we get down to the business of the A.G.M., new Committees, a Christmas Dance and, later, a Yinter Programme. T am sure that the present Committee would like to see YOU at the AGM -— non voting wives tend to congregate and have a natter in the bar. If you've never be:> to an A.G.M before there's always a first time and you won't be ti. only newcomer, The "Regulars" get fed up with the sound of one anothers voices and points of view, so some new ideas or angles on old problems would be very welcome, tleanor Witter, SOME THOUGHTS ON TRAM RACING This season we were "fortunate" in being accepted for the Wraysbury Lake S.C, Autumn Leaf Trophy. Sixteen teams were split into two groups and within the group everyone sailed against everyone else - seven races spread over one and a half days. At Stansgate that would be very grueiling. The shape of the gravel pit is such that the start and finish lines can be some way apart and in fact the lines are served by two separate race boxes so there is never a problem in finishing one group while the other group's starting. Gravel pit sailing can be fun but there was too little wind for the liking of the Marconi team and their efforts on the Saturday were little short of disastrous. It should however be borne in mind that most Clubs we sailed against, regularly took part in team racing -— as often as once a fortnight -— and our team had not sailed together, as. a team, before. By Sunday there was more wind and the team were much more at home. They found that they could initiate manoevres instead of being governed solely by what little wind was available on Saturday.

wD Their final race with Staines S.C. provided the first win of the .week-end. While other peoples protests were being heard the wind got up a treat but by 3 o'clock when the lst semi final was due, the wind had lightened again. Beeston S.C. were beaten by Horning, and then Wraysbury Lake beat Hayling Island. Wraysbury beat Horning in the final in hardly any wind at all. It is significant to note that both these Clubs are lake sailors and Wraysbury were on their home ground, What should we do to get better results? lkntering Open Meetings wakes one up to the standard in other Clubs. It's all too easy to assume that the best Marconi people are "good". It's painfully obvious that in the company of others we are very mediocre, secondly for team racing practice is essential. At Stansgate the fleet spreads out very quickly and often there isn't anyone very close at a buoy. In team racing on inland waters there are always other people very close by and one has to know all the Rules. Putting other people out is a very important part of team racing. his sometimes leads to protest meetings. Our team were rather disturbed about the unpleasant attitude of some of their opponents in this respect - it should always be done in a keen but friendly manner. So . As a Club we need to be more sure of our rishts on the water and be prepared to stick to our guns and assert our rights. If this leads to protests so much the better, We'd all learn much more quickly, It's not just a case of who gets the points for that race but just as much it clears up some of the more obscure interpretations of the rules that enable the next race to be sailed without incident. We came to the conclusion that enclosed water team-racing was a different sport altogether from the sailing we enjoy! ~5 Jackie & Brian Bowsher's Summer Cruise to Holland 28th June to 14th July, 1968 PART 1 — PREPARATIONS We decided on a sailing holiday in Holland around the beginning of the year, though the idea had been in the back of my mind ever since buying the boat four years azo. The Roger Pilkington Small Boat books, and articles in Navizans and the yachtinz press. had painted such an interesting picture of Duropean waterways that we decided it was really time to see for ourselves, We were interested in Holland largely due to the reports from friends telling of the excellent sailing facilities there, and of the friendliness of the sailing fraternity. First thoughts were to sail to the Hook and make our way up the canals to Amsterdam, spending sometime in the Lake of de Kaag north of Leiden, which is a popular sailing area, and is reported to be the Holland of one's imagination, However, the prospect of the North Sea crossing from Imuiden was somewhat daunting, and so we decided to explore the esturies of Zeeland, and to make our landfall in Belgiun. AS vreviously our longest trip had been to Pin Mill, and ny navigation had never had a real tost, I started reading navigation books to more purpose. For a North Sea chart, we chose the Imray, Laurie, Norie and Wilson chart No, %30, which covers Harwich to the Hook and Dover to Calais, and has large scale plans of the main ports. I drew magnetic north iines acro7s the chert, so that I could use a Douglas protractor, as this method or course plotting seems to me the most convenient in 4 small boat with ro fixea navigation table, A suitable p’ lot book proved to he a big problem, as the Admiralty books do not give approach and harbour information in yachtsman's terms, and it was a fortnight to cur holiday before I aiscovered a book newly published by Adland Coles entitles ‘North Sea Harlbcurs and Pilotage — BY tT Calais to Den Helder! by FE, th. Delmar-Morfan. Undoubtedly, the single most importaus factor in a sex crossing is the weather, and in ozder to try to urderstand how it changes, I received 2 Daily Yeather Report from the Met, Office for the three months before our holidszy. This is an exsellent service and cost 15/- for one month and °? for three months. ach report consists of four sequential weather -harts, drawn at six hour intervals and covers up to 06,00 the previous day. Our boat ‘Natasha' is a 20 foot fibre-glass Vivacity, which is moored at Stansgate, To prepare for the trip, i fitted the boat with electric navigation lights to be cun from the car battery and provided two independent sources of ligh* for the compacs, After a good deal of metal—bashing a 14 inch radaz reflectér was produced, which could be shackled between the shrouds and heuled up to the spreader. I ran a life-line along each side ieck and made some plywood covers that could be fitted over the ports, as 1 feit these to be « weakness of the design, We bought a barometer, and life belt light, and changed the Seagull Centry Plus for a Penta 5 h.p. outboard. Although the Seagull had always performed faithfully, the small tank was very inconvenient, and the high noise level extremely unpleasant, particularly as we might have to use the engine for a long period. In addition, the Penta has has a lighting output that can be used for battery charging. We already had a pack of mini-flares, but decided to get some more powerful rocket-flares, and a couple of white hand fleres to be used as ship scarers. By this time we had used up 211 our holiday money, and therefore had to eat baked benns for a ronth, Jackie and I were to spend the holiday by curselves, but we thought that it would be sensible to have two men for the crossings, and we were lucky in having a friend Denn:s Taylor who was very willing to help.

On one of our sailing weekend, we checked the steering compass against the hand bearing compass on various courses, and found no disagreement, It was as well to check this, as we had found that ‘ ; te 0 the outboard in certain positions could cause an error of 20°. As we had no real experience of night sailing, particularly in traffic, we decided to have a night run down to the hiedway, but unfortunately a complete lack of wind meant that we only reached the Whitaker Buoy. However, some lessons were learnt, as it was an extremely black night and impossible to see the unlit buoys, which became quite a hazard when entering the Colne later on. I therefore determined to get a mich more powerful spctiight, which additionally, would be a good ship scarer,. A week before our holiday I telephoned the Customs Officer at Maldon, who noted that we were going foreign, and said that if we would ring hin on our return, he would gladly come down to Stansgate to give us clearance, However, he suggested that we might get 2 quicker clearance at Brightlingsea as there are more men on duty there. We planned to sail at 09.30 on Friday 21st June, and with Stansgate high tide at 10,30 would have the best of the tide out of the Thames Istuary: We decided to make for Ostend, as Dennis could easily fly back from there to his home in Southend. Allowing twenty hours for the crossing, we would make our landfall at cawn, and having the advantage of being able to see the powerful Ostend light, and also be able to enter the harbour in daylight. The only disadvantage being that we would have to cross the shipping lenes at night. Although the week started well, the weather gradually deteriorated until the forecast at 06.40 on Friday was S.W. 4-6, due largely to a depression north of Scotland. I rang the London Yeather Centre who told me that the situation was likely to get rapidly worse due to a depression forming west of Ireland, and that gale force winds were likely on Saturday. ve waited until Saturday, which produced the promised weather, and as Dennis had to be at work on Monday, we realised that we muss postpone our trip. ve were bitterly disappointed, but fortunate in being able to delay our holidays for a week, though we felt somewhat sheepish in going back to work on the Monday, as in the eyes of non-sailing people, it kad beéa a fine sailing week-end, I used a Met Pad fcr recording the radio forecast information, and using this, was abi to construct a rouga and ready weather map, which was particularly us.cul when telephoning the Weather Centre. During the following week I listened to the 14.00 forecast each day, and found them extremely gloomy, with high pressure over the Continent and a procession of wave depressions crossing the country. .Friday was a day of torrential rain ard high winds, and I felt the depressions were crossing me as I rang the Weather Centre after work. Much to our amazement, the forecaster was optimistic, and said that the present depression would be clear by iate evening, and that we should have at least 24 hours of light southerly winds, before a deep depression of 984 millibars started to effect western districts. Not able to believe my ears, I wang the Mildenhall Weather Office for a second Opinion, and they confirmed the situation and said that the cold front was crossing them et the moment, I phoned Dennis, and we were ali down on the boat by 21.00, the wind having died completely. ie deflated the bow section of the Even dinghy and tied down the dinghy securely on to the coachroof, not realising that it would remain there for the rest of the holiday. As high tide at Stansgate was not until 03.30 we decided to have 2 short sleep, and I set the alarm for the 02.00 weather report. Part 2 — The Crossing in December Navigans.

The Club membership is ever increasing, in fact by 80 in 1968. Consequently it is inevitable that the duties of the Officers and Committee become rather demanding, It is envisaged that there must be changes in our outlook and administration for next year and with the much needed co-operation of members it is hoped that we can ease the situation by delegating some of their duties. SATLING SECRETARY'S REPORT 1968 1968 has seen an increase in the number of boats in the Club, 166 dinghy and 44 eruiser registrations were made compared with 114 dinghies and 44 cruisers last year. Among the dinghy classes there are 30 Enterprises, 30 GP14's, 19 Mirrors and 13 Hornets. A few more helmsmen have entered races but not regularly, so that in the points series the number of entries is nearly the same as last year, However, inclusion of the reorganised Helmsman of the Year series brings the total number of race entries in 7 closed events 10% above last years figure. The Cruisers have not been able to run any of the Barnacle Series and the only races were those in the Regatta including a fairly successful race for the Maldon Yacht Club Silhouette Trophy. The Open Hornet Meeting, ably organised by our fleet, was again a successful occasion and appears to be established in the Hornet Association's programme. The timing of this event one week before the Regatta was an aid in securing Hornet entries in our Regatta. The Regatta during the Spring Bank Holiday was an excellent dinghy event, but the Cruiser side was disappointing (It is thought that the Cruiser Cup would be better held at an ordinary week-end). Trophies raced for were the Enterprise Triple K Cup, the GP14 Commodore Cup, The Fleetwind Designer's Trophy and a new Gem Trophy for Graduates and there were good entries in the Hornet, Finn, Snipe and Mirror classes. My thanks go to John Witter who undertook the secretarial work of the Regatta, We were successful in the Hornet Team races with Saltcote S.C and also the Enterprise team race with Osea S.C. The Hornet Invite Series with Stone S.C. got off to a good start but interest slackened towards the end of the year, Only one week-end (14th-15th Sept) had such bad weather as to prevent Sailing but a midweek gale in July damaged several moored boats.

-5- The reorganised Helmsman of the Year series went well but it seems that 8 weekends may be too many and next year the 8 races could be kept to 4 days. The dinghy cruise in company wnd the pursuit race were both enjoyed. The two main rescue launches have been used for many rescues — some from serious situations - but neither boat has been completely satisfactory and on occasion the 14' with outboard has had to be used. Brazil has been used less this year possibly because there are other boats Suitable for tuition including one owned by the Apprentice Association, In general the mooring situation has been satisfactory but there have been 2 few mishaps particularly when the gales in July and September revealed one or two inadequate moorings, My thanks go to Pat Black for dealing with the allocation and positioning of moorings. Several race marks were lost this season and a new set will be BES Some materials have been purchased but were not used this year, I should like to thank Richard Benwell for being Race Officer on 2 number of days and to others who undertook the job at short notice on other occasions, It has not been easy to get race officers and rescue boat crews this year and we were recommending that a rota of members prepared to do these duties should be included in next seasons programme. I have enjoyed much of the sailing secretary's work but have not had time at work at E.E,V to contact people (through the external phones) and confirm arrangements for each weekend. Hence I have come to face the fact that something or someone Will be missing at Stansgate and as the season progressed it became something of a chore to make the visit. In these circumstances I do not wish to continue as Sailing Secretary and I hope we can all try to make my sucessor's job as smooth and pleasant as possible. P.H. Batey. Sef tee * PART 2 of BRIAN BOWSHER'S SUMMER CRUISE THE CROSSING The forecast was 5.1-3. The barometer had risen to 1013, and by 03,00 we were on our way, with the genoa and main pulling gently on a faint breeze from the S.W¥, At the Bench Head we ran out the log, and as the wind had died completely started the outboard, which was to run till noon. The Spring Tide was now ebbing at it's peak, and by 06.00 we were at -the Wallet Spitway, and 07.00 saw us at the Sunk Beacon, having set a course via the N.E. Middle and Barrow No.3. buoys. For tidal information on the Thames Estuary I used an Admiralty Tidal Atlas, in which I marked in advance the actual times of use for each page. I kept an hourly log of the barometer, wind and log reading, and on the chart I marked the time, log and new course-at each significant point, be it actual or dead-reckoning. I found it convenient to keep the hourly log time in terms of the tidal reference time, and could then quickly tell the tidal set to allow when plotting a position. From the Sunk Beacon, which is on the N.B&. edge of a drying section on the Sunk Sand, wé set a course to take us midway between two drying sections on the Long Sand. This seemed to me the most direct course to take to Ostend, but at low tide there is very little water, and I would not have attempted it in bad weather. While crossing the Sunk Sand we monitored the echo-sounder, partly to avoid running aground, but also alias to note when we had reached the Black Deep. This appeared with a sudden jump of 40 feet and we found ourselves crossing in front of two large tankers coming out of the Thames, I checked their bearing against the rigging and noted that we would comfortably pass ahead, but the bone in their teeth could be seen distinctly, The Black Deep was marked by buoys, but as our chart was not, they were of little use navigationally. At 08,10 the echo-sounder made another dramatic leap, and we were crossing the Long Sand. It was now near low tide, and being the peak of a Spring Tide, we were down to Chart Datum. However, in crossing the sands we never recorded anything less than 10 feet, although there were several 5 foot depths on the course line. When the echo-sounder showed deep water again, we had réached Knock Deep, and we set a course to take us between the Middle Knock and South Knock buoys, which are about 2 miles apart, At 10.10 wé picked out the South Knock, and declared ourselves in the North Sea. We changed over from the Thames Estuary to the North Sea Chart, and set a course to the Fairy Bank Buoy, using the tidal diagrams incorporated hr in the chart. The buoy was 26 miles on, and although the vishbility was good I must confess I had little confidence in picking it up. However, the West Hinder Light Ship was 8 miles beyond the buoy, and would be easier to find. ; Since leaving the Bench Head, we had found no wind at all, and the sea was a glassy calm, but around noon a good sailing breeze came up from the South, and thankfully we were able to stop the outboard motor. Until then the sky had been overcast, but suddenly the clouds dispersed, and we had a perfect afternoon, Jackie made some lunch, and being well fed and content, we basked in the sunshine, while the boat furrowed on, rising and falling on a gentle swell. All weather symptoms were good. The barometer had risen steadily to 1020 and was still rising, and the weather. forecast suggested that the S.E. of lngland was coming under the influence of the high pressure over the Continent, while the deep Atlantic depression was taking a more northerly course. At 15.00 we were crossing the South bound shipping lane, and an hour later the North bound traffic appeared. Luckily the traffic was light, and we never found ourselves in the embarrassing position of being run down. Much to my amazement at 16.10 we sighted a buoy to starboard, It was very indistinct, and a running fix put us 2 miles to the North. Assuming this to be the Fairy Bank Buoy we set a.course for the West Hinder, which we passed at 17.45, giving and receiving a wave from the crew, From the lightship it was a three mile hop to the East Dyck buoy, and a further eight miles to the Middelkerk buoy. The wind now began to lighten until none remained and we were forced to start the outboard again.

a) -7- The tidal current off the Belgian Coast behaves very stangely, as the tidal set makes a complete circle every 12 hours, and I found it useful to refer to the tidal diagram in Delmar—Morgan's Pilot Book. From the Middelkerk, the buoys are spaced at about 2 mile intervals, and it was just a case of buoy hopping into Ostend. However, it seemed the longest part.of the trip, as the coast was in view for about three hours, and until the last hour, never seemed to get closer. Approaching the Binnen Stroombank buoy just outside Ostend, we pulled in the log line which had recorded 87 miles from the Bench Head. It was just getting dark as we approached Ostend and I switched on the navigation lights, There were quite a few fishing boats about, and a couple of ferries came in, which were the first we had seen, I would have worried about entering Ostend at night had it not been for theexcellent Pilot Book, — which gave such good pictures and information, that I had no doubts, The incoming ferries turn round half a mile outside the entrance, and then enter stern first, and it is important not to try to squeeze in ahead of then, There are traffic signals on the end of the N.E, breakwater and it is advisable to obey these if there are any ferries about, though the local fishing boats do not seem to worry. Just as we came up to the entrance we received the go ahead signal, and we ran along the S.i/. breakwater, until we reached the first break to 2=starboard which is the entrance to MontZomery Dock. Turning to starboard inside the dock, we found ourselves at the North Sea Yacht Club pontoon, and were lucky enough to find a vacant berth there. The time was 23.15 and we moored with our bow to a buoy and our stern to the pontoon, and then stepped ashore for a quick stroll round the harbour to get our land-legs, before climbing very contentedly into our sleeping bags. On Sunday morning we woke up to a clear blue sky, with the nine o'clock sun already quite warm. We flew our courtesy Belgian ensign, and, in common With several other yachts, raised the yellow Customs flag, only to find that Sunday is a Customs day off. The North Sea Yacht Club overlooks the yacht basin, and we were made very welcome there, We had a drink on the verandah and watched the ferries docking just passed the entrance to Montgomery Dock, and noted the flashing light that warns those in the harbour not to venture out when a ferry is on the move. The harbour at Ostend is delightful, with ocean racers and day boars huddling together with gin palances in the deep well of the dock, while the fishing boats bustle about feeding the market in the main street above. Later that morning we took a walk around the town, and were fortunate in seeing 'The Procession of the Blessing of the Sea’, This is a most interesting and colourful procession, involving perhaps 400 people, many of them wearing the most elaborate costumes, 'Kach year the various groups recall the gratitude of the fisherman to God, the Almightly, Creator of the Sea, their struggle for their livelihood and their hope of returning safe and sound to harbour! By now it was so hot that we were glad to escape into the cool shade of a restaurant on the seafront. This was a mistake however, because, ajthough the food was good, the price made us thankful that we had brought so much food with us. Dennis had to fly back in the afternoon, and Jackie and I spent the rest of the day lazing on the beach and swimming to keep cool. That evening we ate on the boat, and just sat in the cockpit watching the harbour. PART 3 — JANUARY ISSUE OF NAVIGANS.

To the Mediterranean - Dr, Donald iicKm@mdrick les Iles d'Hyeres (the Golden Isles) lie about 25 miles east of Toulon, We had previously taken our five tonner there and decided to rcpeat these highly successful holidays in 1968, The 'Jayess' is a 23 foot bilge keel Gnapdragon in which we have cruised widely during our four Yours of ownership, On this occasion our i. consisted of myseli, my wife Evelyn, Sally (daught er? and Sally (friend) - two pretty (sic) inexperienced but kcen 15 year olds, To reduce the driving in lrance we cross Newhaven- Dieppe. Tovwing with a 2.2 litre Ensign estate has proved no problem in the past but on the way home this year we boiled excessively on some of the hills (the cer had done 80,000 miles!) so it has now been replaced by a Land Rover for future trips. We left Arkley (Herts) at 1400 hours on Thursday August 8th. ~° With a large tow one gets very favourable treatment on ferries and is among the first both on and off, jrriving in Dieppe about midnight we pulled off the road on to the ample parking space on the front, climbed into our sleeping bags and slept in comfort until the morning. At midday on Sunday (24 days latex we drove into Toulon where unfortunstely we were met by the police with a message from home which meant Evelyn had to fly home imnacdiately. £%-0800 hours on iionday morning we were expertly craned into the water in a matter of minutcs. There was a strong mistral blowing so after getting the mast up we motored to a more protected berth at the Societe des Regattes where we lay in comfort head on to the pontoon. On Tuesday the mistral still blew. This is a favourable wind for the Golden Isles so the Sallys and I set off with the working jib end 8 rolls, bathing costumes instead of oilies -in the force 5 plus, a not unusual combination in this part of the world, We were in fact over-reefed so after five miles I shoook out the reefs and we made better progress, ie had a good run to Porquerolle - the main’island in the group - where we turned into a small sheltered bay. There we dropped the hook, took a stern line ashore to a convenicnt trec in the accepted manner and all thankfa dived overboard to get cool, We spent thrce weeks in this delightful cruising ground. If you like hot sun’ and warm bathing in deep blue crystal-clear water with the bottom visible at-ten fathons quite often and three fathoms always, if you like watching the wondrous ways of the French dropping their anchors at full speed ahead - always done bt the wife with the husband at the tiller giving advice at twenty to the dozen, if you like 1 eace and quiet in idyllic scenery, then come to the Golden isles, ic visited the mainland occasionally but always were thankful to get back to the tranquillity of the Islands. Porquerolle has numerous beachss and even more simall rocky bays most of which can only be reached b3 boat. Fort Cros is the pretticst of the three islands where the gold of the rocks is really striking in certain lights. It has two main bays - Port Cros and Port hian - one of which will amost certainly give protection against the prevalent vands of the summer, although during this holiday they were cach to give us their measure of excitement, There are no stores at Port itan but the third island - Levant - is only a mile away. This-‘is the island famous because it favours nudism, where indeed one fecls rather overdressed in the grocers if one is wearing more than a G-string. ut the nudists attrect the tourists and’we only visit Levant Tor shopping. We had a lot of wind this year. {Two nights stand out. The first was in Fort Man which is a dcep bay where we were sheltering from a strong notrth-westerly which nevertheless bounced off Levant and appeared to blow straight in. During a very restless night nearly all of the 40 odd boats dragged. The Jayess, an Atalanta and a Hillyard did not, no doubt because English yachts tend to carry much heavier ground tackle than most of the French boats in the iicditcrranean,. The other night was one we will long remember and occurred soon after Evelyn had rejoincd us in Porquerollc. We were back in Port Cioss end at anchor on a rater dull évening. Evelyn and the Sallyshad gone ashore with friends from another boat and I stayed on board because I did not much like the look ci the sky. The storm began dramatically just as the shore party were rcturming and this very crowded anchorage turned into chaos in séconds. age.n we were protected, this time

=o from the 'Levant' which is the notorious casterly of this reri of the world, so therc was really nothing of © séa. Yet the gusts laid us well over and this is the only time in my sailing career I have renoved while at anchor well lashed down foresails, boarding ladder and everything else possible from deck in order to reduce windage. During the next four hours the ventimeter repeatedly registered force ten, and this of course in a sheltered anchorage. The storm took its toll of at least one boat in the area and I believe there was another also with loss of life, We were safe enough in Port man although we dragged at first like everyone else, We ended up well secure with 25 fathoms of chain on the main, 20 fathoms on the kedge and a 100 fathoin line to a bollard ashore. One of the many interesting features of this exciting evening was the sudden appearance of f'rogmen who dived repeatedly in 30 feet of watcr leading boats to better holding ground and finally apparently hooking anchors on to rocks on the sea bed. We love the sun and the bathing from the boat. the sailing is mixed - plenty of wind at times but the engine is often required for passage making as there is no help from tides - a deficiency more than compensated for by the pleasure of anchoring in three feet of water on any sandy beach. A Snapdragon is an idcal type of yacht for the Mediterranean with its large cockpit and airy cabin. Therc is always plenty of room for sunbathing and a lilo aft of the mast is a fevourite spot whether sailing or at anchor, Whatever the wind it is always possible to get shelter and there is now a good - harbour in Porquerolle for those who like to be in port at night. We don't too many pcople, too much noise but worst of all no pro-breakfast swin, Except when the wind is from the Mast, which is rare, therc is almost continuous sun, . The Mistral blew hard at the end of our holiday as it had at the beginning. It usually eases off a bit at night so we sailed for Toulon at 2300 -hours on September Ist. It was a pitch dark moonless overcast night and we had a fairly wet: beat back so I was glad I had bcen persuaded to put in our oilics byEvelyn ('just in case') as I had wanted to leave them at home. The Jayess was on her trailer by lunchtime on Monday and we were home in our beds in Arkley in the carly hours of Friday 6th, The journcy is no probleu, indeed it is very much part of the holiday (once we came home vis Paris to the constermation of the camp sité in the Bois de Boulogne). We would be very happy to supply details of the practicalities to anyone considering a similar holiday. We will certainly be there again next summer. te et et ee ee vo ~ MAKING .ND BREAKING RC RULES One of the Merlin-Rocket class's carly classics was a Sussex coast meeting when a race was started bcfore the first mark was laid. The boat carrying the buoy could not overtake the fleet and the leaders set sail for the only speck on the horizon, a fisherman snoozing over his rod, After the first six ierlins had roared round his lonely outpost the fisherman decided to up anchor and row to a niore peaceable spot. PAR? 111 of Jackie & Brian Bowsher's Summer Cruise Ostende to the Veersemeer On Monday the Customs men appeered, but when approached they seemed more concerned about any bonded stores that might be needed. I made a mistake here, because I decided to wait until later, and in fact Ostend was the only place we visited where it was possible to buy bonded drink for a yacht, We left for Blankenberg at Midday, thereby having the best of the tide along the coast. “We had wondered whether to go inland on the canals to Terneuzen, but it was so hot agein, that we felt it would be cooler at sea. ‘The breeze was very erratic, but it was only cight miles along the coast, and we sailed along leisurely, reaching Blankenberg in three hours. We will always remember the blast of heat at the harbour entrance, It was quite withering. Looking back at the dreadful weather of the summer, we realise our good fortune in having the two hottest days of the summer during our holiday. Slankenberg has a very attractive little harbour behind the sea front, and it is hard to imagine that 18 years ago it was completely silted up. The entrance is still shallow, but once inside there is a reasonable depth of water by the pontoons, The town is a fairly large seaside resort, and appeared rather uninteresting during the day, but in the evening everyone was “gut- strolling elong the streets and gazing in the busy shops, and we were contcnt to~spend a couple of hours walking to and fro with the crowd. Tuesday .came with a slightly overcast sky, which soon cleared, giving us another hot day. The wind was $8.2 and we set sail at 11.00 for Breskens, 20 miles along the coast. We kept close to the shorc, apart from giving the Zeebrugge iuole a wide clearance as suggested in the Filot. The wind coming off the shore gradually increased, and presented our travelling Compansion, a Westerly 22, with e FINA plastic canoe, and shortly afterwards gave us an enormous beach bail. 4s we approached Holland we ceme under the influence of the flood-tide into the Wester Scheldc, and with the wind now 8.4 we made good progress reaching Breskens just after 16.00, Soon after we arrived a violent thunderstorm loomed up and we were thankful not to be sailing, but the rain soon passed, leaving a pleasantly cool and refreshing evening. The yacht basin is new and most impressive, holding perhaps 390 boats on pontoons, but possibly due to being nationally run, it seemed a cold and uninteresting place to us. There were plenty of people about, but everyone kept themsclves to themselves, and I do not think that we spoke to a soul. There was a toilet, shower and a couple of men's stand-ups in @ block house overlooking the basin, and we could only think that the harbour was for men only, as there appesred to be no other facilities about. We noticed that our yellow flag was the only one flying, and after three hours we took it down again, Having become somewhat relaxed by the Customs! approach in Belgium, we fclt that we had done our bit in entering Holland, but lesrnt later from friends in Rotterdam, that the Dutch view things differently, and that imnigration clearance is essential. Had we entered Flusing we would have been cleared quickly, but «8s breskens has no Customs Office we should heve reported to the local Police Station. In the evening we walked around the quiet fishing town and it seemed a thousand miles from Blankenberg. All the streets were incredibly neat and tidy and the living rooms of the houscs, with their lights on and curtains undrawn, almost forced you to look in at the tidy rooms full of flowers and pot plants, That night the wind blew hard from the west, causing a tremendous din in 500 masts.In the morning thewind wes Wi, from a clear sky, and there appeared to be quite a séa ruming with the wind against tide. We donned waterproofs and with working jib and four rolls in the main we stood out of the harbour. Directly outside a wave shot up and broke across our
