Tele W'house Lane Bxt.296 Reviews Three Boys in a Boat by David Brook Do not be misled by the title, to expect a new Jerome K Jerome; the book owes nothing to that style, though it is written with a light and humourous hand, It could as well have been entitled "Peter Pan on the Bast Coast" or "How I brought up three boys and became a yachtsman", and any of these titles would have been incomplete, David Brook tells how he was faced with the job of raising three sons who lost their mother, without foregoing his own life and leisure if he could avoid it. Living on Mersea Island, he owned, and occasionally sailed, a "tore-out" 20-footer, and was a casual member of the W.M.Y.C., but would never have called himself a keen yachtsman, Indeed, he admits that he felt no affinity for the offshore-racing crowd that piled into the clubhouse when there was a big race, However, he took the boys on a cruise in a chartered boat up to the Deben, decided they would take to the water’ but wanted a handier yacht, and presently bought Kim Holman's prototype "26" fresh from a successful Burnham Week. "Nymphet" showed her paces from the beginnings after reading of the chilly reception he got from winning his first major race in spite of a monumental (and public) bloomer, one may well feel there should be a handicap penalty on any Holman designed boat, to be doubled if it was Holman - tuned! I am sure the crack Class 1 crews must have felt so when they were pipped by a few minutes in that race, There are some fine pieces of descriptive writing of heavy weather in the North Seas of ‘the inevitable squabbles of a family together (never sail close to leeward of a light vessel about 12 o'clock; the boys'. tongues will hang out agonisingly as you pass by the galley ventilation); of cruising in the Netherlands and the Channel Isless of EAORA races in calms and near-gales and blind-man's buff navigation of the Rays'n channel. After "Nymphet" came "Bandit", Brook did not have the benefit of the magic touch of Kim Holman's tuning (only the design this time) and he obviously felt he was slow in getting her to sail to her ratings but <—~~4 offshore his growing williness made up for 2 good deal. No more would he be seen keeping out of the tide after it had turned in favour, (unless there was a deeper game to play). Though he does not admit as much, I seem to recall that it took Holman himself to put "Bandit" out of the money in any of the 1964-65 offshore races. As fer the "happy ending" you must read the book for that. Anyone who sails the East Coast will surely eajoy it. Jackie & Brian Bowsher's Sumner Cruise to Holland. PART 1V — Delta Marina to Rotterdam Beyond the lock we would be in the tidal waters of the Easter Schelde, and it was important to judge the time of departure for the next day. We decided to leave at 06.00 in order to have the best of the tide up to Zijpe and Willemstad, but we would have to battle against the Easter Scheie for about four miles, A friend lent us some recent Dutch estuary charts, and we supplemented these where necessary, and also bought some tidal charts, For general infomation we borrowed 'Inlend Waterways of Holland' and 'Thorpe's Yachtsman's Guide to Dutch Waterways' from Chelmsford Library, though these are rather out of date now. We sct off on Saturday in e stcady drizzle, which soon developed into a continuous downpour. We passed through the lock with two motor yachts, end then battled into the wind and tide, The rain continucd to gct heavier until visibility was very poor, and it became increasingly difficult to pick out the navigation buoys. With several sandbanks around to worry us, we decided to call it a day, and so we ran back to the iuarina,. However, on this occasion the Lock-keeper did not seem inclined to let us in, and we cruised around for about three-quarters of an hour in the lock entrance, unable to moor due to the swell, until eventually a ferry appeared and took us through. It rained solidly until 6 o'clock that evening, and we were cold, wet and miserable, but Sunday arrived bright and clear, and so we set off again in the early inorning. This time we could just hold a course for Zierikzee, and so fighting the tide was not such a problem, Due to the estuaries being inter-connected, the tides have unfamiliar ways, and at this time the Easter Schelde was flooding strongly while the Keeten Channel to. Zijpe was just on the turn, Just before the Oosterscheldebrug connecting Noord-Beveland to Schouwen Duiveland, we turned up the Keeten Channel, and joined the heavy barge traffic to and from the Zuid-Leéveland Canal. This is one of the main waterways of Europe and the air was full of the rythmic thud of diesels «S an unending procession of international barges passed us on their way to Antwerp or Rotterdam, These barges are also homes and have window boxes and washing lines, play-yens and swings, and to the children this is the normal way of life, The wind slackened to a gentle breeze from the west, but with the tide building up its strength beneath us, we soon reached Zijpe, and turning into the Volkerak Channel, we ran gently on our way to Willemstad, The sun was shining, and secing all the barges with their washing lines full, Jackie proceeded to fill the backstays with towels and tea cloths, and yesterday's wet clothing. Just before Willemstad we went through an enormous new lock, which could swallow perhaps a 1000 Vivacities, and yet we were through in no time at all. It was intcresting to compare this lock with the large lock at Veere, which took half an hour's hard labour by the Llock-keeper and his mate to bring a boat through. luckily, it is only the larger barges that use this lock, Out of the lock, we turned into the Hollandsch Diep, and soon to starboard saw Willemstad hiding behind its fortifications, Running in beside the nole, and through the narrow entrance in the walls, we were presented with an unforgetable picture of this little harbour, jostling with boats, and overlooked by the newly-restored windmill standing four square at the end of the quay. The time was 14.00 and we were 50 miles from the impersonaility of the Marina and back into the world of Veere. The Harbour liaster put us five boats out from the shore and added another two to us, leaving room further along the quay for the bigger boats that might come later, Scrambling ashore, we climbed up on tb the carthen walls, and watched the boats come and go, and noted the new marina being built outside. _ That evening it rained quite heavily and though the weather on the whole was good for the rest of our holiday, the heat-wave had finally passed.

7 -8= 2 oe We joined the barge procession at 12.00 the next day. °° A time that had to be judged carefully, so that we would reach Dordrecht at high tide, and thereby have the tide with us to Rotterdam. Just before the Moerdijk railway and road bridges we turned off to port into the River Kil, finelly leaving behind us the broad estueries, As we approached Dordrecht we lowered the mast, knowing that a low railway bridge would soon confront us, and having passed this obstacle, we re-rigged thinking our height problems were over, We rather regretted not stopping at Dordrecht, as the old waterways branching off into the town and crossed t; - sunter-balanced bridges, looked full of interest. However, we had determined to reach Rottcrdam that day, and so we turned into the Noord, on its way to meet the Lek and the Hollandsche Ijssel to form the broad and powerful Nieuwe Meas, which finally reaches the sea at the Hook. ‘Although it was soanabite to sail in the Noord we felt a little uneasy with all the t affic about-us, and so we motored on past all the shipyards and noted that the water was still clean cnough for children to be swimming from the occasional garden that ‘come down to the river. As we approached Rottérdam the traffic became very heavy, with motor barges everywhere; and floating derricks and crancs, and great pusher- tugs shoving enormous lighters, and all these criss-crossed by the worrying furrowing tugs and ferries, unmindful of the out-of-place yacht, The floating timber provided another hazard, and scveral times we a ran hard into a heavy log floating just below the surface and I was particularly worried that a glancing blow might damage the outboard motor. We knew there was a railway bridge in Rotterdam but it appeared from out information that we would have six foot clearance, but on approaching ‘the bridge it became obvious that we were not going to make it, so down came the mast again. The water was: now in so much turmoil due to the passing traffic, that it was the devil's own job to stop the inast leaving the boat altogether and I found mysclf sitting on the coachroof as though riding at a rodéo, while Jackie ‘steered the best course she could between barge and bridge. Having reached the other sidc, the situation was no better and after a few hopeless attempts to get the mast up again, we bolted into the first hole we saw. Here we were asked if we wore stopping, and when I replicd 'no, we will be going on to the Royal Meas Yacht Club’, he pointed at his boots and we realised that we had arrived. The Club has @ delightful harbour, situated as if in a London Square . with Plane trees all around, end an air of tranquillity heightened by the hustle and bustle which surrounds it. Being the premicr yacht club of o_, Holland, and the place where Princess jcatrix keeps her yacht, the Club offers a standard of scrvice far above normal, and the Harbour hastcr, more English than the English, runs everything with a military precision, Previously we had: always to pay a nightly mooring charge of about threc shillings, but here thé mooring was free for the first weck, That evening we had a meal in the Clubhouse with some friends of fricnds from Southend, and admired the view over the river to the liners docked on the other side. We «* an Indoncsian dish callcd Nasi Goreng, which though cooked superbly, had the most strange cffect on us the next day - or was it the drink we had? On Tuesday we saw the new City Centre and latcr climbed the Euromast which gives a fascinating view of thc. docks and: river below. We took the train to Amsterdam on Wednesday, and returning on Thursday cvening saw the devastation of that day's gales. This gale was thé onc that caused so much damage at Stansgate, and around the yacht harbour great branches had been wrenched off the trees and the strcéts were covered in debris. CRUISE TO THE SCILLY ISLES by JOHN TODDS Mor-An-—“Ira is an attractive 18'6" glassfibre sloop of the Hurley 18 class. During the summer of 1968 she was moored on the Helford River in Cornwall and I had sailed in her there a few times with Robbie, her owner. Friends of his had offered to lay the boat up in the Scillies, so when September came we made our plans for sailing her there. For both of us this was to be our first real cruise, since 311 our previous sailing experience had been gained in racing dinghies. The channel pilot, when talking of the Scillies, speaks darkly of not approaching them without local knowledge or a pilot, but we decided that the warning was intended for larger ships than Mor-—An—Yra and made our pians accordingly. In order to arrive in daylight we would have to sail part of the journey by night, since we had a distance of about 55 miles to cover. ‘We'd decided to attempt the trip in one hop, since Penzance, the nearest good harbour to the Scillies, was still 40 miles from them, and about 30 from the Helford, It seemed that the navigation would be fairly straightforward, provided the visibility remained good, since these waters are well provided with light and bouys. The weather forecast on Thursday, the 12th September, was for winds S to SW, force 3 to 4, with a slight chance of some fog early the following morning, we decided that this was a good enough forecast to enable us to leave that evening, so, after moving the boat from her mooring to Helford quay to load our gear, we finally got away at 19.30 hours under the power of the Seagull Century. As we motored down the river we hoisted the sails and heated some water which was put in the thermos for coffee later in the night. The outboard was then stopped, taken up from its well and stowed away, and the Compari dinghy was deflated and stowed in the stern locker. The evening seemed very quiet and the wind fairly light as we sailed out into the open sea. It was dark perhaps an hour after we had left, but our first mark, the Manacles Buoy, was easily seen, flashing in the distance over our starboard bow. To the north of us lay the lights of Falmouth, with the lighthouse on St Anthony's Head nearby. One light out to sea puzzled us for a time. It was flashing red, but our charts Showed no bouys in that direction. Eventually we realised that we had been taking bearings on 2 helicopter from the Culdrose Naval Air Station, hovering out at sea on night exercises! At about 22.15 we came upon another yacht idling around. Having no fixed navigation lights we shone a red-shaded torch over our port side at then. This drew forth a startled oath, followed by the sound of a motor starting. The yacht sailed round ahead of us and then headed back towards Falmouth. During the interlude the moon had risen so that we could see her quite clearly. She carried self-stecring gear on her stern. Shortly after this encounter I took the helm from the skipper and continued what was by now a slow beat down the coast. I could see the dark outline of the land by the loon of the Lizard light beyond. Slowly we passed the Manacles and then the light of Coverack. We had intended to pass close to the Manacles Buoy, but because of the wind direction we went well outside it, in the eastern white sector of St. Anthony's light, As we tacked to the south we frequently passed from this white sector back into the red sector, which gave us a good position line, . Eventually the Lizard Lighthouse came into view, yet we were Still not quite abeam of it when Robbie took the helm again at 02.00. The signal station flashed us, but the skipper couldn't make out the message, so we made no reply. Later we saw the station talking to other ships in the vicinity, and we watched them answer. ‘We had informed the coastguard of our plans, so the signal station probably knew who we were. It was low tide when we reached the Lizard, and we were anxious to keep clear of the many rocks which lie off the shore. Ye finally decided we had enough water when we found ourselves passing rather close. to a couple of small coasters, which smelied warmly of diesel engines. From there we were able to set course, due west magnetic, for the scillies, about 40 miles out into the Atlantic. There had been quite a

ae TS lot of shipping about just off the Lizard, but once past the point we were able to relax. The wind had gone southerly and freshened a little, So we were naking quite good speed. I went below to try to get some sleep, but the movement of the boat made it impossible. I lay listening to the rush of water past the hull, and wondering if I felt seasick, till eventually I was dozing fitfully. At about 0500 the skipper raised both the Longships Lighthouse, off Land's End, and the Wolf Rock lighthouse, Our course lay a nile or two south of the ‘iolf. Day was beginning to break when I took the helm at 0600, and we were Still reaching merrily along with the wind from the south. Robbie went below and managed to sleep for an hour, which was no mean achievement as the seas were building up. The existing wave p2ttern had built up with the previous few days westerly winds, so the sea was getting lumpy. At about 0730 abeam of the ‘olf Rock, I said that I thought we should change the jib as I was having to spill wind. In a calm sea the wind ifgself would have been perfect, but with the waves rolling us the boat was becoming overpowered, so the skipper, encased in waterproofs and life jacket, went forward to set the storm jib. He had to do this sitting on the fore-deck with his back supported against the pulpit because of the movements. (Mor-An-"ra is also fitted with a taffrail and guard-lines, and these were certrinly essential out on the open sea), A little later, after watching a large liner head nobth between us and the mainland, we wound 2 couple of rolls down on the main to balance the boat better, Mor-—An-vra was still tramping xzlong, but she proved 2S very dry. We shipping nothing but a couple of dollops of spray on the whole trip, so there was no chance to test the efficiency of the self- draining cockpit. Considering the state of the sea this was a very reassuring performance from a pretty small boat. The weather had been cloudy for some hours, but now the sky to the west began to look black and ominous as the Wolf Rock lighthouse slid past our starboard bean, The skipper wondered if a storm was brewing. To me the clouds seemed more like rain than wind, and as there had been no gale warning on the radio we decided to press on. Cornwall was gradually fading from view, and so our only landmark was the lighthouse astern. With no sign of our landfall, the dark sky and heaving Atlantic combined to produce a slightly frightening atmosphere. We were constantly checking our compasses, for now we had nothing to aim for. From the cockpit the horizon was only a couple of miles away. Suddenly I saw a sleek blue grey shape leap clear of the water dead ahead - a porpoise. I c2lled Robbie, who fetched his camera, and soon a whole school of these creatures was playing around the boat. They were leaping ang in twos and threes on all sides of us, and sometimes a group would play at cutting right across the bows as if to see which could get closest without being hit. ‘We could plainly hear them calling to each other in high pitched squeaks. It seems they were a good omen, in best maritime tradition, for by the time they left the sky had brightened a little, . and very shortly afterwards we sighted the Scillices. With our destination in sight and the wind still fresh on the beam our spirits rose, and we were able to enjoy the experience of Sailing at speed in rough water. Mor-—An-W/ra was a pleasure to handle. In the hard puff of wind just a quick pull on the tiller would be sufficient to hold her on course. We saw one or two fishing craft, and one of the BHA helicopters on the Scillies run from Penzance flew close past us. We gave. him a wave, as he had come a few miles south of his course to look at us. A friend of the skipper works at the Scillies Heliport, and he watched our final twelve miles in through binoculars from the control tower. He later told us that a large submarine had surfaced fairly close astern of us, but neither of us had seen anything of it. We had, however, noticed a strange cloud formation ahead of us over the Scillies, which we jokingly called a waterspout. Only after our arrival did we find that it had been one.

We were naking very good time, and we began to wonder whether we would beat the mail ship, "the Scillonion" into St. Mary's harbour, as she was due in at about 1130 hours. However, just a few miles fron the islands we saw her corning up fast on our starboard quarter, and she passed us just before the Spanish Lodge Buoy, the first of two red can bouys marking St. Mary's Sound. This Sound is the channel to the south-west of St. Mary's, and here we met 3 patch of the roughest water we'd encountered, probably a combination of wind, tide race, and wash from the Scillonien. We were only in it for a minute of two, and then things were much easier, The sun was by then shining brightly, and the wind had eased a little. I prepnzred the anchor in case we had to use it, and then took the reef out of the main. We sailed north past the Garrison, the westernmost point of St. Mary's and then east to the harbour, which faces north west and is normally fairly sheltered. Feeling rather pleased with ourselves at our first successful cruise, wo picked up a vacant mooring at 12.50, less than 17% hours after our departure from Helford quay. Robbie went ashore in the dinghy while I took off the sails and did a bit of tidying up down below. Having found the Harbourmaster, who pointed out an unused mooring closer to the quay, the skipper returned and we moved the boat under the outboard to the new mooring. After the continual movement and cloudy skies of our Atlantic crossing, it was very peaceful to be moored on calm clear water on that bright late-summer's day. It seemed unlike a Friday the 13th. We'd eaten very little during our trip, so we went ashore for lunch in the "Mermaid", where we realized that we'd have to find our land legs again, The whole bar secmed to be swaying, even before we'd drunk our beer, ‘We spent a few days on the ishand, and had a really great time. The people were very friendly and the scenery was fascinating, especially to anyone who loves boats and water. On return trip, on "The Scillonion" was a less pleasant experience - a force 8 northerly gale built up huge seas which rolled the ship violently, and she was over an hour late getting back to Penzance. SAILING 1969 ~ WHAT'S HAPPENING The Sailing Programme (Year Book) for 1969 has been revised to include more information about the Club and to make the programme itself more readable, In the Programme the name of the Race Organiser (R.O.) is now included, This means that the named individual is responsible for the provision of (for example) race officers for an event, The idea is to relieve the Sailing Secretary of some of his responsibilities and to share the duties more equally between members, The Sailing activities provided differ from last year. There are now two Points series, Spring and Main, for each class except the Hornets who retain their Invitation Points with Stone S.C and just one Points series, - The people who are not ready by Easter will be able to compete on equal terms later in the Season with those who have more time during the winter to prepare their boats. Sunday Points racing will be for Enterprise, Hornet, GP14, Mirror and Handicap fleets. Another new Series is the Saturday Points, This replaces the individual Spoon Races previously held and is designed to make it more interesting and enjoyable as well as to encourage Handicap racing in which all Fleets may participate, If the turn out for this series is good, there is nothing to stop it being divided into two to provide Suitable sailing for both the faster and slower boats, Sailing is scheduled to start on Easter Sunday with a Tuning-Up Race and a Pennant Race. This is all dependant on all the facilities being ready by then and at the present rate of progress it is going to be very difficult to guarantee this. The programme is at present with the printers and if we are not-- -- able to circulate it to Paid Up menibers with this Navigans then it will follow fairly soon, John Witter -— Rear Commodore.

LETTERS Dear Mrs, Witter As a relatively recent convert to sailing, I thought some of my - last season's experiences may be of some interest to other beginners. It is easy to be put off when hearing old hands discussing racing rules, navigation and so on, and this is a pity, for there is a vast amount of enjoyment to be had from sailing, I bought ‘Quackers! -— Mirror 3284 last February, when I was still working and living at my home in Coventry. I joined the Mid Warwickshire Y.C and thus started out as a reservoir sailor. le sailed all year round ‘ there, weather pernitting, and on one or two occasions, the rescue boat nad to go out first to break the ice up! Easter saw my friend John and myself in Torquay for a few days. The harbourmaster was very helpful, although the harbour and slipway fee was a bit steep. The weather remained fine throughout our stay, but the wind tended to be rather blustery. On 2 relatively caln day we crossed Torbay to Brixham, where several people came down to the slipway and said they had watchéd our passage. I didn'r think anybody had noticed! The average speed was about 4 knots over the five miles or so across the bay, and outward bound on a beat it was a good trip. However, on the return journey, ‘the combination of a following wind and sea made poor John feel ill, I think he said he wanted to die or something! On the last day but one in Devon, I was sailing solo in the harbour when a gust caught me on the hop, and I had my‘first (and so far, only) ducking, I inadvertently let the boat get upside down due to my own incompetence. After tying the painter to a handy buoy I righted the boat quite easily. My plimsolls were in the little open fronted locker, and they were still dry. Fortunately, being Baster time, there were not too many people watching, but even so, at least two strangers had a joke on me the following day. At the beginning of July I moved south to Marconi and within a week had joined MSC and brought the boat down. From this point on, all ny sailing from Stansgate has been single—handed, as I have not yet taken up racing, but more of that later, 4&n early sortie was the dinghy cruise to Brightlingsea, Although the wind was light we averaged 34 - 4 knots if my memory serves me correctly. ‘The return trip almost developed into a race, and by taking a short cut through sone very shallow shallows, I found myself temporarily in the lead, I would point out here that this was not a bad risk to take since the tide was rising and the boat was only making a few inches draught with the centreboard up and the rudder about 2/34 up (the wind was following). A very friendly and interesting cruise ended with rain just es I reached the

the slipway. In the summer John and I had 2 week at Teignmouth, and here I was soundly taught a lesson: carry a compass when on the séa, -One day I sailed along the coast to Torquay, which is about: ten miles, We stayed there the night with my relatives, and the next day I elected to sail back again while John went by road in ny car. It started off a fine day but- as I reached the furthest point from land, fog clamped down tightly and the wind dropped, The rolling motion and some apprehension caused me to have my only bout of sea-sickness -_it was horrible. <Anyway, I took ny bearings fron the wind, turned 45° to port, and rowed most of the way home. I was never more pleased to see those towering cliffs of Teignmouth. So you see, even on such a short coastal hop, a compass would have:been useful, If the wind direction had changed, I might have been in trouble as the fog stayed down at sea level until about 9.pn. The second week of our holiday was at Lyme Regis on the south coast, The fee for using the dinghy park and picturesque little harbour was 30/-. At low tide, the harbour dries out as far as the eritranee, and the wind direction made it difficult to get out of the narrow opening. However, once on the sea, the sailing was exhilerating. About a mile and a half to the east is Charmouth, where the offshore wind funnelled down between the hills, rippling the sea over 2 large-area at about force 5. The thrill obtained from beating up past this area and then planing back on a broad reach has never been paralleled in my experience, The boat became alive, and the centreboard hummed merrily in its. case,..This is sailing at its best. This is what it is all about. ~ Jo sail.a small dinghy*in fair weather is fine, but in.a blow, and. on the sea, it is a tremendously exciting experience, It is a aoe Once 9 but one which must be tempered with prudence, for the sea may be a tranquill friend one minute, and it can turn sour on you the next. The wind too is a fickle ally, as the next episode illustrates. One pleasant Saturday morning I left Stansgate at 8.30.am on “the falling ‘tide, crossed the Colne estuary and beached near Clacton for lunch Returning in the afternoon was peaceful in light airs, until it got tighter and lighter. By the time I had made Mersea it was almost non-existant. Progress was so slow that I had barely reached the estuary as the ebb tide began, so I was slowed even more instead of being carried upstream on the previous flood, The sun went down the light began to fade, and as. Quackers passed Bradwell, darkness reigncd. The lights on three Bites anchored near the Power atetion gave soac comfort, but as they receded astcrmn only a few tiny pin-pricks of light remained shead. I judged thesc to be at Stone, andI was right. There was a pale moon highlighting the water to leeward, and from this I was able to fix my position in the river. Thus I had two approximatc bearings from which to-navigate. Stansgate was found without having collided with anything, and I fclt almost guilty about coming Home so late. Hauling the boat up the wet slipway on that heavy. trolley and in the dark was a trying job, as I was getting a bit tired aftcr fourteen ‘hours in the saddle. Anyway it was accomplished by attacking the slope at an angle, and as I drove home ina: Saale to Writtle, there was time to ponder on the day's happenings. ' So, that was the season that was, very full and quite eventful. There were many other trips both up and down the river, other than those I have related; following the Barge racc, and Old Gaffers Race for example. The boat is back at Coventry waiting to be repainted and this coming Easter, with a bit of luck, thc two of us will be back at Torquay. The best way to learn is by experiéncc, although it is sometimes the hard ways Mistakes are bound to occur but so long as no-one is harmed, nothing is lost. Nothing venturcd, nothing gained, aftcr all. Next season I shall break newground (for myself) by starting to race. So if anyone rcquires a crew in a dinghy or cruiscr carly in the season, I shall be glad to oblige (Baddow extn.97). I have no doubt that an experienced sailor would have made light

ws ne of my difficult situations, but I also fecl that a beginncr such as mysclf should not bc too tinid about cxperinenting and finding out his limitations. Sailing is a great pastimc, ané@ onc which is becoming open to more and more people. And if any person has learned anything from reading this, then I am pleased, for I have achicvcd my objective. Brian S Lidstonc. CONTINUING JACKIE & BRIAN BOWSHUR'S SUMMER CRUISE TO HOLLAND PART 5 ROTTERDAM — HOLib On Friday we picked Dennis up from the airport and prepared to leave for home at 08.00 on Saturday, 13th July. The time was chosen with reference to the Pilot Book which suggcstcd leaving at three hours after Hook H.W. Before leaving England Demis rang Mildenhall Weather Office and this information, togethcr with the radio forecasts, gave a weather picture of high pressure, arcas ovcr Germany and to the $.W. of Iceland, and a shallow depression of 1004 millibars moving slowly towards the Southwest Approaches, For more local. information I could have thoned the Weather Centre at the Hook but the situation seemed fairly stable. The 06.40 weather forccast gave S.E. 1-2 and by 08.00 we were on our wey with hardly enough wind to fill the sails, but with 25 knot tide thrusting.us along, we motored rapidly pest mile after mile of docks. We passed..a.tanker burnt and twistcd, with a gaping hole.in its side, and noticed the roofs missing from several houses nearby. Early the previous morning, Rotterdam had becn shaken by a tremendous explosion which occurred when the ship's tanks were being cleancd. In Rotterdam the river traffic had been light but as we approached the Europoort the shipping built up, and so we kept well over and left the super-tankers to themsclvcs. Rotterdam's position as the premicr port of Europe is quite possibly due to the small tidal range of only seven fect, but this docs not mean that the currents are any the less. Twenty foot below the surface the currents can be twice the surface speed, which means of coursc, the ships can be affcctcd by a five knot tide, We reached the end of the Hook breakwater at 10.350 and noticed the turbulenec as this great mass of water met the sea, Et must be a terrifying place for yachtsmen in bad wcather, We rcached the Goeree Lightship at 13.20 having by now cscaped the great mass of shipping surrounding the Hook, and with the wind non-cxistcnt we motored on a course duc East, heading ultimately for a point midway between the Galloper and Outcr Gabbard Lightships. These would be the first navigation marks we would sec in sixty miles, but during the day we were reminded that our course was correct by the occasional Hook to Harwich Ferry or by running into the waste thrown overboard from them, «at one stage the outboard came to a stop wedged firmly into a cardboard box filled with packing wool, and later, with the outboard running normally, imagine our surprise at coming to a gentle but complete stop, only to find a great wicker basket caught bctwoen the bilge keels. By the evening there was still no wind and not the slightest movement in the sea, The weather report said that the depression off Ircland had dcepened slightly, but was still slow moving, and they forecast S.W. 4-5 in the Thames area on Sunday. With our 24 hour supply of fuel now half finished, it looked as if wo would need this wind to gct us hone, With night approaching, Jackie snuggled into the warmth of her sleeping bag, while Demis and I put on extra clothing and donned our Pitt. regalia of watcrproofs, life jackcts and safcty harnesses. Vié raised the radar reflector and prepared to switch on the navigation lights whenever a ship was sighted.

< Bias _ dust as night fell Fred the racing pidgcon, aiming for the mast head, hit the slack mainsail,. and came tumbling down to the side deck. Recovering his self~possession, and: aftcr a quick look through the port at Jackie slecping down below, he settled down to wait patiently for dam, Several times ships passed us at a distance, and we found it very difficult to judge their direction from the lights, but hopcfully, I had visions of Officers of the Watch straining their cycs for the 5000 ton boat that showed so clearly on their radar screens. At 03.10 we picked up the Outer Gabbard light but visibility was not good cnough to catch it dipping, and thercforcewc did not gct an immediate fix. Taking a running fix over an hour put us almost cxactly midway between the two lightships, and soon afterwards we pickcd up the Galloper light. We then set a course for the Sunk Lightship, and wondered whether the, wind would come before: the petrol ran out. At day-break Fred stretched, came down to the cockpit, checked the- COMPASS, and pen. flew ahtaigne off without so much as a nod. ! sus. keene 08.00 we felt a breath of wind and by 09.15 we were at the Sunk Lightship and sailing. hard on the wind, with working jib and five rolls in the main, ive were doubly fortunate that soon afterwards the wind. backed :slightly enabling us to head down the Wallet,:and in addition we: just caught the start of the flood tide. It rained heavily© and blew:hard, but. the rain soon passed and we had an cxhilarating sail in home waters again, »« 4t 14.30 we ran into Brightlingsea to pick up the Customs having logged 119 Miles from the Hook, and it only remaincd to “" pick up our’mooring at Stansgate to complete a really cnjoyable holiday. CRUISE TO CHRISTCHURCH IN 'HULLAB4LOO by L.A. Payne. MAY/ JUNE 1968 Having a son, Roger, et the Signals Resesrch and Devclopment Establishment (S.R.D.TM) Christchurch, I was anxious to accept his long- standing invit ition to visit him by sea, so made enquirics about. finding a crew. I knew that Walter Standing from the Marconi Sailing Club -had disposed of his Kingfisher cruiser and was without a boat and that he had frequently given me a hend in the race box at Stansgate so I approached him and was dcelightcd to find that not only did he accept, but that he was able to supply a further hand, Colin Edmund, whose father is the skipper of the famous gaff-cutter Theodora, belonging to the Ocean Youth Club. It was decided to make the cruise to Christchurch during the Spring Bank holiday, which gave us three clear days as both Walter and Colin had to return to their duties on the Tuesday, and a few days beforé the start were occupied with loading up the Atalanta cruiser ‘Hullabaloo with water, petrol, stores and generally checking the boat and her gear, although as she had been afloat for only about a month there was not much doubt about this. The great day arrived: the Walton Coast Guard was advised of our sail nunber, time of departure and destination; the crew turned up in good time so that we were able to make our first entry in the log:- 155C hrs. Left mooring at Blackwater Sailing Club: Wind S.E. force 3, -, Colin had already obtained the weather report, by telephone, which was - favourable and the weather was fine and clear; but as the wind was dead _ against us and we were anxious to cross as much of the Thames as possible “in daylight, we proceeded under engine, hoping to set sail after rounding --Osea pier, However, it was not bcfore Stone that we sect sail and then only just managed tc weather Thirsle: spit beacon and as the next board would have teken us into St. Lawrence Say and out of the tide, we decided to hand sails and continue under engine. 1/3C hrs: Passed Cradwell Nuclear Power Station: Wind nowE.3. It was not until we were well past Bradwell that we were able to set sail and then, with the tide under us, we soon passed the Bench Head, New. Knoll, Eagle and Knoll; but with wind against tide, there was by now quite a choppy sea which was not quite so pleasant for those down below poring over the charts planning our course over the sands, and it was not long before both my crew succumbed, It speaks well for their fortitude and strength of will that they were both Soon able to carry on with theiz duties despite the discomfort. 1915 hrs, Passed the Wallet Spitway, sailing fast. As it was nov’ half tide we found there was plenty of water through the Spitway, and we passed in grand style the Whitaker and Heaps and we soon saw the light from the Barrow Deep light vessel, as it was now dusk. 2100 hrs. Barrow Deep left to port: Wind Eb foree 3 and twentyfive miles of our journey completed; average specd 5 kt. Here we nearly had a major ‘disaster. A sheet fouled thc compass supporting ring which sprung and allowed the compass to fall from its gimbals on to the deck. Fortunatcly the compass appeared to be undamaged and it was soon sprungback into its gimbals: This timc we tock the precaution of securing it by a thin nylon line, With visibility excellent and the wind holding, we decided to go through Fisherman's Gat so bore away, and leaving the Sunk Beacon to. starboard, picked up the Black Deep 8 where, although now about low water, we found plenty of depth ard after leaving No.10 to port soon saw the welcome light from the Tonguc L.V as by now it was quite dark. I was unable to persuade either of my crew to partake of any refreshment ~ not even a cup of Bovril - so being fairly confident of our course, I sent them both below for a well carned rest, Bcing now alone on dcck and having been at the helm since’ leaving the mooriugs, I soon realised that I was ravanously hungry. I had taken the precaution of stcwing vast quantities of food in the cockpit - locker, so now treated mysclf to a considerable meal, at.‘the samc time realising how wonderfully my crew had carried on in spite of their disability

and without a grumble, i ; 2400 hrs, Leaving Tongue L.V to starboard. Flood started; wind dying. After my ample repast I was feeling that so far we had not done too badly when my complacency was rapidly brought to an end by the presence of the Thames traffic, and as the beam from the Tonguc L.V. swung round, it was evident that there was a considerable amount of shipping about. However, the North Foreland lighthouse red sector was picked up and, after what scemed an interminable time, the white sector. This we held for some time but with the wirji dying and the flood carrying us up the Thames, we were again back in the red sector. The shipping was now causing anxiety and I reluctantly decided to call Walter and togethcr we decided to drop sail and continue under engine and with navigation, mest head light and stern lights all switched on we were soon.on cur way again and back in the white sector. The shipping seemed to we very kind to us and on several occasions vessels which seemed to be heading straight for us eventually bore away and although we were doing only two to three knots against the tide, we were nevertheless able to take avoiding action. As I could still not prevail on Walter to partake of any refreshment and as he scemed to be quite happy at the helm, I went below and turned in, N.Goodwin L.V. was seen to port in the distance during the night, and the sea was confused while rounding N.Foreland, but by dawn Broadstairs Knoll buoy was passed followed by the Gull Stream and South Black off Deal. Although there was very little wind we set sail in order to show our number to the Coastguard, the Walton-station of which had bcen informed of our departure and route. 0835 hrs, Dover abeam; Wind light variable: Weather overcast. Possibly owing to the port strike, no traffic was entering or leaving the harbour at either entrance, so we passed without incident. The Harbourmaster had very obligingly hoisted his black ball allowing us to enter, but we continued doggedly on our way and passed the Hythe buoy. Here we saw the iialdon cutter Rikki-Tikki-Tavi, much to Colin's joy; as he knew the crew. 11.30 hrs. Dungeness abeam, Wind still light cariable; sails not doing much good so engine left running at tick-over., The engine, although a 16 hsp. Coventry Victor, ran so smoothly and started so readily at the press of a button, ‘that Colin named it "the sewing machine"and throughout the cruise it was thus referred to. On passing Dungeness I went below and made a brew-up and then turned in, the long haul of some 50 miles across the bay being too much for my patience. When I came on deck again we were approaching Beachy Head and I found that Colin had set the Spinnaker and was having a great time trying to get it to draw. However, it was not doing us much good and again we had to resort to "the sewing machine". We were now well-over the half-way mark on our outward cruise. By this time I was anxiously measuring the petrol depth in the tank and making ‘calculations about our ability to reach out destination should there still be no wind, As Newhaven was so very little off our course we decided to call in to re~fuel and strétch our legs and we reached the harbour at 20,15 hrs. We tied up at the petrol float and unhappily the attendants had gone home, so Walter and Colin very nobly agreed to go ashore with the spare cans and find a garage. By now the Harbourmaster had followed us down from his office and told us that we might not stay without paying harbour dues but that’ if we could get away by 2100 hrs he would let us off. I invited him on board and plied hin with sherry and cigarettes, but in the end I had to pay up as the crew did not get back in time, The Harbourmaster was at some pains to explain that this would entitle us to tie up in harbour for the night, but as Walter and Colin had had to walk quite a long way before finding a petrol station, they took advantage of the occasion to refresh themselves at the same tine and on returning would not hear of staying for the night, so we left, with a' wave from the Harbourmaster from the top of the pier. It was dusk with en off-shore breeze, and we sped along happily with large. genoa set. I sent tis Grow beiow For a snooze. It seemed an interminable time passing the lights of Brighton and towards widnight I found myself dozing so was obliged to call Colin to do a spell, and didn't he need some wakening: When I came on deck again at 0400 hrs, Littlthanptmwas ‘faintly visible astern, and what there was of it, the wind was back to the East. © (i Phere were a lot of fishing boats about and big ships were passing towards

on KY a Goes ‘ Portsmouth, but after 56 1.4.46 of drifting we were rather worried about our position and could find neither the Nab tower nor the Owers L.V and could get wireless signels from neither. Walter therefore got busy with the wireless and with bearings from Le Havre, Cape Barfleur and St. Catherine's Point obtained a series of error triangles which showed that we were, in fact, too much South, Our course was duly correctcd and to our relief, Dunnose Head on the Isle of Wight appcars througn the murk on our starboard bow, 1640 hrs. St. Catherine's Point abeam wand light from E, sca calm, After the prolonged spdl of castcrly winds, quite a swell of very long wave- length had developed and it was fascinating to sve that when in the trough nothing but sea could be secn on the horizon, whilst on a crest the Isle of Wight and all the shipping came inte view. We crossed Freshwater Bay with wind dying and the Needles were soon picked up. As we passed the Needles a large steamer was clearing the Shingles ani it stopped to pat her pilot off on to the boat which had been following, Having passed astern of this boat, we set course for Christchurch Bay, the iast lap of cur outward passage. Hengistbury Head was seen on our port bow, and the white inflated rubber dome cnclosing Roger's satellite dish acrial at S.R.D.E was soon spotted on the clifs right ahcad, «As we approached the buoys at the entrance to the harbour several yachts and fishing boats were anchored waiting for the flood, as the pilot handbook warns sailors that the ebb (known as ‘the Run') may reach as much as 9 knots and there is very little depth over the bar. However, as it would have mcant waiting two hours for the flood, by which time it would have been dark, we decided to make a dash for it. This is where the great advantage of the Atalanta, with its adjustable keels and powerful engine, became apparent. We therefore raised the keels to 2.5 ft and got the anchor ready, while Colin stood by with the lead line, We got safcly over the bar, although the rudder did touch, it was qickly lifted and then wemet the full force of the cbb. "The Sewing Machine" was opencé out to give its full 16 hp and although it still ran very quictly there was a dintinctly healthy burble heard from the stern of the boat, There was a look of concern on the faces of the Fisherman who lined the quay watching our hazardous entry as we made about 1 kt over the torrent; but once in the hsrbour we made for the only mooring buoy which was vacant, which, in fact, turned out to be the mooring which Roger had arranged for us in collaboration with the local Cruising Association boatmen, Within a very host time Walter end Colin were getting themselves ready to go ashore whilst I launshed the rubber dinghy which had been carried fully inflated on the stern. and they set off for the quay to Telephone Roger to come to see us and to the Coastgoard tc inform Walton of our safe arrival. After Roger's visit we had a splendid mcal on board and turned in, Needless to say, none oF us needed any rocking that night: The distance was just about 200 miles and it had taken us 52 hours, the average spced being 3.85 kt, The mooring which we used was on the cdge of the channel up to Christchurch and with certain conditions of wind and tide we took the ground, but as it was beautiful soft golden sand this did not mtter at all - in fact - it was an advantage, for during my daily swimming I was sable to scrub down and touch up the mull and topsides, so that by the cnd cf our stay all were in perfect condition, During our stay in Christchurch I wes abie to visit Roger's satellite communications establishment where, as a retired harconi engineer, I was very gratified to note that the equipment was largely liarconi, Therc was a very popular pub on the quay where the local boatmen assembled and they were always very helpful in obtaining vetrol and stores and providing local knowledge. Provisions and newspapers we got from the cafe on the beach, and therc were several standpipes from wiich drinking water could be obtained. As my crew were not available the following week-end, I had to stay two weeks in harbour, but this was not a bit too long and with spendid weather and plenty of yachts coming and going, there was never a dull moment. I took the opportunity of running over the whole ship anc engine in preparation for the return journcy but found everything was in first class order and apart from cleaning up, there was nothing to be done, Return trip ~- Christchurch to Heybridge in next issue of Navigans.

CHRISTCHURCH TO HEYSRIDGE An A At slack water I cast off the mooring which had served us so well whilst in harbour and brought Hullabaloo alongside the quay, where our friends the Fisherman took our lines, All our fenders were needed to keep us off the quay and as by this time the flood had started, and being stern on, it was almost impossible to move the rudder, such was the force of the tide. Also whilst awaiting my crew, the wind which had been off-shore, now started to veer and increase in force which added to my difficulty in fending off, However, the wind eventually died and by this time ‘alter and Colin arrived with Roger who had collected them from the station. Within minutes, they had donned their sailing garb and we were soon away from the quay. The wind was now light and dead against us and as there was still quite a lot of the flood left we decided to make use of it and make the passage inside the Isle of Wight thus giving ourselves the satisfaction of having made the trip round the island. 1920 hrs, Cast off moorings from Christchurch quay. wind &, Light vars course 120° for North, Channel buoy to avoid the shingles sands and Hurst Castle abeam at 2045 hrs. Passed close to Hurst Point with overfalls rather ominous; heavy shower, Wind now completely gone so proceeded under engine. As visibility was not too good we decided to cross at once to the Isle of ‘ight where we picked up the Albert Fort on the cliffs and proceeded up the Solent in great style with the tide still under us. The rain had now ceased and ~ the night was fine although still overcast. By now it was dusk and by | 2100 hrs we had the ilghts of Yarmouth abeam. The Hamstead buoys off Newtown and eventually Egypt Point off Cowes were passed. It was now quite dark and we were obliged to use our searchlight as the numerous unlighted buoys caused us some anxiety. 2200 hrs. Gurnard buoys and lights off Cowes passed — no traffic about. Towards midnight we sew the lights of Ryde with what we thought was its brilliantly—-lighted pavilion looking resplendent in the pitch—black darkness, We had been at the helm for quite a spell and both “alter and I thought we must have been dowing for it sesmed the pavilion was moving out to seas of course we soon realised that it was the Southampton Ferry boat which was then moving away from the pier, which we were seeing! As we approached the forts off Seaview the shipping from Southampton down the Spithead became considerable and we prudentiy kept our course Well to the south of the channel. The France, brilliantly illuminated an’ with her name under the bridge, passed us at an incredibly high spced and was soon out of sight. Having set course for the Looe channel with the light of the Nab on our starboard bow, I turned in — not without some misgiving as conditions were suggesting that we might encounter fog. I had not been asleep for long before I was quickly brought back to my senses by Colin rushing down into the Cabin calling for the foghorn. I at once came on deck and was alarmed to find dense fog and to ry horror the towering stern of a large cargo boat passing ahead of us. The distance looked like 100 ft but in all probability it was nearer 100 yards but still unfomfortably clese. We blew our horn frequently but it would probably have been of no avail and I expect that the cargo boat had not even seen us, Fog horns were ahead from all directions and we spent an anxious half hour on deck with our eyes skinned until, to our great relief, at dawn the fog began to lift. As we possessed no proper radar reflector, Colin had most enterprisingly hoisted an aluminium saucepan in the rigging in the hope of giving an improved radar response to that due only to our rigging. ‘Is it possible that the cargo boat we had so narrowly missed had actually got a response and, in fact, taken avoiding action? We had altered our course to get us clear of the main deep water shipping channel, and as daylight came we found ourselves amongst numerous boats which were fishing off Selsey Bill. We had quite a time and went considerably off course in avoiding their nets. However, fog came down again and we passed rather close to a large yacht and we heard the Nab blowing his fog horn but the coast was not visible. Nevertheless, we were able to pick up the Pullar and Street buoys marking the Looe passage.

se 0910 hrs. Passed Hast Borough Buoy: Fog lifted: Wind & light var. We heard the Owers L.V. blowing but it was entered in the log as being just a smudge — our eyes were strained by now and none of us was certain. By mid-day it was bright and clear with a little breeze - albeit ahead -— we were able to set sail and with our course set for Beachy iiead, Brighton and Newhaven were picked up, the chimneys of Shoreham Power station also, and bearings were taken on then. A high-speed R.A.F. rescue launch came out from Newhaven and circled us, but as we appeared to be doing no harm and proceeding nicely, they left us unmolested, 1830 hrs. Passed Beachy ilead: Wind astern, light variable, so set spinnaker but did no good so resorted to "the sewing machine". We now started the long haul of about 30 miles to Dungeness, coming well into Pevensey Bay to avoid the worst of the tide. Although we could have done with 2 good breeze to enable us to sail we also thought of the consequences of getting caught out in a storm in the middle of the bay with very long distances to ports of shelter — Newhaven to the west and Folkestone to the east. Dungeness was passed at 0215 with the new power station plainly visible and another long haul to Dover in prospect. Fortunately: there was now no fog, but the wind, what there was of it, still right ahead. The Hoyal Sovereign L.V was. just visible on our starboard beam and we realised that this would probably be the last time we should see it because it is to be replaced by an unmanned automatic lighthouse now being assembled in an engineering works in Grays -— the firm which made a similar lighthouse for Dun Laoghaire in Dublin Bay The lights of Hastings. and Fairlight were visible in the distance and we : VY wondered whether we should be able to find our way into Rye harbour in the event of trouble for it was a long way to any other ports of shelter. Passed Dover at 0645 hrs and were not inconvenienced by traffic entering or leaving: Misty morning but still very little wind and what there was of it, dead ahead, Set sail to Deal to show our number to the Coastguard and tacked for:quite a while with little progress and tiring ourselves in the process, Had the wind held from the East we should have sailed very well after rounding South Foreland but luck was against us, for as we turned northwards, the wind backed and headed us. By this time we had run the engine quite a lot and I made calculations as to whether our fuel supply would hold out. Ramsgate was dead ahead and I considered it prudent to call in and replenish our supplies. As we approached we got the signal from the Harbourmaster that we might enter the harbour, but as we did so, we noticed a Hovercraft coming towards us at great speed and throwing off huge clouds of spray and evidently also wishing to enters so although he appeared to wish to give way to us, we considered it | more prudent to let him enter first and we therefore made a wide turn and follow in his wake. In the harbour we soon spotted to the south a floating petrol station and tied up alongside when a hose was passed aboard and we filled om tanks to our heart's content with the precious liquid. We were asked to move away as soon as possible so were not able to stretch our legs ashore. It soon became obvious that the urgency was due to the Putney—Calais—Putney speedboat..race, and high speed motor boats were coming and going in great numbers, some to take petrol. It was fantastic to see the way they shot into the air with engines roaring when they hit the waves and it speaks well for the fibreglass hulls that they withstood the impact when they came down on the water again with great force. 1300-hrs, Left Ramsgate, ‘ind N. Force 2/3. Overcast. sea agitated. We. soon passed Broadstairs and by 1400 hrs we were with North Foreland lighthouse abeam, At this moment we thought we saw Colin's father's boat Theodora proceeding towards Edinburgh Channel. As the wind was now blowing quite strongly we considered how best we could use it to our advantage and although it entailed some careful navigation, we decided to take a northwesterly course to the Swin. We therefore tacked first to the Margate Sand beacon, the Pan Sand beacon and the Shivvering Sands tower, where the illicit broadcasting station was situated, and so into the West Swin. Here at dusk, it was tantalising to see the wireless towers on Foulness, so near yet so far!

I at once came on deck and was alarmed to find dense fog and to ny horror the towering stern of a large cargo beat passing ahead of us, The distance looked like 100 ft but in all probability it was nearer 100 yards but still unfomfortably close. we blew our horn frequently but it would probably have been of no avail and I expect that the cargo boat had not even seen us. Fog horns were ahead from all directions and we spent an anxious half hour on deck with our eyes skinned until, to our great relief, at dawn the fog began to lift. As we possessed no proper radar reflector, Colin had most enterprisingly hoisted an aluminium saucepan in the rigging in the hope of giving an improved radar response to that due only to our rigging. Is it possible that the cargo boat we had so narrowly missed had actually got a response and, in fact, taken avoiding action? We had altered our course to get us clear of the main deep water shipping channel, and as daylight came we found ourselves amongst numerous boats which were fishing off Selsey Bill. We had quite a time and went considerably off course in avoiding their nets, However, fog came down again and we passed rather close to a large yacht and we heard the Nab blowing his fog horn but the coast was not visible. Nevertheless, we were able to pick up the Pullar and Street buoys marking the Looe passage.

7 0910 hrs. Passed Bast Borough Buoy: Fog lifted: Wind I light var. We heard the Owers L.V. blowing but it was entered in the log as being just a smudge — our eyes were strained by now and none of us was certain. By mid-day it was bright and clear with a little breeze - albeit ahead - we were able to set sail and with our course set for Beachy iiead, Brighton and Newhaven were picked up, the chimneys of Shoreham Power station also, and bearings were taken on then. A high-speed R.A.F. rescue launch came out from Newhaven and circled us, but as we appeared to be doing no harm and proceeding nicely, they left us unmolested, 1830 hrs. Passed Beachy ileads Wind astern, light variable, so set spinnaker but did no good so resorted to "the sewing machine". We now started the long haul of. about 30 miles to Dungeness, coming well into Pevensey Bay to avoid the worst of the tide. Although we could have done with 2 good breeze to enable us to sail we also thought of the consequences of getting caught out in a storm in the middle of the bay with very long distances to ports of shelter — Newhaven to the west and Folkestone to the east. Dungeness was passed at 0215 with the new power station plainly visible and another long haul to Dover in prospect, Fortunately: there was now no fog, but the wind, what there was of it, still right ahead. The Hoyal Sovereign L.V was just visible on our starboard beam and we realised that this would probably be the last time we should see it because it is to be replaced by an unmanned automatic lighthouse now being assembled in an engineering works in Grays -— the firm which made a similar lighthouse for Dun Laoghaire in Dublin Bay The lights of Hlastings and Fairlight were visible in the distance and we Vw wondered whether we should be able to find our way into Rye harbour in the event of trouble for it was a long way to any other ports of shelter. Passed Dover at 0645 hrs and were not inconvenienced by traffic entering or leaving: Misty morning but still very little wind and what there was of it, dead ahead, set sail to Deal to show our number to the Coastguard and tacked for: quite a while with little progress and tiring ourselves in the process. Had the wind held from the East we should have sailed very well after rounding South Foreland but luck was against us, for as we turned northwards, the wind backed and headed us. By this time we had run the engine quite a lot and I made calculations as to whether our fuel supply would hold out. Ramsgate was dead ahead and I considered it prudent to call in and replenish our supplies, As we approached we got the signal from the Harbournaster that we might enter the harbour, but as we did so, we noticed a Hovercraft coming towards us at great speed and throwing off huge clouds of spray and evidently also wishing to enter: so although he appeared to wish to give way to us, we considered it more prudent to let him enter first and we therefore made a wide turn and Followy in his wake, In the harbour we soon spotted to the south a floating petrol station and tied up alongside when a hose was passed aboard and we filled om tanks to our heart's content with the precious liquid. We, were asked to move away as soon as possible so were not able to stretch our legs ashore. It soon. became obvious that the urgency was due to the Putney—Calais—Putney speedboat race, and high speed motor boats were coming and going in great numbers, some to take petrol. It was fantastic to see the way they shot into the air with engines roaring when they hit the waves and it speaks well for the fibreglass hulls that they withstood the impact when they came down on the water again with great force. 1300 hrs, Left Ramsgate. Wind N. Force 2/3. Overcast. sea agitated. We soon passed Broadstairs and by 1400 hrs we were with North Foreland lighthouse abeam. At this moment we thought we saw Colin's father's boat Theodora proceeding towards Edinburgh Channel. As the wind was now blowing quite strongly we considered how best we could use it to our advantage and although it entailed some careful navigation, we decided to take a northwesterly course to the Swin. We therefore tacked first to the Margate Sand beacon, the Pan Sand beacon and the Shivvering Sands tower, where the illicit broadcasting station was situated, and so into the West Swin. Here at dusk, it was tantalising to see the wireless towers on Foulness, so near yet so far!

~ 7- By now, although the wind held, it had veered and was now blowing at force 3 from the N.i, so that it was necessary to tack past the Maplin buoys and the Whitaker, which called for considerable concentration and we were very relieved when we eventually picked up the welcome flashing of the Swin Spitway, We were now able to bear away and sailed through the Spitway without once touching the bottom although our keels were lowered to their full 5'6" and it was nearly low water, One boat had not been so successful and was aground about half way across gwaiting the flood to carry her off: had we not been so occupied with our cwn safety and beamed our searchlight on her we should have discovered that it was Theodora, which we had previously seen coming up the Edinburgh channel. The wind had almost gone and was anyway dead against us so we pressed the button and proceeded under engine, Leaving “alter at the helm, I went below to sleep. When I came on deck at dawn we were passing Bradwell nuclear power station and before going below Walter related how during the night he had mistaken the lights of the power station for an anchored fishing boat and had sought to take avoiding actions he had been with the charts almost continuously since leaving Margate and was doubtless very tired. I took over the helm and proceeded up the river and eventually picked up my mooring at the Blackwater Sailing Club at 0500 hours. The dinghy was launched and Walter and Colin were soon ashore and were able to get to Colin's house at Maldon in time for breakfast and to report that Theodora would probably be back on the evening tide. Neither was late for his duties that morning but after their strenuous night I don't know how they managed to see the day through. The total time taken for the trip was 57 hours including the stop at Ramsgate. This gave an average speed of abour 3.5 kt. The amount of petrol used was 15 gallons. , The cruise was very successful. ‘Ye were favoured with good weather and calm seas but owing to the lack of time the crew was able to allow, it was necessary to use the’ engine more than I should have liked. The Atalanta gave every satisfaction and never any cause for anxiety; it proved very comfortable and the galley was most efficient. The engine behaved remarkably well and its reputation as "the Sewing Machine" was well justified, its petrol consumption being in the region of 0.3 gall/hr and it was generally run at quarter throttle. It would have been nice to have made the trip under sail alone, but there are not places like the Pyfleet where one can put in should the weather turn bad along the south coast and with a climate such as ours there is a lot to be said for motor sailing. Great credit is due to ny crew who carried out their duties without ever a grumble and those who have sailed with me know how fussy I can be! I hope, however, that this would be put down to my age! B.A. Payne. Summary of Classes rceognised by the iarconi Sailing Club OR What not to sail The General Purpose 1h ft dinghy. commonly known as the G.P.1h This is one of the oldest classes sailed on our river, fhe first one having been introduced in the mid cighteenth century sailing under the name of 'Victory'. In 1805 her helmsman, one Horatio Melson was Killed during a rather notted up protest in a regatta off Cape Trafalger. Although this class has been greatly modified in size and sail area, its weight has remaincd largely unchanged. The International fiornet Class, The fly in the ointment. This boat was designed esnecially for the helmsman who doesn't like his crew. It is equipoed with many anti-crew devices such as ejector seat(Sliding board )or hanging noose (trapeze). We suggest that anyone who has. -trouble with Hornets. should consider a new insecticide spray, Govelovoed by Anti Hornet Enterprises Ltd. at 9/-. The fulrror Class This class is a formidable opponent to any other class on the River) - relying on sheer weight of numbers and high handicap rather than on speed or mancouverability,. A good example of this was when an eight strong fleet of Mireballs engaged a forty strong fleet of Mirrors in a Regatta late last year, One “ireball ce accounted for....three Mirrors sunk, ecight protested out and one swamped in his wash. Yet the Mirrors still won the race outright. The lational :interorise Class, This boat can be sailed in three positio s> a) The vertical or dry position, ‘This position is used entirely by experts and takes a great deal of si:ill and experience to retain, b) The horizontal or damp position, -nterorises can be found sailing in this position almost anywhere round the coast, Although this metnod tends to be a little slow it is extremely stable. c) The waterlogged or sunk position. This method is the least common of the three. It involves sailing with about three feet of the mest protruding above the surface. Commonly used by spear Fisherman, Tim Digden

AUG. 9th CRUISER - Passage race to Pin Mill TODAY, Take Navigans home and let the whole family read the various important notices from the Commodore and catch up on the race results etc, EDITORIAL The editorial this month concerns messages I've had from several people about swimming, Firstly, in the last three weeks two little girls have found themselves out of their depths when only a few feet from the water's edge. Fortunately their respective Mums were close at hand and it was they and not their daughters who were scared. Parents — please be careful to watch the children, especially the non-—swimmers. The beach does slope very steeply and the children should be encouraged to swim or paddle parallel to the shore. The strength of the tide shouldn't be under estimated either. Secondly, boats sometimes approach the hard very fast and with a flick of the helmsman's wrist they are almost stationary, head—to-—wind and completely under control. Although I quite agree that swimmers have as much right to use the water as the sailors, boats are bigger than a Swimmer's head and it would seem sensible if swimmers would not swim from the hard when dinghies are-coming in. The gravel at the Stone end of the hard really is a safer place to swim. Hedmsmen please try to come in slowly if you think its swimming weather,

Thirdly, for Cadets (and those under 10) who like Swimming, why not make a point of going swimming with your friends in the summer holidays at a particular time. For Mum's benefit I'm suggesting Wednesdays, Thursdays and Fridays. Now that the Market is right beside the swimming pool, park in the short stay car park, have a swim with the kids, do your shopping and then go home, duty and pleasure combined, Already several families with under 10's are making arrangements, now what about some of the over 10's getting themselves organised. LEAVING THE COMPANY I have received enquiries recently from Full Members who are contemplating leaving the Company but wish, if possible, to retain their membership of the Sailing Club. The Marconi Sailing Club is primarily for employees of the Marconi Group of Companies and is a section of the M.A.S.C (and if you wish one of the ‘Perks! of being a Company employee. ae On termination of Company employment it is automatic that full membership of the M.A.S.C and the Sailing Club are also terminated. THE PRIVACY OF STANSGATE For Some years now members have been able to enjoy the facilities at Stansgate in comparative ease and privacy. . _In recent weeks however, this situation has ceased by the influx of guests and non-members who have had little or no. right at all to be at Stansgate, It must be remembered that the Club hold an exclusiv e | lease to Stansgate and last year the Club, assisted. by members donations, spent £1000 on repairing the access road. Consequently we must: protect our own interests, In'a recent check, one member turned up. at the Club with his wife |

a Boe and family in one car and later two more cars arrived filled with his guests. to clarify the position under Rule 17 and Byelaw 25 In order’ members have the privilege: of introducing not more than two occasional visitors in one day. It is further expected that their names shall be entered in the visitors book to be found on the Clubhouse bar. The Officers and Committee are determined to ensure that members comply with the Club Rules and see that day trippers are sent packing. A swing gate has been installed at the entrance to the Club and members are expected to close it after use, Further periodic checks will be made and membership cards will have to be produced, To some, these steps may be irksome but they are in the interest of the Club and it's members, A.S. SOCIAL SCREED The Barbecue started with a lovely still evening, and as we watched the sun setting over Osea Island and across the river, it looked like it was going to be a fine night for our over 150 guests who turned up. Brian Hull and his music from Colchester provided some good dancing music and everyone was able to sit around at the tables on the hard under floodlight and coloured.lights enjoying themselves. Steaks, beefburgers, sausages and chops were served from the barbecue range, and there was plenty to eat for everybody. As soon as darkness fell the bonfire was lit, and many guests took the opportunity to sit around and perhaps warm themselves from the cool of the evening. As the crowd was much smaller this year, the helpers were able to cope much better and an excellent job was done by all who assisted in making the Barbecue such a successful evening. Social Secretary. FIRST TIME OUT. From the shore, the water sparkled invitingly in the spring sun and a light breeze fluttered through the red, white and blue sails of the waiting boats. It was a gay colourful scene. Happy laughing sailors in yellow anoraks and bright yachting caps busied themselves about their craft, setting sails and adjusting strange gadgets to their satisfaction. My helmsman and boat appeared calm and serene on the shore-line as they waited for me - the all important crew, to climb aboard. 0, it was all such fun!! At last, at last, I was going for a real live sail! Ten minutes later, I was perched uncomfortably on top of a jambing cleat with strict instructions to "pull the jib sheet hard in". I nobly tried to please by pulling hard on a jib sheet, but unfortunately it was the wrong one. This brought forth a stream of incomprehensible commands from my helmsman in the stern, who had suddently turned into a fearsome ogre speaking a strange language.

-5- I could understand the adjectives, which were rather distressing, but the rest was couched in obscure technical terms. For the next hour or so, I bounced gaily from deck to centre- board box to shroud, collecting more bruises at every tack, and frequently landing on my posterior in two inches of water in the bottom of the boat, feet flailing uselessly in the air. WNotsuch fun after all. I was rapidly learning about the dastardly crew- traps in an Enterprise -— that kicking strap, highly tensed and waiting to slice off an unsuspecting ear, that centreboard box with special knobs to give extra special bruises and those toe-straps specially designed to trip up the crew when tacking, And how was I supposed to look out for boats on starboard tack when my field of vision was totally obscured by a massive wall of blue sail?? When it actually happened, I was just beginning to relax und enjoy myself, We were skimming along quite pleasantly on what the helmsman called a "run". The wind appeared to have dropped right off and I began to look around and take an interest in some exciting water skiing on the other side of the estuary. Sailing wasn't so bad, after all......cuddenly the whole world tipped at an alarming angle and I received yet another almighty blow across the head as the boom swung across. Then, slowly, but Oh so surely, we were lowered into the icy depths of Blackwater estuary. For a moment everything was splutter and choke and I dogsy—paddled around uselessly until I realised that my feet were tangled up in the mainsheet and I wasn't getting anywhere fast. The freezing water gradually seeped through layers of clothing and I couldn't breathe, it was so cold. Helmsman righted the boat at the second attempt, the first try ending in an ignominious dive backwards off the centreboard amid gurgled curses. (This was quite the highlight of the day). Eventually the rescue launch arrived and I was heaved on board feeling very much like a freshly caught walrus. Then we were putting for home. But the humiliation of that walk up the beach!!! As & squelched up to the clubhouse, I was surrounded by grinning faces and greeted by cheerful hearty jeers. Happy laughing DRY sailors in yellow anoraks and bright yachting caps, Fool me. They had never left the shore. Now I know what they're laughing about, NOVICE. - Tin: MR.UNDERDOWN OUR CARETAKER. It is most unfortunate that we are very soon to loose the services of Mr. Underdown. He has served the club and members extremely well over the past few years, he has done his job well and has shown a special aptitude for the various tasks concerning boats. He is leaving Essex and hopes to settle down somewhere in the West Country. I am sure that you would all join me in wishing him the very best of good fortune for the future and a very happy retirement. The Club will endeavour to find a replacement for George, meanwhile members must be more careful on the question of security. Personal gear must not be left "laying around" and the clubhouse must be locked after use. Moocings must be looked after too since there will be no Mr. Underdown to report that a certain boat is adrift. A.o. Bigden — Commodore. RESCUE LAUNCHES — COXSWAINS WE NEED YOUR HELP!! Rescue launch coxing can be very enjoyable and rewarding and is avery necessary part of Club activities if we are to look after the safety of all our members and in particular the novices. It is not always necessary to be on the water when one is on duty although it is still necessary to observe from the shore. It is at times when trouble is least expected that tragedy can strike. Many new members and even established members may not have thought that at present very few people are devoting a great deal of time to looking after their safety not always adequately due to the load falling on too few people who do not have unlimited time to spare. .. The response to the appeal in the May issue for potential Coxswain was very disappointing and with the few people who have come forward it has not been possible to provide as complete a Service as is necessary to cover all Club activities whether organised or not, Personal problems have delayed the training of some volunteers but this is to be remedied in the immediate future and further volunteers are required to provide full coverage without over working those who have. already come forward, : To ensure that we have not omitted anyone who has already volunteered would all interested please re-confirm their willingness to either Bill Mortimer or myself or by signing the list in the clubhouse at Stansgate as soon as possible. On receipt of names, sessions will be arranged to familiarise volunteers with the details of operating the in-board engines which each have their own peculiarities.
