EDITORIAL May I start by saying that the Editorial usually consists of my own thoughts on happenings at the Club and though it may be 'vetted' by John it is not necessarily the Committee's view. If anyone objects to what I write about I do wish they'd send me a stinking letter to print in Navigans, Although the incidents were small, the principles involved were somewhat greater, The incidents — several rowing dinghtes fairly near to the shore on a very sunny day and a dead flat calm. One thing noticed was children standing in a boat and another was that none of the youngsters were wearing lifejackets. Even on a calm day it is only common sense to make sure that Cadets do not do silly things in boats. It is one thing to go swimming voluntarily from the shore, and another to be tipped into the Blackwater unexpectedly. There is a Club Sailing Byelaw, which was made by your elected Committee and not by a nebulous "them!" to spoil everyone's fun, that days that all Cadets under 18 shall wear personal bouyancy when sailing from Stansgate. I suspect that the "sailing" was meant to imply rowing and even outboard motoring. I suppose that if a parent does not wish a child to wear a lifejacket the correct course would be to join a club without the rule (which seems rather a harsh solution) or approach the Committee to have the Byelaw amended, There must be other byelaws and rules that are not adhered to and my own view is that the committee would be pleased to hear from members who wish to suggest amendments or new rules.

oe Bow Personally I feel that the lifejacket rule for Cadets is sensible and most of the senior Cadets set a good example and wear their life- jackets everytime they go out for a sail or row. EAST SCHELDE LANDFALL (1968): I had heard several yachtsmen speak of the East Schelde or Roompot as the most attractive entrance to the Netherlands. Some were probably reminiscing of the days when you could sail straight into Veere, and the Patent Agent of larconi's (alias Hon. Navigation Instructor, L.S.C) may have regarded it as an intriguing problem in navigation; but in a few years' time it will be closed by a dyke in the course of the "Delta Plan", the current master-plan for the shortening of the immense length of the Dutch sea-defences, Also it would be a good exercise in D.F. navigation, for which 2 "Seafix" was available; there are few off-—lying marks, but cross—-bearings could be taken from the radio beacons on the Noord Hinder and Goeree light vessels. (There is nothing intoxicating about the Roompot, by the ways; "Room" in Dutch is cream. Delicious, or possibly "easily whipped up")? Weather was generally anticyclonic, with actual wind about ESE force 3-4, and forecast wind NE force 3-6. We left Harwich at 1500 of 12th June under "Kazarka's" favourite cruising rig of main and No.2 Genoas a few tacks took us out past Landguard Point and over the N. tip of the Cork Sand, Still nearly close—hauled on port rack, we passed Roughs Tower at 1702. Backing wind and the North—-going tide allowed sheets to be eased as we went on towards the Sunk, indeed we were being set up towards the Shipwash. Checked the "Seafix" on the Sunk L.V and got sharp nulls and accurate alignment between radio and visual (boresight, the Americans would call it). Sensitivity was also OK on beacons at full nominal range. I laid off courses for E Schelde, W. Schelde, Zeebrugge and Ostend, but the first choice seemed to be "on" unless the wind headed us severely. Maggie took the helm from cast-off until past the Sunk, while I worked out the navigation plan, rested and passed up hot soup. The sky was clear and it was getting cold already when I relieved her after 1900. We crossed the Galloper, well North of the light vessel; in the fairly slight sea there were strong tide-ripples, although the chart gave 2 fathoms plus, There was not very much shipping until near the N. Hinder L.V., and even there most of it was not on cross tracks and there were no close-quarters situations. Passed 1 mile North of the N.Hinder at 0155. Thursday, and traffic soon decreased to less than one ship per hour until we were quite near the Dutch coast, About 0230 I lashed the helm and went below, leaving "Kazarka" nearly close—hauleds; not the ideal course but good for self-steering, One day I'll make a self-steering gear! Although no-one was on deck, I could keep watch through the cabin windows, while being out of the wind and cold, and within reach of food, and charts. I started DF's about 0400, getting N. Hinder 250 T and Goeree 066 T.3 nearly in line, a poor fix but it showed we must bear away to close the coast so I would have to take the helm again. The sea was absolutely featureless after losing N. Hinder, for we were too far out to pick up the shore lighthouses before dawn. But on a course of 124M,, later (and not wisely) 145M., the DF lines gradually opened up. To save repeated plotting, I had prepared the chart with compass roses on the two beaconss a very useful dodge suggested by Mary Blewitt in "Navigation for Yachtsmen". But hour after hour there was no visual check. Ultimately I spied a tower, rather hazy. I hoped it would be Domburg church on the NW shore of Walcheren island, but it could also be Westkapelle lighthouse at the W. tip (it was about 8 miles away). This was about 0930. Later, and very slowly, we caméup on a green wreck-buoy nearly due W of Westkapelles I was surprised to find the tide past it nearly West-going as a result of the streams out of the E and W Scheldeg the tidal atlas gave it as more SW-going, i.e. along the main coast line, This was our first buoy since the N, Hinder group. Close-hauled now, we needed a few tacks to make Westkapelle. some large ships were in the deep Oostgat near the coast, but their channel was narrow and well marked, We had to dodge the Botkil to the W. of Westkapelle, by transits on the smaller Noorderhoofd lighthouse and the OG 1 buoy, The wind was now NNE 5 and a small but

=O= J lumpy sea was being set up. '"Kweerens" and "Domburger Rassen' were names on the charts "queer 'uns" we felt described the waves here. Fram 1200 we could expect a fair tides we should carry it right up to Zierikzee. At 1240 we had Domburg church abeam (no doubt this time). Rather hard pressed and with the mainsail usually eased, I hoped it would be better in a mile or two when we could bear away a little. But by 1315 it was evident that we were still over-canvassed, the jib was pressing down our bows and "Kazarka" was carrying massive weather helm. Took off jib and didn't put up anothers a little later, started the engine. Some of the channels ran nearly to windward and I didn't want to miss stays in the trickier spots, with a short wind- against—-tide sea running. I reckoned it a full force 6 when taking the No.2. Genoa off. Past the Veeregat dam the channel funnels down and is called "Schar van Onrust''s roughly "the strait of unrest', In these conditions this was good Anglo-Dutch understay¥ement, On the North Side is the Hompels shoal which dries at low water, Waves were breaking heavily on it, but were also breaking for about a mile across the Schar itself; very short and steep waves like a weather-going tide in force 7 off Stansgate, “only more so", Nothing to do but keep her going, in the channel, and hold on! That was a full-time job pspecially in the narrowest part of the channel, for the tide appears to spill over, as it were, and sets partly across the Hompels., However, we kept the transits moving the right way on the buoys, and came through with our teeth still in their sockets. After all, it was a spring flood, and wind rising force 7 against it. Another time we'll take it with Wind and tide, and see if it is a little less "onrustig". On to Zierikzee it was just a hard punch, mostly to windwards a lot of spray flying, but we were used to it now. The difficulty was to see the buoys and their numbers through well-salted eyes, The Zierikzee entrance canal is* mile before the Oosterschelde bridge, which the most salt—blinded sailor could sees but because of the Size of the bridge, it seems much nearer, Not wishing to go down-tide of the entrance, we went up to a light-buoy to read its number! The entrance is clear when you come to its we entered at 1545, 24° hours and 105 charted miles out from Harwich. We weren't the only yacht out that afternoons a small Dutch yacht entered with us, under jib only. But they knew better than to go through the Schar van Onrust -— they had come up close under the lee of the North shore! A.M. Adan. I suppose all sailors who aspire to owning their own boat go through the agonics of decision - making when the time comes to buy the first or subscquent boat. Three seasons ago the choice for me was fairly simple and was solved .. .-. mainly on financial grounds coupled with the need for soicthing that I could manage both ashore and afloat and the need for a craft that would not dump myself and family in the water at the slightcst pretext. The creft chosen was “a Mirror dinghy which was cheap, safe and light. Having joined the Marconi Sailing Club it began to dawn on me that there were other factors to consider, The most important of these was the necessity to be able to sail against the current in a light breeze and to be able to point reasonably close to the wind. It was also irksome to be the tail end charlie in a handicap race, arriving home to find the other crews changed and having tea, The Mirror, being short hylled and gunter rigged was inclined to be slow and not terribly close winded, having a Portsmouth rating of 122. In the Autumn of this year, we said goodbye to the Mirror, banked the money, and started looking around for the next choice. It was soon evident that certain criteria had to be ratified. Firstly we decided to go for a dinghy with a fibreglass hull, if possible, about 1),' long but not too heavy. It should have a Portsmouth rating of 90 to 100 and it should not cost more than about £250. Later we found that the dimensions. of beam and height of the hull wcre important in determining whether the hull would pass sideways through a door in the garden wall for winter storage behind the house. Having obtained a cheap trailer car topping was no longer a criterion but due regard nccded to be paid to whether the boat should be one of the established classes at the club in order to avoid handicap racing, although quite a lot of pottering was also envisaged for the benefit of the non-racing mcembers of the family. It scemed that the choice had to be one of four boats, the GP14, the Enterprise, the Scorpion and the Lark. The first two were obvious candidates as they were well cstablished and thriving club classés, Wie fell in love with the Scorpion at the boat show and the Lark was chucked in for good measure as the second non club class as it was a modern design,

wa: o we All four boats could be purchased in stage 3 kit form or secondhand and could be used in minimun sailing trim i.e. no. spinnaker or other extras, for around £250 mark. The Scorpion was the only one of the 4 which was not available with GRP hull. Research showed that the GPl4. was purchasable from agents or builders within 20 miles radius of Chelmsford, it was a good secaboat and compctitive with the genoa increasing the sail area but it was inclined to be heavy (293 lb plus) and it looked as if those door posts would have to come down in order to pass the hull through sideways, especially as the glass hull had moulded in washboards (the Mark 11 version). The Scorpion was fairly quickly eliminated because of its non GRP hull and it secmed to have characteristics which were similar to the Enterprise or the Lark, The builders were also in Devon, although no doubt the boat could be bought more locally. The Enterprise merited a very long scrutiny indeed. It has a spacious hull, is very popular both at the Club and throughout the country, and comes very close indeed to buing an ideal’choicc. However demerits were its rumoured hull weakness in glass, its need for a smaller main for pottering, especially in a blow, and its apparent desire to broach on the run if indifferently helmed. It was now the turn of the Lark. Hull very similar to the Enterprise but round bilged and reputedly easily driven, with some characteristics reminiscent of the National 12. Small wonder for it was designed by Michael Jackson and markcted by Dick Wyche, both of them having close associations with the National 12. It is claimed that this boat will casily achieve its Portsmouth Rating of 9 3 with the modest sail area of 105 square feet. It is also claimcd that it will stand up to a blow without scrious crew discomfort by hardening down on Cunningham hole and kicker. Shceéting can be on a centre or transom horsé and the alloy centreplate is controlled by a lanyard brought out to each side deck. My interest was sufficiently aroused that I went down to see Dick iiyche at Chichester and had a look at the real thing. Dick reccived me very couteously and patiently answered all my questions so that I decided that if I choose the Lark, he would supply it. As far as I could sce the only problem would be that mine would be the only Lark in the club, indced, probably on the Blackwater. However I talked myself into waiving this little difficulty and despatched my order and cheque. I am now waiting anxiously for Dick to tcll me to collect. Iam looking forward to bringing the Lark to Stansgate next season and, who knows, she may generate sufficient intcrest to pcrsuade othcrs, who are undecided what to go for next, to start the nucleus of a flicet. The Club's boats will require similar treatment. To finish even the more necessary tasks befére a new season's sailing helpers will be required each weekend fron now on. The reliability of the rescue launches is in inverse proportion to the Winter's work and the amount of extra naintainance that has to be carried out during: the Sailing Season. As the amount of that work which : can be completed in the time available depends on the assistance received Will "you" please help for a few Sundays (or Saturdays if you prefer) during the winter, A large part of the work is cleaning and preparing the bonts for re-painting for which no great skill is required, so that

This year to achieve continuity and an improved organisation it is hoped to have someone with an over2ll knowledge of the work to be done and who will be in charge of the work for each working day at Stansgate. In addition it is intended to break down the projected work into a number of areas and to ask volunteers to undertake, as Task Leaders, to organise the individual tasks. It is envisaged that the job of the Task Leaders will be to organise any necessary help, tools, materials etc for his individual project, to arrange for continuity of effort on working days at Stanszete and on a rota basis to assist the overall Orcaniser. (c) The essential work will only be partially completed, resulting in decreasing the. reliability of the boats during the Szason, increasing the maintainance during that period, and addinz to next winter's work. None of these situations should arise if the response to this appcal is adequate but the onus is on you. Beavins Ken( Associate) COMMODORE'S REPORT 1969 Over the last few years we of the Marconi Club have enjoyed to the full sailing from a site which must be considered one of the best in Essex. Unfortunately during this time we have not been able to enjoy a sense of security. There has always been doubt in our minds as to how long we shall be sailing from Stansgate. In spite of the efforts of Officers past and present in 1968, and although we were still at Stansgate; we could not boast of security of tenure, During the latter half of 1968 your Vice Commodore, Stan Allerton, and behalf of the club. It was quite a comprehensive development involving some ? I spent some considerable time in prepsring a plan to develop Stansgate on / three acres, with a new Club House and anciilary buildings with maps, detailed drawi’ gs and costing and above all details of justification. The scheme involved the purchase of three acres of land or a long term lease of no less than 21 years with a built-in incentive for our landlord. On the following Sunday Stan and I met Pat. Sparrow to present our proposals, but before we could do so were informed by Mr. Sparrow that he was negotiating the sale of his two farms to Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge and that a draft contract was in the process of being drawn up. Should we therefore wishto discuss an extension of our lease, we had best contact their Agent, Mr. Stafford Smith. To say the least, Stan and I came away somewhat dejected. On December 14th, 1968 I again went to see Mr. Sparrow and was introduced to Mr. Stafford Smith who went into great detail to outline a development scheme he had in mind for Stansgate. I do not propose to go into detail of this very ambitious scheme, but as I alone could not commit either the club or the Company (who were being asked to get involved), I suggested that I convene a meeting between Company Representatives, Mr. Stafford Smith and myself. At this stage I was offered the services of Mr. Riddel, the Company Property Of:icer, as a legal representative who was briefed on all aspects, including the past history of the club. [COREE a5

> To sum up, the results of the meeting with Mr. Stafford-Smith were negative since he was not in a position to commit himself eat tnis stage. The contract of the sale of the farms was signed in March, 1969. Mr. Riddel and I have met Mr. Stefford-Smith on two occasions since and we have a very good understanding; he is aware of our requirements and we have reason to believe we know of his. He has not, as yet, had much Success with the development, but the scheme he has in mind will take time to progress, Both Mr. Riddel and I are of the same mind thet eventually the situation will resolve itself and that we, the Marcon i Sailing Club, will one day have the security we have been seeking over the years. What of the future, assuming we are successful in our endeavours. We may one day still have the opportunity to purchase or have a long lease. Should this come about, we shall have to have a development scheme of our own to include a larger Club House with better facilities. This, of course, will cost money and as our main source of income is subscriptions, it is inevitable that we shall have to dig deeper into our pockets. This has been my last year in office - not a particularly fruitful year, frustrating, in fact. I would, however, like to thank the Officers and Committee who have supported me over the past three years. -I would also like to thank all the members who have ziven their time, labour and donations to the various appezls I have made. The ladies of the Club, as always, have given me their support. Margaret Cottam who organised the Galley services, Ann Smith on social work, Joyce Polley for helping David our Treasurer. There are many others of course, but I must mention my wife Connie who has been very tolerant and helpful over the years, especially at times when club work came before the home. Two ladies who need special mention are Avril Stevens «ss Social Secretary and Eleanor Witter, the Editor of Navigans. They have both done trojan work for the Club and their services, I am sure, are appreciated by all Club members, I would like to close by wishing your new Officers and Committee Success in the future, and may the Club achieve the security it has earned Over the past fifteen years, SECRETARY'S REPORT 1969 Committee meetings have -been held on the first Monday of each month and Committee members! attendance has been fairly good. Sub-committees were formed to deal with the various activities of the club. The appointment of a Dinghy Park Secretary scems to have worked quite well, relieving the Sailing Secretary, enabling him to concentrate on sailing. In my opinion the Sailing and Social activities for the past year were an improvement on the previous year, partly due to the reorganisation and partly due to those responsible for these activities. However, there was still a lack of sufficient volunteers to assist in the manning of the rescue launches, thus placing a heavy burden on those few who were willing to undertake this task. ices wee

Ken Monger SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT 1969 From the sailing point of view I feel 1969 will go down as a very good year. Average entries for points races have gone up, in some cases by an exceptional amount. Individual attempts at Open Meetings and Class Championships have also met with great success. The reorganised Helmsman of the Year series has returned an average entry of 15 which is an increase of 25 on last year's figure. The total entry was 127 and suzgests that the right formula has now been found. The three main fleets have been consistent and in most cases have attracted more entries than last year. This is particularly true of the Enterprise Fleet whose average entry is up 80% on last year. The three disappointments this year I think have been firstly, the non- emergence of the Mirror fleet which was mainly due to the discontinuity caused by the resignations of two fleet captains during the year, secondly the failure of the Handicap fleet to stage any race this year, and thirdly the failure of the Barnacle Points Series for cruisers. The Silhouette Cup run by us this year attracted only three entries too. This year five new points series were introduced. The Spring Points series for GPl4s, Enterprises, Mirrors and Handicap Fleets and the Saturday Points series. Once again with the exceptions of the Mirror and Handicap

fleets, these proved satisfactory and- we hope n next year. to stage them agai The three pursuit races this year proved to be popular once mid week races. more as were the The Regatta this year was extremely successful and I believe is fast becoming the big attraction of the year on the Blackwater. At this point I would like to thank John and Elesnor Witter for their invaluable help .in looking after the Regatta and somchow managing to get everything running so smoothly. The Challenge Cup this year attracted 51 entries as opposed to 30 last year, an increase of 70%. Team racing has not been one of cur stronger points this year, although we must congratulate the Hornet team for winning their team race versus Salcote S.C., the GP.14 team for bringing the Lawson and Cuthbert Cup home for their defeat of M.Y.C. and also the team skippered by Julian Bigden which achieved second place overall in the John Lewis Partnership team race event at Poole. This year the greatest individusl success has been achieved by Simon Darney who came second in the Hornet Nationals at Herne Bay and well up in the field at the World Championships at Hayling Island. The rescue launches hve been far more reliable this yeer and I think this is due to the amount of work put in on the boats by the Bosun Ron Greygoose and Bill Mortimer, the Coxon, and I would like to express nay thanks to both of them and to Brian Urry who has helped Bill out on many an occasion. We have found, though, tht we still have not got enough coxons to even out 'the load' sufficiently and so next year the Race Organiser will be asked to provide a coxon as well as a Hace Officer. This idea of a Race Organiser has incidentally proved most satisfactciy and we hope to carry it through to next year. The race marks have stood up to a lot this year - certainly more boats going round them, and my thanks go to Chris Cooper who has been looking after them this year. I would also like to thank Nick Tovey for his work on the racing programme, especially as the time for its preparation comes round once more. Looking forward to next year, we have been lucky enough to have been asked to staze the Interprise East Cosst Area Championships at Stansgate which will I'm sure be the success that is becoming a frequent visitor to the Marconi Sailing Club. igs LADY ANNE'S SUMMER CRUISE 1969 Lady Anne is an eight ton auxiliary cutter. She was designed and built near Burnham in 19355, and was owned by my father for ight years from 1947-1955. She is a reomy boat, shoal draught, centreboard, not too good to windward in a short sea, but very strong and sound. We have every confidence in her, The crew were to consist of myself, Frances, our two children, Fiona (4 years) and Nigel (24 years) and Trixie our black and tan terrier. During my father's ownership Lady Anne had been cruised in the Isle of Wight area, and I longed to take her back there. When my younger brother and his wife purchased a 45 ton cruiser last winter, we arranged to mect at Newtown Creek on the Isle of Wight. He keeps 'Freedom' at’ Weymouth, 60 miles west of I. of W. and we keep Lady Anne on the Blackwater in Hssex 150 miles east of I. of W. His holiday was limited to a fortnight, whereas we had a month. Detailed plans were not made, as I wanted to keep time in hand to prevent my having to give the crew a hard bashing ut sea just to maintain a tight schedule. Broadly the plan was a week to I. of W., two weeks pottering, a week back home, 7. | Pr ee At the last minute Frances' brother Tony agreed to accompany us for Friday 18th July, 1969 17.30 Phoned London Weather Centre for Thames forecast. S to SW 3-4, 5 on Saturday, maybe 6, visibility good but some fog patcnes. We'll go! Phoned Walton coastguards and gave an accurate description of Lady Anne and details of safety gear aboard. The only item I really should have had was an inflatable dinghy or a liferaft. Our eight foot stem dinghy had bouyancy fitted, and was lashed on the coach roof. The other gear included life jackets, lifebouy, flares, smokes, 4 fire extinguishers, (Lady Anne has Calor, petrol and a coal stove!), torches, searchlight and two radio receivers. <A total of 16 galiions of petrol gave a duration of about 24 hours. | Picked up Tony and made haste for Stansgate. Several trips in Puffin were needed to ferry a vast pile of gear and provisions aboard whilst Frances \ was getting the children into their fo'csle bunks. All gear was carefully stowed, the sail covers and boom crutch were buried for the duration. Finally a cup of coffee and a good meal, during which Tony and I ran over the proposed course. 22.30 The great moment, under all plain sail we quietly slipped our mooring and waved farewell to 'home'. The wind was SW 2-3 and just enough to let us creep downstream against the flood. It was a mild, dry, but very dark night with nine tenths cloud. = Once under way, Frances turned in and seemed to doze off all right. Voices were kept low and lights out to allow her to sleep. Saturday 00.10. / , 4 The cloud was down to three tenths, but as there was no moon, it was pretty dark. The breeze was now a shade firmer, still from SW. 0110 Estimated position off Sales point and set our first heading of 115 deg. for N.W. Knoll. 0115. Picked up lights of N.W. Knoll and estimated that we whould be able to see bouys up to 2$ miles off. For vractice both Tony and I took bearings of Knoll, Colne entrance and Bradwell breakwater. The results were accurate to @ quarter of a mile an? agreed with our estimated position. By 0230 we were

able to pick up both Spitway bcuys. The wind had freshen:d to about force 5 and Lady Anne was rushing through the night throwing lots of spray about. The course was about SE and we were now on a broad reach. I+ was a grand sail for a while, but as the wind seemed intent on freshening we decided to put a couple of rolls in the main and furl the jib. This eased the motion and heel for the benefit of Frences and children. We still seemed to be tramping along at about © knots and life wes good, made perfect by a cup of coffee and chunk of cake. 0500. We were by now up to the Mid Barrow lightvessel, and it was broad daylight. Dawn at seaadlways seems a bit pale and cheerless after a full night at the helm, and I appreciated having Tony on watch with me, A call from Frances below brought the unwelcome news that Fiona had been seasick in her bunk, Frances comforted Fiona and after a short while things were shipshape and secure again. The motion in the bows is much more severe than in the cabin or down aft, and we decided then that no-one should sleep in the fo'csle at sea. Fiona is prone to sea motion sickness and we had a remedy on board thathed been orescribed by our doctor, When Nigel finaliy woke at 6 O'clock Fiona was proud to teil him that She had been sick, 'Some in the bucket!! We all had a cold breakfast ‘with a cup of coffee, the ebb was hard away now and at tines we had to put in a tack to wriggle across the sands down to the Wdinburgh Channel. By seven O'clock we were reaching along the Edinburgh and the wind had freshened to about SW6 and we were making about 65 knots despite a lumpy sea. With the children about now, we found it prudent to put a full 5 rolls in the min. At that we were able to sheet in harder and printa bit closer. Tony turned in about 0800 but only dozed, and came up again Shout 0900, so I turned in for about an hour. : 1022, We put Lady Anne abouc onto the port tack near the Gull Buoy off the N. Goodwin lightvessel. The wind had dropped tc SW 5 and it had turned into a really beautiful day. After our rest, and a further cup of coffee,‘ spirits rose and we shook out 3 rolis and realiy set to sailing the boat. 1130. Close in towards Pegwell Bay we tacked again and battled cff to the SE. Frances was asleep again claiming a disturbed night below! Ten minutes later a series of bumps and thuds from belowshowed that we were off course and had located the Brake sands. Quickly the engine was started, sheets let fly and we put her head to wind to get the 34 cwt. centre plate up. This is always a struggle, and is nigh impossible with the sails SO OLENTES I was relieved to get it right up, as I have a fear of bending the dinch bronze brute. As soon as it was home I yelled to Tony to put her back out to sea. She paid off and sheets were made fast and as I made my way aft she was off like a scalded cat, reaching with the engine on. Imagine my horror as I reached the after end of the weather side deck to see that we were settling by the stern, the water level was almost up to the rubbing strake! I dived into the saloon, hurling Frances out of my way, and ripped up the floorboards. There seemed to be a lot of bilge water, but not enough to account for our state. Back in the cockpit I pumped urgently and got her dry in a remarkably short time for a doomed vessel! We still seemed down by the stern, but repeated checks showed a dry bilge, so .eluctantly I relaxed and tried to puzzle it out. The full answer came a week later: when my brother sailed in company with us. In brief, as we bore away, Lady Anne heeled and- accelerated to her water-line maximum speed. She is an ample old girl and at 6 knots she makes large bow and quarter waves with a great dip amidships. Also under power she tends to sit owittcee as her great prop squirts all the water from under her. From a standing position on the weather deck when she is well heeled, this effect, if not exvected, is startling to put it mildly! On this occasion it was so startling that it was decided to fo.go thoughts of Dover, and hopes of Newhaven as the next port of call, but turn tail for the peace and tranquility of Ramsgate outer harbour. Incidentally the plate only touched at the bottom of three successive waves, and a more careful check on our position showed that we had strayed 5 mile too close to land from the Gull Stream channel. The echosounder was on the feet range, but was not being properly watched.

a) = On the run backto Ramsgate we got the mainsail stowed and warps and fenders ready. 1230. We entered the harbour and were directed to the Western wall where we made fast alongside the yacht 'Sixpence'. Trances made a welcome lunch which was constantly interrupted by a fender coming loose or a warp needing adjusting due to the long low swell which was making all craft, but the catamarans, roll their heatts out. At one stage aseries of sweils got Lady Anne going and she rolled thirty degrees each side. Tony and I longed for sleep, and as high water approached it was obvious that we must enter the inner harbour for rest. Vessels locking in and out awoke us to a werm, calm night. We had a cup of tea, ut had no difficuity in dropping off to sleep again, not to awaken till the shipving forecast. As we could only lock out at high water, the next leg to Newhaven had to be made despite the foul tide. 70 miles at 4 knots gave 18 hours run, but for that we would only have a fair tide for a few hours, SO we prepared for a long trip. The forecast was W2-3 with fog patches. 1500. We departed Ramsgate under engine, visibility 10 miles plus and adead - nose ender of about force 2. I turned in for an hour's sleep in the Foc'sle, away from the engine AND the children, 1730 We were alongside the Deal Bank Buoy, wind S2 slight cloud, ‘superb visibility, estimated over 2U miles. 1800. Forecast W-3 fair chance of fog patches in Channel. 1900. We could just set sail and motor sail hard on the starboard tack. It didn't help the speed, but seemed more 'proper!. 2000. Two miles off EB Dover, wind SW 3. By now we could ease sheets a bit and sailwithout losing too much to the tide. Land far off our Port bow was assumed to be France. 2030. Checked fuel and put in three gallons totop the tank. This indicated & consumption of two hours per gallon which is 0.K. for light throttle settings. The wind died away to SW 1-2 and reluctantly we started motor sailing again +n the Starboard tack out towards the Yarne bank and then we tacked towards Hythe flats.

i.r —9= 2210. We were at the Sandgate Buoy off Folkestone, heading for Dungeness on 230 deg. Wind SW 2-3 with a gentle swell and small waves. Unsure of what I had seen, (a flare, an aircraft, car tail lights) I noted the bearing and the layout of the shore lights and kept a close watch on the spot as we steamed on. I also alerted Frances, who was not yet. asleep. A few minutes later we saw another light. No mistaking it this time - a red flare archine up and over before extinguishing. The international Signal for .a vessel in distress, all vessels bound tc assist, We turned in towards the shore and started to get sail off, in the process of which we lost a batten and two elastic sail ties overboard. Again after a few minutes we saw a third flare, and estimated it to be fairly close inshore. At this stage we were about 4 miles SE of Hythe, and heading in at about 4 knots. I was reluctant to go faster as I did not know what we were looking for and it was again a dark night. A large coaster was bearing down on us from Dungeness point and es Frances took the helm I tried to call her up with our searchlight and a hand lantern. ~ She passed about #4 mile astern of us and apparently did not see $.0.S. flashed at her bridge for about 20 minutes. I had hoped she would heave to and send a launch with a more powerful light than our 60 watt searchlight, So we were on Or own, ani now getting a bit closer inshore. I checked that our echosounder was 0.K., and fixed our vosition as best I could, in between searching with our lights in the immediate area and showing as much light as possible to show our presence. It seemed prudent to search straight in towards the shore as far as 15ft. on the echosounder, and then search up and down. On our run in we saw another flare, this time of a distinctly yellow/orange colour, that wes a new one on me and I still do not know what it W&S 2315. We were now in as close as I dare, seemingly about 300 yards off the promenade. We could see car roofs cver the sea wall, and the blue street lights reflecting off the sea gave a good chance of seeing anything inshore of us. Every so often we-had stcpped the engine and shouted, but saw and heard nothing. A decision was now needed, to continue on our passage, to search longer or to get ashore and alert the coastguard. Landing at Hythe was out of the question due to the darkness and the swell, so we decided to go full ahead for Folkestone and report from there. , The tension had'been intense and Francés was all in, so she went below and slept till we were alongside the lighthouse on the pier. As she came on deck she spotted a great steel hawser running out from the B.R. Steamer at the pier and warned me just in time. They evidently use this to warp the steamers away from the pier. There were several vessels at anchor, but as luck would have it a Pilot cutter was leaving as we cane in. A funny 7cituation then developed as we flashed lights and turned to close on her, she ‘took avoiding action. We got her cornered before she could use her speed, and finally she hove to and we came alongside. We passed our report to a crew member who said th>y would alert the coastguards on VHF radio. We were now free to push on. .
